case20v1-cust.persona.build:
Atithi Systems: Three Personas in Nine Days

A decision case on turning interview research into personas a product team will believe

1. Opening

On Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Geetika Kapadia, head of product at Atithi Systems, sat in the company's Pune office with a wall of yellow notes in front of her and a calendar open beside it. Planning for the next two quarters would be locked at a leadership review on Friday, 23 October, and sprint planning for 22 engineers in Bengaluru and Pune would begin on Monday, 26 October. Every line would be argued by reference to "the customer", and leadership did not agree who that was.

Six weeks of interviews had just ended. Geetika now had to decide how the research would become personas, and whether those personas would be ready, and believed, in nine days.

2. Company background

Atithi Systems, founded in 2019 by Gaurav Khurana, sells a billing, inventory and order-management app to independent restaurants and cloud kitchens. The product prints GST-compliant bills, reconciles UPI payments from PhonePe, Google Pay and Paytm QR codes against the till, and merges orders arriving from Zomato, Swiggy and, increasingly, ONDC buyer apps into one screen. It competes with Petpooja and Posist, and with free billing tools bundled by aggregators and payment apps.

At the end of September 2026 Atithi had 6,400 paying outlets. The average outlet paid ₹1,520 a month (total monthly subscription revenue divided by 6,400 outlets), which gave monthly recurring revenue of ₹97.28 lakh and an annual run-rate of about ₹11.67 crore.

Until this year, "the customer" at Atithi meant Gulshan, a persona written on a single slide in 2021: a forty-five-year-old owner of a family restaurant in a tier-2 city, wary of technology, who wants bills printed quickly. Gulshan had been drawn from Gaurav's memory of his first twenty customers.

3. The situation

In June, three roadmap proposals reached Geetika from three directions. Sales wanted aggregator-commission dashboards, support a simpler onboarding, the founder a kitchen display system. Each proposal named a different user and each cited Gulshan. She asked Gautami Kurian, the lead researcher in Bengaluru, to run a proper study. Between Monday, 24 August and Friday, 2 October, Gautami and two colleagues conducted 42 interviews in Pune, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Jaipur, Lucknow and Kochi.

Three clusters emerged on the wall, each defined by what people were doing rather than by who they were: the owner who cooks or works the counter in a single outlet; the owner of two to six outlets who manages through reports from a distance; and the cloud-kitchen operator who lives on aggregator dashboards and sells under several brand names from one kitchen. The clusters did not map to Gulshan. Each rests on six or more interviews, but the sample was not drawn to be representative.

Exhibit 1 compares the interview sample with the customer base. Cloud-kitchen operators supplied 12 of the 42 interviews (28.6 per cent of interviews) but account for 960 of 6,400 outlets (15.0 per cent of outlets), because they were easier to reach on video and talked more. Single-outlet owners are 55.0 per cent of outlets but 38.1 per cent of interviews.

Exhibit 2 puts money and retention beside the clusters. Single-outlet owners contribute ₹38.72 lakh of the ₹97.28 lakh monthly revenue (39.8 per cent), multi-outlet owners ₹36.48 lakh (37.5 per cent) and cloud kitchens ₹22.08 lakh (22.7 per cent). Churn is the other half of the picture. Of 5,800 outlets active a year earlier, 1,064 left, which is 18.3 per cent of that starting base. The simple average of the three cluster rates, 21.0 per cent, overweights the small cloud-kitchen group and should not be quoted. Cloud kitchens lose 35.0 per cent of their starting outlets; multi-outlet owners lose 8.0 per cent.

Geetika's team also sees the study differently from where each member sits. Gabriela Kovacs, the lead designer in Budapest, who works three and a half hours behind Pune until the clocks change on 25 October, had already drawn screens for a kitchen display and wanted a persona she could design toward. Gathoni Karanja, who runs customer success from Nairobi, warned that personas drawn from six Indian cities would be quoted as universal.

4. The people

Geetika Kapadia, head of product, Pune, owns the roadmap and the decision. She wants a persona set that survives the first hostile question in the review.

Gurpreet Kohli, head of sales, Gurugram, closes most new accounts and believes only in what moves a deal. He says Atithi has "two customers, the owner and the chain", and that cloud kitchens are a fad.

Gautami Kurian, lead researcher, Bengaluru, wants the personas to carry the evidence with them: every trait traceable to quotes, every quote to an interview. She distrusts personas that are quickly made.

Gaurang Kakkar, data scientist, Warsaw, three and a half hours behind Pune, can size each behaviour from billing and usage data but warns that his cluster rules are approximations. Gaurav Khurana, the founder, wants the kitchen display system and can be argued out of it.

5. The options

Option A: Adopt sales' two archetypes. Gurpreet's owner and chain archetypes already exist in the CRM and need no new work. The upside is speed. The cost is that the archetypes were built from who buys rather than who uses, merge two clusters with different churn (Exhibit 2), and ignore the segment, cloud kitchens, which pays the highest revenue per outlet at ₹2,300 a month.

Option B: Synthesise three evidence-tagged personas from the interviews and test them against usage data in nine days. Gautami's team would write one persona per cluster, naming Govardhan (the single-outlet owner), Geeta (the multi-outlet owner) and Gagandeep (the cloud-kitchen operator), with each trait labelled by the number of interviews supporting it. Gaurang would weight the clusters by the 6,400-outlet base rather than by interview count, and ten follow-up calls, budgeted at ₹2.4 lakh, would probe the thinnest claims. The upside is a set the team can trace and challenge. The cost is that nine days leaves little room, so the set ships as version 1.

Option C: Commission a survey of 600 outlets first. A research vendor would quantify the clusters at a cost of ₹14 lakh and eight weeks, which would push the roadmap lock from 23 October to Friday, 18 December. The upside is a defensible segmentation. The cost is two months of roadmap argued without personas, across Diwali on 8 November.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, which cluster is the most important to Atithi, and does your answer change if you rank by revenue share, by retention or by outlet count?
  2. Why might 42 interviews be good enough to find behavioural patterns but not good enough to size them, and what does Gaurang's billing data add?
  3. What would make Gurpreet and the founder believe a persona they did not write? What in Gautami's evidence tagging would address that?
  4. Choose between Options A, B and C for the 23 October review, and state what you would do on Thursday, 22 October if the follow-up calls contradict one persona.

7. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. A persona is a synthesis of research patterns given a face; it is credible only when the team can see the path from a trait back to what real people said and did. Gulshan was a persona with no evidence; a survey-first approach would be evidence with no persona, arriving too late. The skill is to build the smallest set faithful to the patterns, honest about its limits, and ready when decisions are made.

One defensible path: Option B. Three personas fit the evidence, because the clusters differ in what they do, what they pay and how long they stay. Option A discards that difference; Exhibit 2 shows cloud kitchens churn at 35.0 per cent against 8.0 per cent for multi-outlet owners. Option C buys precision the decision does not yet need; the roadmap choice is between three or four initiatives, and the clusters already separate them.

Geetika should designate a primary persona using the sized data rather than interview counts. On revenue, Govardhan has the largest share at 39.8 per cent, but Geeta contributes 37.5 per cent at a churn of only 8.0 per cent, and she is the user the cloud-kitchen and chain-reporting asks would both build toward. The review on Thursday, 22 October should present all three with evidence tags, name Geeta and Govardhan as co-primary, and treat Gagandeep as a retention problem to be solved before an acquisition bet. It should flag claims resting on few interviews and state Gathoni's Kenya caveat. The kitchen display system then becomes a hypothesis tested against Gagandeep's workflow, not an article of faith, and Gulshan is retired in the same meeting so that the team does not carry two customers at once.
exp40v2-cust.persona.build:
Building Personas from Research

Turning interview tape and survey rows into people a team will argue on behalf of.

1. Two decisions, three weeks apart

On Thursday 10 September 2026, Upasana Ullal, vice-president of product at Ukti Content Labs in Bengaluru, laid five persona cards on a table. Ukti sells an AI drafting tool: mid-market Indian retail brands feed it a product sheet and it returns catalogue copy and marketplace listings in nine Indian languages. The company had 1,240 paying accounts and ₹57.71 crore of annual recurring revenue. On Thursday 1 October, twenty-one days later, the pricing committee would cut the product into tiers drawn around whichever customers Ukti said it served. Udayan Umranikar, the researcher in Kochi, had run 41 interviews between Monday 4 May and Friday 19 June 2026; Urooj Umarji in Kuala Lumpur had surveyed 620 of the 1,240 accounts, a 50 per cent response rate. Utpal Uchil, the chief executive, asked which of the five Ukti would lose money by ignoring.

Two days earlier, Umesh Utturkar, head of product at Uttung Machine Works in Kolhapur, was reading July's alert data. Uttung bolts retrofit controllers onto older lathes and sells condition monitoring on top: 2,840 controllers in 1,120 job shops across Maharashtra, Gujarat and Tamil Nadu. Between Wednesday 1 July and Friday 31 July 2026 the fleet raised 18,600 alerts, of which 7,254 were acknowledged at all, 39.0 per cent. Two quarters of engineering, roughly ₹2.4 crore, turned on one question: whose product is this? Ulhas Uplekar, the managing director, said the shop owner's, who signs the cheque; Ushma Undale, field-reliability lead in Coimbatore, said the operator's, who stands at the screen at eleven at night. Umesh had until Tuesday 29 September.

Both teams had research; neither had a set anyone would defend. The argument here is narrow: a persona earns its place only when it changes a decision that would otherwise have gone the other way, so building one from research is the discipline of finding the axes along which decisions diverge.

2. The idea, and the camps that will not agree about it

A persona is a fictional individual constructed to stand for a recurring pattern of behaviour and need found in research, described concretely enough that a team can reason from it as from a person. Three clauses do work. Fictional: a real customer's name is a category error, because that customer carries idiosyncrasies the pattern does not. Pattern of behaviour and need: the unit is a cluster in behaviour space, not a demographic bracket. Reason from: the test is inferential — can the team predict from the card how the person reacts to something never asked about?

Alan Cooper set the device out in The Inmates Are Running the Asylum (1998), attacking not ignorance of users but the elastic user: a “user” so undefined that any feature could be justified by invoking him. His second claim is often forgotten: design for one primary persona and accept that others are served imperfectly, because optimising for an average yields a product optimal for nobody.

From there the field split, and the splits are real. An expert referees arguments by locating the disputants, so name what each camp signs and refuses to sign. The goal-directed camp (Cooper, Kim Goodwin) signs: a precise invented individual with explicit goals beats any aggregate description; it refuses: a persona must be statistically representative before use. The data-driven camp (Pruitt and Adlin, 2006) signs: every attribute traces to an observation, and every persona carries a population and a revenue estimate; it refuses: intuition may supply an attribute. The jobs camp (Christensen, Ulwick, Moesta) signs: circumstance predicts behaviour better than the person, so the unit is the job; it refuses: the person's attributes carry design information. The segmentation camp (the Kotler lineage) signs: a group is worth serving only if measurable, substantial, differentiable and reachable; it refuses: one named individual may stand in for a segment in a budget decision. Behind all four, Chapman and Milham argued in 2006 that the method is unfalsifiable: given a persona, no procedure could show it wrong. They sign a persona cannot be validated and refuse therefore stop representing users.

3. Mechanics in depth

Expert practice runs through six stages. Teams describe one, three and five fluently; two, four and six decide the quality and stay implicit.

Stage 1, episodes. Udayan asked each of his 41 respondents to narrate the last specific piece of copy they shipped — what they typed, what they pasted, who read it before it went live — never what they “usually” do. Stage 2, coding, converts those stories into countable units, and is usually done in somebody's head. Udayan split transcripts into single observations, coded them, merged synonyms, then applied the two filters at the heart of the method.

Coding stage (41 interviews)CountNote

Of 64 merged codes, 23 recur and only 9 of the 64 discriminate, 14.1 per cent. Cards filled with the recurrent but undiscriminating are why so many sets read as five people differing only in job title.

Stage 3 produced six candidate ways to cut the base, three firmographic and three behavioural. Stage 4, the separation test, adjudicates. Urooj took one outcome measurable for every account from Ukti's logs — the accept rate, the share of generated lines published without human edit during August 2026 — and for each axis divided the gap between group means by the pooled within-group standard deviation. That ratio is Cohen's d: below 0.5 the axis barely separates, above 1.0 it is a real seam.

Revenue band, industry and seat count truly describe Ukti's customers and say almost nothing about behaviour inside the product. The strongest axis is governance: accounts with a separate reviewer accept 39 per cent of generated lines unedited, accounts without one 72 per cent. That is a constraint, not a preference.

If Ukti's economics are revenue-led, three is defensible and the fourth is a volume play to be argued elsewhere. Stage 6, falsification, is taken up in section 6.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

The conditions are four testable claims. One: behaviour inside the product varies more between groups than within them. Demonstrated at Ukti at ratios of 1.85 to 2.75; unknown at Uttung, which has never measured a per-user outcome. Two: the users are the people whose behaviour you can change. True at Ukti, only partly at Uttung. Three: the distinct patterns are few enough to hold in a team's head, practically two to five. Both pass, at five and three; eleven clusters is almost always a coding artefact. Four: the decision in front of you would differ by which persona you privilege. This fails most often and matters most. Ukti's passes loudly: “Uzma” would pay for approval workflow, “Urvi” for bulk throughput, and those are different products.

Three situations make the idea misleading. In a single-job utility, such as an OTP screen, the job admits one correct design and the user's identity changes nothing. In a market the company is entering rather than serving, personas from current users describe only those who already tolerated the product: survivorship bias, invisible and fatal. And where regulation fixes the design, no persona moves a mandated disclosure.

5. Hard edge cases, and what the seams do

Uttung is the hard case: hardware plus software, sold through a channel into an organisation. July's data showed that choosing between owner and operator was a malformed question.

Who acknowledged (1–31 July 2026)AcknowledgementsShare of acknowledgementsAlerts acted onAction rateShare of actions
Machine operator4,20858.0%1,12226.7%43.0%
Shop owner1,84225.4%59832.5%22.9%

Total7,254100.0%2,61036.0% overall100.0%

Of 18,600 alerts raised, 7,254 were acknowledged and 2,610 acted on — 2,610 of the 7,254 acknowledged alerts, 36.0 per cent, barely one in seven of all raised. The operator acknowledges most and converts least, 1,122 of 4,208 or 26.7 per cent. The visiting field technician, employed by neither Uttung nor the customer but by a regional dealer, acknowledges only 1,204 yet converts 890 of them, 73.9 per cent. He is the highest-leverage person in the system and was in nobody's persona set, being neither user, buyer nor employee.

The lesson generalises past hardware. In two-sided marketplaces both sides must be sized separately, because the constraint on one caps what the other can be promised. In multi-product companies the hazard is a shared persona library that is nobody's: the cards survive, the evidence does not, and a team ends up designing for a person whose transcripts were deleted. In regulated products the compliance constraint belongs on the card as an attribute, or the roadmap it generates is one legal kills. In AI-native products the card must carry tolerance for being wrong, because that and not the task decides whether a generative feature is usable — which is why “Uzma” and “Urvi” differ by 33 points of accept rate. What mature companies do, as distinct from what they say, is keep two layers: two or three enduring personas for strategy, and a disposable set rebuilt for each major decision. Teams keeping only the first layer are the ones whose personas quietly rot.

6. Eight nuances that separate the expert from the competent

The persona must be falsifiable before publication. The competent practitioner asks whether the card feels right; the expert writes down in advance a prediction about behaviour not yet measured, then measures it. Udayan's was that accounts with a separate reviewer would use the tone control three times as often. The tell: ask what observation would have shown the persona wrong. No answer means a character sketch.

Recurrence is not discrimination. A behaviour shared by everyone belongs in the requirements, not on a card; of Ukti's 64 merged codes, 23 recurred and 9 discriminated. The tell: cover the names and see whether a colleague can identify each card. An unidentifiable card holds undiscriminating truth.

Thin cells are hypotheses in the costume of findings. “Uzma” carries 26.2 per cent of revenue on six interviews; a survey sizes a cluster but cannot enrich its portrait. The tell: every card states its interview count on its face, and under about six the honest label is provisional.

Whom you interviewed decides whom you can see. Both companies sampled current customers, so neither set contains anyone who evaluated the product and declined. The tell: count the churned and never-bought respondents; at zero, the set describes the already-converted and understates the objections that cost you growth.

Ordering is the deliverable, not the set. Cooper's single primary persona softens into “here are our five customers”, restoring the elastic user by other means: with five equal personas, any feature serves somebody. The tell: ask which persona the team will knowingly disappoint this quarter. A team that cannot name one has not finished.

Demographics are colour; behaviour is structure. Age, city and firm size make a persona memorable and almost never predictive; Ukti's firmographic axes topped out at 0.43. The tell: delete every demographic attribute and see whether a decision changes. Detail aids recall, and recall of an unpredictive attribute licenses stereotyping.

Fabricated detail is a liability that compounds. Hobbies and favourite films creep on to cards to humanise them, then get reasoned from. The tell: demand a transcript line for every attribute and mark unsourced ones in another colour. Three unsourced out of twelve is usable; the discipline is knowing which three they are.

A persona has a shelf life, and the clock starts at the last interview. Ukti's set is dated 19 June 2026, and for a product shipping monthly, accept rates move materially within two quarters. The tell: a card with no “evidence as of” date is undated food. Treat anything older than four quarters as research debt.

7. Differences by product type and company stage

In consumer products the persona is usually one individual and the axes are situational: urgency, who else is present, what was tried first. In B2B and enterprise the set must be a cast rather than a gallery, because user, approver and economic buyer are distinct people whose interests conflict, and the set should record the conflict rather than smooth it. Ukti's “Uzma” is really a brand manager plus the legal reviewer behind her. In platforms and marketplaces each side needs its own sizing and a map of which supply behaviour caps which demand promise. For hardware the card must carry the vintage of the machine, since Uttung's 2,840 controllers sit on lathes of six eras. For AI products the distinctive attribute is tolerance for error.

Stage changes the method more than most admit. Before product-market fit the survey stage is unavailable and the right artefact is a proto-persona: a written bet, labelled a bet, from eight to twelve interviews, revised monthly. At growth stage, where both protagonists sit, there is enough telemetry for the separation test. At maturity the binding constraint is organisational memory, and the discipline shifts to retiring personas. The logic itself does not change: funnel, separation test and coverage curve are the same everywhere.

8. Three worked examples

Ukti, where it worked by changing the question. The committee had framed the decision as “how many tiers?”; the separation table reframed it as “tiers around what?”, and the answer, governance rather than volume, was not available from the CRM. Existing tiers were cut by seats and words generated; since seats separate at 0.43, Ukti had been charging differently for behaviour that was the same.

Uttung, where the set was incomplete. The owner-versus-operator framing would have sent ₹2.4 crore of engineering into one of two screens. The alert table added a third person who converts 73.9 per cent of what he sees and had never been interviewed, because he appears on no invoice.

Upvan Nutrition Industries, where it failed. Upvan, an Ahmedabad packaged-nutrition brand, launched three high-protein lines on Monday 20 January 2025 against a persona called “Urmila the fitness mother”, built by Unnati Ursekar's team entirely from a syndicated panel survey with no interviews. Urmila was described by age, household income, city tier and self-reported attitude to health: four attributes, none behavioural.

Upvan, 20 Jan to 18 Jul 2025Planned unitsActual unitsAchievement (per cent of plan)
High-protein breakfast mix72,00019,40026.9%
Protein bar, two flavours60,00012,60021.0%
Ready-to-drink shake48,0007,60015.8%
Total1,80,00039,60022.0%

Upvan sold 39,600 of the 1,80,000 units planned, 22.0 per cent, to 14,300 distinct buyers at ₹185 a unit: ₹73.26 lakh of revenue against ₹4.80 crore of launch marketing — ₹3,357 of spend per buyer to earn ₹512. Umair Usgaonkar's post-mortem from Monday 11 August 2025, with 18 interviews, found no fitness-motivated mother buying for herself. In fifteen of the eighteen households the buyer was whoever did the monthly stock-up, and the job was stopping the eleven o'clock argument about what the children would eat before school. Protein was not the benefit; it was permission to stop negotiating. Repositioned on Monday 3 November 2025 against “Uma the household stock-keeper”, the breakfast mix sold 1,06,000 units in the six months to 30 April 2026, ₹1.96 crore of revenue. The first persona was right about who bought and wrong about why, and a persona built from attributes rather than episodes cannot detect that error.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

Missing the seamthe resolver is on no cardwho acts when the system signals?two quarters misaimed

One reading is counter-intuitive. Headcount-only selection looks like prudence, but bets that all customers are worth the same: at Ukti it would have discarded the cluster carrying ₹1,451.6 lakh.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether personas can be validated at all. Chapman and Milham, steelmanned: a persona is a conjunction of attributes, and the probability that a real person satisfies all of them falls geometrically as attributes are added, so a twelve-attribute persona may describe nobody. The reply is that a persona claims not an individual's existence but a region of behaviour space, validated by out-of-sample prediction even when no member matches the card. For the sceptics to be wrong, personas must generate predictions that hold on data they were not built from — testable, and almost never tested.

Person or job as the unit. The jobs camp's strongest case is Upvan: a persona accurate about demographics was wrong about causation, and the job fixed it. The persona camp's is Uttung: the job, keeping the machine running, was known to everyone and explained nothing, while the gap between three people's willingness to act explained everything. The honest position, which neither camp states cleanly, is that jobs carry the causal story and personas carry the agency.

Whether vividness helps or harms. One school holds that names and biography drive commitment, with evidence that teams reason more consistently about a named person. The other holds that vividness imports exactly the demographic inference the separation test shows to be uninformative. Settling it needs a comparison of decision quality, not recall, between teams given vivid and austere versions of the same clusters.

Whether a model can substitute for the research. The case for synthetic personas is cost: Ukti's 41 interviews took seven weeks. The case against is that a model returns the modal description of its training category, which is a competitor's persona rather than yours, while the nine discriminating codes were idiosyncratic to Ukti. For the optimists to be right, a synthetic set must reproduce a separation table computed on real telemetry.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in four ways. They write the decision rule before opening the data, because the rule and not the data determines the answer. They quote a separation ratio when proposing a split rather than asserting that two groups differ. They put the case count and evidence date on every card, and name the persona they are choosing to disappoint. And when a colleague proposes a sixth persona, they ask which decision would change if it were real.

12. What each protagonist decided

On Tuesday 29 September, Umesh told Ulhas Uplekar that the answer to “whose product is this?” was neither option offered. He funded three personas with the visiting field technician as primary for two quarters, arguing that the technician converts 73.9 per cent of the alerts he sees against the operator's 26.7 per cent. The operator became secondary, served by one change: an unresolved alert passes to the dealer's technician automatically. Ushma Undale was asked to run twelve technician interviews, because the new primary persona rested on telemetry and no transcripts — a weakness Umesh stated in the memo.

On Thursday 1 October, Upasana took three personas to the pricing committee rather than five, with tiers cut along the governance axis instead of seats: self-serve for “Urvi”, reviewed-workflow for “Uzma”, multi-client for “Ujjwal”. The three cover 64.9 per cent of revenue; “Ulka” and “Udit” stayed documented as secondary, and she told Utpal that the choice left the remaining 35.1 per cent to tiers not designed for it.

Discussion questions. First: if the governance ratio fell from 2.75 to 0.9 after a year of product change, what would Upasana have to unwind, and would three tiers still be defensible? Second: Umesh made a persona primary on telemetry with no interviews behind it — when is that the right trade, and what would make it reckless? Third: Upvan's first persona was right about who bought and wrong about why; what would you have asked the panel to measure that would have caught the error before ₹4.80 crore was committed?

13. Going deeper

Anatomy of a persona — the fields a card must carry, including the evidence date and case count that make a set auditable. Synthesising research — the rigour behind stages two and three. AI-assisted persona synthesis — where models help and where they return the market's average. The product strategy document — where ordering becomes a budgeted commitment. Telling the customer story — how a persona travels to those who were not in the research. Research debt and stale personas — the decay problem. Market segments vs personas — two objects with different owners, whose conflation drives most persona-count arguments. Why personas and the self-referential design trap — the elastic-user problem they solve and the failure they prevent. Jobs to Be Done and functional, emotional and social jobs — the causal vocabulary that would have caught Upvan's error. Forces of progress: push, pull, anxiety, habit — how a stated want becomes a switch.
exp20v2-cust.persona.build:
Building Personas from Research

How a team moves from forty hours of interview tape to a handful of people it will actually argue on behalf of.

1. A Monday with a Friday deadline

On Monday 20 July 2026, Falak Siddiqui, head of product at Firozi Home Works, opened a document titled "Who are we building for?" and found she had nothing to put in it that she believed. Firozi Home Works runs an app through which households in Lucknow, Indore and Nagpur book plumbers, electricians, carpenters and appliance technicians. It had 2,30,000 active customers, and the board would meet on Friday 24 July to approve a release budget of ₹3.6 crore for the next two quarters.

The trouble was that the company's existing "personas" were two laminated posters on the office wall. One showed "Fareen, 32, working mother, values convenience"; the other showed "Firdaus, 45, homeowner, values quality". Nobody remembered who had written them. Between 8 June and 3 July, Fanindra Hegde, the company's design researcher in Mysuru, had conducted 28 customer interviews. Fouzia Rahman, an analyst working from Auckland, had then run a survey of 1,840 customers. The material was unsorted, and the founder, Faiyaz Lodhi, had asked a blunt question: "Is it two people or five? Because I will not fund five roadmaps."

If Falak chose badly the cost was concrete. Too few personas and the release would be built for an average customer who does not exist; too many and the ₹3.6 crore would be split into slices too thin to ship. This page follows her through the work of turning research into a persona the team believes, and uses her numbers throughout.

2. The idea

A persona is a fictional but evidence-based portrait of a pattern of behaviour, given a name and a face so that a team can reason about it. The word to hold on to is pattern. A persona is not a customer, not an average of customers, and not a demographic bracket. It is a description of a group of people who face the same situation, want the same outcome and behave in similar ways, compressed into one vivid individual.

The device was popularised by the software designer Alan Cooper, whose 1998 book The Inmates Are Running the Asylum argued that teams building software designed for themselves, or for "the user" in the abstract, and so served no one. Cooper's remedy was to design for a specific, named person. Critics such as John Pruitt and Jonathan Grudin later warned that personas fail when they float free of data.

The sentence Falak could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib was this: "A persona is a pattern in what people are trying to do, written down so that we can argue about the pattern instead of about each other's opinions."

3. How it works, step by step

The route from tape to persona has six stages. Practitioners describe the first, third and fifth readily and leave the others implicit, which is where much of the damage occurs.

Collect. Fanindra interviewed 28 customers about the last time they needed a repair, not about what they "usually" do. People remember episodes better than habits, and episodes contain the detail that matters: who was at home and what was tried first. Code. She then broke each transcript into single observations, such as "called her brother-in-law before opening the app", and tagged each with the behaviour it showed. Coding is the implicit step: it converts stories into units that can be counted and compared, and two coders disagreeing on a tag is a finding, not an embarrassment.

Find the axes. A persona set is built along the few dimensions on which behaviour differs most. Fanindra's coded observations kept sorting along two: whether the repair was an emergency or a planned job, and whether the booker alone chose the technician or consulted a family member or landlord first. Choosing axes that are about behaviour and need, not age or income, is the single most important judgement in the whole exercise. Size with a survey. Interviews tell you what patterns exist; they cannot tell you how common each is. Fouzia's survey asked behavioural questions and assigned each of the 1,840 respondents to a cell of the two-by-two.

Falak then wrote each portrait: a name, a situation, a goal, the behaviour that distinguishes it, and the sentence the person would say. Test the persona is the last stage and the loop in Figure 1 exists for it. A persona is shown to people who were not in the room, ideally including customer-facing staff, and asked a single question: "Can you name a real customer who is this person?" If they cannot, the persona is a fiction, not a pattern.

4. A worked example, line by line

Fouzia's survey placed all 1,840 respondents in a cell. Because the sample was random, each respondent stands for 2,30,000 ÷ 1,840 = 125 customers. She then asked the same respondents how many bookings they made in the previous twelve months and the average value of a booking, which gave annual gross booking value (GBV: the total rupee value of jobs booked through the app) per customer.

The arithmetic runs as follows. For cell A, 3.2 bookings × ₹1,450 = ₹4,640 per customer; 76,500 customers × ₹4,640 = ₹35,49,60,000, or ₹35.50 crore. The same operation gives ₹26.89 crore, ₹32.50 crore and ₹24.21 crore for B, C and D, and the four sum to ₹119.10 crore (₹119.098 crore before rounding). Two things stand out. The largest cell by headcount, A, earns less per customer than C or D, while the smallest cell, D, earns ₹6,820 per customer against A's ₹4,640, about 1.5 times as much.

Second pass: change one input. Faiyaz's instinct was to drop any persona under 20 per cent of customers, on the grounds that a roadmap cannot serve a sliver. Apply that rule to the sample shares and cell D, at 15.4 per cent, is dropped, leaving three personas. But the rule measures the wrong quantity. D carries ₹24.21 crore of GBV, 20.3 per cent of the total, which is larger than its customer share by almost five percentage points. Re-run the filter on share of GBV and all four cells pass the 20 per cent threshold. One input, headcount versus value, moves the answer from three personas to four, and moves ₹24.21 crore of annual bookings from "ignored" to "served".

That is an argument for writing the decision rule down before applying it, because the rule, not the data, determined the answer.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Personas are not segments

A segment is a group of customers defined for sizing and targeting, and it is measured at scale. A persona is a representation of a segment for design, and it is written at the scale of one person. They are linked but they answer different questions: the segment says how many; the persona says what they are trying to do and why.

Demographics rarely separate behaviour

Fareen and Firdaus, the wall posters, were split by age, gender and income. In the survey, age explained almost none of the difference between cells; a 28-year-old tenant and a 55-year-old landlord both behaved as Urgent Soloists when a tap burst. Demographics are useful as colour, not as the spine of the persona.

A thin cell is a warning, not a result

Cell D received only 4 of the 28 interviews. The survey could size it, but the richness of its portrait rests on four conversations. A reader should ask how many cases support each persona and treat a number under about six as a hypothesis.

Behaviour describes the present, not the possible

Research shows what people do given today's product. It cannot tell you what they would do with a product that does not yet exist.

Primary and secondary personas

A team can serve many people but design for few. A primary persona is the one whose needs the interface must satisfy fully; a secondary persona is one whose needs are met so long as the primary's are not harmed. Without this ordering, "four personas" becomes four equal claims on the same budget.

The question to ask first

A thoughtful newcomer should ask: "Which decision will this persona change?" If no choice on the roadmap would differ between two personas, they are one persona with two names.

6. How it looks in different products and company stages

In a consumer product such as Firozi's, the persona is typically one person and the axes are situational. In a B2B product the buyer, the user and the person who pays are often three different people, so a persona set must include roles, not just individuals: a plant manager who approves, an operator who suffers. In a marketplace there are two or more sides, each with its own persona set, and the critical research question is how the sides constrain one another. Firozi's technicians form a second set whose own behaviour, such as declining a job in an unfamiliar neighbourhood, caps what customers can have.

Stage matters as well. An early-stage company with 20 customers should build a proto-persona from a dozen interviews and treat it as a bet, because the survey stage has too little data to run. A large company can afford the survey and the sizing, but faces a different hazard: personas become a shared artefact owned by no one and inherited by the next team that has never met the customers.

7. Common mistakes

The averaged person. Symptom: the persona's attributes sound pleasant but any engineer can agree with them. Misunderstanding: the author blended the patterns instead of separating them. Diagnostic: ask whether any attribute would make some colleague disagree.

Invented colour. Symptom: the card mentions a dog, a hobby and a favourite film that appear in no transcript. Misunderstanding: vividness was mistaken for evidence. Diagnostic: for each detail, point to the transcript line; delete any detail without one.

Size-only selection. Symptom: small, valuable groups vanish from the deck, as D nearly did. Misunderstanding: headcount was treated as importance. Diagnostic: recompute the cut-off on value, as in section 4.

The poster that nobody opens. Symptom: no ticket, specification or design review cites a persona by name. Misunderstanding: the persona was treated as a deliverable and not as a working tool. Diagnostic: count citations in the last ten specifications.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Falak's week would have looked like this. She would have written the decision rule on Monday, before opening the survey. She would have stated each persona with its supporting case count, its share of customers and its share of value, as in the table. She would have shown the draft portraits to three call-centre agents, who speak to hundreds of Firozi customers daily, and asked each to name a real caller for every card. She would have recorded a date for revisiting. And she would have brought to the board a single page: which persona is primary, which are secondary, and which decision each one changes.

9. What Falak decided

On Wednesday 22 July Falak settled on four personas with a stated ordering. Cell A, the Urgent Soloist, became primary because it is the largest group by headcount and the highest-frequency user, at 29.8 per cent of GBV. Cell D, the Planned Household, became a funded secondary persona because its ₹6,820 per customer made it the most valuable per head, and because the call-centre agents recognised it instantly. Cells B and C were secondary. She told Faiyaz that the roadmap would carry one primary bet and one secondary bet per quarter, not five parallel tracks, which answered his question: four patterns, two funded at a time. She also flagged that D's portrait rested on four interviews and asked Fanindra for eight more before the October review.

The natural next topics are synthesising research, which governs stages 2 and 3 in more rigour; the anatomy of a persona, which tells you what fields a card needs; and research debt and stale personas, which deals with decay.

Two questions to sit with. First, if Firozi's next pricing change moved the average booking in cell C from ₹3,100 to ₹2,400, would your persona ordering change, and which input would you recheck first? Second, which of your own team's personas could you defend, line by line, to a sceptical colleague who has read the transcripts?
case40v1-cust.persona.build:
Kundan Exchange: Who Is Holding the Phone?

An ambiguous case on building personas from research, set in India's recyclable-materials trade, October 2026

1. The night before

At half past eleven on Sunday night, 18 October 2026, Priyamvada Vidwans sat on the floor of her flat in HSR Layout, Bengaluru, with sixty-three interview summaries in four heaps around her. She had made the heaps three times that evening; they came out differently each time.

At 9.30 next morning, Monday, 19 October, eleven people would gather off Hosur Road for a workshop called "Persona lock — H2 FY27": Pranjal Vemuri in from Mumbai, Purvi Vichare from Pune, Prakriti Vadakkan dialling in from Rotterdam at six her time and Pinaki Vagholkar from Melbourne at three in the afternoon his. On Friday, 30 October the board would get a pack whose first page was meant to name who Kundan Exchange builds for.

2. Kundan Exchange, 2018 to 2026

Pranjal Vemuri founded Kundan Exchange in Indore in August 2018; his family had traded ferrous scrap near Sanwer Road for two generations. From November 2020 it matched sellers of scrap metal, plastic, batteries and electronics with recyclers and secondary smelters, taking a commission and handling weighment documentation, GST invoicing and e-way bills.

One decision still governs everything. In June 2022, racing a GST e-invoicing deadline, engineering collapsed the data model to one account per GSTIN with a single mandatory role: seller, buyer or transporter. A man who owns a yard in Kanpur, runs four trucks and buys aluminium from a neighbour on Thursdays is, in the database, exactly one of those. Every cohort chart, retention figure and persona rests on that field — and the people who move the most tonnage are almost always two things at once.

In March 2023 the company paid Kaushal Partners ₹9.5 lakh for a study based on eleven interviews. It produced Pukhraj, "the dealer who trusts no screen", and Prabhakar, "the plant buyer who needs assured tonnage" — laminated, still quoted, believed by nobody and replaced by nobody.

3. The industry around it

India's recyclable-materials trade is enormous, informal and being formalised from two directions. From below, UPI put real-time settlement into yards that ran on cash; a Ludhiana weighbridge now prints a slip and a PhonePe QR code in one motion. From above, Extended Producer Responsibility obligations under the Plastic Waste Management Rules, the E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 and the Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022 oblige producers to buy recycling certificates through the Central Pollution Control Board's EPR portal.

Demand is visible: Tata Steel, JSW Steel and Hindalco; induction-furnace units in Jamshedpur, Rajkot and Coimbatore; recyclers such as Gravita India and Attero; platforms including Metalbook competing for flow. A sixth of Kundan's non-ferrous tonnage leaves through Mundra and Nhava Sheva, mostly to a smelter in Sohar, Oman — which is why Prakriti Vadakkan sits in Rotterdam. Shredded ferrous held ₹34,000 to ₹41,000 a tonne through 2026, so margins are thin and trust in weighment is the currency.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The EPR line launched in January 2026, and by April three roadmap proposals were in flight, each citing Pukhraj or Prabhakar: a cash advance for yard owners, a photo-assay tool for traders, a documentation module for compliance teams. Priyamvada commissioned fieldwork instead of choosing between them.

Purvi Vichare's team ran it from Monday, 20 July to Friday, 11 September 2026 — fifty-three days, just under eight weeks — with 63 interviews and nine weighbridge observations in Kanpur, Ludhiana, Rajkot, Coimbatore, Guwahati and Mundka, at a cost of ₹18.6 lakh.

Five behavioural clusters came off the wall, defined by what people did rather than what their GSTIN said: the yard aggregator, who buys small lots for cash and lives on the cash cycle; the grade arbitrageur, who treats every grade dispute as the real transaction; the institutional seller, a plant-services manager disposing of a factory's own waste, who wants paperwork and barely notices price; the recycler buyer, who needs assured tonnage at known contamination; and the transporter-operator, who arbitrages the loaded mile.

Three findings have since undercut it. On Thursday, 1 October, Pinaki Vagholkar's rebuilt cluster model left 3,940 of the 26,400 active accounts unclassified (14.9 per cent of accounts), yet those accounts carried ₹29.00 crore of the ₹130.00 crore of September gross merchandise value, 22.3 per cent of GMV. Between Tuesday, 15 September and Monday, 28 September the team audited 1,200 app sessions, with consent from 310 account holders, to see who held the phone: the holder did in 468 of the 1,200 sessions, 39.0 per cent. All 63 interviews had been with account holders. And on Tuesday, 6 October, Kaushal Partners delivered a survey of 900 accounts fielded 21 September to 2 October — overlapping the audit window, but not the same window — in which 504 of the 900 respondents (56.0 per cent) said they entered weights themselves. Both are honest; they cannot both describe one world.

On Friday, 9 October, Kaveri Industries, the Jamshedpur steel and aluminium group that is Kundan's largest buyer, served a shortfall notice for the quarter ended 30 September: against a contracted 18,000 tonnes it had received 16,420, a shortfall of 1,580 tonnes of the 18,000 contracted (8.8 per cent). At ₹38,500 a tonne that is ₹6.08 crore of material, so the 4 per cent penalty came to ₹24.33 lakh — 10.4 per cent of one month's platform revenue of ₹233.30 lakh.

5. The people

Priyamvada Vidwans, vice-president of product, Bengaluru, owns the artifact and wants every trait traceable. Not said: she has drafted a slide reading "we build for the operator, not the owner", and knows 63 interviews with owners cannot defend it.

Pranjal Vemuri, founder and chief executive, Mumbai, wants one persona, the yard owner: a company with five customers has none. His incentive is the Series B tranche. Not said: two of the three yards he cites as evidence are relatives' businesses.

Purvi Vichare, head of design and research, Pune, wants five personas plus a sixth for the operator, each trait tagged with its interview count. Not said: only two of her nine institutional-seller interviews were with compliance buyers.

Prateek Vallath, head of the dealer network, Indore, runs 74 field agents and carries quarterly GMV; there are two customers, he says, the dealer and the plant. Not said: his agents, who introduced most respondents, are paid on verified rather than trading accounts (Exhibit 3).

Prem Vijaykar, head of field operations, Kanpur, insists there is one user: the man at the weighbridge with a phone in one hand and a chalk slate in the other. Not said: his team has shared owners' logins with yard staff for two years, against the terms he sells.

Pinaki Vagholkar, data science lead, Melbourne, five and a half hours ahead of India, lands his runs before Bengaluru wakes; personas are decoration, he says, so ship computable segments. Not said: his model is largely a decision tree over the 2022 role field, and his loaded ₹1.42 crore a year is 4.2 times a Bengaluru engineer's ₹34 lakh.

Prakriti Vadakkan, head of export trading, Rotterdam — three and a half hours behind India until the European clocks change on Sunday, 25 October, four and a half after — notes that unclassified accounts realise ₹55,769 a tonne against the platform's ₹32,500. Not said: her Sohar buyer wants a counterparty list, which would force Kundan to say which accounts are traders, not generators.

Pratibha Vemula, head of regulatory and compliance, New Delhi, wants a compliance-buyer persona: EPR is the only double-digit margin and the only line with no research. Not said until she wrote it down: a yard clerk observed through a consenting holder's screen consented to nothing under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 sets the sample against the book of business: grade arbitrageurs supplied 21 of 63 interviews (33.3 per cent of interviews) while holding 19.7 per cent of accounts and 29.5 per cent of September GMV.

Exhibit 2 carries the arithmetic the Series B milestone turns on. The blended take rate is ₹233.30 lakh of revenue on ₹130.00 crore of GMV, 1.79 per cent, total over total; the simple mean of the five cluster rates, quoted in two internal decks, is 2.02 per cent. The milestone is 1.90 per cent, so the denominator decides whether the covenant is met.

Exhibit 3 is September's onboarding chain by channel. Of 14,600 registrations, 9,490 cleared GSTIN and KYC (65.0 per cent of registrations); 5,124 of those created a first listing (54.0 per cent of the verified); 2,357 of those completed a first trade (46.0 per cent of first listings); 919 of those traded again within 30 days (39.0 per cent of first traders). The four stages compound to 6.30 per cent, and 919 of the 14,600 registrations is 6.3 per cent.

Exhibit 4 is the one keeping Priyamvada awake: 696 of the 1,200 audited sessions (58.0 per cent) were operated by someone other than the account holder, which against the 9.60 lakh seller-app sessions of September is roughly 5.57 lakh sessions in hands Kundan has never interviewed.

Exhibit 5 covers the EPR quarter: 10,125 certified tonnes on 11,350 processed, a yield of 89.2 per cent, at a blended ₹5,017 a certified tonne, total value over total certified tonnes. The ₹6,175 mean of the four stream prices, which overstates the line, reached the September investor update.

Exhibits 6 and 7 set the history against the deadline and the clusters against the milestone.

7. Voices

Pranjal Vemuri, leadership call, 9 October: "I do not need a cluster to tell me who the customer is. He is the man whose money is stuck in a truck."

Prem Vijaykar, field operations, 10 October, 7.12 a.m.: "Sir, with respect: that man is in a Scorpio on a call. The phone is with Pintu at the weighbridge. Pintu has no login. Pintu is your user. We have given him the owner's password for two years and now there is a table about it."

Prateek Vallath, reply to all, 11 October: "Half the GMV is traders — 29.5 and 22.3 in your own exhibit, and anyone who has stood in Mundka knows the unclassified ones are traders. Build H2 for a clerk who does not pay us and I miss the quarter."

Purvi Vichare, workshop pre-read, 16 October: "Six is not indulgence, it is the number of behaviours we found. If you want fewer, tell me which one to stop serving. I will not average two into a person who does not exist: we have one of those on the wall, and his name is Pukhraj."

Pratibha Vemula, note to Priyamvada, 17 October: "Two interviews. That is our whole evidence base for the only customer paying us a double-digit margin. We research the part earning 1.79 per cent and not the part earning 9.0 per cent of certificate value."

8. The options as Priyamvada sees them

Option A: five personas mapped one-to-one onto the computable clusters. Each gets a rule, a size, a GMV share and a take rate, so the persona set and the dashboard agree. The cost is honesty: 14.9 per cent of accounts and 22.3 per cent of September GMV fall outside the five rules, so the set ships with a sixth box called "unclassified", which is not a person, and the 2022 role field becomes the company's vocabulary for two more years.

Option B: two refreshed personas, the yard owner and the plant buyer. Already the house language, three days of writing, adopted at once. It averages the grade arbitrageur into the yard aggregator despite a gap of 0.80 percentage points in take rate, and has no place for the operator of 58.0 per cent of audited sessions.

Option C: four jobs-to-be-done plus one operator persona, and a change to the account model. The jobs: settle a load without a dispute, release cash the same day, assure a furnace charge, file a defensible EPR return. Role-aware accounts cost three of eleven squads for two quarters — 24 engineers at ₹34 lakh each fully loaded, roughly ₹4.08 crore — and no new Kaveri tonnage work in that window.

Option D: delay. Twenty more weighbridge observations and twelve operator interviews would cost ₹7.4 lakh and three weeks, landing Monday, 9 November — the day after Diwali, so realistically 16 November. The board still meets on 30 October.

Every option assumes one persona set, owned by product, used by all. Sales needs a buying unit, engineering a role model, compliance an obligated producer, Kaveri tonnage; one artifact may not be able to be all four.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The workshop is on Monday, 19 October, the day before Dussehra. The board pack closes on Friday, 30 October. Cash at 30 September was ₹61 crore against a net burn of ₹3.4 crore a month: about eighteen months, to roughly March 2028. The Series B second tranche of ₹45 crore requires ₹1,800 crore of annualised GMV at a blended take rate of at least 1.90 per cent by 30 June 2027; September's run-rate is ₹1,560 crore annualised at 1.79 per cent, needing monthly revenue of ₹2.85 crore against September's ₹2.333 crore. The Kaveri contract runs to February 2028 at 18,000 tonnes a quarter with a 4 per cent shortfall penalty. Engineering is 94 people in eleven squads across Bengaluru and Pune, with no hiring budget until April 2027. And the Digital Personal Data Protection Act makes both the method behind Exhibit 4 and the photo-assay feature questions for Pratibha before they are questions for product.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, which cluster matters most, and does the answer change when you rank by accounts, tonnage, GMV, take rate or revenue?
  2. Exhibit 3 supports both "field agents work" and "field agents manufacture dead accounts". What figure would settle it, and is it collected?
  3. Exhibit 4 says the holder operated 39.0 per cent of audited sessions; the survey says 56.0 per cent of respondents enter weights themselves. Neither instrument is dishonest. How should Priyamvada present both, and what would resolve the gap?
  4. Every interview was with an account holder. What class of persona can 63 such interviews support, what class can they not, and what does that imply for naming an operator persona?
  5. Pinaki wants computable segments; Purvi says averaging behaviours invents people. Is that about method, or about who owns the customer definition? And what would you do about the 2022 role field, given that fixing it costs ₹4.08 crore in the two quarters Kaveri needs tonnage?
  6. What should Priyamvada do at 9.30 on Monday, and what would she say to the board on 30 October about who Kundan Exchange builds for — given a 1.79 per cent blended take rate, a 1.90 per cent milestone, and the 640 accounts that are the only thing right of that line in Exhibit 7?

Shortly after midnight she moved one summary to a fifth heap she had not meant to start, then put it back. On the chart paper the operator's name had been rubbed out and written again twice. She had no name for him from the research, because nobody had asked him anything. She turned off the lamp with the heaps still on the floor.
exp40v2-cust.persona.anatomy:
Anatomy of a persona

What a persona must contain to be useful — and the precise point at which it becomes a stereotype

1. Two decisions, four weeks apart

On Tuesday 8 September 2026, in a converted spinning-mill office in Coimbatore, Tanvi Bhide put a question to her engineering lead that the screen could not settle. Bhide runs product at Trinetra Vision Systems, which sells line-mounted inspection cameras and the console software that reads them to auto-component plants, pharmaceutical packaging lines and textile job-shops. The hardware is the moat; the console decides renewals.

Trinetra had 412 plants and 6,180 named console users, and the board had approved ₹1.50 crore for one of two builds. Option A was an inspector-throughput console for the person clearing defect flags at the line all shift. Option B was a defect-cost report for the plant quality head, who logs in twelve times a month and rebuilds the same numbers in a spreadsheet before his review. Every engineer favoured A: the inspectors were the heavy users, the ones who wrote in, the ones the team could picture. The review was Friday 16 October, thirty-eight days later.

Eighteen hundred kilometres north, on Friday 2 October 2026, Tanaya Pingle faced the same problem with none of the same furniture. Pingle heads product at Takhti Learning Systems in Jaipur, an AI tutor for Class 9 and 10 students on the CBSE syllabus. In the July–September quarter Takhti took 7,40,000 installs; 1,48,000 of those students completed a first tutoring session, 20.0 per cent. Its wall carried one sheet: a composite Class 10 student with a cracked screen who wanted to "improve in maths". Pingle had ₹85 lakh and until Friday 13 November to choose between the progress report parents asked for and the streaks students asked for.

Both decisions turn on one defect. A persona is meant to tell a team what a group of users will do; neither sheet could, because each described who the user was, not what the user would do when something changed.

2. The idea, and the five schools that disagree about it

A persona is a named, bounded, evidence-based model of a user group, written so a team can predict its response to a specific decision. It has four parts and the fourth is usually dropped: goals, the outcome the person wants in their terms, never a feature; attitudes, the beliefs and trade-offs that make some routes to the goal unacceptable; behaviours, what they observably do, including the workaround they have built; and decision relevance, which decisions this model can inform and which it cannot.

Everything else is context: age, city, device and income belong only if they predict one of the first three. A persona becomes a stereotype where context outweighs conditionals — a photograph, a hobby, a brand preference, and no sentence of the form "when X happens, she does Y."

The device was invented to end one argument. Through the 1980s the designer Alan Cooper found that teams debated "the user" as though one existed, each participant picturing a version of himself. His answer, in The Inmates Are Running the Asylum (1998), was to make the imagined user explicit, singular and named, so it could be checked. Pruitt and Adlin's The Persona Lifecycle added in 2006 what Cooper left thin: sizing, ownership, an expiry date. Alongside ran the older market-research tradition from Wendell Smith's 1956 segmentation paper, which held that a customer grouping is worthless unless measurable and substantial. The two were never reconciled, and most persona programmes mix them unstably.

Five positions are genuinely held. The goal-directed school signs a design that satisfies everyone satisfies no one, so one primary persona must be satisfied completely but not a persona may be built from analytics alone. The segmentation school signs if you cannot size it you cannot plan against it but not one persona should govern the design. The jobs-to-be-done school signs circumstances cause behaviour, attributes merely correlate but not the person is the right carrier of customer knowledge. The proto-persona school signs a dated hypothesis written in a day beats a six-month study delivered after the decision but not no persona without primary research. The behavioural-cohort school signs the only persona worth having is one you recompute nightly as a query but not narrative adds predictive power. The first and last answer Bhide oppositely.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Name the decision first. It fixes the outcome metric, and the metric fixes which behaviours matter. Bhide's payoff arrives through renewal, Pingle's through paid conversion; the same interviews would yield different personas for each, which is why "build our personas" is never a brief.

Inventory roles before clustering people. Where user, buyer and decider differ, role structure is prior to behavioural structure. Tanushree Barooah, Trinetra's researcher in Kochi, pulled the console's authentication records, which carry a role field set at installation.

Cluster on the decision metric, not on the users. Tithi Bhattacharya, Takhti's data scientist, split the 1,48,000 activated students on first-fortnight behaviour — trickle or burst, whose hands opened the account, dialogue or one-off dump — and traced each to the number that pays the bills.

4. The conditions, stated as testable claims

One: the base is behaviourally heterogeneous on the decision metric. Test with Table 3; Takhti passes at 16.03 per cent. Trinetra passes structurally instead, its roles differing by job description rather than discovered cluster. Where a base is homogeneous, personas add ritual and nothing else.

Two: the decision is sensitive to that heterogeneity. A choice of server region is not; a choice of console is. Both protagonists pass.

Three: beneficiary and payer can be identified separately. Takhti's old sheet merged student and parent. Trinetra failed the other way, ranking known roles by session count — a measure of who benefits, silent on who pays.

Four: the behaviours are stable over the decision's horizon. Personas mislead in a market in structural change, where today's workaround vanishes before the build ships, and where the product's own behaviour is non-stationary — the AI problem, in which last quarter's doubt-dumper is this quarter's engaged learner because answers improved.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product. Libraries collide where bases overlap. The mature answer is one shared vocabulary of roles with product-specific clusters on top: one noun set, many verb sets. The common answer is two incompatible libraries.

Two-sided and marketplace. Personas arrive in opposed pairs and the content is the tension: what delights a supplier often irritates a buyer. Name the decision on which their interests oppose, and settle which side wins.

Regulated. In lending, insurance and health a third party sits in the room — auditor, compliance officer, regulator — neither user nor buyer but able to veto. Experts keep a constraint sheet for them: written as a persona, a compliance officer invites design for her satisfaction rather than her approval.

Hardware plus software. Trinetra's case: the hardware is bought once through a capex process by people who will never use it, the software used daily by people with no budget, and the installed footprint fixes that user population for years.

AI-native. Capability drifts under the user, so behaviour seen in one quarter may be no property of the person. And synthetic personas are cheap: a model yields a fluent archetype in seconds, modelling the training distribution's stereotypes — the very failure personas were invented to prevent.

At the organisational seams. The personas research writes, product plans with and marketing targets drift apart within two quarters unless someone owns reconciliation. The fix is not governance but one shared number — for Trinetra, plant renewal.

6. Eight things an expert sees that a competent practitioner does not

A persona is a conditional, not a description. The tell is grammatical: count the sentences of the form "when X happens, she does Y". An expert's sheet is mostly those, a novice's mostly adjectives. Richer description is not a better model, because description does not constrain prediction. "Price-conscious" rules nothing out; "abandons the form where it asks for a PAN, and has photographed the screen to ask a relative" rules out three designs.

Goals are hierarchical, and feature requests are not goals. Cooper's split between life, end and experience goals survives because it is useful. The tell is a persona whose goal is a feature: "wants a dashboard" is a means in an end's clothes. Trinetra's plant head wanted to arrive at the monthly review able to defend a number.

The three layers decay at different rates. Behaviours change fastest, because products and workarounds do; attitudes are slower, set by one bad experience; goals, within a role, slowest. The tell is a sheet with one revision date rather than three: re-check behaviours quarterly, attitudes annually, goals when the role changes.

Separation matters more than coverage. A library covering every user whose groups behave alike confers false confidence. The tell is the question an expert asks: explains variance in what? Takhti's four clusters covered every activation; so did its city tiers; only one was worth anything.

The primary persona is a commitment to disappoint someone. Choosing one names the users served second, and the tell is that an expert says in public whom the product may disappoint. Teams that cannot have averaged instead. The corollary is the negative persona: attractive, numerous, wrong for this product. Bhide's instinct to serve inspectors was defensible, but she had not noticed whom it disappointed: the people who sign renewals.

Personas drift toward the interviewable. People who answer research calls are biased consistently: more articulate, more engaged, more tolerant of the product as it is. The tell is that an expert asks for the response rate and refusal profile before reading findings. Takhti's doubt-dumpers, 15.0 per cent of activations, never appeared in an interview.

The self-referential trap survives the persona. Engineers in Coimbatore writing a line operator in Ludhiana will, absent discipline, write an engineer's tolerance for configuration. The tell is a persona whose frustrations match the team's own. Tarun Magdum, Trinetra's field engineering lead, caught it: the sheet wanted keyboard shortcuts, while every inspector he watched used a grease-smeared touchscreen with gloves on.

A persona must be falsifiable, and its count follows a decision budget. The right number of sheets is the number of live decisions, usually two or three, and an expert can state for each the decision it settles. Good sheets carry a line reading "we were wrong about —" with a date, and one prediction checkable next quarter.

7. What actually differs by product type and stage

Table 5. Where the anatomy genuinely changes, and each setting's characteristic failure.
SettingWhat the anatomy must carryCharacteristic failure
ConsumerAttitudes do most of the workA lifestyle collage

MarketplaceOpposed pairs, conflict namedStarving one side
HardwareLock-in over the asset's lifeDesigning for the demo
AI productsTraits distinguished from model artefactsReading capability as a trait
Seed stageDated hypotheses, sizes unknownPromoting a stale hypothesis
Growth stageLog clusters, interview-validatedHeaviest users read as payers
Mature companyOwners, dates, one outcome metricA library nobody may retire

Two asserted differences are not real. B2B needs more personas than consumer, not fewer, because the roles are structurally distinct. Nor can enterprise skip attitudes because purchasing is rational: attitudes to blame and audit risk dominate enterprise buying.

8. Three worked examples

Trinetra: the user who is not the customer

Table 1 told Bhide that inspectors were 23.95 per cent of named users and 37.4 per cent of sessions, which the team read as a mandate. The counter-evidence sat in the renewal book. In the year to 31 March 2026, 388 contracts came up for renewal and 357 renewed, 92.0 per cent; the 31 that lapsed carried ₹329 lakh of annual contract value, an average of ₹10.61 lakh each. Barooah and Thanh Nguyen, Trinetra's analyst in Hanoi, called all 31 between 11 and 25 September 2026.

The parent report, ₹85 lakh, was modelled to lift the parent-pushed cluster's paid rate from 24.0 to 33.0 per cent — nine points on 11,100 retained students, 999 subscriptions, ₹23.98 lakh a year, payback 3.5 years. Streaks was what students asked for, and the worse investment by nearly three times.

Tijori Lending Systems: where the method failed

Tijori, in Pune, lends working capital to small retailers through an app, originating against Udyam registration and Aadhaar eKYC. In March 2025 its product head, Tejinder Grewal, received a sheet titled "Tilakraj the Shop Owner": forty-one, owns a 200-square-foot general store, comfortable with UPI, transacts alone and at night. Its evidence base was thirty-four interviews with Tijori's own field agents, describing borrowers. Nobody had interviewed a borrower.

Tijori built for the self-serve night-time borrower for ten months. On Monday 19 January 2026 an audit sampled 900 completed KYC journeys and found 558 of those 900 — 62 per cent — had a field agent present at the shop. The sheet recorded what agents believed about their customers, and was used as a model of the customers themselves.
