The recovery was a different method, not a better persona. Grewal's team ran twenty-two shop-floor observations and rebuilt three clusters around who was present when an application began; the assisted journey, handing the phone to the borrower only for consent, followed. Had the old 9.00 per cent rate held, 52,000 applications would have yielded 4,680 loans; at 12.45 per cent they yielded 6,474, a gain of 1,794 loans and, at an average ticket of ₹1.85 lakh, ₹33.19 crore of extra disbursal in a quarter.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

The proxy persona. Sign: the research cites people who talk to customers, not customers. Diagnostic: whom did we interview? Cost late: Tijori's ten months.

The average persona. Sign: every figure is a tidy mean and forecasts miss when the mix shifts. Diagnostic: which real user sits closest? Cost: Takhti's ₹16.73 lakh error.

The engagement fallacy. Sign: the primary persona is whoever appears most in the logs. Diagnostic: who signs the renewal? Cost: Trinetra nearly spent ₹140 lakh for a 2.43-year payback rather than ₹110 lakh for 0.61.

The frozen persona. Sign: no revision date, or one over a year old. Diagnostic: which behaviour claim should have changed? Cost: a team confidently wrong.

The orphan library. Sign: more personas than live decisions, no owner. Diagnostic: which decision does each settle? Cost: unresolvable reviews, and whoever argues hardest wins.

The synthetic persona. Sign: fluent sheets nobody can trace to a transcript. Diagnostic: show three verbatim quotes with dates. Cost: a stereotype with a document's authority.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Narrative versus cohort. Steelmanned, the cohort position: a cohort is a query, so it is reproducible, sizeable and cannot drift into fiction, whereas narrative adds memorability and also unfalsifiable detail — and detail is what makes stereotypes. For it to be wrong, teams would have to fail to act on definitions they cannot picture. The narrative camp claims that: Trinetra's engineers had the role table for two years and still built for the inspector, because nobody had made the plant head a person in the room.

One primary persona versus a portfolio. Cooper, steelmanned: design is a long sequence of micro-trade-offs under time pressure, and only one primary persona makes them resolvable without escalation. For it to be wrong, products would show no coherence penalty from serving several personas equally — and the enterprise evidence, multi-persona consoles reliably called cluttered, supports him. The portfolio camp's ground is the marketplace, where no primary persona exists in principle.

Person versus job. Steelmanned: attributes correlate with behaviour, circumstances cause it, so the stable unit is the job in context. For it to be wrong, people would behave consistently across circumstances — and Takhti's data cuts against the person, since a crammer in October is often a daily-drip learner in February. The counter: Takhti must still decide who gets a notification, and notifications go to people.

The open question. Nobody knows how much persona work a model can synthesise from real transcripts rather than its training distribution. The optimistic reading is a speed-up in coding and clustering; the pessimistic one, that the value lay in forcing contact with people the team would never meet, so removing it keeps only the artefact.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this opens a persona conversation by asking which decision is pending, and declines if the answer is "all of them". They ask what a persona explains the variance in, and accept 16 per cent. They name the users the product will disappoint, before the people who represent them. And they retire personas visibly, with a date and a note on what the sheet got wrong.

12. The decisions

At the review on Friday 16 October 2026, Bhide recommended Option B: ₹110 lakh against a modelled ₹180.4 lakh of retained annual contract value. Option A was deferred rather than cancelled, because inspectors remain the users whose daily experience decides whether the plant head has anything to report. Her minuted reasoning: the heaviest users were not the customers, and 31 exit calls had priced that confusion at ₹329 lakh.

Pingle, on Friday 13 November 2026, funded the parent report in full and replaced her single sheet with three — Tanmay the Exam-Eve Crammer, Tabassum the Paying Parent, and a daily-drip learner she would not name until a researcher had met twenty. She also wrote Takhti's first negative persona: the doubt-dumper, 15.0 per cent of activations, 100 paying students, not the company's customer.

Discussion questions. First, Option B rests on a modelled four-point renewal lift nobody has observed: what evidence would you require, and by when, before releasing the rest? Second, Takhti's clusters explain 16.03 per cent of the variance in week-4 retention: at what level would a persona set stop being decision-grade, and what would replace it? Third, which persona in your organisation rests on the testimony of people who talk to customers rather than customers?

13. Going deeper

  • Why personas — the purpose this anatomy follows from.
  • Building personas from research — the interview craft behind these layers.
  • Empathy maps — keeping attitudes in view during design.
  • Market segments vs personas — the sizing half.
  • The self-referential design trap — nuance seven in depth.
  • AI-assisted persona synthesis — the open question of section 10.
  • Jobs to Be Done — the rival unit of analysis.
  • Functional, emotional and social jobs — vocabulary for attitudes.
  • Forces of progress: push, pull, anxiety, habit — why a clear goal yields nothing.
case20v1-cust.persona.anatomy:
The Persona on the Wall

Lagan Wedding Collective, Pune, October 2026

1. Opening

On the morning of Monday, 12 October 2026, Padmini Mulay, head of product at Lagan Wedding Collective, stood in front of the whiteboard wall of the company's Baner office in Pune and looked at a laminated card that had hung there for nineteen months. The card showed a smiling photograph and a name, "Shaadi Sonia". Sonia was 27, lived in Mumbai, worked in marketing and had a planned budget of about ₹22 lakh.

The company's quarterly roadmap would lock on Friday, 16 October, and three proposals on the table each cited Sonia as the reason. Padmini had ₹12 lakh of research budget and a suspicion that the card told the team less than it seemed. By Friday she had to decide what a Lagan persona should contain, and how much to spend finding out.

2. Company Background

Lagan was founded in 2022 by Vihaan Mody, a former hotel-industry executive from Mumbai,. The app lets families discover and book venues, caterers, photographers, decorators and make-up artists, and tracks payments and guest lists. Lagan earns a commission from vendors on bookings made through the app. It operates in eleven cities, from Pune and Nashik to Jaipur and Kochi.

The competitive field is crowded. WedMeGood leads discovery, Instagram leads inspiration, and Justdial and word of mouth still decide many caterer bookings. UPI makes it easy for a family to pay a vendor directly and bypass Lagan, so a booking happens only when the family trusts the app enough to pay through it. Demand follows the wedding calendar: bookings climb as the season opens after Diwali and Dev Uthani Ekadashi in late November, and a feature that misses that window waits a year to be tested.

3. The Situation

Sonia had been created in March 2025 from a founder workshop and a pull of app-store reviews. Whenever someone asked whether a feature was right, the answer was "Would Sonia use it?", and Sonia, being fictional, always had an opinion.

Ritvik Mallya, the data scientist working from Hyderabad, was the first to challenge her. In September he joined booking records to the "who is planning" question added to onboarding in January. Exhibit 1 sets out the result for the 2,400 weddings planned in the app between January and September 2026. Only 840 of them, 35 per cent, were led by the bride or groom. In 960 weddings, 40 per cent, a parent or elder relative took the decisions. In the remaining 600, 25 per cent, the couple and their families decided jointly.

The blended average budget of ₹22.3 lakh was almost exactly the figure on Sonia's card, and that was the trouble. No group looked like the average: self-led couples planned at ₹12 lakh, parents at ₹34 lakh and joint deciders at ₹18 lakh.

Exhibit 2 shows the second half of Ritvik's finding. Lagan's paid-booking rate, the share of planned weddings that went on to pay at least one vendor through the app, was 966 out of 2,400, or 40.25 per cent. Splitting by city type barely moved it: 40.0 per cent in the metros and 40.5 per cent elsewhere. Splitting by who decides moved it from 30 to 50 per cent. Sonia's city, age and phone told the team least.

Shobha Mantri, the design lead in Kolkata, noticed in session recordings that parent-led planners ignored the moodboard, went straight to the venue list and phoned. Tarun Mehrotra, who leads sales for the diaspora market from Melbourne, reported that diaspora couples often plan from abroad while parents in Ludhiana or Surat do the booking.

4. The People

Padmini Mulay, head of product, Pune, owns the decision.

Vihaan Mody, co-founder and chief executive, Mumbai, is fond of Sonia, who was drawn from his own sister's experience. He fears "a dozen personas" will become posters nobody remembers.

Ritvik Mallya, data scientist, Hyderabad, believes the answer is already in the data and wants to cluster behaviour at scale. He distrusts vivid stories from twenty-odd interviews.

Shobha Mantri, design lead, Kolkata, wants the personas to be rich enough to design against, with real motives and real frustrations,; a statistical segment gives a designer nothing to picture.

Tarun Mehrotra, head of sales for the diaspora market, Melbourne, wants the persona to recognise people who pay but do not use the app, since his families often book through a relative in India.

5. Exhibits

Exhibits 1 and 2 showed that the decision role, not demographics, separated Lagan's customers. Exhibit 3 shows what each option costs,.

Only one of the two substantial options can be funded, and neither reports before the roadmap locks on 16 October.

6. The Options

Option A: refresh Sonia. Update the card with Ritvik's figures, add a line about family involvement, and carry on. At ₹0.6 lakh and two weeks, it is cheap and keeps the shared language. But it leaves one demographic character at the centre of a company whose customers split into three roles; the 40 per cent of weddings led by parents would still be designed for someone absent.

Option B: role-based personas built from research. Interview 24 recently married families across Pune, Jaipur, Nashik and Kochi, plus the diaspora case Tarun described, and write three personas around what each person is trying to achieve, how they feel about money, family and risk, and what they actually do. At ₹9.5 lakh it fits the budget with ₹2.5 lakh to spare. Upside: depth a designer can use. Cost: eight weeks, and the risk that 24 interviews overstate the vivid.

Option C: data-driven segments. Tag behaviour in the app, survey 1,500 users and cluster. At ₹11.5 lakh it uses almost all of the budget and covers far more people than interviews could. The cost is twelve weeks, a result after the season opens, and clusters that show what people do but not why.

7. Questions for Discussion

1. What, specifically, was wrong with "Shaadi Sonia"?

2. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, which attributes on the old card separated customers in a way that changes a design decision, and which did not?

3. How do the three options differ in what a designer in Kolkata, an engineer in Pune and a salesperson in Melbourne could each do with the result?

4. What should Padmini tell the founder on Friday, and what would make her change her mind?

8. A Note for the Learner

How the topic frames the decision. A persona earns its place by changing a decision. The useful anatomy is goals (what the person is trying to get done), attitudes (how they feel about money, risk, family, trust) and behaviours (what they actually do, including how they decide and with whom). Demographic detail is admitted only where the data shows it separates behaviour. A stereotype is a persona whose details cannot be tested, and an average is a persona that describes nobody. Sonia's ₹22 lakh budget matched the blended ₹22.3 lakh of Exhibit 1 and none of the three groups beneath it.

One defensible path. Choose Option B, scoped tightly. Exhibit 2 has already done much of what Option C would do: it shows that the decision role is the attribute that matters, a 20-point spread in paid-booking rate against half a point for city type. What the data cannot supply is the goals and attitudes behind each role, and that is what interviews provide. Padmini would build three personas, self-led, parent-led and joint, each with a goal, an attitude to money and a behaviour pattern, and would drop the age, phone and job title unless interviews show they matter. Because parent-led weddings are 40 per cent of the total and convert lowest, at 30 per cent, she would interview that group first. Ritvik would test every interview claim against the booking data, which answers his worry about vividness, and the remaining ₹2.5 lakh would fund validation. For Friday, she would hold the three proposals unless each serves a named role, and tell Vihaan that Sonia survives as one of the three, the self-led planner.

What would change the answer. If interviews could not be recruited quickly, or the spread in Exhibit 2 proved an artefact of how the onboarding question was asked, Option C would deserve a second look.
case40v1-cust.persona.anatomy:
Four Men Named Naresh

Utthan Materials Exchange — Indore, November 2026

1. The night before

On the evening of Sunday, 15 November 2026, the Vijay Nagar office of Utthan Materials Exchange held only Dhanashree Vispute, its vice-president of product. On the wall behind her hung three laminated cards. The middle one carried a photograph of a man in a checked shirt beside a hand-cart, under the name Naresh, 38, Tier-2 Collector, and nine lines: married, two children, monthly income ₹28,000, Android phone under ₹12,000, speaks Hindi, prefers cash, uses WhatsApp daily, distrusts banks, wants respect.

The board met at nine the next morning: the H2 product plan, ₹24 lakh of discovery budget, the largest customer. Three of the four proposals began with the same sentence: Naresh needs…

She had spent the weekend with a spreadsheet from Chennai and field notes from Ahmedabad, and the two would not sit together. What troubled her was not that the card was wrong in its details, but that she could no longer say what it was for — what would have to be true on it for an argument in tomorrow's room to be settled by it rather than decorated by it.

2. The company, and the decision that still binds it

Utthan was founded in Indore in 2019 by Sohail Vakharia, a third-generation metals trader, and two engineers. Scrap in India moves through an immense, undocumented chain of collectors, aggregators and traders, and the processors at the end can almost never prove where a tonne came from. Utthan built the layer in between: a price feed, a digital weight slip, a payment rail on UPI, and a chain-of-custody record following material from pick-up to processor.

By FY26 it worked in eleven states and had added a second product: documentation services for brand owners who carry Extended Producer Responsibility obligations and file collection evidence on the Central Pollution Control Board's EPR portal. That business grew faster than the marketplace and now pays most of the bills.

One decision from two years ago still shapes everything. In the three weeks before the November 2024 Series B roadshow, the growth team collapsed a messy internal list of eleven seller types into three persona cards: Naresh the Collector, Ramesh the Aggregator and Corporate Seller. Built for a deck, they were legible and they travelled. The round closed in March 2025. The deck's market slide counted 1.1 crore informal collectors in India and put Utthan's registered collector base at 71,000. That figure then migrated into the board's quarterly scorecard, into the sales collateral, and finally into Annexure C of a customer contract signed in March 2026, which commits Utthan to sourcing from "not fewer than 60,000 registered collectors" for its twenty-four-month term. Nobody writing the deck imagined any of that.

3. The industry

India's recycling market has two halves that barely speak. The formal half — Gravita, Attero, Recykal, the recovery arms of large producers — is capitalised, audited and hungry for feedstock it can document. The informal half collects nearly everything. Policy has been pushing the two together for a decade: the Plastic Waste Management Rules and the E-Waste and Battery Waste Rules of 2022 set recovery targets for brand owners, who discharge them by buying certificates against documented collection. Since the reverse-charge mechanism was extended to metal scrap from unregistered suppliers in October 2024, the tax treatment of a load depends on who the seller is, which pushed thousands of small dealers towards registration and many others further out of sight.

Utthan's exposure runs outward too. Three of its fifteen EPR clients are multinationals whose disclosures are prepared and audited in Europe, to a standard with nothing to do with Indian practice; a two-person desk in London serves them. And the competition for a collector's loyalty is not another app. It is the aggregator two lanes away who has advanced him ₹40,000 against next month's load.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

In February 2026 Utthan launched Sauda, a self-serve Android app that let a seller post a lot, see a live price and be paid within twenty-four hours of weighment. The business case rested on the Naresh card: a cash-preferring, WhatsApp-fluent collector who, given a fair price and a receipt, would stop depending on the aggregator's float. Growth bought installs against that profile.

Exhibit 3 shows what the funnel did. Of 38,400 installs, 9,600 completed verification, 25.0 per cent. Of those, 6,048 posted a first lot, 63.0 per cent of verified accounts; 3,024 completed a first trade, 50.0 per cent of those who posted; and 1,361 traded again within ninety days, 45.0 per cent of first traders and 3.5 per cent of installs.

Through the spring the team read the drop-off as a usability problem and rebuilt the screens twice. In June, Hiral Vazirani spent eleven days in yards in Indore, Jaipur and Erode and came back with a different reading: most of the men using the app were not sellers. They were employees — weighbridge clerks and yard supervisors — posting lots on an owner's instruction, with no authority over price. The independent collector with a cart was there in small numbers and almost never twice.

In September, Shreyas Vellanki, who leads data science from Chennai, cut the quarter by operating model rather than by person. Of the 6,300 active seller accounts in Exhibit 1, route collectors were 4,100, or 65.1 per cent of accounts, but delivered only 17.2 per cent of the ₹20,010 lakh of gross merchandise value. Yard aggregators, 21.4 per cent of accounts, delivered 47.2 per cent; the 230 processor-linked traders, 3.7 per cent of accounts, delivered 20.7 per cent.

Exhibit 2 is the cut the Series B deck had used. By age band, the repeat rate runs from 41.27 to 41.82 per cent; by city tier, from 41.40 to 42.01 per cent. By operating model it runs from 30.0 to 86.1 per cent. The attributes on the card separated almost nothing; the attribute nobody had written down separated almost everything.

Two further things turned out to be wrong. The "registered collector base" in the contract annexure counts accounts ever onboarded since 2019, never deduplicated against PAN or phone. And the three retention figures in Exhibit 5 were produced by three teams over three windows and cannot be reconciled, though all three sit in the same board pack.

5. The people

Dhanashree Vispute, vice-president of product, Indore. Owns Monday's recommendation. Position: the persona model is the root problem, not the app. Incentive: her roadmap is judged on shipped features, and research ships nothing. Unsaid: she wrote the second Naresh card herself, in 2025, and made it warmer.

Sohail Vakharia, co-founder and chief executive, Indore. Grew up in the trade. Position: "we know these people, we do not need a study to meet them." Incentive: the Series B narrative is his, and the collector story is what distinguishes Utthan from an auction site. Unsaid: he thinks the Annexure C number soft, and has told neither client nor board.

Arundhati Veeraraghavan, head of growth, Bengaluru. Built the three cards in 2024 under roadshow deadline. Position: the cards work — cost per verified account fell by a third once creative was aligned to them. Incentive: she is measured on verified accounts and cost per acquisition, which look best when the cheapest audience is the target. Unsaid: verified and trading accounts have drifted apart, and the gap is in her dashboard, not her slide.

Indrajit Vadnere, head of field operations, Jaipur. Eighty-one officers onboard, inspect and chase payments for him. Position: personas are a poster; his officers know every yard owner. Incentive: his budget scales with accounts onboarded, so he resists anything that cuts field headcount. Unsaid: four in five accounts his team books trade through an officer, not the app, and he would rather that were not measured.

Hiral Vazirani, principal designer, Ahmedabad. Position: the unit of design is the situation — a load, a dispute, a payment that has not landed — not the person; a persona should carry goals, attitudes to risk and credit, and observed behaviour, with demographics deleted unless they change something. Incentive: her credibility rests on the June field work. Unsaid: of the thirty-one people she interviewed only four were independent collectors, so the sample is thinnest where her argument is strongest.

Shreyas Vellanki, data science lead, Chennai. Position: segment on behaviour and value; let behaviour define the person. Incentive: his roadmap is the clustering project in Option C. Unsaid: the event data cannot tell an owner from an employee on the owner's login, so his clusters describe logins.

Rehana Valecha, director of brand partnerships, London. Owns the multinational EPR accounts, including the largest. Position: whatever the team does internally, the external story must keep its collectors. Incentive: renewal is March 2028, but the client's audit is early February 2027. Unsaid: that client has begun asking for collector-level traceability Utthan cannot produce.

Salil Vyawahare, head of the processor network, Coimbatore. Position: the product points at the wrong end of the chain; the mills' purchase managers are 230 accounts and a fifth of value, and nobody has written a persona for them. Incentive: his line is the take on completed trades. Unsaid: two large processors have asked for a direct feed that would bypass matching entirely.

7. Voices

"Take the card down if you like. My officers will onboard the same people tomorrow anyway."

— Indrajit Vadnere, operations review, 28 October 2026

"Cost per verified account is down thirty-three per cent since we aligned creative to Naresh. I will not apologise for a card that works. If the trading rate is bad, that is a product problem."

— Arundhati Veeraraghavan, growth review, 2 November 2026

"Two hours with a man in Erode. A goal: close the day owing the aggregator nothing. An attitude: a receipt is a summons unless the money is in hand. A behaviour: he takes four per cent less for cash at four o'clock. None of it is on the card, and all of it decides whether he uses us."

— Hiral Vazirani, written note to Dhanashree, 9 November 2026

"My clusters are built on logins. If Ramesh's clerk posts the lot, my model has learned the clerk. I can tell you what a login does, not whose hands it is."

— Shreyas Vellanki, chat thread, 10 November 2026

"Please do not change the word 'collector' in anything customer-facing before February. Their audit reads our language literally."

— Rehana Valecha, email from London, 11 November 2026

"Nobody here has written down what a mill's purchase manager wants. He decides whether we have a business in Tamil Nadu next year."

— Salil Vyawahare, same thread, 11 November 2026

"Three cards raised ₹210 crore. Thirty will raise nothing. Tell me what you want to do differently on Monday, not what you want to understand."

— Sohail Vakharia, to Dhanashree, 13 November 2026

8. The options as Dhanashree frames them

Option A — rewrite the three cards. Keep the count and the names; replace the demographic lines with a goal, an attitude to credit and risk, and two observed behaviours each. ₹1.3 lakh, three weeks. It preserves the shared language — and the assumption that three is the right number and a person the right unit.

Option B — the field study. Thirty-six sites across the four operating models, sampled by value rather than headcount, with the aggregator's clerk and the mill's purchase manager in scope. ₹17.5 lakh, reporting 26 February 2027. The only option that can tell an owner from an employee — but it lands after the client audit, and Exhibit 4 shows it will not fit beside C.

Option C — instrument and cluster. Rebuild the event layer, ingest weighbridge data from four processors, cluster, validate by phone. ₹21.2 lakh, reporting 19 March 2027. Scale, and a model that updates itself, but Shreyas has said what it will learn: logins. Linking weighbridge records to identified individuals also brings the Digital Personal Data Protection Act into scope, and that consent language does not exist.

Dhanashree has written the three options on a page with a fourth line she keeps crossing out: do none of these; change what the cards are used for. Nothing in Exhibits 1 to 3 says the company needs better personas. They say it has been using a person-shaped object to answer questions about value, authority and situation. A card that described Naresh perfectly would still say nothing about Salil's purchase manager, and would still not settle the argument between Arundhati's cost per account and Indrajit's headcount, because those two are not disagreeing about who the customer is.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The board meets at nine on Monday, 16 November 2026. The H2 plan locks that day; anything unfunded waits for April. The ₹24 lakh discovery budget is the only unspent line Dhanashree controls. Cash is ₹96 crore against a burn of ₹4.2 crore a month, about twenty-three months of runway — so nothing here is existential, and nothing will be extended on compassionate grounds either.

Three hard edges. Annexure C runs to March 2028 and specifies not fewer than 60,000 registered collectors; the audit is early in February 2027, and Exhibit 6 puts Client 1 at 38.0 per cent of a service line that is 69.6 per cent of quarterly revenue. Lalita Vaswani, the partner at the fund that led the Series B, sits as board observer and wrote the market slide the collector count came from; reopening the segmentation reopens the model under it. And the DPDP consent framework Option C needs is undrafted, with counsel contracted two days a month.

And a soft edge that may matter more: Hiral has twice said in writing that she cannot design against the current cards, and designers who say it twice usually say it a third time elsewhere.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Take each attribute on the Naresh card in turn: what decision could it change, and what evidence here says it does or does not separate behaviour?
  2. Exhibits 1 and 2 describe the same 6,300 accounts. Why does one show a 56-point spread in repeat rate and the other less than one point, and what does that say about how the three personas were constructed?
  3. Exhibits 1 and 3 cannot be reconciled, and Exhibit 5 holds three retention figures that contradict one another in effect if not in arithmetic. Which would you take to the board, and what would you say about those you leave out?
  4. Cost per verified account fell by a third under the current cards and the trading rate did not move. Is that a success of the persona, a failure of it, or two teams optimising different things? What would you measure instead?
  5. Utthan's revenue comes from brand owners buying evidence; its product is built for sellers supplying material. Should a persona set follow the money, the material or the screen? Who is Utthan's customer?
  6. It is Monday morning and Dhanashree has ten minutes before the board. What does she recommend, what does the ₹24 lakh buy, what does she say about Annexure C, and what happens to the three cards on the wall before February?

At a quarter past ten she pulled the middle card off the wall, held it, and put it back. A field officer had taken the photograph in a yard in Dewas in 2024; nobody had asked the man what he did for a living. She turned off the light with the three cards still hanging, and drove home with the board pack unopened beside her.
exp20v2-cust.persona.anatomy:
Anatomy of a persona

What a persona must contain to be useful, and what makes it a stereotype

1. The persona on the wall

On Monday 6 July 2026, Devika Pradhan, head of product at Dehari Earnings Labs in Indore, taped a laminated A3 sheet to the glass wall of the team's meeting room. It showed a smiling young man on a motorcycle in a delivery jacket. Beneath the photograph ran a caption: "Ravi, 28, gig rider, Class 12 pass, earns about ₹24,000 a month, uses WhatsApp, wants to save."

Dehari makes a phone app that lets people paid by the day or by the delivery, such as riders, drivers and warehouse loaders, record their earnings and keep a running view of the month. By June 2026 it had 48,000 monthly active users. The team was now deciding whether to spend ₹1.2 crore building a "weekly buffer", a feature that holds back a slice of good days' earnings and releases it on lean days. The decision was due on Friday 17 July. Dilip Narula, the finance lead, wanted one number to defend: how many users would adopt it?

Devika's unease began with a small thing. Her researcher, Damayanti Rao, who works from Coimbatore, had just finished 24 interviews with Dehari users and kept saying that Ravi "does not exist". Nobody in her notes matched him. Some users earned far more than ₹24,000 and spent it anxiously; some earned less and spent it calmly. If the team built for Ravi and Ravi was an average rather than a person, the ₹1.2 crore would be spent serving someone who was nowhere in the user base.

2. The idea

A persona is a described, named, fictional-but-evidence-based person who stands for a group of real users, written so that a team can predict what that group would do with a product decision. The ingredients that make this predictive are three: goals (what the person is trying to achieve, in their own terms), attitudes (what they believe, fear and trade off) and behaviours (what they observably do, including workarounds). Age, city and device are context; they are not the anatomy.

The device was invented to solve a specific failure. In the late 1980s and 1990s, the software designer Alan Cooper found that teams argued about "the user" as if there were one, and that each person pictured a different one, usually themselves. Cooper began using concrete archetypes and popularised the method in his late-1990s book on why software is hard to use. A named person ends the argument about whose imagined user is correct, because the description is written down, checked against research and shared.

The sentence Devika could say in a meeting without sounding glib was this: "A persona is a prediction about behaviour, and we should keep only the details that change what we build." The test of any line on the sheet is whether removing it would alter a decision. Ravi's photograph passes no such test.

3. How it actually works

Figure 1 shows the anatomy as layers. The outer ring, context, is what a team can write from a spreadsheet or a stock photograph, and it is what Ravi's sheet consisted of. The inner rings need research. Goals are found by asking what the person was trying to get done, never what features they want. Attitudes are found by listening for trade-offs. Behaviours are found by watching or reading logs, because people misreport what they do.

The steps run in a fixed order, and practitioners often leave the middle ones implicit. First, state the decision the persona will serve, since this fixes which behaviours matter. Second, gather evidence about goals, attitudes and behaviours from interviews and logs. Third, cluster people by those inner layers, not by demographics. Fourth, and the step usually skipped, check that each cluster is distinct on the decision: do its members behave differently from other clusters in a way that changes what you would build? Fifth, size each cluster. Only then write the named description, keeping the details that earned a place and leaving out the rest.

Damayanti applied this to Dehari. She and her analyst, Dhanraj Menon in Bhubaneswar, ran the clustering on three months of logs: how often users logged earnings, how erratic their weekly income was, and what they did on a lean day. Her interviews supplied the reasons behind each cluster. Table 1 gives the result.

4. A worked example

Table 1. Dehari's 48,000 monthly active users by behavioural cluster, June 2026. Adoption is the share of each cluster that would take the weekly buffer, estimated from the 24 interviews plus a smoke-test sign-up button.
ClusterUsersShare of baseAvg monthly income (₹)Buffer adoptionAdopters
Smoothers: keep a fixed daily spend regardless of earnings14,40030%22,00040%5,760
Chasers: work longer hours when money is short19,20040%30,00010%1,920
Planners: set aside money for a named goal9,60020%18,00025%2,400
Drifters: log earnings rarely, spend as it comes4,80010%20,0005%240
Total / weighted average48,000100%24,20021.5%10,320

Read the table line by line. The weighted average income is the sum of users times income, divided by 48,000: (14,400 × 22,000) + (19,200 × 30,000) + (9,600 × 18,000) + (4,800 × 20,000) comes to ₹1,16,16,00,000 (₹116.16 crore), and dividing by 48,000 gives ₹24,200. Ravi's ₹24,000 was therefore a sound average. It was also a description of nobody: no cluster is closer than ₹2,200 to the ₹24,200 weighted average, and the largest cluster earns ₹30,000. The same trap appears in adoption. Adopters sum to 10,320, so the blended rate is 10,320 divided by 48,000, or 21.5 per cent, yet no cluster has a rate near that figure. Smoothers are at 40 per cent, Chasers at 10.

The money follows. Suppose Dehari charges ₹600 a year for the buffer. At 10,320 adopters it earns 10,320 × 600 = ₹61,92,000, which is ₹61.92 lakh a year, against a build cost of ₹1.2 crore, or ₹120 lakh. Simple payback is about two years, and every figure rests on who is in the base.

Second pass: change one input. Suppose a ride-hailing partnership brings 12,000 new users, all of them Chasers. The base becomes 60,000; Chasers become 31,200, or 52 per cent. Adopters rise by 10 per cent of 12,000, which is 1,200, to 11,520, and the blended rate falls to 11,520 divided by 60,000, or 19.2 per cent. A forecast built from Ravi's 21.5 per cent would predict 12,900 adopters, an overstatement of 1,380 users, or 1,380 × 600 = ₹8,28,000 (₹8.28 lakh). A persona is a claim about a mix, and the mix moves.

5. The nuances

Anatomy versus demographics

Demographics describe who a person is; the anatomy describes why they act. Two 28-year-old riders in Indore, one a Smoother and one a Chaser, share every demographic detail and want different products. Include a demographic only if you can show it predicts the behaviour.

Persona versus segment

A segment is a countable group, defined by a rule, that can be sized and targeted. A persona is the narrative that makes the group's logic memorable. Table 1 is the segment view; Ravi, rewritten, will be the persona view.

Persona versus average

The ₹24,200 earner and the 21.5 per cent adopter are averages. An average blends clusters that behave in opposite ways and can describe no one. The anatomy exists to keep the clusters apart, so check any persona by asking whether its facts are the mean of several people.

Persona versus jobs-to-be-done

A job to be done is the progress a person is trying to make in a given circumstance, whoever they are. A persona describes the person; the job describes the situation. They complement each other: the job explains why Smoothers want a buffer, and the persona explains how they will go about getting one.

One persona, one decision

A persona is built to serve a decision, so one built for pricing may be unhelpful for onboarding.

Evidence has a half-life

A persona carries a date and a sample size. The 24 interviews behind Table 1 are enough to find clusters and too few to size them, which is why the logs matter.

What a persona cannot tell you

It cannot say how many people exist in the cluster, how much they will pay, or whether your solution will work. It tells you what to test. Adoption of 40 per cent among Smoothers came from a smoke test, which measures intent, and intent runs ahead of behaviour.

Questions to ask before relying on one

How many people produced it? Which of its details came from observation and which from imagination? Does each cluster differ on the decision? When was it last checked against behaviour? If nobody can answer, treat it as a hypothesis.

6. How it looks in different products

Table 2. How the anatomy shifts with product type and company stage.
SettingWhat the persona must captureTypical trap
Consumer (Dehari)Personal goals and emotional trade-offs; one person is both buyer and userWriting a lifestyle collage, not a behaviour
B2BSeparate personas for buyer, daily user and approver, each with different goals and attitudes toward riskModelling only the champion who answers your calls
MarketplaceAt least two sides, and the tension between them: what delights a supplier may annoy a buyerBuilding for one side and starving the other
Early-stage companyTwo or three personas from a dozen interviews, held as hypothesesTreating them as proven
Large companyLogs, surveys and interviews triangulated, with owners and revision datesA forty-page library that no one opens

Table 2 compresses the difference: B2B personas arrive as linked sets, marketplace personas in opposed pairs, and the early-stage firm cannot size anything and should say so, while a large firm can size every cluster from its logs and risks personas that are never retired.

7. Common mistakes

The stock-photo persona. From outside you see a named face, a hobby list and a favourite brand, but no sentence of the form "when X happens, she does Y". The misunderstanding is that vividness equals accuracy. The cheapest diagnostic: strike every line that could not change a decision. If a third survives, the rest was decoration.

The average persona. Symptom: the persona's numbers come out as tidy means and the forecast built on them is wrong whenever the mix shifts, as in the 19.2 per cent case. The misunderstanding is treating the middle of a distribution as a person. Diagnostic: ask for the spread, and ask who sits at each end.

The kitchen-sink library. Symptom: fourteen personas, and in review meetings each team cites a different one. The misunderstanding is that completeness is a virtue. Diagnostic: ask each team which two personas matter now; differing answers mean no shared map.

The persona with no research. Symptom: nobody can say who was interviewed. The misunderstanding is that a workshop of colleagues is evidence. Diagnostic: ask for three verbatim quotes and the date of the interview behind each.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Devika's wall carries four short sheets, one per cluster, each dated and each marked with its share of the base. Under "Meena the Smoother" sits a goal in her own words ("I do not want to ask my brother for money in the last week of the month"), an attitude (distrust of locked savings, because a relative once lost access to funds), and a behaviour (she fixes her daily spending at about ₹700 and lets the balance swing). Beneath that stands one line of decision relevance: the buffer must release money without a request or a delay, or Smoothers will not trust it.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

On Friday 17 July, Devika retired Ravi and brought Table 1 to the review. She did not approve the full ₹1.2 crore. She recommended a first release that serves Smoothers, who are 14,400 users and 5,760 of the expected adopters, plus a design test for Planners, and a decision on Chasers only after the ride-hailing partnership showed how that cluster actually behaved. The reasoning was plain: the likeliest adopters were Smoothers, and the largest cluster was among the least likely. Dilip took 10,320 as his base case and 19.2 per cent as the downside.

The natural next steps are building personas from research, which covers how to run the interviews and coding that feed the inner rings, and empathy maps, a one-page tool for recording what a user says, thinks, does and feels, which helps a team hold the attitudes layer in view.

Two questions to sit with. First, if a persona's best-supported detail came from the users who respond most readily to interviews, whom has it quietly excluded, and how would you find out? Second, if the mix of your user base shifted tomorrow, which line on your own team's persona would stop being true first?
case20v1-cust.segments:
Chulha Labs: Who Cooks, and How

A decision case on market segments and personas

1. Opening

On Monday, 19 October 2026, Ila Mandlik sat in the glass-walled meeting room on the fourth floor of Chulha Labs' Pune office, with a laptop and a printed spreadsheet. As Chief Product Officer she had until Friday, 30 October, to put one plan in front of the board. That plan would fix how the company spent its ₹3.6 crore acquisition budget for October to December and what its fourteen-engineer core squad built. Diwali fell on Sunday, 8 November, and the campaign brief was due the Monday after the board meeting.

For three years the company had described its customer as "an urban working woman, 25 to 40". The spreadsheet in front of her suggested it described who the users were without saying much about what they did.

2. Company background

Chulha Labs was founded in Pune in 2021 by Irfan Majumdar and two engineers. Its app helps Indian households decide what to cook on weekday evenings. It suggests a plan, builds a shopping list and sends it with one tap to a quick-commerce partner such as Zepto or Swiggy Instamart. The base app is free; Chulha Plus costs ₹149 a month and unlocks weekly planning, nutrition filters and a pantry tracker.

By October 2026 the app had 12,00,000 monthly active users and 1,80,000 paying subscribers, which is 15.0 per cent of monthly actives. At ₹149 a month, subscriptions brought in ₹268.2 lakh a month, about ₹32.18 crore a year. It competes for attention with YouTube recipe creators on one side and the food features inside Swiggy and Zomato on the other; none sits at the moment between "what shall we eat tonight" and "what do I need to buy".

3. The situation

Growth had been paid for with the segment. The company bought installs on Instagram and YouTube, targeting women aged 25 to 40 in the largest metros, at an average ₹180 per install. Exhibit 1 cuts the user base the way the company always had: by gender, age and city tier. Women 25 to 40 in metros were 7,44,000 of the 12,00,000 actives, or 62 per cent.

But look at the conversion column. It ran from 13.9 to 16.0 per cent across the four segments, against a company-wide 15.0 per cent. The segment that received nearly all the marketing money converted at almost exactly the average. Age, gender and city told the company almost nothing about who would pay.

In August, Ila asked the data team to ignore demographics and cluster users by their 90-day behaviour: when they opened the app, whether they planned ahead, how often they ordered groceries, and whom they cooked for. Four groups emerged,; the team checked them against twenty-two customer interviews in Pune, Nagpur, Jaipur and Hyderabad. The Planner opens the app on Sunday evening and plans five dinners at once. The Rescuer opens it at about 6:30 pm on the day, tired, asking what can be made from what is already at home. The Feeder cooks for someone else's needs, such as a child's school tiffin or a parent's low-salt diet, and uses the app mainly for filters. The Browser reads recipes but rarely cooks.

Exhibit 2 shows how sharply these groups differ. Planners were 25 per cent of actives, and 40.0 per cent of them subscribed, so they supplied 1,20,000 of the 1,80,000 subscribers, two-thirds of the paying base. Rescuers were the largest group at 5,40,000, yet only 5.0 per cent subscribed. Exhibit 3 sets the two cuts side by side: 40.0, 13.8, 5.0 and 0.0 per cent for Planners, Feeders, Rescuers and Browsers, against 13.9 to 16.0 per cent for the demographic segments.

Were personas just demographics in disguise? Exhibit 4 answers. Every segment contained all four personas in broadly similar proportions: in the largest, 25.5 per cent were Planners and 44.4 per cent Rescuers. The persona cut across the segments.

One more fact framed the choice. From 7 September to 4 October, four weeks, the growth team spent ₹20 lakh on a pilot targeting behavioural look-alikes of Planners instead of demographics. It bought about 6,900 installs at roughly ₹290 each; 48 per cent of them, or 3,312, behaved like Planners in their first fortnight.

4. The people

Inderjit Matharu, head of growth, in Gurugram, owns the ₹3.6 crore budget. His case: the segment is large, measurable on every ad platform and has delivered for three years. He distrusts a behavioural audience that costs more per install.

Isabel Marques, design lead, in Lisbon, ran the interviews. She wants the product redesigned around the Planner and the Rescuer, who need opposite screens.

Imtiaz Mirza, data scientist, in Kuala Lumpur, built the clustering. He cautions that personas were fitted on past behaviour, so a new install has no history and the app cannot yet tell on day one which persona a user is.

Irfan wants a plan explainable in a sentence that protects the ₹32.18 crore run-rate.

5. The options

Option A: continue segment-led growth. Spend the full ₹3.6 crore on women 25 to 40 in metros at ₹180 an install, which buys 2,00,000 installs. At the base's 15.0 per cent conversion, that is 30,000 new subscribers, or ₹44.7 lakh a month, at ₹1,200 per subscriber (₹3.6 crore ÷ 30,000). The upside is predictability; the cost is that the app serves every user the same way, and nearly half of each cohort will be Rescuers who rarely pay.

Option B: persona-targeted acquisition. Spend the same budget on Planner look-alikes. Applying the base's conversion rates to the pilot (40.0 per cent for Planners, and 60,000 ÷ 9,00,000 = 6.7 per cent for everyone else) gives about 1,564 subscribers on ₹20 lakh, or ₹1,279 each. Scaled to ₹3.6 crore, that is about 28,000 subscribers and ₹41.9 lakh a month. The upside is a better-fitting audience; the cost is that it is dearer per subscriber than Option A.

Option C: persona-led product. Move the squad to the Rescuer: a "cook from what's at home" screen, and a one-question onboarding ("How do you usually decide dinner?") that routes each newcomer to the Planner or the Rescuer experience. The squad costs about ₹1.34 crore for the quarter (14 engineers at ₹3.2 lakh a month loaded cost, for three months). If Rescuer conversion rose from 5.0 to 8.0 per cent on 5,40,000 actives, subscribers would rise by 16,200, worth ₹24.14 lakh a month, or about ₹2.90 crore a year. The cost is that the gain is a hypothesis and arrives after the festival.

6. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibits 1 and 4, why could "urban working woman, 25 to 40" not predict who would subscribe?

2. What does each persona in Exhibit 2 need, and which need does the app serve least?

3. Compare the options on cost, payback and quality of evidence. Which figures are measured, and which assumed?

4. Which option would you take to the board, and what happens to the unspent budget?

7. A note for the learner

The topic frames the decision as a question: am I describing who my users are, or how they behave, and which matters for design? A segment describes who the customer is, and is useful for buying media because platforms sell audiences that way. A persona models behaviour and attitude, and is useful for design, because screens respond to what people do, not to their age. Exhibit 1 shows a segment that is large but silent on willingness to pay. Exhibits 2 and 4 show behaviours that differ eight-fold in conversion (40.0 versus 5.0 per cent) and that sit evenly across every segment.

A well-reasoned answer therefore does not discard segments. It uses them for what they are good at, which is reaching people, and uses personas for what they are good at, which is deciding what to build. It also respects the evidence limits: personas were fitted retrospectively, and the Rescuer lift is an assumption.

One defensible path is Option C, staged. Build the onboarding and the Rescuer screen first; they attack the largest, weakest group. Hold the ₹3.6 crore rather than spending it all before Diwali, which would pour Rescuers, 45 per cent of a typical cohort, into a product not yet built for them. Release a first tranche of segment-led spend only if early Rescuer conversion shows a lift, and keep Option B as a small continuing experiment to learn whether the persona audience holds up. The sentence for Irfan: keep buying reach by segment, but build by behaviour. The main risk is delay.
exp20v2-cust.segments:
Market segments vs personas

Discovery & Design, Customer Modelling: who your users are, and how they behave

1. A roadmap that fits nobody

On Tuesday, 6 January 2026, Meenal Ghorpade, head of product at Lagan Tutoring Labs in Pune, had until Friday 9 January to submit the first-half roadmap. Lagan sells a mobile revision app to Class 9 to 12 students preparing for CBSE and state-board examinations. It had 1,20,000 monthly active learners, of whom 13,920 paid for a subscription averaging ₹4,800 a year. The board examinations began in mid-February.

The chief executive, Mahesh Kulthe, wanted one flagship feature and a clear answer to a simple question: for whom is it built? Kunal Lonkar, the head of growth, proposed the usual answer: Lagan's reports divided users by city tier and class, as advertising platforms sold audiences. "Metro Class 11 and 12 pays best, at 15 per cent," he said. "Build for them."

Meenal hesitated. Two months earlier, Leela Karmarkar, Lagan's user researcher, had watched a fortnight of session recordings and observed that a Class 11 student in Mumbai and one in Nashik sometimes behaved identically, while two Class 11 students in the same Mumbai building might use the product in opposite ways. Marta Lindqvist, a data scientist working remotely from Stockholm, had since clustered the usage logs and found four stable patterns of behaviour that cut across every city tier. Building for a demographic cell meant designing for an average student who did not exist; building for a behaviour meant defending the neglect of the categories the company spoke in.

2. The idea

A market segment is a group of existing or potential customers defined by shared attributes that can be observed from outside and used to find them: age, class, city, income, industry, company size. Wendell Smith, writing in the Journal of Marketing in 1956, introduced the idea to solve a specific problem. Mass markets were fragmenting, and a single product and message served no one well, so firms needed a way to divide demand into groups they could reach and size. Segments answer "who is out there, how many, and how do I reach them?"

A persona is a concrete, archetypal portrait of a group of users defined by what they are trying to do, how they go about it and what they believe, not by who they are on a census form. Alan Cooper, a software designer, developed the practice in the 1990s and popularised it in his 1999 book The Inmates Are Running the Asylum. His problem was that engineering teams built for an abstract "user" and, in practice, for themselves; a named archetype gave them something specific to argue with. Personas answer a different question: "what is this person trying to get done, and what will they do when we put a feature in front of them?"

Meenal's sentence for the meeting: a segment tells us where to find people; a persona tells us what to build for them once we have.

The two are not rivals; the common failure is to use one where the other is needed. A segment is defined by attributes you can query from a database or buy as an audience. A persona is defined by behaviour and attitude, which you must infer from observation. Behaviour is often correlated with the attribute, which tempts teams to treat the two as one thing.

3. How it works, step by step

The mechanics run in a fixed order. First, name the decision, because the lens follows from it: where to spend advertising money needs a segment; what the product should do needs a persona. Second, build segments cheaply: cross two or three attributes already in the database and count. Third, check whether segments differ in the outcome that matters, here paid conversion. Fourth, and the step practitioners usually leave implicit, ask whether people inside a segment behave alike. If they do, the segment is a good design target; if not, it is a sampling frame, not a description.

Fifth, build the personas. Leela interviewed 22 students and parents, Marta clustered 90 days of usage on session timing, content type and feature use, and the two sets of evidence were reconciled. Sixth, size the personas by assigning every user to the nearest one. Seventh, check how personas map onto segments. That shows whether a demographic cell is a reasonable proxy for a behaviour.

4. A worked example

Exhibit 2 is Lagan's segment view; paid rate is paid divided by users.

Exhibit 3 is the persona view of the same users. Marta found four patterns: Night Sprinter, who studies in bursts before an examination; the Steady Planner, who follows a daily schedule; the Doubt Hunter, who opens the app to get questions answered; and the Parent-Led learner, whose parent bought and monitors the subscription.

The same 13,920 payers appear in both tables; only the grouping differs. Persona rates range from 6 to 22 per cent (16 points); segment rates from 9 to 15 (6 points). Behaviour separates payers from non-payers far more sharply than geography and class do. Marta's cross-tabulation also showed Steady Planners at exactly 25 per cent of every segment cell: 7,000 of 28,000, 7,500 of 30,000, 8,500 of 34,000 and 7,000 of 28,000, which total 30,000. On the first pass Option B nets ₹22.32 lakh against ₹10.80 lakh, roughly twice as much, because the behaviour group is larger. In the second pass one input changes: Marta observes that Night Sprinters buy a short pass, not an annual plan, so revenue per added payer falls to ₹3,000. Option B now nets ₹7.20 lakh and Option A wins. Personas did not lose; the persona told Meenal which input to interrogate, which a segment would never have prompted.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Attributes are not behaviours

Class and city are known without asking; behaviour must be observed, which costs more. Treating the cheap evidence as a stand-in for the costly one is the original error of this topic.

Correlation can make a segment a good proxy

Sometimes a segment is a persona. Where practitioners in one industry share a workflow, the attribute predicts the behaviour well enough. Test it with the step-seven cross-check.

Personas are models, not people

A persona is a deliberate simplification. Real students blend patterns, switching from Steady Planner to Night Sprinter in the last month. Write each with a claim data could contradict.

Segments need reach, personas need access

You can buy a segment on an advertising platform; you cannot buy a persona. Marketing needs a bridge, such as a signup question, to recognise members.

Demographic personas are the usual counterfeit

A "persona" called "Priya, 16, Class 11, Pune, likes cricket" is a segment with a photograph. If you cannot say what Priya does at 11 pm, it is not a persona.

Statistical clusters are not automatically personas

Marta's clustering found groups; Leela's interviews supplied the reasons. A cluster with no explanation may not survive the next dataset.

Neither tells you causes or the future

Both describe the present. Neither shows a feature will move a group, so the 2-point lifts above are hypotheses to pilot.

Questions before relying on either

What decision does this serve? Who is absent from the sample, such as students who churned in week one? How stable is it from one season to the next?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products, early and late

In consumer products like Lagan, attributes are shallow and behaviour varies enormously, so personas differentiate. In B2B products the weight shifts. A segment such as mid-sized Indian manufacturers, as Zoho or Freshworks might define one by employee count and industry, carries real information about compliance, integrations and buying process, so it often is close to a persona.Inside one account a finance approver and a plant supervisor are different personas with conflicting goals. In marketplaces such as Flipkart or Urban Company, each side has its own segments and personas, and they interact, so a persona on one side changes the value to the other.

Scale changes the work. An early-stage company with 2,000 users cannot cluster usage logs; it should interview ten people and treat one or two provisional personas as hypotheses. A large company has data but a political problem: segments are embedded in budgets and targets, and a persona that crosses segments threatens someone's number. At Lagan the persona view had to be translated into segment language before it could be used.

7. Common mistakes

The photograph persona

Symptom: slides of smiling faces with age, city and hobbies. Misunderstanding: demographic detail feels like understanding. Diagnostic: ask what this persona would do differently from the next when shown the same screen; if only "they are older," it is a segment.

Designing for the biggest cell

Symptom: the roadmap tracks segment size. Misunderstanding: size of audience equals size of opportunity. Diagnostic: compare the paid-rate range across personas with the range across segments, as in Exhibit 4. If the persona range is wider, behaviour is what you should be pricing.

Too many personas

Symptom: nine archetypes, no priorities. Diagnostic: ask whether any decision would change if two personas were merged. If none, merge them.

Personas never revisited

Symptom: the same document is used for three years. Misunderstanding: behaviour is as stable as demography. Diagnostic: re-run the cross-tab each season and check whether the shares in Exhibit 3 have moved.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Meenal states the decision first. She uses segments to size and reach, and personas to choose the design. She puts both tables on one page and shows that Planners are 25 per cent of every cell, so segment is not a proxy. She marks each lift as a hypothesis, asks for a pilot, and interrogates revenue per payer for each persona instead of assuming the average. Finally she writes a bridge, a signup question and a seven-day usage signal that tag a new user with a likely persona, so growth can act on what design learned. Kunal's segment reports remain, now with a defined purpose.

9. Closing

Meenal presented both exhibits on Thursday 8 January. She recommended a four-week pilot of the countdown pack on a sample of Night Sprinters, with revenue per payer measured and not assumed, while the metro revision planner stayed as the fallback if sprinter revenue per payer proved close to ₹3,000. Mahesh approved the pilot. Her reasoning: Option B's first-pass advantage rested on an unmeasured number, and a cheap pilot would turn a disagreement about demographics into evidence about behaviour.

Next, study statistical segmentation, the method for finding clusters like Marta's, and then jobs-to-be-done, which asks what progress a person is trying to make. Buyer, user, influencer and blocker follows for B2B settings.

Two questions to sit with. First, think of your own product and write one persona claim that data could disprove; what would you need to observe to discard it? Second, if you could keep only the segment table or the persona table for your next roadmap decision, which would you keep, and what would that choice cost you?
exp40v2-cust.segments:
Market segments vs personas

Discovery & Design › Customer Modelling. Which cut carries the information you need, and how to tell from data you already hold.

1. Two decisions, one week in January

On Monday 12 January 2026, Nupur Palnitkar, vice-president of product at Prastaav Procurement Systems in Bengaluru, had eighteen days before the board met on Friday 30 January to approve the FY27 go-to-market plan. Prastaav sells spend-management software to mid-market Indian manufacturers: 1,180 paying accounts, ₹49.10 crore of annual recurring revenue, and a book in which 1,029 of the 1,180 accounts due that year renewed — 87.2 per cent.

Parimal Nautiyal, who ran sales, wanted the plan in the only language his territory maps spoke: engineering and capital-goods accounts carried ₹5.60 lakh of ARR each and pharmaceuticals ₹5.00 lakh against ₹3.10 lakh in textiles, so hire into the first two and exit the third. Omana Nipani, in revenue operations, had classified every account by who inside it actually drove adoption, and in that view the renewal spread was not four points wide but twenty-three. Nupur's problem was not which lens was true. Both were. Quotas are set in Parimal's language; product decisions in Omana's.

On Wednesday 14 January, Prachi Nadgauda, head of product at Naadi Health Works in Ahmedabad, met the same fault line in hardware. Naadi sells an upper-arm blood-pressure monitor at ₹2,790 with an app and an optional ₹1,490-a-year service, Naadi Plus; in the year to 31 March 2026 it sold 1,96,000 monitors and booked ₹55.73 crore. Nihar Ozarkar, the founder, wanted a Senior Care edition for buyers aged 65 and over — 23,520 of the 1,96,000 devices, or 12.0 per cent, and the band with the lowest app pairing. Pradnya Narlikar's November fieldwork in sixty-one homes found that in many the buyer was not the person wearing the cuff.

2. The idea, and the quarrel inside it

A market segment is a group of actual or potential customers defined by attributes observable from outside and usable to find them: age, income, city, industry, employee count. Wendell Smith named the practice in the Journal of Marketing in 1956 to solve a production problem — mass markets were fragmenting and one offer served nobody well. Segments answer who is out there, how many, and how to reach them.

A persona is a concrete archetype of a user defined by behaviour, goal and belief rather than attribute. Alan Cooper developed it in the early 1990s and published it in The Inmates Are Running the Asylum (1999) against a different problem: teams designing for an abstract user and, in practice, for themselves. A persona answers what this person wants to accomplish and what they will do with a feature.

The traditions were never in dialogue. Marketing had moved towards behaviour without Cooper — Yankelovich argued in 1964 that non-demographic criteria predicted purchase better than demography, and Haley's benefit segmentation (1968) grouped buyers by benefit sought — while design reached archetypes through ethnography. Hence two vocabularies, and four positions a practitioner can hold.

The reach school signs that a customer model is useful only if you can act on it in a media buy or territory plan, and refuses to fund an unaddressable behavioural type. The design school signs that behaviour determines what the product must do, and refuses a demographic cell as a design target. The jobs school, after Christensen and Ulwick, signs that the unit of analysis is the job, not the person. The mass-marketing school, after Ehrenberg and Sharp, signs that buyers of competing brands look far more alike than segmentation decks imply. A reach-school head of growth and a design-school head of product can both be competent, read one dashboard, and want opposite plans.

3. Mechanics: what the choice of lens actually is

The expert move is to stop asking which lens is better and ask a narrower question: for the outcome variable I care about, which grouping explains more of the variance? That is the technique, and it is testable on data most companies already hold. Oskar Nowicki, a data scientist in Kraków, began with Prastaav's firmographic view, Exhibit 1 — every cell countable from the CRM and reachable.

Exhibit 1. Prastaav, firmographic view, year to 31 March 2026. Accounts and ARR sum exactly; ₹49.10 crore = ₹4,910 lakh. Total-row rates are book averages, not sums: 4,910 / 1,180 = ₹4.16 lakh; 1,029 / 1,180 = 87.2 per cent.

Read together, the exhibits produce a second-order effect neither school states. On price the firmographic lens is better: ARR per account spans ₹2.70 lakh to ₹5.60 lakh across industries, 2.07 times, against ₹3.00 lakh to ₹5.70 lakh, or 1.90 times, across patterns — industry proxies plant count and procurement volume. On retention the behavioural lens is overwhelmingly better: 85.0 to 89.2 per cent across industries, a range of 4.2 points, against 73.3 to 96.1 per cent across patterns, 22.8 points.

Nowicki then took the step teams leave implicit. Renewal is binary per account, so total sum of squares is n p(1 − p) with n = 1,180 and p = 0.8720, and between-group sum of squares is the sum over groups of ng(pg − p)². The ratio, eta-squared, is the share of variance explained. Industry explains 0.2 per cent of renewal variance; adoption pattern 6.4 per cent, thirty-two times as much. Both are small, which is instructive: most of the variance is idiosyncratic. Still, the comparison is a calculation, not a preference.

4. Conditions, stated as claims you can test

One: the attribute predicts the outcome you are optimising. Test it with the decomposition above, once per outcome. At Prastaav it holds for ARR per account and fails for renewal; at Naadi, age predicts whether the app gets paired and not whether anyone pays. One company needs opposite answers in one quarter, which is why "we are a segments company" is incoherent.

Two: within-segment behaviour is homogeneous enough to design for. A segment whose members behave alike is a design target; one whose members do not is a sampling frame. Prastaav's textiles cell fails this test usefully.

Three: the behavioural type is addressable. You can buy a segment on an advertising platform; you cannot buy a persona. Without a bridge — a qualifying question, a first-week usage signal — it acts on design and retention, not acquisition.

Four: the type is stable over the decision's horizon. Demography drifts slowly; behaviour can flip in a quarter. A persona built on 2024 research is an assertion about 2026 until re-measured.

The idea turns actively misleading in two places: when a persona is used to size a market, since personas have no denominators of their own; and when a segment is used as a design brief where buyer and user differ — Naadi's trap, and the one in nearly all B2B.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seam

Exhibit 4 dissolves Parimal's argument without contradicting his data. Textiles looks bad because 95 of its 240 accounts — 39.6 per cent — are Mandate-only, against 10 of 165 in engineering. The firmographic cell is a partial proxy for the behaviour, which is the general case. Note what Nowicki refused to do: estimate textiles ARR by multiplying cell counts by each pattern's average ARR per account. ARR per account varies within a pattern across industries, so the product of the margins is not the joint distribution. From billing, the 95 Mandate-only textile accounts carry ₹209 lakh, ₹2.20 lakh each — below the ₹3.00 lakh pattern average — leaving 145 accounts carrying ₹535 lakh, or ₹3.69 lakh each. Exiting textiles would shed ₹209 lakh of bad revenue by surrendering ₹535 lakh of good.

Two-sided situations break the one-model habit. At Nukta Workforce Exchange, matching blue-collar shifts to sites, Poorva Nimkar's supply-side segments barely overlap her behaviours: 1,840 of 46,000 registered workers — 4.0 per cent — are crew leads who bring five to eight others, and they account for 84,940 of the 2,74,000 shifts filled that quarter, or 31.0 per cent. A crew lead fills 46.2 shifts a quarter against 4.3 for everyone else, and no city-and-trade cell isolates them.

In regulated and hardware categories the seam is physical. Naadi's monitor is a Class B device under India's Medical Device Rules, and its clinical advisor, Njambi Opiyo in Nairobi, must validate claims against a cuff, not an app cohort; regulatory files are written in demographic language because trials are stratified on it. AI-native products add a wrinkle: at Pratibimb Insight Labs, a meeting-notes assistant, model behaviour adapts per user, so the persona is partly a product of the product — the heavy editor and the blind truster diverge further the longer each uses it. Mature companies say they run one customer model; they run two registers with a lossy translation layer. At Prastaav, Omana's patterns had to be re-expressed as industry plans before finance would fund them.

6. Eight distinctions between an expert and a competent practitioner

The lens follows the outcome variable, not the company. The tell is a practitioner who asks "retention or price?" before "segment or persona?" The obvious reading, that behaviour always beats demography, is wrong: firmographics predict willingness to pay.

A segment can be a persona, and the test is cheap. Where attribute and behaviour correlate tightly the attribute wins, being also addressable. The tell is an expert who runs the cross-tab first: Prastaav's "other manufacturing" cell is 44.1 per cent Mandate-only.

Buyer and user differ more often than anyone budgets for. The tell is an expert who asks whose behaviour a segment statistic measures. Naadi's 65-and-over band says whose arm the cuff goes on; the purchase belongs to a daughter in another city.

Personas have no denominators until every user is assigned to one. An unsized persona cannot lose an argument. The tell is an expert who declines to discuss one until a count and a share of revenue sit beside it.

Clusters are not personas and personas are not clusters. An algorithm finds groups; interviews supply the reason they exist. A cluster without a mechanism is unstable; a persona without a cluster has no size. An expert treats their disagreement as the finding.

Between-group variance is usually small, and that is information. Both Prastaav groupings explain under seven per cent of renewal variance. The naive reading is that both are useless; the expert reading is that account-level variance dominates.

Segments are load-bearing in the organisation, not only the analysis. Territories, quotas and profit-and-loss lines are cut by segment, so a persona crossing segments threatens someone's number. An expert ships the insight inside the segment vocabulary.

Behavioural types migrate, often because of the product. A Worried Well buyer who receives a hypertension diagnosis becomes a Medicated Self-Tracker: the persona is a state, not a trait. The tell is an expert who asks about transition rates.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products, observable attributes are shallow and behaviour varies enormously, so behavioural models usually dominate — though the mass-marketing school is strongest here, since in low-involvement categories buyers really do look alike. In B2B the weight flips partly back: a firmographic segment carries genuine information about compliance regime, integration surface and procurement process, so at account level it often is close to a persona, while inside the account buyer, user, influencer and blocker are different personas with conflicting goals. On marketplaces each side needs its own pair of models, and the cross-side interaction is the real object of study. In hardware the unit economics intrude: Naadi's device contribution margin is 31 per cent against 86 per cent on Naadi Plus, so a persona generating device referrals beats one that subscribes. In AI products the persona is partly endogenous. Stage matters more than product type: a company with 2,000 users cannot decompose variance and should hold one or two provisional personas as falsifiable hypotheses, while a large one has abundant data and a political constraint, because the segments are in the budget.

8. Three worked examples

Prastaav: pricing the patterns. Four-year contribution per account is average ARR per account × 72 per cent gross margin × (1 + r + r² + r³), where r is the pattern's annual renewal rate. Divided by the cost to win an account, the ratio spans 4.80 to 1.25 — not the ARR ranking, because Mandate-only accounts are hardest to win and fastest to leave.

Exhibit 5. Unit economics by adoption pattern; CAC from sales-cost allocation. The last row holds account-weighted averages: ₹12,062 lakh of contribution over 1,180 accounts is ₹10.22 lakh each, ₹3,811 lakh of CAC is ₹3.23 lakh each, a ratio of 3.17.

Naadi: the funnel the persona explains and the age band does not. Of the 1,96,000 monitors sold, 1,07,800 were paired with the app, 55.0 per cent. Of those, 42,042 still produced four or more readings a month in month three, 39.0 per cent of the paired base; of those, 7,007 bought Naadi Plus — one-sixth of them, 16.67 per cent — or 6.5 per cent of paired devices and 3.6 per cent of devices sold.
