The failure: Naadi Lite. On 1 August 2024 Naadi launched Lite, a stripped-down monitor at ₹1,490 aimed at the under-35 segment, which in FY25 was 29 per cent of buyers and the band with the highest pairing rate: young, price-sensitive, digitally fluent. In the twelve months to 31 July 2025 Lite sold 18,400 units against a plan of 60,000 — 30.7 per cent of target. The deeper damage was in the mix: of the 18,400 buyers, 11,960 — 65.0 per cent — said they would otherwise have bought the ₹2,790 device, forgoing ₹1,300 each, or ₹1.55 crore of revenue; and Lite's pairing rate was 38.0 per cent, so only 6,992 of its units reached the app. Cut by behaviour rather than age, the under-35 band proved dominated by the Worried Well pattern — which pairs readily, goes quiet by month three, converts to Plus at 2.40 per cent and refers at 8.0 per cent. A cheaper device had bought more of the least valuable behaviour and cannibalised the most valuable. Lite was withdrawn on 15 January 2026, a little over seventeen months after launch, with a ₹64 lakh write-off. The recovery was not a new device: Naadi re-pointed the same ₹1,490 price at Naadi Plus, a service only engaged users buy, and rebuilt onboarding around one question — "is this device for you or for someone else?" — the bridge that made the Caregiver-bought pattern addressable at the point of sale.

9. Failure modes, with their early warnings

The photograph persona. Warning: a persona slide whose distinguishing content is age, city and hobbies. Diagnostic: ask what it would do differently from the next persona on the same screen. Cost if caught late: Naadi's ₹1.55 crore of cannibalised revenue and ₹64 lakh write-off.

Designing for the largest cell. Warning: a roadmap whose priority order matches segment size order. Diagnostic: compute between-group variance in the outcome you are optimising, both groupings. Cost: capacity spent where dispersion is four points wide, not twenty-three.

Mistaking a mix shift for a product improvement. Warning: a blended rate moves and nobody can name the behaviour that changed. Diagnostic: hold the mix constant and recompute. Cost: a celebrated launch that was a channel change.

Confusing buyer with user. Warning: a segment statistic whose subject is ambiguous. Diagnostic: ask whether a number measures purchase, installation or use. Cost: Naadi's largest growth engine ran two years unnamed.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The reach position. Steelmanned: a model you cannot act on is a cost, not an asset. Platforms, trade media, distributors and territories all address attributes; behavioural types are discovered after acquisition, so treating them as growth instruments yields plans that cannot be executed. Evidence: the gap between attribute-targeted and untargeted campaigns, and the fact that Prastaav's board votes on territories. It would be wrong if behavioural signals became observable before purchase — which, for products with free tiers, they increasingly are.

The design position. Steelmanned: a brief written in attributes produces an averaged artefact that fits nobody, as Cooper documented across dozens of engagements. Evidence: dispersion of the kind in Exhibits 3 and 8, where behaviour separates outcomes by factors the attribute cut cannot see. It would be wrong wherever attributes and behaviours are tightly coupled — which Exhibit 4 shows happens in specific cells.

The mass-marketing position. Steelmanned: in most categories buyers of competing brands are near-identical in demography and attitude, loyalty follows availability, and segmentation decks rationalise noise. Evidence: decades of panel data on duplication of purchase and the double-jeopardy law. It would be wrong where switching costs are high and a behavioural group has genuinely different requirements — most B2B software, much of health hardware. No synthesis exists that all three would sign; an expert names which position the decision sits closest to.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this argues about segments and personas. Someone who has internalised it names the outcome variable first, runs the decomposition on data already held, and keeps whichever grouping wins for that variable while expecting a different answer for the next. They size every persona and refuse to discuss an unsized one. They check the buyer-user question reflexively. And they translate behavioural findings into segment language before taking them to finance, knowing that being right in the wrong vocabulary is indistinguishable from being ignored.

12. The decisions

Nupur presented on Friday 30 January. She kept industry as the unit of territory, quota and spend, because reach is firmographic and the board's accounts are cut that way. She did not exit textiles: that would shed ₹209 lakh of Mandate-only revenue at the price of ₹535 lakh of good revenue in the same cell. Instead she funded Omana's qualification gate — three questions at deal review classifying a prospect's adoption pattern before discount approval — and capped new Mandate-only bookings, whose ratio of 1.25 does not clear the book average of 3.17. Her line to the board: industry tells us where to hunt; adoption pattern tells us what to shoot at.

Prachi's decision conceded the segment. She approved the Senior Care edition: a 25 per cent lift on 23,520 devices is 5,880 units, ₹1.64 crore of revenue and ₹51 lakh of contribution at 31 per cent — materially more than the ₹23 lakh her caregiver-pairing feature would produce in year one. But she rewrote the brief: the edition's buyer is a 42-year-old caregiver, so packaging, warranty registration and the first-run flow are built for someone setting the device up for another person, and the 25 per cent lift goes to a four-week pilot first. The persona did not replace the segment; it rewrote what the segment's product had to do.

Discussion questions. First, adoption pattern explains 6.4 per cent of Prastaav's renewal variance against industry's 0.2 per cent, yet 93.6 per cent is unexplained; what would you do with that residual? Second, Naadi's Caregiver-bought pattern generates 44.1 per cent of referred devices but 18.8 per cent of Plus subscribers — if the metrics point to different roadmaps, which wins, and what does that assume about where margin comes from? Third, Lite failed because a price cut aimed at a segment recruited a behaviour; what test, runnable before launch, would have caught it?

13. Going deeper

  • The Six Ps framework — persona is its first P.
  • Statistical segmentation — clustering, and how to test a cluster's stability.
  • Early adopters and the chasm — a behavioural segmentation of time.
  • Buyer, user, influencer, blocker — what Naadi lacked.
  • Ideal customer profile — a firmographic definition tightened by behavioural evidence.
  • Modelling multi-sided customers — why Nukta needs four.
  • Segment migration and lifecycle segments — transition rates.
  • Why personas — the case for archetypes over averages.
  • The self-referential design trap — what personas were invented to prevent.
  • Anatomy of a persona — the cure for the photograph persona.
  • Building personas from research — reconciling interviews with clusters.
  • AI-assisted persona synthesis — what models infer, and the new failure modes.
  • Jobs to Be Done — the school that discards the person.
case40v1-cust.segments:
Marham Care Collective: Four Body Parts, or Four Behaviours?

An ambiguous case on describing customers — who they are, and how they behave

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday, 22 November 2026, Suchitra Bhatkhande was still at her dining table in Navrangpura, Ahmedabad, with two printouts that would not agree. The board of Marham Care Collective met at ten the next morning and wanted one plan for the ₹14 crore set aside for 1 January to 30 June 2027.

As Chief Product Officer she had written the paper four times. One printout cut Marham's users by age and city tier, the way growth bought media; the other by what they did with the app over ninety days. The first said the base was homogeneous, the second that it was not. Both came from her own department, from the same September numbers.

September revenue was ₹5.06 crore, an annualised ₹60.67 crore. Twenty-two studios were committed to 31 March 2028. One direct report wanted eight more studios, one wanted the app rebuilt, one wanted nine salespeople.

2. How the company came to be constrained

Marham was founded in Ahmedabad in June 2021 by Sarvesh Birje, a physiotherapist, and Suchitra, who came from a Bengaluru payments company. Indian adults with back, knee or shoulder pain typically see a surgeon once, are given a sheet of exercises and do them for nine days; Marham would supply the missing eleven weeks.

A ₹41 crore Series A closed in March 2023. The decision that shaped everything came in October 2024, for good reasons: patients arrive naming a body part and insurers code by body part. Marham built four journeys — Lower Back, Knee, Neck, Shoulder — and tagged the 1,180-video library, the protocols, the onboarding assessment and the analytics schema that way. In the same quarter it signed sixty-month leases on twenty-two studio sites at an average ₹2.80 lakh a month: ₹61.6 lakh a month, ₹7.392 crore a year, non-cancellable to 31 March 2028. A ₹96 crore Series B followed in February 2025, on a plan for sixty studios.

Two years on, the schema is the constraint. Marham can say how many knee users in Jaipur opened the app last Tuesday; it cannot say who is in an acute flare and who is mid-programme. Of the 2,12,300 onboarding assessments completed between 1 July and 30 September 2026, 94,500 recorded pain at more than one site, 44.5 per cent.

3. The industry around it

Marham sits in a crowded Indian market with no incumbent. Cult.fit and HealthifyMe own the fitness habit, Practo and Apollo 24|7 doctor discovery, Tata 1mg the pharmacy. Max Healthcare and Manipal Hospitals run their own physiotherapy departments, and in Jaipur Marham takes referrals from Marudhar Hospitals Trust. A smaller rival, Mahatva Spine Works, runs no studios.

Physiotherapy is regulated under the National Commission for Allied and Healthcare Professions Act, 2021, so Marham cannot hire more cheaply. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 treats Marham's pain logs as personal data needing specific consent, and only 1,04,000 of the 4,60,000 monthly active users, 22.6 per cent, have consented to their use for marketing audiences. The IRDAI's push on outpatient cover interests insurers such as Niva Bupa and Star Health in musculoskeletal programmes — priced per covered life, not per persona.

Collections run on UPI through Razorpay; the ₹471 monthly charge — ₹399 net of eighteen per cent GST, the figure used in every exhibit here — is as easy to cancel as to take. Marham's one overseas exposure is Masarrah Facilities Group of Abu Dhabi, which wants UAE data residency and a lower price per employee.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Exhibit 1 sets out the sequence. In February 2026 the growth team doubled media spend on a target it could buy on every platform: adults aged forty-five and over in the six metros with studios. The belief was that pain follows age and willingness to pay follows city. Exhibit 2 is that belief measured: conversion across five demographic segments runs from 9.78 to 15.04 per cent against a blended 13.26 per cent.

In April 2026 Samwel Barasa, a senior data scientist in Nairobi, was asked to ignore demographics and cluster users on ninety days of event data. Four groups emerged, named in a June workshop: the Flare Responder, who appears in bursts when pain spikes and vanishes for months; the Programme Finisher, who logs most days and completes eight-week plans; the Clinic Companion, for whom the app is an accessory to studio visits; and the Information Seeker, who reads and never starts.

Exhibit 4 shows the same 4,60,000 monthly actives under that cut, and the contrast is stark: conversion runs from 4.68 to 40.0 per cent, a spread of more than eight times. Programme Finishers supply 31,280 of the 61,000 paying subscribers, 51.3 per cent, while only 9,900 of the 1,98,000 Flare Responders subscribe, 5.0 per cent.

In August a panel asked people to describe themselves, and Exhibit 3 does not match Exhibit 4: the panel puts Clinic Companions at 35.97 per cent of respondents where the event data puts them at 12.00 per cent of monthly actives. Part of the gap is in the footnote — 512 of the 1,240 panel respondents, 41.3 per cent, were recruited in studio waiting rooms, while studio patients are 14,800 of the 4,60,000 monthly actives, 3.2 per cent. The research lead says event logs cannot see intent; Samwel says the panel is a sample of the waiting room.

On 12 November Samwel circulated an unasked-for page. Re-running the clustering on April-to-June against July-to-September, he found that of the 2,94,000 users present in both, 1,01,700 had moved cluster, 34.6 per cent. His reading: the clusters track how much pain a person is in this quarter, not a stable disposition. Snehal Bijlani, the design lead in Amsterdam, drew the opposite conclusion — if a third of users change behaviour within six months, the product must follow the change, which a body-part schema cannot do.

Exhibit 5 was meant to settle whether personas were merely demographics in disguise. It does not. Programme Finishers are 29.35 per cent of the smallest metro segment and 10.87 per cent of both tier-two segments — more structure than Shekhar Bhurke, the head of growth, expected — yet that segment holds only 16,200 of the 78,200 Programme Finishers, 20.7 per cent.

Exhibit 6 reports the one deliberate test. From Monday 5 October to Sunday 1 November 2026 the growth team spent ₹87.92 lakh on a look-alike audience seeded from consented Programme Finishers, buying 31,400 installs at ₹280 each against the ₹180 blended cost of the July-to-September quarter, a premium of 55.6 per cent per install; cost per first payment came out at ₹2,281 against ₹2,727, better by 16.4 per cent. But the columns cover unlike periods: a quarter observed to 31 October against four weeks observed only to Sunday 15 November, a fortnight containing Diwali.

On 17 November Sagarika Bawdekar, the clinical director, mentioned that nineteen of the 132 sanctioned physiotherapist posts were vacant. Exhibit 7 computes utilisation on bays and reports 82.31 per cent; computed on physiotherapists in post, the same sessions imply 96.15 per cent. The first says there is room inside the existing leases. The second says there is not.

5. The people

Suchitra Bhatkhande, Chief Product Officer, Ahmedabad, owns the board paper; her option tranche vests on FY28 revenue, rewarding whichever path books fastest. She does not say that the October 2024 schema was her own written recommendation.

Sarvesh Birje, co-founder and chief executive, wants one sentence he can repeat: Marham is a clinical company with a digital front end. He has not told the product team that his Series C conversations are benchmarked against companies valued on studio count.

Shekhar Bhurke, head of growth, Bengaluru, holds the media budget, about ₹7 crore a quarter, and is measured on cost per first payment. He argues that segments are the only thing ad platforms will sell, and does not volunteer that his best creative is a film about waking up unable to turn your neck — a flare, not a demographic.

Sagarika Bawdekar, clinical director, Jaipur, holds that the clusters are severity bands and that a person in an acute flare needs triage, not a cleverer onboarding screen. She has not put in writing that the vacancies sit in Coimbatore and Jaipur, the studios whose utilisation carries the expansion case.

Snehal Bijlani, design lead, Amsterdam, wants three journeys — flare, programme, companion — and an onboarding that asks one question. She does not emphasise that the persona names came from a workshop rather than the clustering, or that Information Seekers, 27.96 per cent of actives, have no place in her design.

Samwel Barasa, senior data scientist, Nairobi, built the clustering and then undermined it. He has not said that the October seed was drawn from consented users who skew towards the already-engaged, so the pilot’s better rates may be an artefact of the seed.

Sohrab Bhonagiri, enterprise lead, Melbourne, wants nine hires. Nine contracts cover 46,000 employees at ₹1,180 a year, and his bonus is on contract value signed, not activation. He has not said that 9,890 of the 46,000 covered employees, 21.5 per cent, have ever started a programme, that 2,769 of the 46,000 covered employees, 6.0 per cent, were still active in month three, or that two renewing buyers have asked a twenty-two per cent cut.

Shirin Bhatewara, chief financial officer, reads the lease schedule and notes that ₹7.392 crore of annual rent runs to 31 March 2028 whatever the product team decides. She has not told her colleagues that ₹4.1 crore of the ₹14 crore is conditional on a bridge note closing in January.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

Product and growth review, Thursday 19 November, Ahmedabad.

“I am not against personas. I am against a plan that depends on buying them. I can buy women over forty-five in Jaipur tomorrow at a known price. Tell me the line item for ‘Programme Finisher’ and I will spend on it.” — Shekhar Bhurke

“You already did. Your neck film is a persona. You filed it under a demographic because that is the only box in the report.” — Snehal Bijlani

Email, Sagarika Bawdekar to Suchitra Bhatkhande, 18 November, 06:41 IST.

“Be careful with the word persona in front of the board. A person whose back has locked is not expressing a preference. Label them Flare Responder and build a cheerful onboarding, and we have renamed a clinical priority as a marketing type.”

Internal chat, #series-c, 20 November.

Sarvesh Birje: “The comparable set is studio-count based. Eight studios is a number they can model. ‘We rebuilt onboarding’ is not.”

Shirin Bhatewara: “Lucknow opened fifteen months ago and is at 55.6 per cent.”

Samwel Barasa: “Lucknow also has the fewest Programme Finishers per thousand actives, on my cut. Bad site, or different people?”

8. The options as Suchitra sees them

Option A — eight more studios. Fit-out is ₹68 lakh a studio, ₹5.44 crore in all, with ₹2.688 crore a year of new rent and a fresh lock-in. At the blended utilisation of 82.31 per cent, eight studios would deliver about 12,327 sessions a month, worth ₹78.89 lakh at ₹640 a session, or ₹9.467 crore a year at maturity. The case rests on Exhibit 8 and the ₹747 figure; the counter-case on Lucknow and the staffed-capacity footnote to Exhibit 7.

Option B — rebuild around behaviour. Six months of the twenty-six-person squad at ₹3.4 lakh a month loaded is ₹5.304 crore, plus ₹1.2 crore to re-record and re-tag content in five languages: ₹6.504 crore. If Flare Responder conversion rose from 5.0 to 8.0 per cent on 1,98,000 monthly actives, that is 5,940 more subscribers, ₹23.70 lakh a month, ₹2.844 crore a year. The lift is an assumption nothing here supports.

Option C — buy the employer channel. Nine hires for six months at ₹4.3 lakh a month loaded is ₹2.322 crore, against fourteen contracts covering 1,05,000 employees at ₹1,180, or ₹12.39 crore of annual contract value. Cycles run seven to eleven months, so almost none lands inside the funded half-year, and the channel sells by headcount while the product is consumed by behaviour.

What Suchitra cannot write is why they are three. The exhibits suggest two framings with no column in the paper: that the Clinic Companion may be an artefact of having studios rather than a kind of person, and that the unit of this business may be an episode of pain rather than a customer — in which case Exhibits 2, 4 and 5 are counting the wrong noun.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board votes at ten on Monday, 23 November 2026. The campaign brief for the Makar Sankranti and Pongal window of 14 January 2027 is due on 8 December, so any behavioural audience must clear data-protection counsel first. Of the ₹14 crore, ₹4.1 crore is contingent on a bridge note expected in January; rent of ₹7.392 crore a year runs to 31 March 2028 regardless. Nineteen physiotherapist posts are open and cannot be filled with unregistered staff. Behavioural audiences may be built only from the consented minority of the base, and widening that consent needs engineering weeks Option B also wants. Masarrah wants UAE data residency, which no one has priced.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 2 and 4, state what each cut does and does not tell Marham. Which would you buy media with, which would you build from, and why are those not the same?
  2. Exhibits 3 and 4 disagree about the size of the Clinic Companion group. Reconcile them if you can; if not, which goes in the board paper?
  3. Exhibit 8 shows ₹747 against ₹399. What does a naive reader conclude, a careful one, and what would you add to stop the naive reading?
  4. One colleague reads Samwel’s cluster-switching finding as destroying the persona work, another as proving its necessity. Which do the exhibits support, and what evidence would separate them?
  5. Exhibits 6 and 7 each compare unlike things. How much of the ₹14 crore would you commit on evidence of this quality?
  6. It is Monday morning and the floor is yours for six minutes. What do you recommend, what do you refuse, and what do you tell the board about the October 2024 decision you signed?

11. Later that night

After midnight Suchitra drew two columns, one headed who they are and one headed what they do, and stopped, because the first thing she wanted to write — a woman of fifty-two in Coimbatore, three weeks into a knee programme, who stops when her daughter’s exams start — belonged in both and fitted neither. The studios would photograph well in a diligence pack. The rebuild would be right in a way she could not yet put a number against.

Outside, the last Diwali lights were still up. She thought about Sagarika’s line — that a person whose back has locked is not expressing a preference — and about Shekhar’s neck film, filed under a demographic because there was no other box. At ten o’clock she would have to choose a noun.
exp40v2-cust.self.ref:
The Self-Referential Design Trap

Discovery & Design › Customer Modelling: Segments, Personas, Jobs to Be Done. Learning objective: you are not the user. Near-expert treatment.

1. Two rooms, eight days apart

On 3 February 2026 Yamini Rautray, vice-president of product at Rujuta Diagnostics Network, had to choose between two bets for the quarter beginning 1 April, fifty-seven days away. Rujuta sent phlebotomists to homes in Pune, Nashik and Nagpur, completing 6,40,000 home collections in the twelve months to 31 January 2026. Bet A was an interpretation layer that read a household's report history and explained trends in plain language: ₹2.95 crore to build. Bet B was a telephone-and-WhatsApp booking path, a printed report at the door and a shared family record for elders without smartphones: ₹1.60 crore to build and ₹1.95 crore to run for a year, ₹3.55 crore in all. All thirty-four people in Rautray's product organisation had tried Bet A, and twenty-nine had asked, unprompted, when it would ship. Nobody had asked for Bet B.

Eight days later, on 11 February 2026, Rupin Jahagirdar locked Release 9.0 of Uttaran Warehouse Systems in Hyderabad, sold to third-party logistics operators and shipping on 30 June 2026, a hundred and thirty-nine days later. Uttaran had thirty-eight accounts across 412 sites, 14,600 named users and recurring revenue of ₹43.70 crore, an average of ₹1.15 crore per account. Jahagirdar's team was not insular in its own estimation: quarterly reviews with every account, and a Kraków-based researcher, Urszula Zielinska, logging each one.

Both rooms answered the same question with the wrong instrument — enthusiasm in Pune, a contact log in Hyderabad. The trap is a failure of measurement rather than of humility; it is cheap to measure; and the measurement does not tell you what to do. Uttaran, which talked to customers weekly, sat further from its users than the firm that talked to none.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Partition the user population into segments with weights ui, and let ti be the builders' own distribution across those segments. A team forecasting response to a feature with per-segment rates ri will, undisciplined, forecast Σtiri while the market delivers Σuiri. The trap is the systematic use of t where u belongs. Three consequences, each routinely denied: the error vanishes when t = u, so resembling your users is a shortcut, not a sin; it vanishes when r is flat; and its size is the interaction of unrepresentativeness with rate dispersion, so composition alone is never a verdict.

Three literatures converge on the diagnosis: Ross, Greene and House on the false-consensus effect in 1977; Camerer, Loewenstein and Weber on the curse of knowledge in 1989; and Scandinavian participatory design, which argued from the 1970s that workers must co-design the systems governing their work. Software's own contribution was a habit — dogfooding, excellent at finding defects and incapable of finding non-adoption. The remedy came from Alan Cooper in 1998: a research-grounded surrogate user with a seat in every argument.

Five schools divide on the prescription. Goal-directed design, in Cooper's line, signs "no interface decision without a research-grounded surrogate in the room" and refuses "behavioural data can substitute," since logs hold only people who already got in. Jobs-to-be-done, after Christensen and Ulwick, signs the stronger claim that demographic distance is irrelevant once the job is correctly specified. Lean experimentation signs "every belief is a hypothesis with a cheap test" and refuses weeks of prior ethnography. The participatory school, with its Indian tradition of text-free work for low-literacy users, refuses that a persona deck discharges the obligation to put the user in the room. The founder-taste school signs "the sharpest first versions come from builders who are users" and refuses "therefore never test with strangers." Von Hippel's lead users sit across the divide: builder-as-user is sometimes the best source in the market.

The schools agree on the diagnosis and divide on the prescription, because the division turns on a quantity each firm must measure itself.

3. Mechanics: what expert practitioners actually do

Step one: partition by behaviour, not demography. Rujuta's researcher, Ujwala Sapre, segmented by who initiates the booking and who reads the report: salaried self-bookers (S1); family caregivers, an adult child booking for a parent over sixty who receives the report (S2); doctor-referred patients (S3); and employer-sponsored checkups, where the organisation buys and the employee uses (S4).

Step two: measure the builders against the same partition. This is the step that gets skipped, and it is an afternoon's work: Rautray had all thirty-four classify their own last three diagnostic encounters.

4. When the idea applies, as testable claims

One: divergence on behaviour-relevant attributes exceeds roughly twenty points. Rujuta 57.41, true; Uttaran 78.28 against seats, true. Two: measured rates differ materially across segments. Rujuta's span 6 to 38 per cent for A and 7 to 34 for B; Uttaran's pick-confirm rework matters to 10,950 floor users and barely to 438 analysts. Where rates are flat the trap cannot bite. Three: reweighting can reverse the decision's direction, not merely its margin. Rujuta yes; Uttaran only partly, since its analytics workbench is over-funded rather than worthless. Four: someone can act on the answer. Here the idea misleads: at Uttaran the users who matter do not sign the cheque, so moving t towards u without a commercial instrument produces a beloved product with flat renewals. It misleads too in a new category, where no u yet exists.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Uttaran is the canonical enterprise case, and it overturns the intuition that proximity to customers is protection. Zielinska's ledger for the two quarters to 31 December 2025 recorded 580 hours of watching the product in use.

Table 5. Uttaran Warehouse Systems: seats, attention and funding by role

Three hundred and eighteen of the 580 hours, 54.8 per cent, went to managers holding 7.00 per cent of seats; 512 of the 1,240 engineering points, 41.3 per cent, went to features whose primary user is a client analyst or CXO, a role holding 3.00 per cent of seats. The mechanism is not laziness: managers grant meetings and complain by email, while reaching a floor picker means standing in a cold aisle in Bhiwandi at six in the morning. Uttaran's divergence exceeds Rujuta's precisely because it has a contact process, which samples by accessibility. Funding in proportion to seats would nonetheless be the wrong correction.

Points per screen is Table 5's points over screens. User-hours assume 160 pick-confirms per picker per shift at 11.5 seconds, 95 minutes per supervisor, 48 per manager, 18 per analyst; the rounded column sums exactly to 10,013.2.

Per screen the floor is Uttaran's best-funded surface, 38.0 points against 10.2 for managers — which closes the argument for a competent practitioner and opens it for an expert, since three screens used 160 times a shift by 10,950 people deserve more per screen than forty-one occasional ones. Switching the denominator from seats to user-hours barely moves it, 65.52 points of divergence against 65.81: when it is this large the finding is robust to the weighting.

Other seams differ. In regulated products the trap hides inside compliance, where the team models the regulator's intent from the circular rather than from how a branch officer reads it. In hardware plus software the object has users the software team never enumerates: Yugal Cooling Industries designed the door seal of its two-tonne cold rooms for 4.0 minutes of door-open time a day, and telemetry from 1,180 units showed 41 openings a day averaging 46 seconds — 1,886 seconds, or 31.4 minutes, 7.9 times the assumption. The app's user was the trader's son; the door's user was a helper paid by the day. In AI-native products the trap moves into the evaluation set: 201 of the 240 prompts in Rujuta's eval suite for Bet A, 84 per cent, were written by team members about their own reports, which is why it scored 4.3 out of 5 there and 2.9 on ninety prompts drawn from what doctor-referred patients had asked a phlebotomist.

6. The nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The index is a smoke alarm, not a verdict. A competent practitioner computes divergence and concludes the roadmap is wrong; an expert knows bias is divergence times rate dispersion, so a large index with flat rates is harmless. The tell is a memo quoting composition and no rate.

Divergence must be measured on behaviour-relevant attributes. A team can be diverse by gender, language and home state and unanimous on what drives behaviour: everyone owns a ₹60,000 handset. Choosing the partition is the hardest judgement here.

Customer contact is not user observation. Uttaran's 580-hour ledger looked like rigour and was a sampling instrument weighted by who can grant meetings. The obvious reading, talk to customers more, is wrong: the same process yields the same bias with higher confidence.

Dogfooding is a defect detector that emits preference data. It finds crashes cheaply; the danger is the by-product, twenty-nine people asking when Bet A ships, entering the decision as evidence. The tell is a decision log citing internal sentiment.

Over-correction is a distinct failure with the same root. A team that discards everything it personally values has swapped one invented user for another. The tell is a cut justified by "that is just us" rather than by a measurement.

Research sampling inherits the bias and disguises it as precision. Reweighting corrects the estimate and destroys information: Rujuta's 750 interviews were worth 466. The heaviest-weighted segment usually has the fewest observations, so the population you understand least is the one your interval is widest on.

The cost of the error is asymmetric, which is why it survives. Being wrong about a segment you resemble is self-correcting, because someone files the bug; being wrong about one you do not surfaces months later as metric drift. The tell is a bug tracker whose reporters match the team.

Sometimes your own taste is the asset. In developer and design tools, builder-as-user is an advantage the correction can destroy. The distinguishing test is empirical: does the team's preference predict the behaviour of users unlike the team? Rujuta's did not.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

Consumer: the largest builder-user distance, since the population is broad and the team narrow on income, language, device and data cost; the trap shows up as features serving the most fluent users. B2B and enterprise: smaller distance on demography, larger on role, with the contact process reinforcing it as Table 5 shows; the complication is commercial, since user value must convert into a renewal or it dies in the budget. Hardware: worst where the product is operated by someone who appears in no software artefact. AI products: different in mechanism, since the trap enters through evaluation sets and preference labels. By stage: a five-person startup is often its own first user and should be, the index near zero because the market is people like the founders; the trap arrives at the first expansion, when u moves and t does not. In large organisations self-reference becomes second-hand reference, and the index must then be computed on the evidence base.

8. Three worked examples, including one failure

Rujuta, succeeding. Section 3 works the first example in full: a 57.41-point divergence, a ranking reversed by reweighting, ₹11.12 crore net against ₹6.14 crore, and a reversal threshold of 11.32 per cent.

Uttaran, succeeding partially. Jahagirdar's pilot of the reworked pick-confirm flow at four sites over the 48 days from 2 November to 20 December 2025 cut per-line confirm time from 11.5 to 8.2 seconds, a saving of 3.3 seconds, or 8.8 minutes per picker per shift. Across 17,52,000 lines a day that is 57,81,600 seconds — 1,606 hours a day, 4,81,800 hours over 300 working days; at a loaded floor cost of ₹120 an hour, ₹5.78 crore a year. Mis-picks fell from 11 to 8 per 10,000 lines, and 3 per 10,000 of 52.56 crore annual lines is 1,57,680 errors avoided at ₹180 each, ₹2.84 crore. Customer-side benefit: ₹8.62 crore a year, the exact sum of the two rounded components. Uttaran's defensible capture was a 6 per cent renewal uplift on nine accounts worth ₹13.20 crore — ₹79.20 lakh — plus retention of two accounts worth ₹2.30 crore. The gap between ₹8.62 crore created and ₹79.20 lakh captured is the enterprise version of this topic.

Ritambhara Learning Labs, failing. Ritambhara sold Class 10 state-board exam preparation in Patna, Ranchi and Lucknow, with 2,80,000 monthly active learners in January 2025. Its audit was exemplary: twenty of twenty-two product staff were English-medium metro graduates, against a learner base overwhelmingly Hindi-medium and small-town. The team concluded correctly that its instincts were unrepresentative, then drew the wrong inference — rebuilding voice-first and Hindi-only, and removing timed mock tests on the reasoning that scheduled self-assessment was a metro habit. The rebuild shipped 1 July 2025, and over the 91 days to 30 September 2025 monthly actives fell to 2,09,000, a loss of 71,000 learners, or 25.4 per cent. The post-mortem found that in June 2025, 1,64,000 of the 2,80,000 monthly learners, 58.6 per cent, had attempted at least one timed mock, and attempt rates were higher among Hindi-medium learners, for whom the mock was the only objective signal of readiness. Mocks returned on 12 October 2025 in both languages; by 31 January 2026 actives had recovered to 2,66,000, still 14,000 or 5.0 per cent below the pre-rebuild level, at a direct cost of ₹9.50 crore — ₹7.40 crore of engineering and ₹2.10 crore of re-acquisition marketing. The audit established that the team's view was over-weighted; it did not establish which preferences were idiosyncratic, and that is settled attribute by attribute.

9. Failure modes, with their early warnings

The triumphant demo. Sign: high internal enthusiasm, no segment-level forecast. Diagnostic: what share of this room belongs to the segment that is most of our users? Late cost: a shipped quarter, ₹2.95 crore at Rujuta's scale.

Contact mistaken for observation. Sign: a repository where every entry carries a job title and none a shift timing. Diagnostic: show me the observation-hours ledger by role. Late cost: Uttaran's 65.81 points of accumulated funding divergence.

Over-correction. Sign: cuts justified by "that is just us". Diagnostic: which measurement says this attribute is idiosyncratic? Late cost: ₹9.50 crore and 14,000 learners.

Correction without a commercial instrument. Sign: satisfaction rising, renewal pricing flat. Diagnostic: who pays for this value, through which clause? Late cost: a beloved product with the same revenue.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Measure and reweight. Composition is cheap to observe and rates cheap to pilot, and the arithmetic converts both into a defensible decision; the evidence is cases like Rujuta's, where the ranking reversed and survived both a value layer and a sensitivity test. For this to be wrong, three-week rates would have to be unstable enough that reweighting adds precision without accuracy.

Specify the job and the person stops mattering. Segmentation by person is unstable and by job is not, so the answer to divergence is a better job statement, not a representative team. For this to be wrong, execution details — language, literacy, handset, who holds the phone — would have to move behaviour independently of the job, and Ritambhara's 71,000 lost learners argue that they do.

Founder taste beats representative process. Great products are disproportionately built by builders who were users, and the correction's real cost is lost conviction. For this to be wrong, the market entered must differ from the founders' world on an attribute that drives behaviour — normal in Indian consumer markets, abnormal in developer tools.

Representation, not research about representation. A colleague who grew up in the market argues back in real time, where research is a lossy channel. For this to be wrong, one or two hires would have to be an inadequate sample — which, strictly, they are: hiring two caregivers into Rujuta's thirty-four moves the divergence index only from 57.41 to 53.00 points.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this runs a persona workshop and feels better. Someone who has internalised it changes three structural things. Composition and divergence appear in the operating review beside revenue, so the question is asked on a schedule. Decisions carry their reversal threshold — "Bet B unless caregiver adoption is below 11.32 per cent" — so later disagreement concerns a measurable quantity. And access asymmetry is attacked with a budgeted rota that puts every product manager on a warehouse floor each quarter, because the alternative relies on virtue, and virtue does not survive a release crunch.

12. What each protagonist decided

Rautray funded Bet B for the quarter beginning 1 April 2026 and did not cancel Bet A. Her argument to the board was not the divergence index, a diagnostic only, but ₹11.12 crore net against ₹6.14 crore, with the 11.32 per cent reversal threshold on the slide. Bet A was rescoped as a capability investment limited to S1 and S2, its evaluation suite rebuilt from 300 real user questions sampled to population shares, and Sapre was to re-measure the S3 rate on 300 observations rather than 95.

Jahagirdar did not flip his roadmap to match seat shares. He moved Release 9.0's 1,240 points to 430 for the floor, 240 for supervisors, 330 for managers and 240 for analysts and CXOs, cutting funding divergence from seats from 65.81 to 40.32 points and deliberately not to zero, since proportional representation is not the objective. He tied the floor rework to the renewal uplift justified by ₹8.62 crore of customer-side saving, and made an eight-hour floor shift per quarter a condition of employment for every product manager and designer.

Discussion questions. First: Rujuta's reversal threshold rests on a rate measured over three weeks on 190 people — should a board accept a ₹3.55 crore commitment on that basis? Second: Uttaran creates ₹8.62 crore of annual value for its customers' floor staff and captures ₹79.20 lakh; is the answer a commercial instrument, a different roadmap, or a different buyer? Third: name the step that belonged between Ritambhara's audit and its rebuild, and what it would have cost.

13. Going deeper

  • Why personas. The standing remedy for this trap, and the module's vocabulary.
  • Market segments vs personas. Which object the index is computed over: a segment is a share of a market, a persona a decision-making surrogate.
  • Anatomy of a persona. Which attributes belong in the partition — the hardest judgement in section 3.
  • Building personas from research. The provenance discipline that stops the author-shaped persona.
  • AI-assisted persona synthesis. Where the trap re-enters at speed, since a model asked to imagine a user draws on whatever its prompt over-represents.
  • Jobs to Be Done. The strongest rival framing, from the school that denies you need resemble your user.
  • Functional, emotional and social jobs. Why Ritambhara's learners wanted timed mocks: the job was reassurance, not practice.

The Self-Referential Design Trap

Discovery & Design, Customer Modelling. Learning objective: you are not the user.

1. Fourteen people and a route planner

On Tuesday, 14 October 2025, Sunanda Hirlekar, head of product at Subah Commute Network, sat in front of a wall of sticky notes in the company's office in Koramangala, Bengaluru. Subah sold monthly bus-pass renewals and Namma Metro top-ups through an app used by about 1,20,000 riders a month, many of whom boarded BMTC buses at Majestic, Whitefield and Peenya. The engineering lead, Vedant Kamerkar, had just walked her through the proposed centrepiece of the next quarter: a multi-leg route planner that would compare bus, metro and auto combinations with up to three transfers. Everyone who had tried the prototype loved it.

Hirlekar had counted the people who loved it. Of the fourteen on the product and engineering team, twelve were salaried office workers in their late twenties or thirties, comfortable with English-language apps, on unlimited data plans, and accustomed to planning their day on a phone. Two were former students. None had ever depended on a daily wage, a shared handset or a prepaid recharge of ₹19. The quarter's engineering cost was ₹96 lakh, and the planned launch was 24 November 2025, 41 days away. If the planner shipped and the riders who most needed Subah ignored it, the company would lose the quarter and, worse, would learn the wrong lesson from the failure.

The prior question was whose problem is this a solution to?

2. The idea

The self-referential design trap is the tendency of builders to design for the person they know best, namely themselves or people like them, while believing they are designing for the actual user. It is not vanity; it is what any mind does when asked to imagine a stranger.

Three older ideas explain why the default is so strong. In 1977 the psychologists Ross, Greene and House described the false-consensus effect: people systematically overestimate how widely their own choices and preferences are shared. And the software industry developed its own habit, dogfooding (using your own product internally, a phrase associated with Microsoft in the late 1980s), which is valuable for finding bugs but is, by construction, a sample of one kind of person.

The remedy came from design practice. In the late 1990s Alan Cooper, in The Inmates Are Running the Asylum, argued that programmers build for themselves unless forced to build for someone specific, and he promoted personas: concrete, research-based portraits of target users that stand in for the missing person in every product argument.

The sentence Hirlekar could repeat in the meeting: "Before we ask whether we like it, let us check how much of the room looks like the people who pay us."

3. How it works: the mechanics, including the implicit steps

Avoiding the trap is a procedure.

Step one: name the target population explicitly. Hirlekar's first act was to write down who Subah's 1,20,000 monthly riders actually were, using three groups that the company's research had previously identified: office-going commuters (call them Group A), shift workers in garment units, security services and domestic work (Group B), and students (Group C).

Step two: measure the builders against the same categories. This is the step practitioners leave implicit. If the team is a biased sample of the target, you want to know by how much, in numbers, before arguing about features. Step three: find the gap in the evidence, not in opinion. Whatever the team believes about adoption is a forecast from a biased sample, so you replace it with observation: interviews, ride-alongs, or a small behavioural test. Step four: re-weight. Compute the same decision twice, once using the team's implicit picture of the market and once using the measured one. Step five: decide, and write down which assumption would reverse the decision.

Figure 1 shows steps one and two for Subah. The dark bars are the team's composition; the light bars are the rider base. Group A is 85.7 per cent of the team (12 of 14) but 30 per cent of riders. Group B, the largest group of riders at 45 per cent, is absent from the team entirely. Group C is 14.3 per cent of the team (2 of 14) and 25 per cent of riders.

4. A worked example, line by line

Hirlekar asked Tripti Gaikwad, Subah's lone researcher, to test two rough features for two weeks: the route planner (Feature X) and a low-data renewal flow using WhatsApp and a voucher code redeemable at neighbourhood kiosks (Feature Y). Gaikwad measured, for each group, the share of riders who used the feature at least twice in the test fortnight. Table 1 gives the measured rates and the resulting adopters.

Table 1. Rider base and measured adoption (share using the feature at least twice)
GroupRidersFeature X rateX adoptersFeature Y rateY adopters
A: office36,00040%14,40010%3,600
B: shift workers54,0006%3,24035%18,900
C: students30,00020%6,00015%4,500
Total (rates: blended)1,20,00019.7%23,64022.5%27,000

Riders: 30 per cent, 45 per cent and 25 per cent of 1,20,000. Blended rate = total adopters divided by 1,20,000 (23,640 / 1,20,000 = 19.7 per cent; 27,000 / 1,20,000 = 22.5 per cent).

Read it line by line. Group A is 36,000 riders, and 40 per cent of them is 14,400 X adopters; Group B's 54,000 at 6 per cent gives 3,240; Group C's 30,000 at 20 per cent gives 6,000. These sum to 23,640. For Feature Y the same arithmetic gives 3,600, 18,900 and 4,500, which sum to 27,000. Measured against the real rider base, Y reaches 3,360 more riders than X.

Now compare this with what the team believed. If you weight the adoption rates by the team's own composition instead (12 of 14 Group A, 0 of 14 Group B, 2 of 14 Group C), Feature X scores (12 × 40% + 2 × 20%) / 14 = 5.2 / 14 = 37.1 per cent, while Feature Y scores (12 × 10% + 2 × 15%) / 14 = 1.5 / 14 = 10.7 per cent. The team's mental model made X look more than three times as attractive as Y (37.1 against 10.7). The measured market says Y leads by 22.5 against 19.7 per cent. Same data, different audience; the trap is the choice of weights.

Second pass: change one input

A careful reader should distrust the 35 per cent for Y among Group B, which came from a two-week test with a small sample. Suppose it is really 20 per cent. Group B's Y adopters become 54,000 × 20% = 10,800, so total Y adopters are 3,600 + 10,800 + 4,500 = 18,900, or 15.75 per cent of riders, and X (23,640) now wins. The break-even is the Group B rate at which Y equals X: (23,640 − 3,600 − 4,500) / 54,000 = 15,540 / 54,000 = 28.8 per cent. So the decision is not "Y beats X"; it is "Y beats X if shift workers adopt it at better than about 29 per cent".That is testable, and it tells Gaikwad what to measure next.

One caution on what this arithmetic is: adopters count heads, not value.A Group A rider may be worth more.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

The trap is about similarity, not intelligence

Capable teams fall in because the error is structural: nearly everyone at Subah was alike on the dimension that mattered.

Dogfooding is not research

Using your own product catches defects. It cannot tell you whether anyone unlike you would adopt it.

Being like the user is not always a problem

If the product is a developer tool and the team are developers, self-reference may be a cheap and decent proxy.The danger scales with distance between builder and user in income, language, device and context.

A persona is not a stereotype or an average

A persona built from five loosely remembered customers is the self-referential trap with a name attached. A useful persona is traceable to observations, and its attributes are the ones that change behaviour.The "average" Subah rider, part office worker and part shift worker, does not exist.

Confusing the buyer with the user

Families often buy a student's pass. A team can be right about one and self-referential about the other.

Asking people what they want is not an escape

Riders who had never seen a WhatsApp renewal could not request one. Observed behaviour beats stated opinion.

Representation helps but does not finish the job

Hiring one shift-worker's son improves the odds, yet one person is still a sample of one. Use representation as a complement to research.

What the idea cannot tell you

It identifies whose view is being used. It does not tell you which segment is strategically the right one to serve. Group A may be smaller but more profitable; choosing Group B is a strategic decision, taken knowingly, not an automatic outcome of correcting a bias.

6. How it differs by product type and by stage

Consumer products. The distance between builders and users is usually the largest, because consumer populations are broad and the team is narrow. Language, data cost and shared handsets vary enormously, and the trap shows up as features that suit the most fluent users.

B2B products. The trap takes a different form: building for the buyer you meet in demos (a senior manager) rather than the clerk who uses the system daily. The cure, sitting beside them on a work shift, is cheap but often skipped.

Marketplaces. There are at least two populations, and teams usually over-identify with one. The test must be run on every side, with each side's builders-versus-users gap measured separately.

Early versus large. A five-person startup is often its own first user, and that is a legitimate way to start: founder-user fit can produce a sharp first version. The trap arrives at the first expansion, when the product leaves the founder's world. Large companies suffer layers of intermediaries, so self-reference is replaced by second-hand reference.

7. Common mistakes

"The demo went wonderfully." The symptom is a launch where internal metrics and enthusiasm are high, but adoption is flat in groups nobody on the team belongs to. The misunderstanding is treating the audience in the room as the audience in the market. The cheapest diagnostic is the one Hirlekar ran: tabulate team versus customer composition on three or four behaviour-relevant attributes. It takes an afternoon.

The persona who is secretly the author. The symptom is a persona whose goals, vocabulary and habits read like a flattering version of the team. The diagnostic: ask for the source of each attribute; any that points to "we felt" rather than an interview or log is a guess.

Research with the reachable. The symptom is interview notes that cover only people who responded to an in-app survey, or friends of the team. The misunderstanding is that any customer is a representative customer. The diagnostic is to compare the research sample with the rider base, using the same table as Table 1: if Group B is 45 per cent of riders and 5 per cent of interviewees, the evidence has the same bias as the team.

8. What good looks like

The team would state the target population in writing, measure its own composition against it, and publish the gap in the roadmap review. It would test the two options on every group, reweight the results by the real rider base, name the single input that would reverse the decision (here, Group B adoption of Y at about 29 per cent), and schedule the measurement that resolves it.It would keep the planner on the roadmap, because it is genuinely good for Group A; the point is sequence and evidence.

9. Closing: what Hirlekar decided, and what to learn next

On 16 October Hirlekar took the numbers to Kamerkar and the leadership group. She did not cancel the planner. She split the quarter: the low-data renewal flow went first, with Gaikwad extending the Group B test to the 28.8 per cent threshold, and the planner was slotted for the second half of the quarter, scoped for Group A and Group C. The decision was never "which feature is better" but "which group do we owe the next quarter to", and the evidence favoured the group with the most riders and the fewest builders.

To go further, study personas themselves: why they exist and how to build them from observation, since personas are the standing remedy for this trap. After that, learn segmentation and jobs-to-be-done, which turn the single act of checking into a method for choosing which customers to serve first.

Two questions to sit with. First, on which two or three attributes would your own team look least like your customers, and have you ever written that down? Second, if your best measured result came only from people who answered a survey in English on a smartphone, what would you conclude about everyone who did not answer?

The Dashboard Nobody in Malharganj Asked For

Dhwani Systems and the Insights 2.0 decision

1. Opening

On Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Jayashree Nerurkar sat in a glass meeting room on the fourth floor of Dhwani Systems' office in Bengaluru's Indiranagar and watched a screen recording that she had asked for and did not enjoy. In the recording, a Dhwani field executive held a phone for a provisions-store owner in Indore, Jeetu Narang, and asked him to open the new cash-flow forecast. Mr Narang, fifty-one, looked at a smooth green line curving upward through the next ninety days, said in Hindi that it looked like the stock market, and added that he had customers waiting.

Ms Nerurkar was Dhwani's vice-president of product. Co-founder and chief executive Jatin Nayyar had given her until Friday, 30 October 2026 to confirm how the company would spend the second-half product budget of ₹3.6 crore (₹360 lakh), almost all of it earmarked for "Insights 2.0", a larger analytics suite whose forecast feature the team had loved since January. Diwali falls on 8 November, and the engineering plan needs a start date either way. She had about two weeks to decide whether Dhwani was building for its merchants or for itself.

2. Company background

Dhwani Systems, founded in 2019 by two former product engineers from Bengaluru, sells Dhwani Khata, a billing and ledger app for small shopkeepers. A merchant records a sale, sends a bill by WhatsApp, tracks customer credit (udhaar) and collects by UPI. The company has raised ₹42 crore in venture funding, employs 140 people across Bengaluru, Pune and by September 2026 had 1,20,000 registered merchants. Of these, 41,000 were monthly active (34.2 per cent of registered), and 14,500 paid ₹2,400 a year for the premium plan, which is ₹3.48 crore in annual subscription revenue. The ₹360 lakh budget was therefore slightly more than a year of subscription revenue.

The competitive set is crowded and well known to every Dhwani employee. Khatabook and OkCredit won ledger-keeping with simplicity, Vyapar bundles billing and inventory, and Tally remains the accountants' default. PhonePe for Business and Paytm's Soundbox sit on the counter and already see the UPI money. NPCI's rails make payments close to free, so the contest is over the shopkeeper's daily habit. Dhwani's own advantage had been speed, and the team prided itself on shipping what it found useful.

3. The situation

That last phrase was the problem, though nobody had called it that until recently. Dhwani's product team of 38, all of whom used the app daily as "internal testers", had built the analytics dashboard and the forecast because those were the things they wanted from a business tool. The board demo on 12 January 2026 was a triumph, and Figure 1 sets out the calendar that followed.

Figure 1. Insights 2.0 timeline. Dates are as stated in the text; spacing is not to scale.

In August 2026 the company fielded a merchant survey of 1,200 active shopkeepers, and the data scientist Jasleen Nanda, working from Sydney, put it next to the profile of the internal testers. Exhibit 1 shows the gap. The merchants are older, use ₹8,000 to ₹12,000 Android phones, and mostly run the app in Hindi or another Indian language.

Each location saw it differently: Bengaluru saw momentum, Amsterdam saw beauty, Sydney saw usage data and Indore saw the shop counter.

4. The people

Jayashree Nerurkar, vice-president of product in Bengaluru, owns the decision. She had championed the forecast and uses it herself, which is precisely what worries her.

Jelle Noordhoek, lead designer in Amsterdam, drew the dashboard and is proud of it. He argues that a merchant who has never seen a good chart cannot ask for one, and that Dhwani should lead rather than follow. He has never visited a kirana store.

Jasleen Nanda, data scientist in Sydney, wrote the survey analysis behind Exhibits 1 and 2. She wants a pause but is cautious about overclaiming from usage logs, which show what a merchant did and not why.

Jagannath Nigam, head of field sales in Indore, manages twelve executives who visit shops daily. He wants simple things: Hindi screens, bigger buttons, faster voice. He fears a research pause will leave his team nothing new to sell.

5. The options

Ms Nerurkar identified three distinct courses. Exhibit 3 summarises their costs.

Option A: build Insights 2.0 as specified. The full ₹360 lakh goes to the dashboard, the forecast and an investor-ready analytics story, with a launch on 29 January 2027. The upside is momentum and a polished board narrative. The cost is that the evidence in Exhibit 2 suggests a small audience, and a year of revenue is committed to it.

Option B: translate and localise. Keep the design but translate it into Hindi, Marathi, Telugu and Tamil, at ₹210 lakh, holding ₹150 lakh. This answers the language gap quickly. The cost is that it leaves untouched the question of whether a weekly chart-reader exists among the 92 per cent of merchants (1,104 of 1,200) who do not open one.

Option C: stage the spend behind field research. From Monday, 2 November to Monday, 14 December 2026, six weeks, designers, engineers and the data scientist would sit in 60 shops across Indore, Nagpur, Coimbatore and Lucknow, including through Diwali week. ₹40 lakh funds the research; ₹120 lakh is released in January 2027 against what is learned; ₹200 lakh stays held. The upside is that the money follows evidence. The cost is a delayed launch.

Exhibit 3. The three options against the ₹360 lakh budget.

In Option C, the held-back ₹320 lakh is ₹120 lakh (January tranche) plus ₹200 lakh (reserve). The ₹40 lakh is 11.1 per cent of the ₹360 lakh budget.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, describe the person Dhwani's team has been designing for, and the person it sells to. Why did the team not notice?
  2. Exhibit 2 shows revealed use. What does it prove about the forecast, and what can it not prove? What would Ms Nanda's caution lead you to ask next?
  3. Option B treats the problem as language. Is it? What would have to be true about merchants for translation alone to succeed?
  4. If you were Ms Nerurkar, which option would you confirm on 30 October, and what evidence would make you change course in January?

7. A note for the learner

The self-referential design trap is the habit of treating your own preferences as customer needs. It is hard to spot because everyone in the room likes the thing. The corrective is the plain reminder that you are not the user, and the tools that serve it are personas, segments and jobs-to-be-done, which replace "what I would want" with "what this person is trying to get done".

Here the signs are all present. The testers and merchants differ on every row of Exhibit 1. The feature the company loved most is used by 2.0 per cent of active merchants, while reminders and voice entry were cheap to build and well used. A good answer names the trap, uses the numbers, and does not overcorrect into "the team knows nothing".

One defensible path is Option C. It is the only option that treats the choice as a question about the user before spending against an answer. It commits ₹40 lakh, 11.1 per cent of the budget, to observe the actual jobs: the shopkeeper recording a sale with one hand while serving with the other, chasing credit before Dhanteras, and getting GST paperwork ready for an accountant. Option A bets a year of revenue on the team's own taste; Option B improves the wording on a product that may still be the wrong one. Voice and reminders can keep improving meanwhile, and the visits give Mr Nigam's team customer contact.

The path has conditions. Set in advance what would release the January tranche, for example a clear and repeated merchant job that the forecast serves, and set equally what would redirect the money to voice and language. Put Mr Noordhoek in a shop in Indore, because watching someone use his work is the best argument.
case40v1-cust.self.ref:
The Console and the Karur Clerk

Nirgam Works and the second-half plan, Bengaluru, October 2026

1. Opening: Sunday night

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Sunday, 11 October 2026, Tanaya Chellappa sat at her dining table in Bengaluru's Jayanagar with two printouts on it. In fourteen hours she would commit Nirgam Works' second-half product budget of ₹9.6 crore for the year ending 31 March 2027.

The first was Friday's slide: Nirgam Console 4.0, a shipment control tower with an immutable audit trail, a buyer traceability pack and an analytics page Ms Chellappa opened most mornings. Everyone in the product organisation liked it. She liked it.

The second was a transcript. On Friday, 11 September 2026, Toral Chimanlal, Nirgam's head of customer success, spent three hours at Nilaya Home Textiles in Karur, a ₹6 crore-a-year exporter of table linen. The proprietor, Trilok Chowgule, fifty-six, had passed the customs broker's examination in 1998. Asked to show how he used the product he had paid for over eleven months, he opened WhatsApp — photographs of a packing list, an invoice, a voice note in Tamil about a container at Tuticorin — and only then Nirgam, on the shared desktop, logging in with the password on a Post-it and uploading the same documents so the record would be there if the bank asked. Nine minutes; he never opened the analytics page. What he wanted, he said, was for the product to send those documents to his bank.

What unsettled Ms Chellappa was not that he used the product badly, but that he used it exactly as well as it deserved, and nobody had designed it for him.

2. Nirgam Works: seven and a half years

Nirgam was founded in March 2019 by Thyagarajan Cherukuri, an enterprise-software product manager, and Tirthankar Chakrabarti, an engineer with six years on bank integrations. An Indian exporter's paperwork is a relay — invoice, shipping bill on ICEGATE, bill of lading, then the evidence a bank needs before the Reserve Bank of India's realisation certificate releases the RoDTEP scrip and the IGST refund — and every handoff is where a document goes missing and working capital stalls.

Nirgam's answer was the Console. By 2026 it held 2,128 paying customers and ₹17.39 crore of annual recurring revenue, employed 212 people across Bengaluru, Pune and Coimbatore, and had raised a ₹68 crore Series A on 6 March 2024 led by Nirmaya Partners of Mumbai.

One early decision still governs what can be built. In August 2022, chasing twelve large customers — garment houses in Tiruppur with compliance departments — Nirgam committed to a single canonical shipment record: one object per consignment, every action attributed to a named individual, every change in an append-only log that would satisfy an auditor's inspection. That promise won the accounts, and it means a document cannot enter Nirgam except through an identified user acting on a chosen shipment: a photograph from a shared handset in Karur has nowhere to land. A second decision, in 2024, reserved the ICEGATE and EDPMS integrations — the two things Mr Chowgule wanted — for customers paying above ₹3 lakh a year. Figure 1 gives the sequence.

Figure 1. The decision's timeline; spacing is illustrative.

3. The industry

India's export paperwork sits inside a dense, digital and unforgiving public infrastructure: the Directorate General of Foreign Trade for scrips, ICEGATE and the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs for filing, GSTN for refunds, the RBI for realisation, ECGC for credit insurance, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 over all the data.

The software market around it is fragmented. Nirgam's large customers have usually bought ERP from Infosys or TCS and treat Nirgam as the trade layer on top; the middle runs on TallyPrime and Zoho Books with a broker handling the rest; the bottom, by count almost all of it, runs on WhatsApp, a shared Gmail account and the broker's clerk, and Amazon Global Selling has taught such sellers to expect export paperwork to be free.

Two forces pressed in 2026. European importers were beginning to demand documentary traceability Indian suppliers had never had to produce; and bodies such as the Federation of Indian Export Organisations and the Tiruppur Exporters' Association ran camps where a thousand small exporters could be met in a weekend, which made acquisition look cheap.

4. What happened, and what has turned out wrong

On Monday, 19 January 2026, Nirgam launched Console 3.0 to its customers and its board. It was, by any craft standard, excellent. In the eight and a half months since, two beliefs underneath it have come apart.

The first was that the small-exporter segment was the same product sold cheaper. On Wednesday, 1 April 2026, the board approved a plan to reach 20,000 exporters shipping less than ₹10 crore a year, at ₹24,000 a year, sold through association camps; nineteen field executives were hired on eleven-month contracts. Exhibit 5 shows what the first half produced.

The second was that enthusiasm in the installed base was evidence about the market. On Monday, 17 August 2026, Teresia Chege, data scientist in Nairobi, delivered the cohort analysis behind Exhibits 1, 2 and 4: the segment behaving like the people who built the product is the one that pays, renews and expands. Twenty-five days later came the Karur transcript, which says something else — that small exporters are not failing to understand the product but using a narrow part of it well.

Between the two, on Friday, 3 July 2026, Nordhaven Textiel B.V. of Rotterdam, which buys from 31 of Nirgam's customers, told its Indian suppliers that from 1 April 2027 it would accept shipments only with a per-consignment document trail of the kind the Console's audit log produces. Those 31 accounts carry ₹312 lakh of recurring revenue, 17.9 per cent of the ₹1,739.44 lakh total. Mr Cherukuri circulated it as "the market is coming to us".
