6. The people

Tanaya Chellappa, 34, vice-president of product, Bengaluru, owns the decision. Nirgam, she says, has been designing for its own reflection. Not said: she wrote the analytics specification and is the heaviest user of a feature 12.9 per cent of Exhibit 3's operators open weekly.

Thyagarajan Cherukuri, 41, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru, wants Console 4.0 and the traceability pack: Exhibits 1, 2 and 4 say the money is at the top. Not said: his Series B term sheet conditions on net revenue retention above 100 per cent for the year to 30 September, the blended figure is 101.6 per cent, and Tier C alone drags it down.

Tirthankar Chakrabarti, 43, co-founder and vice-president of engineering, Pune, holds that a WhatsApp-first product is a second platform, not a feature, because the 2022 record demands a named actor and a chosen consignment: twenty-two engineers for seven months. Not said: four of his best engineers will leave if the roadmap becomes document uploads in Tamil.

Tomás Cordeiro, 37, principal designer, Lisbon, cites his July study, in which 26 of 30 participants completed the filing task, 86.7 per cent: people cannot ask for what they have never seen. Not said: participants were screened for English fluency and laptop access — the 17.9 and 21.7 per cent slices of Exhibit 3 — and he has never been to Karur.

Teresia Chege, 31, staff data scientist, Nairobi, produced Exhibits 1, 2, 4 and 6 and footnoted all of them: the panel proves nothing, the five-year cap does the work in the LTV comparison, and the Tier C figures describe a sales motion, not a segment. Not said: she was twice asked for one blended number on a slide, and twice agreed.

Toral Chimanlal, 39, head of customer success, Ahmedabad, has visited 71 small exporters since April: Tier C wants a different object, not less Console. Not said: for five months her team has run an unofficial WhatsApp desk, taking documents from about 400 Tier C customers and uploading them by hand.

Travis Colbeck, 46, head of enterprise sales, Chicago, has eight named targets asking for the traceability pack, against a plan that spent nineteen headcount for 331 customers. His commission is weighted to deals above ₹20 lakh. Not said: two of the eight will wait for Rotterdam to settle.

Tilottama Churi, 50, partner at Nirmaya Partners and a director, led the Series A on a slide about one lakh Indian exporters: the market cannot be 2,128 customers. Not said: the 20,000-customer plan was largely her idea, and her investment committee has not seen Exhibit 5.

7. Voices

"Read Exhibit 2 again. Tier A renews at 96.8 per cent and expands at 128. Tier C loses 596 of 1,254 customers in a year. Tier C is not a software market yet."

Thyagarajan Cherukuri, product review, 2 October 2026

"Or we built a product only a compliance department can use, sold it to people who do not have one, and now read their exit as a verdict on them."

Tanaya Chellappa, same meeting

"Can we stop quoting 44. The panel has three numbers — 74, 48 and 9 — and which one is 'the' score depends on who you have decided the customer is. Weight it to the base and you get 14."

Teresia Chege, internal mail, 5 October 2026

"Mr Chowgule passed the broker's examination in 1998. He knows more about a shipping bill than this floor. He is not confused by our product; he is finished with his work before our product becomes relevant."

Toral Chimanlal, chat thread, 11 September 2026

8. The options as Ms Chellappa sees them

She has three, each spending the whole ₹9.6 crore — 55.2 per cent of annual recurring revenue.

Option A — finish the Console. ₹620 lakh to Console 4.0 and ₹340 lakh to the traceability pack, ₹960 lakh in all, shipping in March 2027 ahead of Nordhaven's deadline. It serves the 73.7 per cent of revenue in Tiers A and B, protects the ₹312 lakh exposed to Rotterdam, and lifts the covenant number. The 20,000-customer plan ends quietly; Exhibit 3 is unanswered.

Option B — build Nirgam Docket. ₹410 lakh to a WhatsApp-first intake that accepts a photograph from a shared handset and routes it, ₹250 lakh to field operations, ₹300 lakh held back, ₹960 lakh in all. It answers Exhibit 3 and Ms Chimanlal's desk, needs the consent and identity layer the DPDP Act and the 2022 undertaking demand — twenty-two engineers for seven months — and bets against the 0.67× in Exhibit 4 without knowing whether that figure belongs to the segment or to how Nirgam sold to it.

Option C — reach Tier C through brokers. ₹180 lakh to a broker portal, ₹120 lakh to decommission the direct motion, ₹660 lakh to the Console, ₹960 lakh in all. A broker serves perhaps forty exporters, so 1,906 Tier C customers imply a few hundred brokers. The user becomes the broker's clerk, paid to file, and perhaps the only one in the chain who wants a dashboard.

The framing has two seams. All three treat Tier C as one segment, when Exhibit 3's 240 operators contain an owner who files his own shipping bills, a clerk who only photographs documents and a firm that exports twice a year — three jobs at one price. And all three ask which user to build for, when Mr Chowgule asked only that his documents reach his bank — a job the Console does, and sells above ₹3 lakh a year.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The budget is committed at the board meeting on Monday, 12 October 2026 and cannot reopen until April. The term sheet lapses on Monday, 30 November 2026 with its retention condition. Nordhaven's requirement begins on 1 April 2027, and Mr Cherukuri has written to the 31 affected customers. The nineteen field contracts end on 31 March 2027; not renewing is cheap, rebuilding that network is not. The 2022 undertaking is a contractual term in the Tier A agreements, which carry ₹684 lakh of ARR. Engineering can staff one platform-scale programme this half-year. And either way the ₹27.74 lakh half-yearly Tier C support bill and Ms Chimanlal's desk continue until named.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. From Exhibit 3, describe the person Nirgam has designed for. Which rows show a design error, and which only that builders and users differ?
  2. Exhibit 6 yields +26, +14 and +44 from one survey. Which is right, and what question is each the right answer to?
  3. Exhibits 2 and 4 say Tier C destroys value, while Exhibit 5's footnote shows its CAC depends on the denominator. What would you need before concluding that nobody can serve Tier C profitably?
  4. Mr Cordeiro's 86.7 per cent and the Karur transcript are both true. Design one study that could tell them apart, and say what result would change your mind.
  5. Suppose Nirgam built for itself. Suppose instead that the segment resembling Nirgam is the right beachhead and going downmarket is the error. What evidence here separates the two readings, and what is missing?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Ms Chellappa commit the ₹9.6 crore to, with what tripwires; what does she tell Ms Churi; and what does she say to Mr Chowgule?

11. Sunday night, continued

By a quarter to one she had drafted three first slides and deleted them. The spreadsheet from Nairobi lay on one side of the table and the Karur transcript on the other, and she could not make them disagree in a way she could take to a board. Every number said the company should finish the product it had; every hour spent watching people use it said the company did not know who it was for. She typed a note and closed the laptop: Ask tomorrow who in this room has ever filed a shipping bill.
exp40v2-cust.jtbd:
Jobs to Be Done

Discovery & Design › Customer Modelling: Segments, Personas, JTBD. Objective: frame demand as the progress a customer is trying to make. The question: what progress is the customer trying to make, regardless of my product?

1. Two decisions, nineteen days apart

On Thursday 5 February 2026, Mrudula Phansalkar, head of product at Odhani Apparel Industries in Pune, was studying a number her founder wanted smaller. Odhani sold women's occasion wear, workwear and separates direct to consumers. In the twelve months to 31 December 2025 it shipped 2,84,000 orders at a blended average order value of ₹2,643 — ₹7,506.12 lakh, or ₹75.06 crore. Of those, 87,330 came back, a return rate of 30.75 per cent, and each cost ₹310 to collect, inspect and repack: ₹270.72 lakh.

Nandita Oak, the founder, wanted the return window shortened. Mrudula hesitated. She had spent January reading 54 switching interviews run by her research lead, Moinak Dasgupta, in Kolkata, which said something awkward: for her best customers, a garment going back was not a failure of the purchase but part of how it worked. Charging for returns would cut orders, not returns. The choice was worth ₹2.40 crore, and the board review was Thursday 9 April 2026, nine weeks later to the day.

Nineteen days later, on Tuesday 24 February 2026, Ovais Lakdawala met the same problem in another shape. As VP Product at Nirukta Practice Systems in Hyderabad he sold appointment, billing and records software to independent physiotherapy and dental clinics: 4,120 paying clinics at ₹1,850 a month, ₹914.64 lakh of annual recurring revenue. Nirukta had lost 1,133 clinics in the year, 27.5 per cent of the base. Ovais suspected the funnel's middle, broken because Nirukta sold three kinds of progress under one name and managed the average. Mrinalini Deshmukh, his co-founder and chief executive, gave him fourteen weeks, to Tuesday 2 June 2026, and ₹1.10 crore if he defended it.

2. The idea, and the four schools that disagree about it

A job to be done is the progress a person or organisation is trying to make in a specific circumstance. The customer hires a product to make it and fires it when something else does better. The unit of analysis is a circumstance paired with a desired outcome. A well-formed statement names no product, feature or demographic: it must survive your company never having existed.

It repairs a defect in segmentation: demographic and attitudinal variables correlate with purchase without causing it. Levitt's quarter-inch hole is the compressed version. Anthony Ulwick built the first operational method in the 1990s as outcome-driven innovation; Bob Moesta and Rick Pedi developed the switching interview; Clayton Christensen gave the canonical framing in The Innovator's Solution (2003) and Competing Against Luck (2016).

Practitioners who share the phrase disagree on what it licenses. The switching-interview school would sign: causation lies in the circumstance, and a few interviews with recent switchers recover it. It would not sign that jobs can be enumerated or scored. The outcome-driven school would sign: a job is a stable functional process decomposing into 50 to 150 measurable desired outcomes, which a survey of several hundred respondents can rate for importance and satisfaction. It would not sign that twenty interviews are evidence, nor that emotional jobs rule. The progress-making-forces school holds that a job is never a task but a desired change in life situation, and rejects outcome lists as feature-thinking by the back door. The category-entry-point school, from the Ehrenberg-Bass tradition associated with Byron Sharp, grants that buying situations are measurable — as cues in brand memory, not deep struggles — and denies that interviews recover causation.

3. Mechanics, including the steps usually left implicit

Expert practice has seven steps; the second, fifth and seventh are the ones amateurs skip. First, sample recent switchers, within sixty days of a purchase, cancellation or refusal, because memory of the deciding moment decays fast. Second, sample those who solved the job without you: 11 of Moinak's 54 interviewees browsed Odhani and then went to a tailor. Third, reconstruct a timeline rather than ask for reasons: first thought, passive and active looking, deciding event, first use. Fourth, code each story into circumstance-outcome form and cluster those sharing both.

Fifth, and this converts a workshop into a decision, attach each cluster to behaviour already recorded, so every job carries a number. Odhani's checkout asked “what is this for?”, with four options Moinak's coding had made meaningful.

Sixth, where the job is a repeatable process, quantify it. For “get paid for work already done without an argument,” Ovais had 212 clinic owners rate desired outcomes for importance and satisfaction out of ten, then computed the opportunity score, importance + max(0, importance − satisfaction). “Cash payments go unrecorded”: 8.8 and 3.1, so 8.8 + 5.7 = 14.5. “Time to know which patients owe money”: 9.1 and 4.2, so 9.1 + 4.9 = 14.0. “Effort of a reminder the patient acts on”: 8.4 and 5.6, so 11.2. “Time to produce a GST-ready statement”: 6.2 and 7.4 — a negative gap floors at zero, opportunity 6.2. Seventh, re-cut the funnel by job: Nirukta's 14,500 trials from the year to 31 March 2025, tracked twelve months past conversion, give Figure 3.

The second-order effect matters most: blended retention is a weighted average, so it moves when the intake's mix changes, though no job is served better. Nirukta's marketing had bought search traffic against slot-filling queries, raising the share of a job served at 33.3 per cent; retention fell; the company funded a reliability programme.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Four testable conditions decide whether the framework earns its cost. One: the customer had an alternative. Where demand is compelled — a statutory filing, an accreditation requirement — there is no hiring decision, only a specification. Two: the purchase has a traceable deciding moment. Habitual purchases leave no timeline, and memory structures explain them better. Three: outcomes vary more than people do. If buyers want the same thing and differ only in willingness to pay, price segmentation works better. Four: behaviour can be attached to each candidate job. Without step five you have a vocabulary, not an analysis.

At Odhani all four hold: Figure 1's alternatives are mostly outside the category. At Nirukta the first fails for the panel job, whose outcome insurers and administrators specify; the clinic chooses only who prepares it. Hence its middling 50.0 per cent: a product serving it competes on compliance accuracy, not insight.

It misleads in three cases. Where supply, not demand, binds, job language dresses a capacity problem as discovery. In fast-moving goods bought in seconds, job statements have failed to out-predict distribution. And in a two-sided market one side's job can be fully served and produce nothing.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Multi-product. When several products serve overlapping jobs, the honest unit is the job, which no product manager owns. At Nirukta, “get paid without an argument” runs through billing, reminders, payments and support: four teams, four roadmaps. Mature companies appoint a job owner holding the metric but no engineers.

Two-sided. The two jobs are asymmetric. Nagara Transit Network's riders wanted not to lose a fare on a missed connection; its bus operators wanted settlement within 48 hours. Serving only the rider job produced trips the operators disliked, and two depots stopped accepting app tickets.

Regulated. Here the job often belongs to neither user nor buyer — for panel claims, the administrator who adjudicates. Write it from the vantage of whoever can refuse, then ask what your user must do to stop being refused. The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission's identifiers, GST invoicing and the DPDP Act's consent rules constrain it first.

Hardware plus software. Mandhan Equipment Works, which makes therapy ultrasound units for the physiotherapists Nirukta serves, has a job clock in years: a clinic hires a machine for a decade. Its product head, Nitin Vaidya, treats software and hardware as separate hires with separate firing conditions: a clinic tolerates a mediocre app on a trusted machine, never the reverse.

AI-native. Where a model does the work, the job collapses from process to outcome; the seam, priced in section 8, is that model quality rather than feature scope becomes the product.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

A return can be part of the purchase, not a defect in it.

The tell is a quality metric that worsens as satisfaction improves. Odhani's occasion job returns at 45 per cent because customers buy fit certainty by ordering alternatives; the same sizing yields 10 per cent on the replacement job. Ask what a metric prices.

The average of a set of jobs is a number nobody experiences.

The tell is a blended target with no owner who can move it: Nirukta's 60.0 per cent retention, Odhani's 30.75 per cent return rate. Both are dominated by mix, and improving mix looks identical in aggregate to improving the product.

Interviews recover circumstances; instruments size them.

The tell is twenty vivid stories and no numbers, or 400 survey responses and no idea why anyone bought. Moinak's 54 interviews told Mrudula what the four checkout options should say; the 2,84,000 orders priced them.

The decisive job is often held by someone who never logs in.

The tell is excellent usage data and inexplicable churn. In Nirukta's clinics the receptionist uses the software and the owner pays; she wants the day to run without conflict, he wants the month to reconcile.

A job only a minority can hold is a segment in disguise.

The tell is a precondition buried in a well-written statement. “Commute without thinking about the fare” presupposes a predictable month and income; for 58 per cent of Nagara's riders neither held. The job was right; its incidence was guessed inside the app.

Firing is more informative than hiring.

The tell is a research programme with no churned customers. Of Ovais's 41 interviews, 18 were with clinics that had left, and those gave the chair-hour finding: what beat Nirukta was a receptionist's WhatsApp waiting list, free and better at judging attendance.

Competing against non-consumption is a different problem.

The tell is a healthy win-rate alongside stalled growth. When the alternative is doing nothing, the obstacle is anxiety and habit, so the right intervention cuts what the customer must commit, not what they get.

Experts write job statements so that they can lose.

The tell is a statement no observation could contradict. “Customers want a seamless experience” cannot fail. “Occasion buyers will accept one guaranteed 48-hour exchange instead of a free return, and the covered return rate will fall from 45 to below 34.6 per cent” can.

7. How this differs by product type and stage

Table 3. Where the difference is real, and where it is not.

Stage changes the constraint, not the method. A company with 40 customers can interview all of them, risking over-fitting to three loud buyers. At Nirukta's scale there is abundant data and almost no contact, so jobs risk becoming a slide that reaches deciders. Mrinalini Deshmukh sat in on six of the 41 interviews, which is why the chair-hour finding survived the sales plan. At enterprise scale the constraint is organisational: reorganise around jobs, or accept that nobody owns the number.

8. Three worked examples

One: Odhani's Event Date Promise. Mrudula proposed capturing the event date at checkout and, for the 14 cities with same-city exchange capacity — 60 per cent of occasion orders, 59,640 a year — guaranteeing delivery six days early plus one free exchange inside 48 hours. An exchange costs ₹190, not ₹310, the replacement shipping on the pickup leg.

Downside: logistics cost rises ₹4.17 lakh, exchanges added without returns falling far enough, and 5,964 extra kept orders are worth ₹119.40 lakh, netting exactly ₹1,15,22,448 — ₹115.22 lakh, where the rounded rows would give ₹115.23.

Two: Nagara Transit Network, the failure and the recovery. Nagara ran a bus-ticketing app in Indore and Nagpur with 1,80,000 monthly active riders and 3,10,000 ticketed trips a month — 1.72 trips per rider — earning a ₹2 fee per ticket: ₹6.20 lakh a month, ₹74.40 lakh a year. Narmada Krishnan, its head of product, ran 44 in-app-recruited interviews and coded one job: “commute without thinking about the fare.” Nagara spent ₹1.85 crore from January to June 2025 on a pass and trip planner, launched Monday 2 June 2025, targeting 12 per cent of riders: 21,600 buyers at ₹900 a month on a ₹90 margin, ₹19.44 lakh a month. Take-up was 2.5 per cent — 4,500 buyers, ₹4.05 lakh a month, a fifth of target.

The diagnosis was sampling, not coding. Of the 44 interviewees, 38 held salaried jobs and all had data plans, while 58 per cent of riders earned irregularly, and a ₹900 pass demands certainty the modal rider lacks. Thirty riders re-interviewed at bus stops in July 2025 gave another circumstance: “when the bus I need does not come, I do not want to lose the fare I already paid.” The recovery, to March 2026, was a free second leg within 45 minutes, cash top-ups at 1,250 kirana counters and a ₹20 minimum wallet, costing ₹62 lakh. Trips rose from 3,10,000 to 5,27,000 a month, exactly 70 per cent, lifting fee revenue from ₹74.40 lakh to ₹126.48 lakh a year, while pass buyers drifted to 6,300, or 3.5 per cent, adding ₹19.44 lakh of margin. Incremental contribution of ₹71.52 lakh a year repaid the ₹62 lakh recovery in 10.4 months. The ₹1.85 crore needs a further 2.59 years; Nagara wrote it off.

Three: Nirukta's panel drafter. Nirukta offered its 203 retained panel-job clinics a model that drafts the claim narrative from session notes; 147 enabled it, 72.4 per cent. Those clinics average 50 panel claims a month, so 7,350 claims, and rejections fell from 18 to 12 per cent — 1,323 to 882, a fall of 441, or one third. At ₹1,450 a claim that releases ₹6.39 lakh a month, ₹4,350 per clinic, 2.9 times what they paid Nirukta. Repricing the panel tier from ₹1,500 to ₹2,400 then took these clinics' monthly revenue from ₹2,20,500 to ₹3,18,000 — 118 accepted, 29 reverted to the ₹1,200 base tier — up 44.2 per cent, or ₹11.70 lakh a year.

9. Failure modes, their early signs and the cost of lateness

Rewriting the persona in job language. Sign: statements opening with an age or a role. Diagnostic: delete every demographic word and see whether the sentence still asserts anything. Caught late: the same roadmap, better rhetoric.

Smuggling the solution in. Sign: the job mentions an interface. Diagnostic: could someone who had never heard of your product hold it? Caught late, you have specified a feature and validated it against itself.

Sampling the reachable. Sign: every interviewee came from a channel you own. Diagnostic: what share chose something else? Cost: ₹1.85 crore.

Coding one job per customer. Sign: every story fits one narrative. Diagnostic: count distinct circumstances; fewer than four in 40 interviews means leading questions.

Leaving jobs unattached to data. Sign: the output is a deck, not a column in a table. Diagnostic: can you state each job's share of revenue and its retention?

Managing the blend. Sign: an improvement target with no owner. Diagnostic: if the mix froze, would the number still move? The most expensive late catch: reliability programmes aimed at mix problems consume quarters and fix nothing.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Can an interview recover causation? The switching-interview school says yes: decisions have a structure, and a timeline interview recovers it, because people report what happened even when they rationalise why. Its evidence is a record of such interventions that worked. The Ehrenberg-Bass reply is that retrospective accounts are reconstructions, purchase is driven by availability and memory, and the successes are selected after the fact. It would be wrong if job-interview designs beat category-entry-point designs in matched tests, which nobody has run.

Is a job stable and enumerable? Ulwick's school holds that the functional job is stable for decades while solutions churn, which makes outcome lists worth building; its evidence is the durability of job maps in medical devices. The progress-making-forces school calls that stability an artefact of mechanical categories, holding that in consumer software the desired progress shifts as the possible changes. It would be wrong if today's opportunity scores still ranked the same in five years.

How many jobs does a product serve? One camp holds that a focused product serves one, and multiplicity signals drift. The other holds that a platform necessarily serves several, and forcing one destroys real revenue: Odhani's two largest jobs are 72.4 per cent of it. It turns on whether the jobs share a delivery mechanism.

Do emotional jobs decide, or decorate? The interview school points to purchases that make no functional sense without them. The outcome school replies that emotional language is unmeasurable and so unmanageable, and that where emotion matters it surfaces as an outcome about effort or risk.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this produces job statements. Someone who has internalised it changes what they measure: they insist on interviews with people who chose otherwise, and count them; they write statements a named observation could falsify; and they say aloud what the framework cannot settle — price, incidence, willingness to pay — rather than letting a quotation stand in for a number.

12. The decisions, and three questions

On Thursday 9 April 2026, Mrudula did not ask for ₹2.40 crore. She asked for ₹38 lakh to run the Event Date Promise in four of the 14 cities for one wedding season, with a pre-committed criterion: the covered return rate must fall below 34.6 per cent. Table 4's columns imply a net benefit of 597.83 − 1,378.88r in ₹ lakh, so the ₹120 lakh a year that repays ₹240 lakh in two years needs r = 34.65 per cent. Her reasoning: the 45 per cent rate is a price customers pay for fit certainty, so the only interventions worth funding supply certainty more cheaply than three parcels do — and Table 4's weakest number is a behavioural assumption a pilot can price.

On Tuesday 2 June 2026, Ovais asked for the full ₹1.10 crore to rebuild onboarding around the get-paid job, so a clinic's first session ends with a reconciled list of who owes money, not a configured calendar. His model: onboarding completion rises from 35.0 to 45.0 per cent, giving 6,525 onboarded of 14,500 trials; conversion holds at 40.0 per cent, giving 2,610 paid, 18.0 per cent of trials; retention at twelve months rises to 70.0 per cent as the mix shifts, giving 1,827 retained against 1,218, a gain of 609 or 50.0 per cent. At ₹2,000 ARPA that is ₹438.48 lakh of retained ARR against ₹274.05 lakh — up ₹164.43 lakh, payback in 8.0 months. The downside: dropping slot-filling from the pitch could cut trials from 14,500 to 12,000, a fall of 17.2 per cent, leaving 1,512 retained — still 294 more than today, ₹362.88 lakh of ARR, ₹88.83 lakh of improvement, payback in 14.9 months. Both clear the hurdle.

Three questions. First: Odhani's occasion and gift jobs both return at 45 per cent, for different reasons. One problem or two, and what in Table 1 settles it? Second: Nirukta's chair-hour job retains at 33.3 per cent against a free, human competitor. Serve it better, stop selling to it, or stop measuring it — and what does each do to the blended 60.0 per cent? Third: Narmada's job statement was correct and her product failed. If the error was incidence, not insight, what should she have measured before spending ₹1.85 crore?

13. Going deeper

  • Why personas — what this reacts against, and what jobs add.
  • Functional, emotional and social jobs — the layers section 10 argues over.
  • Forces of progress: push, pull, anxiety, habit — why a real job yields no switch.
  • Pains and gains — lighter vocabulary linking jobs to a value proposition.
  • Customer journey mapping — the job's timeline, instrumented.
  • Writing a problem hypothesis — makes a statement a pilot can falsify.
  • Competing on the job, not the category — the strategy Figure 1 implies.
  • Job hierarchies and job maps — the decomposition behind opportunity scores.
  • Market segments vs personas — how the three coexist.
  • The self-referential design trap — what produced Nagara's planner.
  • Anatomy of a persona — what keeps it compatible with job evidence.
  • Building personas from research — the sampling discipline Nagara lacked.
  • AI-assisted persona synthesis — models on corpora, without laundering assumptions.
  • Service blueprints — for jobs spanning people and systems.
exp20v2-cust.jtbd:
Jobs to Be Done

Discovery & Design, Customer Modelling. The question this page answers: what progress is the customer trying to make, regardless of my product?

1. A product that was loved by the wrong description

On Tuesday, 14 July 2026, Dipti Rajadhyaksha, head of product at Eklavya Skills Network, opened a spreadsheet she did not enjoy reading. Eklavya sold online courses in spreadsheets, data analysis and business writing to working adults, at a flat ₹9,000 per course. In the previous twelve months it had sold 12,000 courses, or ₹10.8 crore (1,080 lakh) of revenue. Yet only 5,076 of those 12,000 buyers had finished, a completion rate of 42.3 per cent, and the chief executive, Eshaan Trivedi, wanted a plan for the board on Friday, 31 July.

The company's working picture of its customer was a persona called "Priya": 28, an analyst in Bengaluru, ambitious, short of time, comfortable on her phone. Eshaan's proposal followed from Priya. Shorten every course into ten-minute lessons, add streaks and badges, and send nudges at nine in the evening. Dipti doubted it, because Priya described who the buyers were but said nothing about why a person pays ₹9,000 and then stops opening the app. Before the board meeting, she and her research lead, Farhan Qureshi, spent the ten days from 15 to 24 July interviewing 48 recent buyers. At stake was whether to spend two quarters of engineering on engagement mechanics for Priya or on something else; a wrong guess would burn roughly 120 lakh and leave the completion problem untouched.

2. The idea

A job, in this framework, is the progress a person is trying to make in a particular circumstance. A customer does not buy a product for its own sake. The customer "hires" it, as one hires a person, to make that progress, and "fires" it when something else does the work better. The analytic unit is therefore not the customer and not the product but the pairing of a circumstance with a desired change.

The idea was invented to repair a weakness in conventional segmentation. Demographic and attitudinal profiles (age, income, city, "ambitious") correlate with purchases but rarely explain them. Two people who match on every demographic can buy for opposite reasons, and two people who look nothing alike can buy for the same one. The Harvard Business School professor Clayton Christensen and his collaborators, including Anthony Ulwick, who built the "outcome-driven innovation" method in the 1990s, and Bob Moesta, who developed the interview technique, shaped the idea through the 1990s and early 2000s. Christensen popularised it with the milkshake study, in which commuters were found to hire a milkshake to make a boring drive bearable and keep hunger away until mid-morning. Its competitors were bananas, bagels and boredom.

Dipti's one-sentence version, for the meeting: "We should stop asking who our buyer is and start asking what she is trying to get done that day, because that is what she is actually paying for."

3. How it works, step by step

The mechanics have five steps, two of which practitioners often leave implicit. The first is to choose whom to talk to: recent buyers, within roughly sixty days of the purchase, because memory of the moment of decision fades quickly. Farhan chose 48 from the 12,000, deliberately mixing finishers and abandoners. The second step, usually unstated, is to include people who considered Eklavya and bought nothing, since a job is easiest to see where it was served by something else. Farhan added buyers who had cancelled before the first lesson.

The third step is the interview itself. It reconstructs a timeline: the first thought that something was missing, the passive search, the active search, the deciding moment, the first use. Each interviewee is asked what else they considered, including doing nothing. The fourth step is coding: each story is reduced to a job statement in the three-part form of Figure 1, and stories that share a circumstance and an outcome are grouped. The fifth, again often implicit, is to measure each group on behaviour the company already holds, such as completion, refunds and repeat purchase, so that a job is tied to evidence of how well the current product serves it.

At Eklavya the coding produced three jobs. In the first, the buyer was changing roles: "When I have decided to leave my current line of work, I want proof that I can do the new one, so that an interviewer will take me seriously." In the second, the buyer was keeping up: "When my team adopts a tool I do not know, I want to catch up quietly, so that no one sees me struggle." In the third, the buyer was seeking recognition: "When my appraisal is approaching, I want a visible credential, so that my manager has something to point to." Priya fitted all three.

4. A worked example, with a second pass

Farhan then mapped all 12,000 buyers onto the three jobs, using each buyer's answer to the order-form question "why this course?". The result is in Table 1. Every revenue figure is buyers multiplied by ₹9,000; every completion figure is buyers multiplied by the completion rate.

Table 1. Eklavya buyers by job, last twelve months
JobBuyersShare of buyersRevenue (₹ lakh)Completion rateCompleters
Change roles5,04042%453.625%1,260
Keep up3,96033%356.460%2,376
Earn recognition3,00025%270.048%1,440
Total / average12,000100%1,080.042.3% (avg)5,076

Completion for the total row is 5,076 divided by 12,000. Revenue of 1,080 lakh equals ₹10.8 crore.

The table overturns the premise of the board paper. The weakest completion, 25 per cent, sits with the largest group, the role-changers, who were not short of discipline so much as short of an outcome a ten-minute lesson could deliver: an interviewer wants evidence of a portfolio, and a badge is not one. Streaks would help the keep-up buyers, but they already finished at 60 per cent. Engagement mechanics aimed at the average, 42.3 per cent, would have been aimed at nobody.

Now the decision. Dipti proposed a "Career Switch" bundle at ₹15,000: a portfolio project, two mentor reviews and a recruiter-facing certificate. Delivery would cost ₹4,000 per learner against ₹1,500 for a standard course, so contribution (price less delivery cost) is ₹11,000 against ₹7,500, an increment of ₹3,500 for each role-changer who takes the bundle instead of the standard course. Building it would cost ₹1.2 crore, or 120 lakh. If 40 per cent of the 5,040 role-changers take it, that is 2,016 learners and an increment of 2,016 × ₹3,500 = ₹70.56 lakh a year. Payback is 120 ÷ 70.56 = 1.70 years.

Second pass. Change one input only: take-up, from 40 to 60 per cent. Then 3,024 learners generate 3,024 × ₹3,500 = ₹105.84 lakh a year, and payback falls to 120 ÷ 105.84 = 1.13 years. Everything turns on whether role-changers feel a deadline. The interviews suggested that they did, because nine of the twenty role-changers Farhan interviewed named a specific application date. That is evidence, not proof.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

A job is not a task, and not a feature.

"Complete module 3" is a task; "have something to show an interviewer" is a job. The test is abstraction: a job survives the removal of your product. If the statement only makes sense inside your app, you have described a feature wish.

A job is not a segment.

One person holds many jobs at different times, and one job is held by many kinds of people. A buyer who keeps up in March may change roles in November. Segments describe people; jobs describe moments, which is why a job can be targeted but a person cannot be "assigned" one.

Functional, emotional and social jobs coexist.

The keep-up buyer has a functional job (learn the tool), an emotional one (not feel anxious) and a social one (not be seen struggling). The last two commonly decide the purchase.

Circumstance matters more than characteristics.

The same appraisal-season buyer behaves differently in October and in May. Record when, where and what had just happened; the trigger often explains more than any attribute.

The competitor is whatever else gets the job done.

For the role-changers, Eklavya's rivals included a friend's referral, a free YouTube playlist, an unpaid internship and inertia. Defining competition by category under-counts the field.

Interviews are retrospective and therefore biased.

People reconstruct decisions to sound sensible. Anchor on concrete facts and be sceptical of tidy motives. Twenty role-changers is a signal to test, not a population estimate.

What it cannot tell you.

It does not size a market, set a price or prove willingness to pay. Table 1 relied on company data to attach numbers to the jobs, and the ₹15,000 price remains a hypothesis until someone pays it.

Questions to ask before relying on it.

Are the interviewees recent buyers or convenient friends? Does every job statement survive without the product name? Is there behavioural evidence that separates the groups? If the answers are no, you are doing persona work with new vocabulary.

6. How it differs by product type and company stage

Table 2. Where the job sits in different products
SettingWho holds the jobWhat changes
ConsumerOne person, often with an emotional or social job often dominantTriggers are life events; interviews are short and honest
B2BSeveral people, each with a different job on one purchaseThe user, the buyer and the approver must be interviewed separately
MarketplaceTwo sides, each with its own jobA job on one side is only served if the other side shows up

In a B2B product, an HR head purchasing Eklavya for 300 employees has a job (show the board that the firm invests in skills) quite different from that of the employee who must use it. Interviewing only users would miss the purchaser's job entirely. In a marketplace such as a freelance-tutor platform, the tutor's job (fill empty evening hours) and the learner's job (clear a test on a fixed date) interact: neither is served unless both are.

Stage also matters. An early-stage company with twenty customers can interview all of them. A large company has more data but less contact, and the risk is that jobs get delegated to a research team and reach product managers as a slide. The remedy is for deciders to sit in on a few interviews.

7. Common mistakes

Describing the user again. The symptom is a "job statement" that opens with "As a 28-year-old...". The misunderstanding is treating the framework as a new template for the persona. The cheapest diagnostic: delete every demographic word and see if the sentence still means something.

Smuggling in the solution. The symptom is a job like "I want a mobile course with streaks". The underlying error is writing down what the team already intends to build. Diagnostic: ask whether a person who had never heard of your product could hold this job.

Stopping at one job per customer. The symptom is a roadmap serving one tidy story, though people hire products for several jobs. Diagnostic: count the distinct stories among your interviews; if every one matches, the questions were leading.

Interviewing the happy. The symptom is glowing quotes and unchanged metrics. Satisfied loyalists rarely recall the original struggle. Diagnostic: check what share of interviewees abandoned or nearly did.

8. What good looks like

A well-run version of this decision would have looked like Dipti's, with one addition. She would arrive at the board with three job statements, a table tying each to completion and revenue, and a pilot proposal rather than a promise. She would also say what the framework did not settle: the price, the size of take-up, and whether recruiters would honour the certificate. A good session leaves the board debating those uncertainties, not Priya's taste for streaks.

9. Closing

On 31 July, Dipti did not ask for 120 lakh. She asked the board for a 20-lakh pilot of the Career Switch bundle with 300 role-changers and a stated trigger: if take-up reached 50 per cent, the full build would begin. Her reasoning: the jobs are served so unequally that one engagement programme would target an average no one lives in, and the ₹15,000 price, the weakest assumption, could be tested cheaply.

The natural next topic is the distinction between functional, emotional and social jobs, since the keep-up buyers' anxiety was invisible to the first coding. After that, the forces of progress (push, pull, anxiety, habit) explain why a person with a job still does not buy.

Two questions to sit with. First: think of a product you used this month, and write the job statement without naming it; what else could have done that job? Second: Eklavya's role-changers completed at 25 per cent. Is that a failure of the product, or evidence that the course was never the whole job?
case40v1-cust.jtbd:
Trinetra Diagnostics Network: What Is the Report For?

A teaching case for discussion. Jobs to Be Done is the lens, not the answer.

1. Sunday night, 18 October 2026

The Ahmedabad office of Trinetra Diagnostics Network was empty except for the receiving bay two floors down, where Sunday's collections were being logged. Tejal Vaidya, Chief Product Officer, had the room to herself and one slide she had rewritten eleven times. At half past nine next morning she was to put the FY2027 plan before the board's product sub-committee: ₹9.60 crore and thirty-four engineers, against four proposals wanting ₹15.60 crore and sixty-eight engineers.

The slide was titled "What the customer is hiring us for". Beneath it she had written four sentences and deleted all four. Evidence was not the problem: in four months Trinetra had run 112 interviews, a survey of 4,800 households, a twelve-month cohort analysis and a continuous in-app survey. The instruments disagreed about why anyone came back — and the option the chief executive had half-promised the largest investor was the one the cohort treated least kindly.

2. Nine years, and one decision that will not let go

Trinetra was founded in Ahmedabad in 2017 by Umang Tirodkar, who had spent eight years in last-mile logistics, and Dr Urvi Talwar, a pathologist from Rajkot. The idea was narrow and good: a phlebotomist on a two-wheeler, dispatched like a courier, drawing a sample in the patient's drawing room at seven in the morning. By 2026 it ran five processing laboratories and a collection network across five states.

Two early decisions shaped what followed. The first was commercial. On 1 April 2020, short of capital and facing a pandemic, Trinetra signed a seven-year exclusive processing agreement with Udgaar Pathology Industries, which performs all specialised assays at fixed per-test fees against a twenty-four-hour turnaround. It expires on 31 March 2027. Six and a half years in, it is why the cost per test is predictable and why it cannot be cut this year.

The second was architectural, and it was the one keeping Tejal awake. In 2021, to satisfy insurer panels and to stay clear of the line between testing and diagnosing, Trinetra rebuilt ordering around a doctor's prescription: an order begins with a photograph of one, the test menu follows from it, and the report goes to the prescribing doctor. The decision won three insurer panels. It also left the data model with no notion of a test ordered without a prescription, none of the same person tested repeatedly over years, and none of an account holder who is not the patient. Every option on Monday's slide runs into one of those absences.

3. The industry around it

Indian diagnostics in 2026 is a market where everybody can reach the doorstep. Dr Lal PathLabs and Metropolis Healthcare bring brand and accreditation; Thyrocare competes on price per panel; Redcliffe Labs and Healthians sell bundled "full body" packages; Apollo 24|7, Tata 1mg and PharmEasy attach a test to a consultation or a medicine order.

The rules matter as much as the rivals. Laboratories need NABL accreditation, which Trinetra holds at all five sites, and diagnostic services are exempt from GST, so input credits cannot be set against output tax. ABHA identifiers under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission are turning a report into a record that follows the patient — easier for Trinetra to build on, and for a rival. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 has made consent a board matter: a son in Doha cannot simply be handed his mother's reports because he paid for them. Roughly one order in nine is paid from outside India, mostly by adult children in the Gulf, North America and Australia arranging tests for parents in Indore, Nagpur and Jaipur. They pay without arguing and ask for a call afterwards, a comparison with last year, and an explanation of what a number means.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

For nine years the strategy had one sentence: be the fastest reliable way to get a prescribed test done at home. The pandemic validated it — volumes tripled and "report by evening" sold itself — and the lesson has not been revisited: speed is the product.

FY2026 closed on 31 March 2026 with revenue of ₹157.282 crore across 12,40,000 orders and an EBITDA loss of ₹24.562 crore. In April 2026 the board set a FY2028 target of ₹300 crore with positive contribution after product spend and fixed the FY2027 envelope at ₹9.60 crore. Tejal, who had joined that January from a payments company, asked for four months to learn what customers were buying before she spent it.

Exhibit 2 was the first surprise. J1, the job the company was built around, produced 49.4 per cent of orders at the thinnest margin of the three consumer jobs. J3 produced 10.8 per cent of orders at 42.9 per cent margins on an order nearly twice the size. J4, which Vineet Umrigar's team had been celebrating, gave ₹166.40 lakh of the ₹5,213.80 lakh total, or 3.2 per cent of contribution from 16.8 per cent of orders. Nor could anyone agree how big the jobs were.

Read naively, Exhibit 3 makes the caregiver job either a quarter of the business or a twelfth of it. Read carefully, it says something worse: the job is small counted as new households and large counted as households still here.

The cohort upset the company's self-image: the job Trinetra was built for keeps barely one household in five. J2 and J3 together are 62,400 of the 2,42,000 first-time households, or 25.8 per cent, and ₹3,543.79 lakh of the ₹5,878.11 lakh of twelve-month revenue, which is 60.3 per cent. Exhibit 5, quoted by growth in every review for two years, says the opposite.

By Exhibit 5, J1 is the happiest customer; by Exhibit 4, J1 is the one who leaves. Exhibit 6 adds a third frame: how households arrive.

The interviews produced something no exhibit captures. Asked what they had fired, households named different incumbents: the collection centre and the outpatient queue for J1; a free blood-pressure machine at the chemist, a diary, or nothing at all for J2; a cousin who could take Amma to the lab for J3. Asked what they did when the report came, more than half of the J2 and J3 interviewees described the same defeat: they could not tell whether anything had changed, and either rang a doctor or let it go.

5. The people in the room on Monday

Umang Tirodkar, co-founder and chief executive, works from Mumbai and spends his week with investors. He wants the same-day promise, because a Series C conversation needs one sentence. He is not saying that he has already told Trayi Capital Partners, who led the Series B, that Trinetra is "largely done building" it.

Dr Urvi Talwar, co-founder and Chief of Lab Medicine in Ahmedabad, is hostile to the care plan: a trend chart implying a diagnosis puts a laboratory where none should be. She is not saying that two of her laboratories missed the twenty-four-hour turnaround on one order in six last January.

Vaibhav Udeshi, VP Growth in Bengaluru, holds that the prescription-led customer is cheapest to acquire and that chasing retention in this category is a fantasy. His variable pay rides on first orders. He is not saying that his cost per first order has risen for five quarters, nor that Exhibit 5 is his team's instrument.

Trisha Venkatraman, Head of Customer Research in Chennai, believes the company has mistaken its most frequent transaction for its most valuable job. She is not saying loudly enough that her panel came from recent orderers, or that she has no evidence about caregiver households outside it.

Vipin Tulpule, VP Engineering in Pune, is the only one who can price the options, and prefers the same-day work: a routing problem his team has solved. He is not saying that the family account is, privately, two quarters of consent plumbing dressed as one, because the schema binds a patient to an account.

Tripti Vasavada, Principal Data Scientist, works from Melbourne and talks to Ahmedabad at seven in the morning her time. She built the cohort and defends it. Outside her appendix she does not volunteer that the job labels came from a classifier which, on a hand-coded sample, agreed with the human coder on 1,920 of 2,400 orders, or 80.0 per cent — so one order in five in Exhibits 2, 3 and 4 may be in the wrong job.

Vineet Umrigar, Head of Enterprise in Gurugram, has the company's only contracted revenue: ₹9.40 crore a year from Udyot Business Services, whose forty-one thousand employees take an annual panel. It obliges Trinetra to deliver an employer portal by 31 March 2027, against ₹1.20 crore of damages. He has already shown Udyot a design, which he has not mentioned.

6. Voices

"Fifty-three per cent of our customers rate us nine or ten. The prescription customer rates us sixty-two. You want to spend the year building for the one who rates us forty-four." — Vaibhav Udeshi, product review, 2 October 2026
"My mother is seventy-four, in Nagpur, and I am in Doha. I do not want a faster report. I want to know whether she is worse than in April, in one sentence." — interview transcript 61, August 2026
"Every option on your slide is a feature. Which changes what a customer would say they hired us to do?" — Tripti Vasavada, chat message, 17 October 2026

7. The four options, as Tejal currently frames them

Option A defends the brand, the chief executive's narrative and the largest body of orders. It aims at the job with a 22.0 per cent twelve-month repeat rate, in cities where Dr Lal PathLabs and Apollo 24|7 can also be fast, and it wants laboratory headroom in the window when employer panels fill the machines. The five laboratories process 12,500 tests a day; FY2026's 12,40,000 orders carried 29,76,000 tests, an average of 8,153 a day, or 65.2 per cent of capacity — but the January peak ran at 11,900 a day, or 95.2 per cent.

Option B aims at the best repeat rate and the second-best margin, and is the one Dr Talwar will contest clinically; at eight months it lands in June 2027, after the Udgaar contract has been renegotiated or lost. Option C is the cheapest consumer option and aims at the highest-margin job — the one whose size nobody can state: 23.0 per cent of surveyed households, 10.8 per cent of orders, 8.2 per cent of new households. It needs consent machinery the DPDP Act makes unavoidable and the schema makes expensive. Option D is barely a product decision.

What Tejal has not written is that the four-way framing may itself be the error. All four are features bolted to existing segments, and none answers the sentence that recurred in the interviews: nobody tells me what the number means. If that is the job — interpretation, not collection — it cuts across J1, J2 and J3, and would make Trinetra a different company.

8. The deadline and the hard constraints

The sub-committee meets at 9.30 on Monday, 19 October 2026 and expects a funded plan; Uttam Thakar, the chief financial officer, says the envelope will not reopen in December. FY2027 spend is capped at ₹9.60 crore and 34 engineers, and no option can be half-funded without losing its launch window. The Udgaar agreement expires on 31 March 2027, with a one-month renegotiation window opening on 1 January 2027; until then per-test fees are fixed, so no variable cost in Exhibit 2 can move. The Udyot portal is owed by 31 March 2027 against ₹1.20 crore of damages, and the DPDP Act governs any product that shows one adult another's reports. Trinetra held ₹38.90 crore of cash on 30 September 2026; at FY2026's burn of ₹24.562 crore, or ₹2.05 crore a month, that is about nineteen months.

9. Questions for discussion

  1. State each job as a circumstance, a motivation and a desired outcome, naming no Trinetra feature. For each, what is the household firing in order to hire Trinetra?
  2. Exhibit 3 gives three sizes for the caregiver job. Which denominator is right for a roadmap decision, and what would you measure to size that job outside Trinetra's own customers?
  3. Exhibits 4 and 5 point in opposite directions. Reconcile them. What does the in-app survey measure, and what would you change before using it again?
  4. Variable costs are fixed until 31 March 2027, and the budget is committed before the renegotiation window opens. How should that sequencing change which option you fund?
  5. The classifier agrees with human coders on 80.0 per cent of orders. If one order in five is mislabelled, which conclusions in Exhibits 2, 3 and 4 survive, and what test would you run to find out?
  6. It is Monday morning. What do you fund, what do you refuse, what do you measure to know within a quarter that you were wrong — and what do you say to a board told the six-hour promise is "largely done"?

10. Half past eleven

Tejal read the slide title again: what the customer is hiring us for. On the whiteboard behind her somebody from growth had drawn the funnel from Exhibit 6, the 8.05 per cent circled twice in red. Beside it, in her own hand from Friday, were four words from interview transcript 61: whether she is worse. Downstairs the receiving bay logged the last of Sunday's samples, every one a prescription photographed by somebody who wanted something the prescription did not say. She had nine hours, four options, three sizings of one job, two exhibits that contradicted each other, one classifier she had not stress-tested, and a chief executive who had already used the word "done" in a room she had not been in.
case20v1-cust.jtbd:
Hamraah Learning Systems: Hired for What?

A short teaching case on Jobs to Be Done

1. Opening

On the evening of Tuesday, 20 October 2026, Garima Gadkari stayed at her desk in Hamraah Learning Systems' Pune office after the others had left for the Diwali sweets hamper being handed out downstairs. As Head of Product, she had until Friday, 30 October to freeze the second-half roadmap. The board had approved a ceiling of ₹100 lakh for it. Three proposals sat on her screen, each backed by someone she respected, and no two of them could be funded together.

What troubled her was not a shortage of data. It was that the same twelve hundred customers had told the company three different things about why they paid. Before she chose a feature, she needed to decide what job the app was actually being hired to do.

2. Company background

Hamraah was founded in 2019 by two former teachers and an engineer. Its app lets a student in Classes 9 to 12 photograph a stuck question from a CBSE or state-board textbook and receive a worked, step-by-step solution, typically within four minutes, from a pool of 900 part-time tutors backed by search and automation. The annual plan costs ₹2,400, and almost all buyers are parents paying through UPI. By September 2026 Hamraah had 1,85,000 paying households, which at ₹2,400 each is annual subscription revenue of ₹44.4 crore.

The category is crowded. Doubtnut offers a similar photo-to-solution flow, PhysicsWallah sells low-priced live batches, Vedantu sells live tuition, and Google Lens answers a surprising share of questions for nothing. Hamraah had always described itself as "India's fastest doubt-solving app", and every roadmap since 2021 had been a variation on one idea: be faster than the others.

3. The situation

In August, Garima commissioned a research sprint. Ishrat Naqvi, the customer research lead, interviewed and surveyed 1,200 paying households, asking one deliberately plain question: "What was the main thing you were trying to get done the last time you opened Hamraah?" Answers were coded into four jobs. The coding, shown in Exhibit 1, surprised the team. A job counts only if the customer describes a situation and an outcome, not a feature request.

The largest group, 34 per cent, used the app exactly as the company had always imagined: a student with a question and a deadline. But Ishrat also tracked who renewed after twelve months, and Exhibit 2 shows a different ranking.

The job that attracts the most households keeps the fewest. A student unstuck on homework gets an answer and leaves; nothing about tonight's question creates a reason to be there next April. Households hiring Hamraah for revision and for tuition replacement renew at three in four. Hugo Ferreira, the data scientist working from Lisbon, added a pattern that the survey could not show: the revision users cluster in the fortnight before unit tests, and in January and February before the board examinations, when usage runs at several times the normal level. Exhibit 3 places these moments in the academic year.

4. The people

Hasan Merchant, head of growth, based in Mumbai, argues that the 34 per cent are the heart of the business. Acquisition costs are lowest among students who arrive with a question in hand, and a rival that answers in ninety seconds would take them.

Harshad Kopparam, engineering lead in Hyderabad, would rather do something he can ship in a quarter. He points out that the answer pipeline has a known bottleneck and the work is well understood.

Ishrat Naqvi, working from Lucknow, believes the survey proves that the company has misread its customer, and wants the roadmap built around revision and the exam calendar. She is also candid that she cannot say how far the 336 revision households can be scaled.

Irene Kamau, who runs support from Nairobi for the late-evening queue, hears a recurring parental complaint: "I pay, but I never know what he is doing." Hugo Ferreira in Lisbon sits between camps, offering to model any option the others can specify.

5. The options

The three proposals are summarised in Exhibit 4. Any two together would exceed the ₹100 lakh ceiling: 60 plus 45 is 105, 45 plus 90 is 135, and 60 plus 90 is 150.

Option A defends the largest group and the brand promise, and Harshad is confident of delivery. Its cost is that it improves the job with the weakest renewal; a faster answer does not make a student come back next year, and Google Lens may be free but is also fast. Option B is the cheapest and answers Irene's callers. Its risk is that it serves reassurance rather than progress, and a report on a child who is not improving may only sharpen the parent's doubt. Option C reaches the two best-renewing groups and ties Hamraah to the moments the family cares most about. It consumes nearly the entire ₹100 lakh and takes six months, so a build begun in November would finish in May 2027 and miss the January peak altogether.

6. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, state each of the four jobs as a situation, a motivation and an outcome, without naming a feature. What is the customer "firing" when she hires Hamraah for each?

2. Why might the largest job produce the weakest renewal? What would you need to learn about the 408 homework households before treating that as settled?

3. Hamraah calls itself the fastest doubt-solving app. Compete against which alternatives for the revision job? Who is the competitor when the job is reassurance?

4. Which option would you fund, with what test before full commitment, and what would change your mind?

7. A note for the learner

Jobs to Be Done asks what progress the customer is trying to make, regardless of the product. The usual segmentation of Hamraah would have produced "Class 10 CBSE student, urban, mobile-first", which tells a team who is buying but not why the purchase recurs. Reading demand as jobs separates four different reasons for paying, and exposes that the loudest reason is also the most perishable. The mistake the case invites is to equate size with value; another is to treat the survey as a verdict, when 504 households is a small base for a ₹90 lakh bet.

A well-reasoned answer therefore does three things. It defines jobs from customer circumstances rather than from features. It sets job size beside job durability, as Exhibits 1 and 2 do; revision and tuition replacement together hold 42 per cent of households (504 of 1,200) but 378 of the 762 renewals, or about 49.6 per cent. It also treats the plan as a sequence of de-risking steps rather than a single leap.

One defensible path. Fund Option C, but in stages. Spend the first ₹30 lakh on the revision sheets and mock tests alone, which need no live tutors, and release them by mid-December, in time for the January peak; the full six-month build is not needed for that. Measure two things with Hugo's help: whether revision households that use the new mode renew at or above their current 75 per cent, and whether the live tutor slot is used by the tuition stand-in group. Release the remaining ₹60 lakh only if both hold. Reserve nothing for Option A, since the current four-minute answer already satisfies the homework job adequately; keep the lightweight half of Option B, a short monthly WhatsApp summary built on existing data, as a low-cost experiment inside the revision release, because parents are the buyers in every segment.

The reasoning is that Hamraah should be hired for exam-readiness, which families value enough to renew, rather than for speed alone. Option A is not wrong; it is aimed at a customer who has little reason to stay. The staged design also respects what Ishrat cannot yet say, that revision demand will scale, and it keeps the brand's speed promise intact while moving the roadmap towards the job that sustains the business.
case40v1-cust.buyer.user:
Mausam Energy Works: The Saving Nobody Owns

A case on who pays, who uses, and who can quietly refuse

1. Sunday night, Koregaon Park

A little after eleven on Sunday, 25 October 2026, Mrinalini Oak sat at her dining table in Koregaon Park, Pune, with three documents before her: the channel agreement between Mausam Energy Works, which she had co-founded, and Nigraani Facility Services; Nigraani's term sheet of 2 October, offering renewal with national exclusivity and its margin raised from 30 to 35 per cent; and Monday's board pack.

The agreement ran to 30 November 2026 and renewed automatically for three years unless either side gave notice by 31 October — six days away. On Monday the board would ask her, as head of product, whether to sell through facility-management contractors or around them. She suspected that was the wrong question.

What made it feel wrong was Exhibit 3, assembled on Friday. Of the ₹320.4 lakh a year of savings the installed base was producing, the landlords who signed and paid kept ₹40.68 lakh, the contractor who could refuse to act on the software kept ₹32.4 lakh, and the tenants — who paid Mausam nothing — kept ₹247.32 lakh.

2. How Mausam got here

Mausam was founded in March 2021 in Pune by Milind Oturkar, an HVAC commissioning engineer, and Mrinalini Oak, six years in product at a building-controls firm. It sells a kit — flow meters, probes, chiller vibration sensors, an edge gateway — and a cloud service that re-tunes chilled-water temperature, pump speed and air-handler setpoints. A plant run by software, the claim goes, uses materially less electricity than one on a commissioning schedule.

The first product was not this. Until late 2022 Mausam sold a dashboard to the chief engineers who ran the plants, at ₹80,000 a building a year; fourteen took a paid trial, two renewed, and none of them could sign anything. In January 2023 Mausam rebuilt it as closed-loop control, for landlords.

Then came the decision that constrains every option. In most Grade-A Indian parks the plant is run under contract by a facility-management firm, so rather than fight for access building by building, Mausam signed an exclusive channel agreement with Nigraani on 1 December 2023 for western and southern India: Nigraani bought at a 30 per cent discount and billed the client, and Mausam agreed not to sell directly into any building Nigraani operated. Deal cycles fell from eleven months to under three. Mausam raised ₹22 crore in November 2024, after ₹3.5 crore of seed money in 2021, and held ₹11.6 crore on 30 September 2026.

3. The industry

India's institutional office stock sits with a few owners — Embassy Office Parks REIT, Mindspace Business Parks REIT, DLF and a tail of family offices — leased to occupiers like Infosys and TCS. Air conditioning is the largest line in a building's electricity bill, and the bill is usually not the landlord's expense: it is recovered from tenants through common-area maintenance, mostly at actuals.

Regulation has made efficiency visible without making it anyone's profit. The Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022 brought large commercial buildings into the Bureau of Energy Efficiency's ambit, and SEBI's BRSR Core disclosures oblige listed REITs to report energy intensity — which is why asset managers have efficiency slides but no efficiency budget. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 matters oddly: Mausam's newest module infers occupancy from air-flow and carbon-dioxide patterns, and a tenant's counsel has asked whether that is personal data. Blue Star, Voltas, Daikin and Carrier bundle their own controls free with new chillers.

Exposure beyond India is small but loud in board meetings. Mahali Estates Partners, owner of a 14 lakh square foot Nairobi portfolio, wants a proposal: Kenyan tariffs near ₹14 a unit against the ₹9 Mausam assumes put ₹140 of HVAC spend per square foot a year behind a building rather than ₹90. But the hardware needs re-certification and Nigraani is not there.

4. What happened, and what has turned out to be wrong

Figure 1. The sequence behind the installed base

Nakshatra Business Park in Hyderabad, five towers and 12.0 lakh square feet, went live on 1 March 2025 after a pursuit begun that July. It was sold as the theory said it should be: Meenakshi Ozarkar, head of asset management at the owner, Nakshatra Realty Partners, ran the evaluation and signed, and the engineers are on the landlord's payroll. It is Mausam's best site on every measure.

The other three arrived differently. At Mandakini Office Park in Pune, live on 1 August 2025, Mausam never met the owner, Mandakini Estates House: Nigraani had won the park's five-year operations contract in May 2025 with Mausam's software written into its bid, and ordered the kit. Oorvi Tech Park in Bengaluru went live on 1 November 2025 after a tenant, Madhyam Software Services, complained about rising common-area charges; the finance director signed, and Nigraani, which runs the plant, was told afterwards. Mithila Business Centre in Kolkata, also owned by Nakshatra Realty Partners, went live on 1 March 2026 on its general manager's signature.

Four beliefs have since cracked. First, that the landlord is the buyer: in two of four accounts the asset team did not run the purchase, and in one did not know for a month. Second, that whoever pays captures the saving. Third, that the chief engineer has preferences but no veto — a nine-week legal review at Oorvi, opened in April 2026 by Madhyam's counsel over the occupancy module, froze the deployment and closed on 15 June with the module disabled, and on 9 July Nigraani's regional director asked that all recommendations be routed through his Pune control centre. Acceptance at those parks has not recovered. Fourth, that the savings were the product's: on 14 September Oorvi's asset manager put renewal in doubt, and Mumbi Oyier spent five weeks rebuilding the attribution model, delivering Exhibit 5 on Monday, 19 October.

5. The people

Milind Oturkar, co-founder and chief executive, Pune. Renew and take national exclusivity: 12 of 28 towers pursued were won, 5 through the channel in under three months, and his Series B talks rest on tower count. Not saying: two investors have asked why revenue per tower is falling.

Nayantara Moghe, chief financial officer, Pune. Nothing that puts hardware on the balance sheet. Not saying: her model shows ten shared-savings parks absorbing ₹9 crore of the ₹11.6 crore of cash.

Mohnish Odedra, head of sales, Gurugram. The channel is the only thing that works; direct deals take seven months and lose, and his quota is towers. Not saying: Nigraani's bid teams call the software "our optimisation layer".

Noopur Mahale, head of engineering, Bengaluru. Acceptance is not a product problem and no feature will fix it. Not saying: she agrees with Mafalda Noronha, the design lead in Porto, that the workflow assumes an operator who wants help.

Mumbi Oyier, data scientist, Nairobi. Restate the savings before a customer does — and she wrote the method any shared-savings contract would rest on. Not saying: her model's error bands are wide and unwritten.

Meenakshi Ozarkar, head of asset management, Nakshatra Realty Partners, Hyderabad. She will add nothing until Mausam shows a return she keeps; she is measured on net operating income, which pass-through savings never reach. Not saying: her BRSR energy-intensity number improved largely because of Mausam — worth something to her chairman that no business case will hold.

Nagesh Modak, regional director, Nigraani Facility Services, Pune. He wants national exclusivity, 35 per cent, and all advisories through his control centre. His contracts carry energy guarantees against a fixed baseline and he keeps half of savings beyond it. Not saying: at retender the baseline resets to actual consumption, which at Mandakini alone would cost him the ₹32.4 lakh a year he now earns from Mausam's savings.
