7. Voices

From the sales review, 6 October:

"Five of our twelve towers came through Nigraani, median two and a half months against seven for a landlord-led deal. You want me to give that up over a clause we cannot change."

— Mohnish Odedra

"The fastest towers are the worst-used. Mandakini and Mithila close 90 of 250 recommendations a month. We sell installations, not savings."

— Mrinalini Oak

Nagesh Modak's email of 9 July:

"Please route all setpoint advisories through our Pune command centre rather than to site engineers. Our contracts carry comfort and uptime obligations; the site team cannot act on third-party instructions without our sign-off."

— Nagesh Modak, Nigraani Facility Services

Mangesh Ohol, chief engineer at Mandakini and a Nigraani employee:

"Ma'am, if I take the chilled water down to 6.5 degrees in April and one floor complains, it is my name on the register. If I save ten per cent nobody writes my name anywhere."

— Mangesh Ohol

Oishika Mundhe, workplace lead at Madhyam Software Services, a tenant at Oorvi:

"Our CAM is running about ₹10.8 a square foot a year lower and I am grateful. But twenty-five complaints in a month about cold mornings and warm afternoons — and I cannot take a line item to my finance team for a system in a building we do not own."

— Oishika Mundhe

On the internal channel, 20 October:

"We publish 16 per cent at Nakshatra. I can defend 11. In a shared-savings contract the number we can defend is the number we get paid on."

— Mumbi Oyier

"Then we are not an energy company, we are a measurement company, and we have never priced measurement."

— Nayantara Moghe, in reply

8. The options as Mrinalini sees them

A. Renew on national exclusivity. Nigraani's 30 per cent applies today only to the ₹69.6 lakh billed in its territory, so Mausam nets ₹123.12 lakh of the ₹144.0 lakh. Exclusivity would route every park through it, putting the whole book in scope: at 35 per cent Mausam nets ₹93.6 lakh, a fall of 24.0 per cent against today. The wider scope costs more than the higher rate: the whole book at today's 30 per cent would return ₹100.8 lakh. Nigraani's offered minimum of ₹1.5 crore a year returns Mausam 65 per cent, or ₹97.5 lakh — less than it nets today. It buys a sales force Mausam does not pay for, closing at 71.4 per cent, and hands the customer to the party whose economics improve when savings prove temporary.

B. Give notice and go direct. The non-solicit survives termination for buildings Nigraani already operates: seven of the twelve live towers and ₹86.4 lakh of the ₹144.0 lakh of gross subscription, or exactly 60 per cent. Mohnish estimates Nigraani or its two large peers hold 38 of the 60 Grade-A parks on his list. It also means selling asset managers a return Exhibit 3 says most never receive.

C. Re-aim at the tenant. Tenants keep ₹247.32 lakh of the ₹320.4 lakh. At one seat per 80 square feet the installed base holds 37,500 seats; at ₹25 a seat a month that is ₹112.5 lakh a year, below today's ₹144.0 lakh gross, from a customer who cannot touch the plant, cannot sign for the building and whose counsel already stopped one module.

D. Shared savings. Mausam funds the hardware and takes 35 per cent of verified savings: ₹112.14 lakh a year on the current book against ₹123.12 lakh net today, or ₹89.15 lakh on Exhibit 5's figures. Ten new parks would absorb ₹900 lakh, leaving ₹260 lakh against a ₹58 lakh monthly burn — four and a half months.

Mrinalini had written a fifth line on the pack and crossed it out: the unit we are selling may not be the building. At Nakshatra the saving is produced by five towers, captured by some ninety tenants, paid for by one asset manager and permitted by engineers on a fourth party's payroll.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The 31 October notice date cannot be extended; silence renews the agreement to 30 November 2029, and Nigraani's term sheet lapses on 15 November. Cash is ₹11.6 crore against a September burn of ₹58 lakh a month, so twenty months, and Nayantara will not approve a plan leaving less than twelve. Nakshatra renews on 28 February 2027; Meenakshi Ozarkar will renew it and add nothing. Oorvi's landlord has made renewal conditional on complaints; the park logged 25 in September, 3.8 per lakh square feet. The occupancy module stays disabled pending a data-protection position Mausam has not written, and Diwali takes three weeks out of whatever is approved.

At a quarter to one Mrinalini turned to the last page of the pack, blank but for a heading typed on Friday: "Who is our customer?" She had Exhibit 3, which said the money went to people who did not buy; Exhibit 4, which said the fastest buyers were the worst users; Exhibit 5, which said a fifth of the savings might not be hers; and six days.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. For each account in Exhibits 1 and 2, name the buyer, the user, the influencer and the blocker. Where does one person hold two roles, and what then?
  2. Using Exhibit 6, what saving must a 10.0 lakh square foot park produce for the payer to break even in year two, and who decides whether it gets there?
  3. Exhibits 3 and 4 point in opposite directions. Which would you trust for next year's sales effort?
  4. Nagesh Modak is at once Mausam's largest channel, the employer of its users and the party that loses money if savings outlast a retender. Partner, customer or blocker?
  5. If Exhibit 5 is closer to the truth than Exhibit 1, which options become unviable, and what should Mausam tell Meenakshi Ozarkar?
  6. It is Monday morning, 26 October 2026. What do you do about the notice, what do you ask the board to fund, and how do you answer a director who asks who the customer is?
exp20v2-cust.buyer.user:
Discovery & Design · Customer Modelling

Buyer, user, influencer, blocker

1. A pilot that went well

On Monday 14 September 2026, Bhavna Ugale, a product manager at Upkaran Medical Systems in Pune, sat down to read the results of a six-week pilot. Upkaran sells a bedside medication-verification system: before giving a drug, a nurse scans the patient's wristband and then the drug pack, and the system confirms that drug, dose and patient match the doctor's order and records the administration. The customer was Bageshwari Hospitals Network, six hospitals with 900 beds in all. The pilot had run from 3 August to 14 September, which is 42 days, across three wards, 90 beds and 48 nurses.

The numbers were good. Thirty-one of the 48 nurses, about 65 per cent, scanned on most shifts, and Babita Ubale, the nursing superintendent, wrote that her staff were "asking when the other wards get it." Uday Bhosle, Upkaran's head of sales, wanted it signed before 30 September. The quote was ₹8,500 per bed per year, or ₹76.5 lakh annually for 900 beds, plus a one-time rollout fee of ₹18 lakh.

Bhavna was uneasy for a specific reason. Everyone who had praised the product was a person who would use it. The person who would pay for it, Bipin Unnikrishnan, the group chief financial officer, had attended one demonstration and asked a single question about the contract term. Balaji Urs, the head of information technology, had attended nothing. If she treated nurse enthusiasm as proof of a sale, Upkaran would lose a quarter chasing a signature, or win a contract that Bageshwari's own systems team would quietly starve of integration work until renewal. The question was not whether the product worked but who had to say yes.

2. The idea

A buyer is the person who controls the money and signs. A user is the person who operates the product in daily work. An influencer is someone with no authority over the purchase whose opinion the buyer trusts. A blocker is someone who can stop or stall the purchase, without owning the budget, by controlling something the product depends on: security approval, integration, a compliance sign-off, or simply a calendar. These are roles in a purchase, not job titles; in a small clinic one doctor holds three of them.

The vocabulary solved a problem sellers met repeatedly in the 1960s and 1970s as products moved into large firms: winning the enthusiasm of those nearest the product and still losing the order. Frederick Webster and Yoram Wind named the decision group in 1972, the buying centre, listing users, influencers, buyers, deciders and gatekeepers within it. Practitioners later compressed the list to the four roles used here, which also split product requirements: the user decides whether the product is pleasant, the buyer whether it is affordable, the blocker whether it is permitted.

Bhavna's sentence, which she could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib: the person who loves the product, the person who pays for it and the person who can stop it are usually three different people, and each needs a different reason.

3. How it actually works

The mechanics have five steps, and the last two are usually skipped. First, list the people the purchase touches. Bhavna started from the pilot's email trail, not the organisation chart, since email shows who actually got copied. Second, assign roles: who signs, who operates, who is consulted, and whose refusal would stop the work? Third, write down what each role is trying to achieve, in their words rather than yours. Bipin was judged on the group's cost per bed. Babita was judged on shift coverage and nurse retention. Dr Usha Bhatnagar, the chief medical officer, was judged partly on medication-safety indicators needed for hospital accreditation by NABH, the national accreditation board. Balaji was judged on uptime and on never explaining a data incident.

Fourth, and usually left implicit, find the conversion path of each person's benefit: how the value that role experiences becomes something the buyer can see. A nurse feels saved time; the finance head sees only the ledger. Fifth, find the power asymmetry: whose approval comes last, and who can say no at no cost. A blocker is rarely against the product; he is protecting something its designers never asked about.

Exhibit 2. Role map for the Bageshwari deal
PersonRoleWhat they are judged onWhat they can do to the deal
Bipin Unnikrishnan, group CFOBuyerCost per bed; cash paybackSign, delay or ask for a cheaper alternative
Babita Ubale, nursing superintendent; 48 pilot nursesUser (and sponsor)Shift coverage; nurse retentionAdopt, work around, or stop scanning
Dr Usha Bhatnagar, chief medical officerInfluencerMedication-safety indicators for NABHFrame it for Bipin as safety, not a gadget
Balaji Urs, head of ITBlockerUptime; data securityRefuse integration with the hospital records system until his checklist is met

4. A worked example

Bhavna first translated each role's value into the buyer's currency, rupees of cash, starting with the users because the pilot gave her data. Nurses reported saving 12 minutes per patient per day on charting and double-checking. Bageshwari's occupancy was 80 per cent, so the occupied beds were 900 × 0.80 = 720. Daily time freed was 720 × 12 = 8,640 minutes, or 144 hours. Over a year that is 144 × 365 = 52,560 hours; at a loaded nursing cost of ₹300 per hour, 52,560 × 300 = ₹1,57,68,000, or ₹157.68 lakh.

That is 2.06 times the annual licence of ₹76.5 lakh (157.68 ÷ 76.5), which is why nurses called the system a bargain. But Bipin pays for cash that stops leaving, not freed minutes. Only the share of freed time that replaces overtime or agency-nurse shifts shows up in the ledger, and Bhavna assumed 25 per cent: ₹157.68 lakh × 0.25 = ₹39.42 lakh. The second benefit is fewer medication errors. Bageshwari recorded 60 adverse drug events a year, averaging ₹1.2 lakh each in extended stays and settlements. If scanning prevents 40 per cent, that is 24 events, worth 24 × 1.2 = ₹28.8 lakh. Cash benefit to the buyer: 39.42 + 28.8 = ₹68.22 lakh.

Exhibit 3. The same system seen by user and buyer (₹ lakh per year)
LinePass 1: 25% of time convertsPass 2: 40% of time converts
Value of nurse time freed (52,560 hours × ₹300)157.68157.68
Share converted to cash25%40%

Total cash benefit68.2291.872
Annual licence76.576.5

Read the first column as the buyer would. The users see a 2.06-times return; the buyer sees 0.89 times, and 0.72 in year one once the rollout is added. For the second pass Bhavna changed one input: Babita agreed that if scanning worked, she would cut agency-nurse shifts and fill vacancies more slowly, raising the convertible share from 25 to 40 per cent. Cash from time became ₹157.68 lakh × 0.40 = ₹63.072 lakh, the total ₹91.872 lakh, and the ratio 1.20. The sale depended not on a better product but on a user committing to convert her benefit into the buyer's currency.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Roles are not titles

The nursing superintendent is a user in her wards and a sponsor in the boardroom. Ask what each person does in the purchase, not what is printed on a card; mapping by title produces tidy diagrams of the wrong people.

The payer is not always the decider

Bipin signs, but he may sign what Dr Bhatnagar has already settled. Holding the budget and deciding the question are often separate; find the second person by asking who would be embarrassed if the purchase failed.

Influencers are not just advocates

An influencer's opinion signals that a product is safe or standard; user enthusiasm signals only that people like it. A chief medical officer can turn a gadget into a compliance necessity; fifty happy nurses cannot.

A blocker may be correct

Balaji's refusal to connect an unreviewed vendor to the hospital records system protects patient data under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Treat his objections as design requirements; a blocker beaten by escalation returns as slow cooperation after signing.

The roles describe a purchase, not a segment

Segments group customers who behave alike; personas describe typical individuals within them. Each segment contains buyers, users and blockers, so a persona needs a role label; otherwise a "hospital CFO persona" stays silent about the nurse.

Questions to ask before relying on it

Who has refused a vendor before, and why? Which approvals are written down and which are merely customary? A role map cannot tell you how much each role weighs; if you cannot answer these, you hold a hypothesis, not a map.

6. How it differs by product type and by stage

Exhibit 4. Where the four roles sit in three kinds of product
ProductBuyerUserInfluencerBlocker
Consumer (a children's learning app)Parent, with a household budgetChildTeacher, friends, reviewsThe other parent; the child's refusal to open it
B2B (hospital medication system)CFO or boardNursesChief medical officerIT, legal, procurement
Marketplace (supplier exchange)Whichever side pays the feeBoth sides, differentlyIndustry associations, large anchor accountsRegulators, payment partners, an anchor account that refuses to list

In consumer products the roles are compressed and emotional: a parent buys, a child uses, and both must be satisfied. In B2B they are separated and procedural, and the blocker is often a function with a written checklist. In marketplaces the side that pays may not be the side whose participation is scarce, so the buyer for revenue and the user for liquidity are different customers.

Stage matters too. An early-stage company often sells to a single founder who is buyer, user and blocker at once, and the role split hardly appears. As customers grow, buying committees form, and a startup whose story rests on one enthusiastic user meets its first stalled enterprise deal. A large company knows its blockers well and loses touch with its users.

7. Common mistakes

Selling to the champion alone. Symptom: glowing pilot feedback and a contract that does not move. Misunderstanding: enthusiasm is mistaken for authority. Cheapest diagnostic: ask the champion, "Who else will have to say yes, and have they seen this?"

Pricing to the user's value. Symptom: users say the product is cheap, the buyer says it is expensive. Misunderstanding: benefits are counted in a currency the buyer cannot spend. Cheapest diagnostic: rebuild the business case from ledger lines only, as in Exhibit 3.

Meeting the blocker last. Symptom: a verbal yes from the buyer followed by weeks of silence. Misunderstanding: the blocker is seen as a formality. Cheapest diagnostic: in the first meeting, ask for IT's and legal's checklists before quoting.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled Bageshwari decision looks quiet. By the pilot's second week the product manager has a one-page role map of names, not titles. Each person has been interviewed separately, and Balaji was asked about hosting, access control and integration, not the nurses' screens. The business case is written in ledger lines, each assumption owned by the person who can make it true, and the blocker's checklist is a contract milestone rather than a surprise. Everybody has been given a reason that belongs to them.

9. What Bhavna decided

She declined to ask Uday for a signature by 30 September. Instead she offered Bipin a revised proposal at the same ₹8,500 per bed, with three changes. First, Babita would sign a plan to reduce agency-nurse shifts, so the 40 per cent conversion assumption became a commitment rather than a hope. Second, 30 per cent of the year-one licence, ₹22.95 lakh (0.30 × 76.5), would fall due only after Balaji's team accepted the integration and the data-hosting arrangement. Third, Dr Bhatnagar would present the adverse-event figures to the board as an accreditation matter. Each role now had a reason of its own to say yes, and the blocker had become an acceptance gate.

Next, learn interviewing in B2B, since a role map is only as good as the conversations behind it, and the buying committee, which extends these roles into an account map. Two questions to sit with. In a product you know, who holds an unnamed veto, and how would you find out? And when the user's benefit and the buyer's benefit cannot be converted into each other, should the product be redesigned or priced differently?
exp40v2-cust.buyer.user:
Discovery & Design · Customer Modelling

Buyer, user, influencer, blocker

Who pays, who uses, who can quietly veto — and the arithmetic when those are three different people.

Section 1Two desks, seventeen days apart

On Monday 7 September 2026, Vrinda Walke read the closing report of a 92-day pilot. She was group product manager at Wahan Telematics Works, an Ahmedabad firm selling cold-chain telematics: probes inside a refrigerated trailer, an AIS-140 gateway, a driver tablet and a dispatch console. The pilot had run from 1 June to 31 August 2026 on 40 of Vahini Cold Chain Carriers' 420 reefer trucks.

It read like a success. Excursion alerts arrived twenty to forty minutes before a load was lost. Vaishali Thakkar, who supervises Vahini's twenty-six dispatchers, measured fifty minutes a day saved each. The shipper's quality head, who holds no budget at Vahini, wanted her cartons on instrumented trucks.

The quote was ₹34,000 of hardware per vehicle, one time, plus ₹1,250 per vehicle per month: for 420 vehicles, ₹142.80 lakh of hardware and ₹63.00 lakh a year of software, so ₹205.80 lakh in year one. Vikrant Wadke, managing director and majority owner, signs capital expenditure above ₹25 lakh himself and applies a two-year payback rule. Eleven days after the review, on 18 September, Virendra Kashelkar, head of transport operations, objected for the first time: fitting probes takes a truck off the road for six hours, and he would not explain a new box to four hundred trip-paid drivers before Diwali. The capital window closed 27 days later, on 15 October.

On Thursday 24 September 2026, in Bengaluru, Vinati Kurup faced the same problem differently arranged. She was head of product at Vishram Elder Care Network — a wrist wearable, an in-home hub and a monthly nurse visit at ₹3,200 a month plus ₹9,600 of hardware — with 14,200 active subscriptions on 1 September 2026, about ₹54.5 crore of annualised revenue.

In seven subscriptions in ten the payer lived abroad. Varsha Menon, a hospital administrator in Melbourne, paid for her father Vasudevan Menon, 74, in Kochi; she read the weekly report, rated Vishram nine out of ten and renewed. Her father found the wristband humiliating and left it on the dressing table. Across the base the device was worn eight hours a day or more in 5,680 of the 14,200 subscriptions — 40 per cent.

Section 2The idea, and what it was invented to fix

Define the terms tightly; loose use is where the frame fails. A buyer controls the budget and bears the consequence of the spend. A user operates the product in their own work or life. An influencer has no authority over the purchase but changes the buyer's reading of risk. A blocker can stop or indefinitely delay it without owning the budget, because the product depends on something they control: a security review, a vehicle's downtime, an integration. These are roles in a purchase, not job titles; one person can hold two or four of them, and different roles in two deals at one firm.

The vocabulary comes from industrial marketing in the 1960s and 1970s, when sellers kept losing orders they had apparently won. Frederick Webster and Yoram Wind's 1972 buying centre named users, influencers, buyers, deciders and gatekeepers, with the group as the unit of analysis. Practitioners compressed five roles into four and changed the purpose: Webster and Wind explained purchasing behaviour, while product managers use the roles to decide what to build.

Three schools sit uneasily together. The selling school, visible in every sales methodology since Miller Heiman's strategic selling, treats the roles as a map of consent navigated deal by deal; it signs that no large purchase closes without the blocker neutralised, and will not sign that roles should set the roadmap. The design school, descending from Alan Cooper's persona work, treats the user as sovereign and will not sign that buyer-facing features are first-class product work. The jobs-to-be-done school rejects the taxonomy as organisation charts rather than progress sought: roles are a consequence, not a primitive.

Section 3Mechanics in depth, including the arithmetic

Expert practice has five steps; the last two separate a role map from a coloured org chart. One: enumerate from traffic, not structure. Vrinda built her list from pilot email headers, tickets and invitations; Virendra appeared on no invitation and fourteen maintenance tickets, which is the signature of a blocker. Two: assign roles by the question each person can answer — who signs, who touches it daily, whose opinion the buyer repeats, whose refusal costs them nothing. Three: write down what each role is measured on. Vikrant on return on capital employed, Vaishali on consignments dispatched on time per dispatcher, Virendra on fleet availability and driver attrition, the shipper's quality head on temperature excursions under the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation's distribution-practice rules.

Four: trace each role's value into the buyer's currency. This step is usually implicit and it is where business cases break. A dispatcher experiences saved minutes; a managing director sees only cash that stops leaving. The conversion is never automatic, is always owned by somebody, and the converting fraction is a decision, not a fact. Five: find the power asymmetry — rank roles by the cost of saying no. Virendra's no costs him nothing.

Step four looks like Exhibit 1. Vahini runs 150 consignments per vehicle a year, so 63,000 across 420 trucks; 1.2 per cent are rejected on a temperature excursion, which is 756 consignments, and its contracts leave it carrying about ₹0.24 lakh of each — an annual exposure of ₹181.44 lakh, which earlier alerts cut by 35 per cent in the pilot. Diesel runs ₹2,520 lakh a year and idling discipline saved 1.5 per cent, or ₹37.80 lakh, part of which leaks into trip allowances rather than the fuel account. Twenty-six dispatchers saving fifty minutes a day across 300 working days frees 6,500 hours, worth ₹16.90 lakh at ₹260 an hour loaded — 2.6 dispatcher-years at 2,500 hours each. The insurer offered 4 per cent off a ₹96 lakh premium, and ₹54 lakh of detention penalties could fall by a fifth.

Read the gross column as the dispatch desk reads it and pass 1 as Vikrant reads it. Against year-one cost of ₹205.80 lakh, pass 1 returns 0.52 times and pass 2 returns 0.69 times; in steady state, when only the ₹63.00 lakh software fee recurs, they return 1.70 and 2.24 times. The binding constraint is the payback rule: ₹142.80 lakh of hardware against net annual cash of ₹44.32 lakh pays back in 3.22 years and fails, while ₹78.42 lakh pays back in 1.82 years and passes. Nothing about the product changed; two non-buyers agreed to convert their benefit into his currency.

The second formal tool is the conjunctive gate: if every role whose refusal can stop the deal must assent independently, the probability of closing is the product, not the average, of the individual probabilities. Vrinda's estimates were 0.80 for Vikrant, 0.90 for the dispatch desk, 0.70 for the quality head, 0.50 for Virendra.

Because the joint probability is a product, the marginal value of effort is highest at the smallest factor. Raising Virendra from 0.50 to 0.85 lifts it by 70 per cent; raising an already-happy dispatch desk from 0.90 to 0.99 lifts it by 10 per cent. Almost every team's instinct is the second move.

Section 4When the frame applies, and when it misleads

Four testable conditions. The roles must be held by different people: name who signs and who logs in daily. At Vahini they are four distinct parties; at Vishram the buyer is in Melbourne and the user in Kochi. For a ₹499-a-month tool sold to a solo architect the condition fails and the frame is overhead. Refusal by a non-budget holder must be materially costless: Virendra loses nothing by stalling a quarter, and Vasudevan Menon gains dignity by leaving the wristband off. Interests must differ in direction, not degree. And assent must be conjunctive: where an executive overrides a security review by fiat, the blocker's 0.50 is wrong.

Two situations make the frame misleading. A role map can substitute for understanding the job, so a team knows who signs and not why anyone wants the thing. And independence can be assumed where it does not hold: if Virendra's refusal would itself lower Vikrant's confidence, the probabilities are correlated and multiplying them understates the risk.

Section 5Hard edges

In multi-product companies the roles invert across the portfolio: the information-technology head who blocks one module buys another, so a vendor who beat him once now faces a person with a memory. In two-sided marketplaces the paying side is usually not the scarce side — a freight exchange earns its fee from shippers and dies without trucks — so treating the fee-payer as the customer produces revenue without liquidity. In regulated settings the blocker is sometimes not a person: Vishram's overseas buyers meet the Reserve Bank of India's e-mandate rules for recurring card payments, which only design answers.

In hardware-plus-software the blocker is often physical — Virendra's six hours times 420 trucks is 2,520 truck-hours of real cost, which belongs in the business case, not an objection-handling script. In AI-native products a new blocker has appeared: whoever is accountable for what a model says to a customer, often newly appointed and therefore unusually cautious. At the seams the roles diverge inside the vendor — sales is paid on the buyer, support measured by the user, security review answers to the blocker. Mature firms say one account plan resolves this; what they do is arbitrate case by case.

Section 6Eight things an expert notices

One: the user is often also the blocker. The obvious reading treats blockers as functions — security, legal, procurement — but Vasudevan Menon is user and veto at once, and exercises the veto by non-use rather than objection. Tell-tale sign: healthy billing alongside falling engagement and no complaints. Complaining requires caring; silent non-use is the cheapest veto.

Two: a champion's enthusiasm is information about the champion, not the account. One who cannot name the next three approvals has never done this before. Tell-tale sign: they offer to handle procurement, then go quiet for three weeks. The obvious reading mistakes willingness for capability; ask what political capital they have ever spent.

Three: blockers are usually right about something. Virendra's objection is arithmetic, not resistance — 2,520 truck-hours Wahan's proposal had omitted. Tell-tale sign: the objection is quantitative and the vendor's answer is about process. Escalation buys a signature then eighteen months of slow cooperation.

Four: the buyer's currency is not the user's, and conversion is owned. The naive move computes total value and shows everyone. Exhibit 1's two passes differ by about ₹34.1 lakh with no product change, because converting freed minutes into cash takes a hiring decision somebody must make. Tell-tale sign: benefits with no owner's name.

Five: influencers work on the buyer's perception of risk, not of value. Teams recruit influencers to say the product is good, which is nearly worthless; what they supply is the judgement that choosing it is not reckless. Tell-tale sign: the buyer repeats the influencer's framing in a sentence containing no product features. If Dr Vishal Pai, the Menons' physician, stops endorsing Vishram, Varsha cannot defend the spend to her brother.

Six: roles rotate within a deal and across the renewal. The person who bought is often not the person who renews, and renewal turns on the user's behaviour, not the buyer's satisfaction. Tell-tale sign: a renewal conversation opening with usage statistics never discussed. Deals are won on the buyer's case and lost on the user's indifference.

Seven: a buyer–user split shows up as a retention mixture, not an average. Vishram's 63 per cent annual retention is two populations at 87 and 47 per cent, and one number understates the asset by 36 per cent (Exhibit 3). Tell-tale sign: a lifetime-value model with a single churn input where payer and user differ.

Eight: in family firms one person holds the roles at different hours. Vikrant Wadke is the buyer, and when a probe fails at two in the morning he is the escalation path too. Tell-tale sign: an owner asking an oddly operational question in a pricing meeting. The obvious reading is micromanagement; the accurate one is that the roles are not separated at all.

Section 7Across product types and company stages

In consumer products the roles compress into a household and the currency is emotional: Varsha buys relief from guilt and her father is buying nothing at all, which is why Vishram's user-facing work is harder and yields more. In enterprise products the roles are separated and the blocker arrives with a written checklist — good news, since a written veto can be designed for. In platforms the roles split across sides, so there are two user populations and one payer, and the scarce side holds a permanent informal veto. In hardware the blocker owns physical access; in AI products the new element is an accountability role, not a new taxonomy. What does not survive examination is the claim that consumer products have no blockers.

Stage changes the frame more than category does. Before product-market fit the founder sells to someone holding all four roles, which is why the first enterprise deal stalls. At Vishram's scale the roles are statistically visible and manageable with cohort arithmetic. At full scale a company knows its blockers and has lost touch with its users.

Section 8Three worked examples

Vishram: the retention mixture

Vinati Kurup took the 2,400 subscriptions that began in September 2025 and measured them on 1 September 2026. Of those, 1,512 were still active — 63 per cent. Split by whether the wearable was worn, 835 of the 960 wearers survived (87 per cent) and 677 of the 1,440 non-wearers survived (47 per cent). Monthly contribution is ₹1,280 on ₹3,200 of revenue, so ₹15,360 a year. Lifetime value as annual contribution divided by one minus annual retention gives ₹1,18,154 for a wearer and ₹28,981 for a non-wearer; weighted 40 to 60 the base is worth ₹64,650. The blended 63 per cent retention gives ₹41,514: an understatement of 36 per cent, or a true value 1.56 times the blended one. Acquisition cost averages ₹24,000 a subscription — ₹18,000 of marketing and referral fees plus ₹6,000 of onboarding visit and device fitting.

The strategic question follows. Vishram's proposed passive option — in-home sensing with nothing to wear, at ₹2,900 a month, contribution ₹920 a month, estimated 80 per cent retention — is worth ₹55,200, or 2.30 times cost. That is below the blended base and far below a wearer, which is why the growth team opposed it. But it nearly doubles a non-wearer's 1.21, and non-wearers are 60 per cent of the base. A mix of 40 per cent wearers and 60 per cent passive is worth ₹80,382, or 3.35 times cost — 24 per cent better than today.

Wahan: the blocker as owner of the business case

Rather than escalate Virendra to Vikrant, Vrinda restructured. Hardware would be rented at ₹1,050 per vehicle per month instead of bought, making the annual cost 420 × ₹2,300 × 12 = ₹115.92 lakh of operating expense with no capital approval needed; fitment would use Virendra's own workshop slots over eleven weeks after approval; and the trip-allowance revision would be his proposal. Against ₹115.92 lakh, pass-1 cash of ₹107.32 lakh returns 0.93 times and pass-2 cash of ₹141.42 lakh returns 1.22 times.

Vidyankur: the failure, and the recovery

Vidyankur School Systems sells fee collection to private school chains. From 4 August 2025 it pursued Vasundhara Vidya Trust — nine schools, 23,400 students — at ₹180 per student per year, or ₹42.12 lakh annually. Three principals were delighted and pilot parents preferred UPI to queuing. On 7 July 2026, eleven months in, the trust declined for a reason never discussed: fee reconciliation ran through a collection product its bank bundled free with the overdraft, and the honorary treasurer would not disturb that relationship for a software fee.

Direct pursuit cost was ₹68 lakh — ₹19 lakh of sales effort, ₹34 lakh of implementation engineering, ₹6 lakh of travel, ₹9 lakh of pilot hardware — against a historic win rate of 1 of 9 pursuits, or 11 per cent. The recovery was not a better pitch. Vidyankur added two first-meeting questions: who holds the trust's current account, and is fee collection bundled into that relationship? Of its next 14 prospects, 6 disqualified, saving an estimated ₹28.8 lakh at ₹4.8 lakh of pursuit cost each. For the remaining 8 it built a bridge posting into the bank's file format instead of replacing the bank, and closed 5 of those 8 — 63 per cent — for roughly ₹130 lakh of annual contract value, an average of ₹26 lakh each.

Section 9Failure modes and their early warnings

The fourth row is hardest to see from inside a product organisation. Buyers answer emails, attend reviews and ask for features; users do not. A roadmap built from the loudest channel is a buyer roadmap, looking data-driven while the asset degrades. Vishram shipped five buyer-facing features and one user-facing feature in a quarter; buyer satisfaction rose sixteen points and the wear rate moved from 39 to 40 per cent.

Section 10Where experts genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is whether the buyer deserves product work at all. The design position, steelmanned: products are renewed on use, use is created by users, and buyer-facing features are a sales cost masquerading as product — evidence being enterprise tools bought and abandoned, and Vishram's 47 per cent non-wearer retention. The selling position: there is no renewal without a first purchase, and reducing a buyer's evaluation risk creates value — evidence being deals like Vahini's, where no user delight clears a two-year payback rule. For the design position to be wrong, buyer-facing work would have to lift long-run retention, not merely first-year conversion.

The second is whether to engage blockers or route around them. Engagement treats the objection as a requirement and pays in cycle time; routing treats it as friction and pays in post-signature cooperation. Engagement's evidence is the escalated security review that becomes an eighteen-month backlog; routing's is that some blockers are rent-seeking. Neither camp has a test for which kind is in the room.

The third is whether the taxonomy is a primitive or a derived artefact. The jobs-to-be-done position holds that roles are an artefact of how a firm has organised itself and change when it reorganises. The buying-centre position holds that money, hands and veto are structural in any non-trivial purchase, and that the jobs framing cannot distinguish wanting an outcome from being able to sign for it.

Section 11What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this draws a four-box diagram and feels prepared. Someone who has internalised it spends their scarcest hours on the least willing required party, because the gate multiplies; attaches every conversion assumption to whoever can make it true; disaggregates retention by role before believing it; and holds that a blocker is both obstacle and requirement.

Section 12The decisions, and three questions

Vrinda Walke withdrew the capital-expenditure proposal four days before the 15 October board meeting and replaced it with the rental structure: ₹115.92 lakh a year of operating expense, fitment on Virendra Kashelkar's calendar, the trip-allowance revision presented as his initiative. She accepted lower first-year revenue to move the gate's weakest factor. Vinati Kurup committed two quarters to passive sensing rather than the buyer dashboard, on the argument that 3.35 beats 2.69 and that the non-wearers' 1.21 is the only genuinely broken number in her business — while noting the 80 per cent estimate might be wrong.

Q1. Vrinda's rental structure cuts Wahan's year-one revenue from ₹205.80 lakh to ₹115.92 lakh. Was Virendra's cooperation worth ₹89.88 lakh of deferred revenue?

Q2. The passive option is worth less per subscriber than a wearer. On what evidence should Vinati proceed, and what would disconfirm it in two quarters?

Q3. Vidyankur's recovery disqualified 6 of 14 prospects. Is a role map that shrinks the market a success or a confession?

Section 13Going deeper

  1. Market segments vs personas — without the split, a segment hides three customers.
  2. B2B vs B2C: the basic distinction — why buyer and user separate.
  3. Interviewing in B2B: users, buyers, blockers — the conversations a map rests on.
  4. Ideal customer profile — Vidyankur's two questions as a repeatable filter.
  5. Shopper vs consumer — buyer in the aisle, user at home.
  6. The buying committee — four roles extended into real groups of six or more.
  7. Account personas and buying-centre maps — a role map a sales team can keep.
  8. Why personas — the case for archetypes, where role labels become inputs.
  9. The self-referential design trap — roles make building for yourself visible.
  10. Anatomy of a persona — what a persona must contain, role label included.
  11. Building personas from research — archetypes without inventing people.
  12. AI-assisted persona synthesis — role structure is what a model least infers.
  13. Jobs to Be Done — each role pursues a different job, hence the clash.
case20v1-cust.buyer.user:
Dhanvantari Ward Systems: Who Really Decides?

A product decision about buyers, users and the people who can say no

1. Opening

On the morning of Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Divyanka Gaikwad sat in a glass-walled meeting room in Pune with three printed pages and a deadline. On Friday, 30 October, she would present to the board of Dhanvantari Ward Systems a single recommendation: how the company should aim its product, its pricing and its sales effort during the second half of the financial year. Whatever she proposed would be funded from a cash balance of ₹12.6 crore.

The three pages were a list of hospitals. Next to each name sat the title of the person who had first said yes to Dhanvantari. The pattern was uncomfortable. The people who loved the product were not the people who paid for it, and the people who paid for it were not the people who used it. Divyanka, head of product, had to decide whom the company was really building for.

2. Company background

Dhanvantari Ward Systems was founded in 2021. It sells a bedside medication-verification application that runs on a rugged handheld. A nurse scans the patient's wristband, then the drug strip, and the application checks the dose, the time and the patient against the doctor's order. Each administered dose also goes to the pharmacy billing desk, so nothing given to a patient goes unbilled.

The company targets mid-sized private hospitals of 100 to 300 beds in tier-2 cities. The large chains, such as Apollo Hospitals, Max Healthcare and Narayana Health, buy centrally, so Dhanvantari had deliberately gone below them. Accreditation under NABH has made documented medication safety a board-room subject, and the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission has made data handling more visible. Dhanvantari had raised ₹14 crore in two rounds, employed 38 people, and spent about ₹70 lakh a month, so ₹12.6 crore gave it 18 months.

List pricing for the product was ₹1,200 per bed per month. A hospital also bought handhelds at ₹18,000 each, about one for every five beds, and paid a one-time ₹4.8 lakh to connect the application to its existing hospital information system.

3. The situation

Over four quarters the sales team had worked twelve hospitals seriously. Three had signed paid pilots. Nine had not. Eklavya Sawant, the sales head in Hyderabad, logged who inside each hospital first championed the product (Exhibit 1). Nursing heads were the most frequent sponsors, five of twelve, and also the weakest converters: one in five signed. Finance heads sponsored two and converted one; IT heads sponsored two and neither signed.

The loss reasons were more telling. Of the nine hospitals that did not sign, four stalled in an IT security review, three were stopped by finance or procurement over price, and two were lost when the nursing leadership changed mid-negotiation. Each rejection was a veto exercised by a person the sales team had not planned to meet.

The three pilots, summarised in Exhibit 2, showed the same divergence in use. At Dnyaneshwar Memorial Hospital in Nashik, where the chief nursing officer had sponsored the pilot, nurses scanned 81 per cent of doses. At Ekta Multispeciality in Indore, where the finance head had pushed it through, the figure was 54 per cent. At Fulchand General Hospital in Raipur, sponsored by the medical director, it was 22 per cent.

Elsa Lindqvist, the user researcher in Gothenburg, had spent a fortnight on video calls with ward nurses at all three sites. Her report said that nurses in Raipur had stopped scanning because the integration with the hospital's older information system took nine seconds to confirm each dose. The IT head there, absent from the original sale, had also delayed integration by seven weeks to review patient-data flows under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act.

4. The people

Fenella D'Souza, chief nursing officer at Nashik, is the product's most committed user-side advocate. She wants fewer medication errors and no extra clicks, and has no budget of her own.

Dilip Ephraim, finance head at Indore, signed because the leakage recovery looked like cash. He wants the licence to pay for itself within the year.

Devendra Fulzele, IT head at Raipur, controls access to the hospital's systems. He is measured by the absence of incidents and gains nothing if the product succeeds.

Eklavya Sawant wants a shorter sales cycle and would sell to whoever holds the cheque. Elsa believes a product that nurses quietly abandon will not renew. Exhibit 3 draws Divyanka's whiteboard map.

Exhibit 3. Who holds which role in a typical hospital purchase

5. The economics

Exhibit 4 prices a 200-bed reference hospital. Licence is ₹2,40,000 a month, or ₹28.8 lakh a year; with ₹7.2 lakh of handhelds and ₹4.8 lakh of integration, year one costs ₹40.8 lakh. Recovered leakage depends on how well nurses scan. At Nashik's ₹2,000 per bed per month, 200 beds recover ₹48 lakh a year; at Indore's rate, ₹24 lakh; at Raipur's, ₹18 lakh.

Only the hospital whose nurses used the product heavily came out ahead, yet the nurses had no say in the purchase.

6. The options

Option A: sell to the cheque-holder. Hire two enterprise sales executives at about ₹60 lakh a year each, ₹1.2 crore in all, and build a return-on-investment pitch for finance heads and medical directors. This follows the highest signing rates. The cost is that it ignores the evidence that heavy use drives the return; hospitals sold this way may sign and then leave at renewal.

Option B: build for the nurse. Put three additional engineers, about ₹90 lakh a year, on handheld speed and workflow, and offer free ward-level trials so that nursing heads can prove value before anyone talks about budget. The cost is that nursing heads cannot buy, and Exhibit 1 shows their sponsorship alone converts only one hospital in five.

Option C: map the committee before the pilot. Spend about ₹45 lakh on a security and data-protection documentation pack and a standard integration kit, and change the sales process so that no pilot starts until the buyer, the clinical user lead and IT have each named a person and agreed a usage target in writing. The cost is a slower start, and the sales head fears losing deals that would have signed on one sponsor's easy yes.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, who is buyer, user, influencer and blocker at each pilot hospital? How would you tell, in a first meeting?

2. Why might the sponsor with the highest signing rate (finance) and the sponsor with the highest usage (nursing) be different people, and what does that imply for renewals?

3. Using Exhibit 4, what usage level must a 200-bed hospital reach for the finance head to break even in year one? Who inside the hospital controls that level?

4. Which option would you take to the board on 30 October, what would you ask the team to stop doing, and what evidence in the next two quarters would tell you that you were wrong?

8. A note for the learner

The topic frames the case with a single question: who pays, who uses, and who can quietly veto? Dhanvantari had treated the hospital as one customer; it contained four roles with four incentives. A good answer begins by separating the roles, then asks what each can do to the deal. The buyer can refuse to pay. The user can refuse to use. The blocker can refuse to integrate.

Break-even in Exhibit 4 sits at a recovered rate of ₹1,700 per bed per month, because ₹40.8 lakh divided by 200 beds and twelve months is ₹1,700. Only Nashik clears it. That is the key insight: the buyer's payback is produced by the user, and the user is held up or enabled by the blocker. A strategy that wins only one of the three is fragile.

One defensible path is Option C, with two refinements. First, make the written usage target a pilot condition and report scan rates to the finance head monthly, so the buyer sees the link between use and money. Second, fix the nine-second confirmation delay before onboarding another hospital. Option A would sell more of the Raipur outcome; Option B builds delight for the one role without budget. Option C is slower, but it tests whether all three roles can agree in the same quarter. A sensible board metric is the share of new pilots reaching a 70 per cent scan rate within 90 days, not pilots signed.
case20v1-cust.pains.gains:
Gantavya Network: What Hurts a Delivery Rider Most?

A product decision on which pains and gains to serve

1. Opening

On the morning of Thursday 15 October 2026, Pooja Hosur, head of product at Gantavya Network, pinned a single sheet of paper above her desk in Bengaluru. It carried two columns, one headed "What hurts" and one headed "What would delight", and nine lines of handwriting in each. The board would meet on Friday 30 October, nine days before Diwali, and would fund exactly one major build for the next two quarters. Pooja had to bring a recommendation: which of the riders' pains should Gantavya set out to relieve, and which gain should it promise in return?

She had the research. Her difficulty was that every line on the sheet was true, and the company could afford to act on only one or two of them.

2. Company background

Gantavya Network was founded in 2025 by two former payments engineers in Mumbai. Its app lets gig workers, mainly riders delivering for Zomato, Swiggy and Zepto, set aside small amounts toward a named goal such as a new bike battery or a child's school fees. Deposits move over UPI, and the money is held with a regulated partner. The company was never meant to compete with PhonePe or Paytm for payments. It was built for a narrow group those apps treat as one more segment: people paid weekly, spending daily.

The product launched in August 2025. By October 2026 it had 1,80,000 downloads. Of these, 54,000 riders had made a first deposit, an activation rate of 30 per cent, and 21,600 were saving in any given week, which is 40 per cent of activated users and 12 per cent of downloads. Gantavya had raised ₹14 crore and employed 31 people. Around it, Jar and Groww courted small savers, while lenders such as KreditBee pitched quick cash to the same riders. The Reserve Bank of India's digital lending directions, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, shaped what any new feature could do with rider data and money.

3. The situation

Between August and September 2026 the team ran 40 long interviews and then surveyed 400 active and lapsed riders in Bengaluru, Pune, Hyderabad and Guwahati. Each rider named their top three pains and top three gains around one job, which the team had written as: "Keep my household running between one payout and the next." Exhibit 1 shows the pains and Exhibit 2 the gains.

Opinions inside the company had already hardened. In Bengaluru, Pooja read the data as a mandate for an earned-wage advance, since the cash gap was both the most common pain and the most intense daily one. In Pune, engineering lead Kamlesh Hussain warned that lending meant a partner NBFC, collections, and a risk model his team had never built. In Lisbon, designer Saloni Hooda, who had watched interview recordings late into her evenings, pointed out that riders spoke of accidents in a different register altogether: voices dropped, and several mentioned a colleague who had been hurt. She doubted a survey count captured that weight. In Mumbai, partnerships head Manoj Hiray was already holding a conversation with an insurer and thought an accident cover could be live in eight weeks.

A time gap of roughly five hours between Lisbon and Mumbai meant the debate ran in written notes. Saloni's note on 9 October was the one that stuck: "We are ranking by how often people complain. We should also ask what they would be afraid to be without."

4. The people

Pooja Hosur, head of product, Bengaluru, owns the recommendation and wants a choice that grows weekly usage without risking the company's balance sheet. Kamlesh Hussain, engineering lead, Pune, wants a scope his team of nine can ship before the festive peak and fears a lending build that never ends. Saloni Hooda, design lead, Lisbon, wants the product to honour what riders fear most, not only what they mention most. Manoj Hiray, head of partnerships, Mumbai, wants revenue the board can see within two quarters, and has an insurer, but no lender, ready to sign.

6. The options

Option A: build an earned-wage advance. Riders could draw part of money they have already earned from the platform, through a lending partner, before the weekly payout. Its upside is that it answers the leading pain and leading gain together, and would plausibly turn a saving app into a weekly habit. Its cost is the highest build, ₹90 lakh, the regulatory load of the RBI's digital lending rules, credit losses, and a skill gap in the Pune team.

Option B: deepen the slow-week buffer. The existing savings engine would learn each rider's income rhythm and set money aside automatically. Its upside is low risk and close fit with what the company already does. Its cost is thin revenue, ₹5 lakh of year-one contribution, and an answer to only the second-ranked gain, one riders could partly improvise themselves.

Option C: bundle accident and hospital cover. Manoj's insurer partner would underwrite a low-premium policy sold inside the app. The upside is the strongest year-one return in Exhibit 3, ₹72 lakh, and relief from the pain riders rate most severe. The cost is that the pain is rare, so the product may sit unused in the app, and that riders may read an insurance pitch as a product for people who expect to get hurt.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, rank the pains and gains. Which ranking rule would you use: count, severity, frequency, or a blend? Defend it.
  2. Why does the one gain Gantavya serves today sit last? What does that say about how the original product was chosen?
  3. Saloni argues that fear and frequency are different things. Where, if anywhere, should fear override a survey count?
  4. Which option would you take to the board on 30 October, and what evidence would make you change your mind before then?

8. A note for the learner

Pains and gains describe the friction and reward around a job. Here the job is keeping a household running between payouts. A good answer ranks pains on at least three dimensions, how many riders feel them, how hard they bite and how often, and treats the survey as stated preference from a sample of existing users, not as proof of behaviour.

One defensible path is a staged Option A with Option C attached. The cash gap leads both the pain and gain lists, and at 3.1 episodes a month it is the only top pain that recurs weekly, which is exactly what a habit product needs. But a 30,000-rider assumption on a base of 21,600 weekly actives is too fragile for a ₹90 lakh commitment. So ask the board for roughly one-third of it, ₹30 lakh, to pilot a capped advance with 6,000 riders through an NBFC partner, with gates on repayment and weekly active use before the rest is released.

Alongside it, ship the insurer's cover within Manoj's eight weeks, offered at the moment of an advance, since a rider thinking about money risk is most receptive then. This honours Saloni's point that the most severe pain deserves an answer, and it funds the pilot cheaply. Option B waits, because it serves the weaker gain. Credit answers that separate frequency, severity and revenue, and test what they cannot yet verify.

Pains and Gains

What hurts most, what would delight most, and why the two cannot be ranked on one list

1. Two decisions, seventeen days apart

On Monday, 14 September 2026, Gautami Phalke had to close a roadmap she did not believe in. She was vice-president of product at Gulmohar Hospitality Systems, Bengaluru, whose housekeeping software ran 212 mid-market hotel properties across 34 groups: 24,960 rooms at ₹240 per room per month, or ₹7.19 crore of annual recurring revenue. Nineteen engineers, two quarters, three candidates, two slots — a room-attendant application with Hindi and Tamil voice input; predictive maintenance alerting; an owner-facing labour-cost view.

Three groups, 22 properties, had declined to renew that year, and Garima Bhatawadekar, who ran customer success from Jaipur, found one sentence in all three exit notes: the software was loved by the housekeeping floor and invisible to whoever signed the cheque. Gunjan Mahulkar's team in Kochi had returned from eleven properties with 61 pains, and 61 items is not a decision.

Seventeen days later, on Thursday, 1 October 2026, Gorakh Pandhare sat in a Vijayawada warehouse with a renewal number. Gahraai Aqua Systems made a tethered sensor buoy for vannamei shrimp ponds, logging dissolved oxygen, pH, temperature and salinity every six minutes. Gahraai had 2,400 buoys across 1,560 ponds in the Krishna, West Godavari and Bapatla districts, at ₹26,500 plus ₹1,450 a month. After the first crop cycle, 912 of the 1,560 ponds had renewed: 58.5 per cent. Gitika Parasuram in Visakhapatnam could show the buoys worked; Ghanshyam Betkar, in field agronomy at Bhimavaram, could show farmers liked them. Neither could explain the lapses.

Gorakh's decision was positioning and price: lead with the pain — your pond will crash at two in the morning and you will not know — or with the gain — you will harvest more kilograms at a better count.

Both decisions turn on one craft: putting the friction and the reward around a job into an order a company can act on. The ordering holds nearly all the difficulty, and the costliest mistake in the field is ranking the sufferer's pains while selling to the payer.

2. The idea, and the four camps that disagree about it

A job is the progress a person is trying to make in a circumstance. A pain is whatever obstructs, frightens or costs them on the way; a gain is an outcome beyond the minimum they would accept. Both belong to the person and the circumstance, not to any product, and they are not mirror images: the absence of a pain is a baseline, not a delight.

The vocabulary was assembled, not invented. Noriaki Kano's 1984 work on quality attributes established the asymmetry; Anthony Ulwick's What Customers Want (2005) supplied the machinery of outcome statements with importance and satisfaction measured separately; Clayton Christensen gave the circumstance its central place; Alexander Osterwalder's Value Proposition Canvas fixed the words from 2014. All of it answered one pathology: teams rated their own features for importance, got a wall of eights and nines, and built what the most senior person preferred. The field never converged, and a practitioner who cannot name the camps will mistake disagreement for incompetence.

The outcome school: the only defensible unit is a metric-bearing statement, such as minimise the time it takes to know a room is sellable. It would sign: a ranking without a satisfaction measurement is not a ranking. It would not sign: a vivid pain from six interviews justifies a roadmap slot.

The narrative school: the ranking lives in a switch story. It would sign: the pain behind the last twenty switches outranks the pain 60 per cent of a panel reports. It would not sign: a seven-point importance scale measures anything stable.

The economic school: a pain is worth what it costs in money. It would sign: if you cannot put a figure on it you cannot price against it. It would not sign: emotional pains deserve equal billing with functional ones.

The asymmetry school, after Kano: merging the lists is a category error, since relieving a pain buys permission to compete and creating a gain buys preference. It would sign: two lists, reconciled by judgement, never by addition. It would not sign: a pain score and a gain score are commensurable.

3. Mechanics in depth

Published versions list four or five steps; competent practitioners perform about eight, three never written down.

Fix the circumstance, not the persona. Gunjan's team researched the two hours either side of the 2 p.m. check-in peak at a 120-room property above 65 per cent occupancy. An inventory written for a role lists grievances; one written for a circumstance has a clock in it, and a clock makes severity measurable.

Decide whose pain counts before collecting any. Three people stand around this job: the attendant who suffers, the manager who chooses, the officer who pays. Fixing the weighting afterwards lets a team endorse the project it already wanted.

Write each item as an observable statement — "poor coordination" cannot be counted, "the front desk promises a room housekeeping has not released" can — then put money on it. Gulmohar modelled a reference property: 120 rooms at 70 per cent occupancy, or 30,660 occupied room-nights a year.

Measure importance and satisfaction separately. Rupees miss whatever never reaches a ledger, so 318 respondents across the three roles rated each outcome for importance and present satisfaction. Three second-order effects bite even flawless execution. Relief destroys its own evidence, since lifting satisfaction lowers that outcome's score next cycle. Relief manufactures new pains: the alerting wakes a duty manager about a compressor nobody can fix till morning. And gains decay once a rival delivers them.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions, as testable claims. C1: the job is stable enough that today's ranking still holds when the work ships. Gulmohar passes; Gahraai only partly, since disease pressure moves between crops. C2: the person can articulate the pain. Gulmohar's attendants and owners can; its supervisors ask for "a better dashboard". Gahraai's farmers state pains precisely but misattribute causes, blaming hatchery seed for a night-time oxygen trough. C3: you can service it. C4: satisfaction is measurable, which needs an incumbent way of doing the job.

C4 is where the idea misleads. In a new category there is no satisfaction to measure, and the algorithm becomes an importance ranking in a formal hat. Under a regulatory mandate the pain is "I will be penalised" and the ranking collapses to a binary. In products bought for status, stated pains are falsified: admitting the pain admits the motive.

5. Hard edge cases

In a multi-product company the inventory fragments by product while the job does not. Granth Retail Systems, Indore, sells billing, inventory and a credit ledger to 11,400 independent hardware shops whose owner has one job, staying solvent this month, split across three teams, none owning the ranking.

In a two-sided business, pains on one side are manufactured by the other. Gumti Market Exchange, a Nashik produce platform, found the grower's top pain to be payment delay and the buyer's quality variance. An instant payout does not remove that risk; it moves it onto the platform's balance sheet.

In a regulated business there are pains you may not relieve. Gopath Credit Services lends against inventory to small retailers; the fiercest pain is "I need the money today", and disclosure rules stand in the way. The constraint is part of the circumstance, so the serviceable pain becomes certainty rather than speed.

In hardware plus software the product adds pains that cannot be patched away: Gahraai's buoys biofoul, drift when a tether chafes, and need calibration no farmer can perform. An inventory omitting them ranks a software feature above a cleaning schedule.

In AI-native products a new pain class appears. Gyanmudra AI Labs, which drafts support replies for Indian service teams, found that relieving composition created verification: agents now had to decide whether to trust the draft. Satisfaction becomes a distribution whose tail drives churn.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

A pain is not a missing feature. The tell-tale sign is an inventory reading like a backlog: "no offline mode", "no loyalty tier". An expert rewrites each line as "the customer cannot…" and discards what will not take it: a request encodes the customer's theory of the solution.

Incidence and severity are different objects, and multiplying them hides which is driving. The sign is a team that cannot say whether its leading pain is common or awful. A common mild pain is a design problem; a rare savage one, a reliability problem.

The sufferer is usually not the payer. The sign is Garima's combination of user affection and lost renewal. In Table 3 the attendant's best outcome ranks fourth once influence is applied, and the hope that love converts fails wherever budget sits above the keyboard.

The information is in the satisfaction column. The sign is an importance distribution with no spread, as in Table 2 where five of six outcomes sit between 7.4 and 9.1. Importance screens; satisfaction signals, because a well-served outcome is where rivals already spent.

Gains are not negated pains. The sign is a gain list in which every item mirrors a pain: the research never left the complaint frame. Gahraai's farmers wanted to stop driving out at two in the morning, but also to show a neighbour a clean oxygen chart.

The most-wanted gain is often one you cannot deliver. The sign is a deck whose headline finding lies outside the company's capability. Pivoting towards it is usually wrong; the expert brokers it. Gorakh's farmers wanted price certainty, and Gahraai is a sensor company.

Pain relief saturates; gain creation compounds. The sign is two consecutive releases against one pain where the second moves no metric. The first eighty per cent of relief holds nearly all the value, so a flat second release means change target.

Emotional and social pains are not softer, merely less measurable, and they are often why your data is wrong. The supervisor who will not log a fault implying her floor failed, and the farmer who will not admit a crash that touches his standing, are describing how your functional data became incomplete.

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products sufferer and payer coincide, so role weighting disappears and recall becomes the problem. In B2B and enterprise weighting is the whole game, and the economic buyer's fiercest pain is about proof rather than work: "prove labour cost" scored 16.00 for the COO and 2.00 for the attendant, and that spread is the enterprise signature. On platforms the two inventories must be built jointly; in hardware the inventory must include the pains the product itself introduces; in AI products verification is a new pain class.

Where the difference is claimed and is not real: the method. Incidence, severity, satisfaction gaps and rupee costing work identically across all five. What changes is who answers, how they are weighted, and how fast the answer decays — never the arithmetic.

Stage matters once. Before product-market fit the leader should be obvious, and needing a weighted model to find it suggests no beachhead has been chosen. At scale the model earns its keep: the obvious items are relieved and what remains is clustered, as 13.49, 12.10 and 12.01 show.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Gulmohar is the first example, and its lesson is a collision between two defensible rankings: Table 4 puts the owner's view at zero, while Table 3 ranks it third of four and makes it the only candidate that answers Garima's churn.

Gahraai. Gitika modelled a one-hectare pond stocked with 4,50,000 post-larvae. Farmers who acted on the night-time oxygen alerts and the early white-faeces warning lifted survival from 62 to 70 per cent, and survival compounds: 62 per cent of 4,50,000 is 2,79,000 animals, which at 25 grams is 6,975 kg; 70 per cent is 3,15,000 animals and 7,875 kg. Feed follows biomass at a ratio of 1.40, so it rises too.

Granth, where the method failed. In mid-2025 Granth ranked shopkeeper pains from 1,340 support tickets and 40 interviews with its most engaged users. The leader was monthly GST return preparation, and Granth spent two quarters and ₹1.9 crore on a one-click filing export, shipped on Monday, 2 February 2026. Six weeks later, 1,482 of the 11,400 shops had used it — 13 per cent — and monthly churn was unchanged at 2.8 per cent. Most owners had already outsourced filing to a chartered accountant, so the relief accrued to a third party who neither chose nor paid for Granth.

The recovery began on Monday, 16 March 2026, six weeks to the day after that launch. Gulshan Alvares re-ran the instrument on a random sample of 300 shops rather than complainants, Geetika Ranganathan added a column for who bore each pain's cost, and the team weighted by payer. The new leader was customer credit: a median ledger of ₹4.6 lakh per shop, of which ₹71,000 was over 120 days old. Reminders and part-payment tracking shipped on Monday, 18 May 2026. By September, 5,244 of the 11,400 shops were using it — 46 per cent — and monthly churn had fallen from 2.8 to 1.9 per cent: 217 shops lost each month rather than 319, about 102 retained monthly and 1,224 over a year, or ₹1,17,50,400 of annualised revenue at ₹9,600 a shop. Twelve-month retention rises from 71.1 to 79.4 per cent.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Ranking from complainants. Warning: the sample comes from a support queue. Diagnostic: what share of a random sample reports this? Cost: Granth's ₹1.9 crore.

Ranking the sufferer's pains where someone else pays. Warning: strong usage, flat renewals. Diagnostic: for each top pain, name the person with budget authority. Cost: churn a renewal cycle late.

Solutions smuggled into the pain column. Warning: lines beginning "needs" or "wants". Diagnostic: attempt the "the customer cannot…" rewrite. Cost: a roadmap transcribing the loudest customer.

Treating importance as the ranking. Warning: no satisfaction measurement exists. Diagnostic: show the satisfaction distribution; without one the ranking is opinion. Cost: investment where rivals already deliver.

Letting a ranking outlive its fieldwork. Warning: an undated priority slide. Diagnostic: when was satisfaction last measured, and what shipped since? Cost: building against a gap a rival closed.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Rupees or felt severity? The economic position, steelmanned: only a monetised pain survives a pricing decision, and costing forces a team to specify the pain precisely enough to be wrong; its evidence is the reliability with which value-based pricing beats cost-plus in B2B. It would be wrong if the largest pains were unmonetisable — which the narrative school asserts, citing anxiety, embarrassment and fear of blame. The narrative position: the only validated ranking is one a real switch revealed, since a switch is behaviour and a survey a claim. It would be wrong if switch interviews held only for recent, high-involvement purchases.

Does the opportunity algorithm predict, or merely describe? The outcome school points to a long practitioner record and the logic of the floor at zero. Critics note the published record is consultant case material without out-of-sample tests, and that scores shift when item wording changes. A pre-registered test would settle it: ship against the middle of the list and see whether the top items did better.

One list or two? The asymmetry school holds that merging over-funds relief, because pains are reported more vividly. The single-list camp answers that two lists merely relocate the trade-off into an undocumented conversation.

11. What mastery looks like

Masters declare the weighting before collecting data and record who chose it. They keep incidence, severity, satisfaction and rupee cost as separate columns, resisting the composite that makes a slide cleaner. They name aloud the highly ranked pains the company cannot service, treating those as a partnership agenda. And they date every ranking, and will tell a leadership group that last year's number is no longer evidence.

12. The decisions, and three questions

On Thursday, 15 October 2026, thirty-one days after the meeting that opened this page, Gautami took predictive maintenance alerting and a stripped-down owner view. Predictive maintenance was the easy half: highest weighted opportunity at 13.49, largest modelled relief at ₹4,87,356. The owner view relieves nothing in Table 1, but Table 4 measures relief at the property while Table 3 measures influence over renewal, and the COO's opportunity of 16.00, from an importance of 9.6 against a satisfaction of 3.2, best explains the 22 lost properties. She shipped a monthly labour-cost statement, not a dashboard, and recorded the cost of deferring the attendant application: the attendant is the source of the fault data the alerting depends on.

On Friday, 23 October 2026, twenty-two days after his renewal review, Gorakh led with the pain. The oxygen and disease early warning was the highest-allocated item in Table 6, Gahraai could deliver it alone, and ₹43,900 was defensible against a ₹4,05,360 margin swing. He declined price discovery despite its 22 points, signing referrals with two processors and telling his board he was handing away 22 per cent of customers' stated value. He also funded a biofouling and calibration programme on no gain list, reasoning that his own hardware's pains best explained the 648 lapsed subscriptions.

Three questions. First: Gautami's weighting of 0.15, 0.35 and 0.50 is a judgement, and it alone moves the attendant application from first to last — what evidence could four weeks produce to justify or overturn it? Second: Granth's GST feature relieved a genuine pain and changed nothing. Is the lesson that pains must be weighted by payer, or that the ranking should never have come from engaged users? Third: defend Gahraai's referral decision against becoming a trading intermediary, and name the figure in Table 5 or 6 that would reverse your answer.

13. Going deeper

  • Jobs to Be Done — without a fixed job, severity has nothing to be severe against.
  • Writing a problem hypothesis — turns a ranked pain into a falsifiable claim.
  • Value Proposition Canvas — pairs pains with relievers, exposing relievers that answer nothing.
  • Kano model — formalises the asymmetry and the survey design for it.
  • Opportunity scoring — the full treatment of the instrument in Tables 2 and 3.
  • Market segments vs personas — decides whose pains you rank; a re-cut inverts rankings.
  • Why personas — the case for a named person carried through the ranking.
  • The self-referential design trap — how a team's own pains enter the inventory unnoticed.
  • Anatomy of a persona — where pains and gains belong, and which fields are decoration.
  • Building personas from research — the audit trail from transcript to ranking.
  • AI-assisted persona synthesis — why synthesised severity is least trustworthy.
