Forces of Progress: Push, Pull, Anxiety, Habit

1. The trader who said yes and did nothing

On 14 July 2026, Harini Hiremath, head of product at Gaddi Ledger Works in Hyderabad, sat down with chief executive Girija Hosmani to defend a number. Gaddi sells a phone-based billing and stock app to small traders: hardware shops, kirana stores and cloth wholesalers, at ₹6,000 a year. Of the 1,600 shops that started a free 60-day trial between 1 January and 31 March, every trial had ended by 30 May. Only 400 were paying by then, a conversion rate of 25.0 per cent. The other 1,200 had said, in surveys, that the app was "better than what I have". Then they had gone back to their notebooks.

Two proposals sat on the table for the 5 August board meeting. Product engineering wanted a GST e-invoicing module, four engineers for six months, budgeted at ₹60 lakh. Harini wanted to spend ₹9 lakh on something unglamorous: staff who would move a trader's old records into the app. If she was wrong, Gaddi would spend a quarter of its roadmap polishing a product that people already admitted was better, and the 75.0 per cent who walked away would keep walking.

The crux was a question: why had they not switched already? Harini had spent three weeks, from 20 June to 10 July, interviewing 50 trial users. One of them, Ganpat Hundekar, who runs a hardware shop in Begum Bazaar, summed it up. He liked the app. His son Ilesh had set it up. For two months the shop kept both the app and the red cloth-bound ledger, and when the trial ended he simply stopped opening the app.

2. The idea

The forces of progress are four pressures that act on any decision to change from one way of getting a job done to another. Two push toward change: push, the dissatisfaction with the current way, and pull, the attraction of the new one. Two push against it: anxiety, the fear that the new way will not work or will cost more than it appears, and habit, the comfort and inertia of the current way. A "job", in the jobs-to-be-done vocabulary, is the progress a person is trying to make in a particular circumstance; Ganpat's job is "know at closing time who owes me what", not "use billing software".

The model grew out of the work of Bob Moesta and colleagues, who built on Clayton Christensen's jobs-to-be-done theory in the 1990s and 2000s. They interviewed people who had recently bought things as different as houses and software, and found that "features beat competitors" explained surprisingly little. It was invented to answer one puzzle: why do better products lose to the status quo?

The sentence Harini could repeat in a meeting is this: "A customer switches only when the pressure to leave the old way, plus the attraction of ours, exceeds the fear of the new and the comfort of the old."

3. How it works, step by step

Figure 1 is a balance, not a checklist. The mechanics have five steps, and practitioners usually leave the first two implicit.

Step one: fix the unit of analysis. The forces belong to one person in one circumstance. Ganpat, the owner, bears the anxiety about wrong stock counts; Ilesh, who types, bears little. The forces are measured per decision-maker, not per account.

Step two: fix the comparison. The competing alternative is rarely a rival product. For Ganpat it is the ledger, which costs nothing and has never crashed. Pull is always pull relative to the thing actually in use.

Step three: find push. Push comes from an event, not a mood. Ganpat's shop was audited in March 2026 and he could not produce stock records quickly. That event created a few weeks of real push, and Gaddi's trial happened to start inside that window. Push decays.

Step four: name pull, anxiety and habit in the customer's words. Ganpat's pull was "the GST invoice goes to the customer's WhatsApp"; his anxiety was "if my entries vanish, I have nothing"; his habit was a ledger his father had kept the same way for thirty years.

Step five: weigh them. Moesta's teams interview switchers and non-switchers and compare.

4. A worked example, with a second pass

Harini coded all 50 interviews, scoring each force from 1 (barely mentioned) to 10 (the reason in the person's own telling). Twenty traders had converted to paid; thirty had not. Table 1 shows the mean scores. "Forward" is push plus pull; "friction" is anxiety plus habit; "net" is forward minus friction.

Table 1. Mean force intensity from 50 trial interviews, scale 1 to 10. Forward = push + pull; friction = anxiety + habit; net = forward − friction. Figures are means of coded scores per group.
GroupnPushPullAnxietyHabitForwardFrictionNet
Switchers207.06.53.53.013.56.5+7.0
Non-switchers305.04.07.06.09.013.0−4.0
Second pass: non-switchers, anxiety 7.0 → 4.0305.04.04.06.09.010.0−1.0

Read the first two rows line by line. Switchers: 7.0 + 6.5 = 13.5 forward, 3.5 + 3.0 = 6.5 friction, net +7.0. Non-switchers: 5.0 + 4.0 = 9.0 forward, 7.0 + 6.0 = 13.0 friction, net −4.0. The gap between groups in anxiety is 3.5 points, in pull 2.5, in push 2.0 and in habit 3.0. The feature the engineers wanted to build attacks pull, which is not where the groups differ most.

Second pass. Suppose migration help cuts non-switchers' anxiety from 7.0 to 4.0 and nothing else changes. Friction falls from 13.0 to 10.0, so net moves from −4.0 to −1.0. Three quarters of the gap closes (3.0 of 4.0) but it does not tip. The question becomes economics. Table 2 treats the assisted group as the 600 trials that book help, at ₹1,500 each, so the cost is 600 × ₹1,500 = ₹9.00 lakh. Assume they convert at 40 per cent against a 25 per cent baseline: 240 shops instead of 150, an extra 90, or ₹5.40 lakh a year at ₹6,000. Overall, 240 + 250 (the other 1,000 trials at 25 per cent) = 490 payers, or 30.6 per cent of 1,600.

The case is thin: break-even arrives only in year two, before the cost of serving those shops. If the assisted group converts at 32 per cent, not 40, the extra shops fall to 42 (192 less 150), and the two-year revenue is 42 × ₹6,000 = ₹2.52 lakh plus 33.6 renewing shops × ₹6,000 = ₹2.016 lakh, about ₹4.5 lakh, roughly half the cost. The conclusion is hostage to one input, so that input must be measured.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Anxiety is not habit

Anxiety is forward-looking fear about the new thing ("will it lose my data?"); habit is backward-looking comfort with the old ("my ledger works"). They need different remedies: reassurance and guarantees for the first, a cheaper first step for the second. Blurring them produces generic "ease of use" fixes that address neither.

Push needs a trigger

Dissatisfaction that has existed for years has not produced switching, so it is not push in the sense of this model. Push is felt pain plus a reason to act now: an audit, a failed delivery, a new regulation.

Pull is relative, not absolute

A customer rates your product against what they currently use, not against the market. A superior product facing a ledger that is free and familiar may generate little pull at all.

Forces are perceived, not factual

Whether the migration is actually risky matters less than whether Ganpat believes it is. The model measures belief, and beliefs can be wrong in either direction.

The scores are ordinal judgements

A 7.0 from coded interviews is a disciplined reading, not a physical quantity. Adding scores, as Table 1 does, is a heuristic for comparing groups; it does not mean the net of −4.0 has units or that −1.0 will convert half the group.

It is not a persona, a segment or a survey

Segments describe who customers are; personas summarise them; forces explain a single decision. The same trader can show high push in March and none in June. Asking people to rate the four forces on a questionnaire invites rationalisation; the evidence comes from reconstructing a real switch.

It cannot predict size or price

The model says why a group stays, not how many will move or what they will pay. For willingness to pay you need a separate test.

Ask before relying on it

Whose decision is it? What is the real alternative? Did I interview non-switchers as well as the happy ones?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early-stage and large

In consumer products, habit dominates and switching costs are small but numerous: a streak, a saved playlist, a family routine. Anxiety is mostly social ("will others follow me there?"). In B2B, forces split across people: the buyer carries pull, the end user carries habit and the finance or security reviewer carries anxiety. Gaddi sells to owners, so one person holds all four, which is unusual in B2B and part of why a small interview programme works. In a marketplace, each side has its own forces and each side's pull is the other side's presence, so the forces are coupled: a seller's anxiety about no orders is cured only by buyers, and the reverse.

An early-stage company usually faces high anxiety because it has no references; its cheapest remedy is a concierge service of the sort Harini proposes. A large company faces mostly habit, since customers have built processes around its product, and the dominant risk is to ignore push that its customers feel about its own legacy.

7. Common mistakes

Treating "no" as a product problem

Symptom: trial users praise the product and do not pay. Misunderstanding: assuming a lack of pull. Cheapest diagnostic: ask five lapsed users to narrate the last week before they stopped, and listen for fear and routine, not features.

Interviewing only winners

Symptom: every interviewee describes a smooth switch. Misunderstanding: believing the converted explain the unconverted. Diagnostic: require a non-switcher quota, as Harini's 30 of 50.

Pumping up pull when friction is the problem

Symptom: the roadmap fills with features and conversion stays flat. Misunderstanding: assuming the customer weighs a feature list. Diagnostic: compare group means as in Table 1, and check which force differs most.

Believing your own scores

Symptom: a spreadsheet of forces that shows no uncertainty. Misunderstanding: taking coded judgements for measurements. Diagnostic: have a second person code ten transcripts blind and compare.

8. What good looks like

A well-run version of Harini's decision starts with a stated alternative (the ledger), interviews drawn from both groups, and a table of forces with the quotations behind each score. It separates what the data says (anxiety is the widest gap) from what it does not (whether ₹9 lakh will pay back). It proposes a test that could prove the team wrong, sized so that a failure costs little, and it names the number at which the idea would be abandoned.

9. What Harini decided, and what to read next

She presented the forces table to Girija Hosmani on 21 July, and then the economics. Break-even at 40 per cent was not convincing and at 32 per cent failed. The risk was that traders who book help are already motivated, so the observed conversion would overstate the effect. She therefore proposed a pilot: offer assisted migration to a randomly chosen half of the next quarter's trials and nothing to the other half, so that any difference in conversion would belong to the help rather than to the kind of trader who asks for it. The e-invoicing module would wait one quarter. The pilot would be judged by one number agreed in advance: at least a 15-point lift among the offered group, which is the 40-against-25 gap the case assumed.

Girija agreed. Next, read about non-consumption and workarounds (the ledger is one), switch interviews, which are the method behind Table 1, and measuring willingness to switch, which turns the forces into forecasts.

Two questions to sit with. If the pilot lifts conversion by only 8 points, which force have you misread? And which of your own customers' "yes" answers have you been treating as pull, when they were only politeness?
case20v1-cust.jtbd.forces:
Charkha Systems: Better Books, Same Bahi-Khata

A case on the forces that decide whether a customer switches

1. Opening

On the evening of Tuesday 13 October 2026, Pooja Deshmukh sat in Charkha Systems' Pune office with a dashboard she had stopped trusting. Downloads of the company's Gujarati-first billing and ledger app, Charkha Khata, had passed 2,40,000 in six months. Almost every download had been, by any marketing measure, a success. Yet when she filtered for traders who were still sending invoices in their third month, the number was 14,400.

Diwali fell on 8 November. Across Surat, traders would open new account books on Chopda Pujan, the one moment when changing how you keep accounts feels natural rather than risky. The board would meet on Friday 30 October. Pooja, Charkha's Head of Product, had to recommend how to spend between ₹30 and 60 lakh before that window closed, and she could not say why people who liked the product were not staying.

2. Company background

Charkha Systems was founded in 2022 in Pune and sells software to small textile and garment traders, beginning with Surat, where thousands of wholesalers, brokers and powerloom owners work out of markets such as Millennium Textile Market and the Ring Road complexes. A typical customer has two to six staff and chases payments by phone. Charkha Khata handles GST invoices, party-wise ledgers, payment reminders over WhatsApp, and e-invoice generation through the GST portal. It has 62 employees and has raised ₹38 crore.

The competition is real and crowded. Khatabook and OkCredit own the digital udhaar ledger; Vyapar sells billing to small shops. Tally, installed on desktops across Gujarat for decades, remains the default of every chartered accountant, and Charkha's pitch was narrower: a product that understood a trader's world, with party names in Gujarati, bale and metre units, discount patterns by market, and broker commission fields. In demonstrations, traders called it better than what they had.

3. The situation

The company's growth had come cheaply. Installs cost about ₹25 each. Exhibit 1 shows what happened to the 2,40,000 downloads. Only 14,400, or 6 per cent, were still invoicing in the third month.

In September, Pooja asked the team to listen to the people who left. Sarika Dutta, the designer, and Padmini Divekar, the analyst, interviewed 60 traders who had registered, created at least one invoice, and then gone silent. They coded every reason a trader gave against four forces. The framework, from Jobs to Be Done, holds that switching happens only when push (dissatisfaction) and pull (attraction) together outweigh anxiety and habit. Exhibit 2 summarises the result.

Exhibit 2: Reasons cited by 60 lapsed traders, coded by force of progress

The pull was not the problem: more than half the lapsed traders praised the product. The push was weak, since only 21 of 60 described real pain with their existing method. Anxiety and habit dominated. Traders feared a half-entered ledger, staff who could not learn a new screen before the season peaked, and an accountant who would refuse a phone app. Several said that moving online would put their sales in front of the GST department in a way paper did not. The team had not designed for that perception.

From the field, Ranjit Dhawan, who leads sales from Surat, offered a blunter version. "A trader does not wake up wanting software," he told Pooja. "He wants his money back from three parties and a quiet audit. We keep selling him a better ledger."

4. The people

Pooja Deshmukh, Head of Product, Pune. She owns the recommendation. She worries that a plan built on fear and habit sounds like an excuse for weak growth.

Ranjit Dhawan, head of sales, Surat. He wants to sell through chartered accountants, whom traders trust when a GST notice arrives.

Sarika Dutta, product designer, Kolkata. She conducted most of the interviews and wants the team to design an easy first fortnight for people who keep paper books.

Padmini Divekar, data analyst, Coimbatore. She is wary of conclusions drawn from 60 interviews and wants any plan to be tested before the board sees it.

Sarika and Padmini worked from different cities; interviews ran in Gujarati and Hindi.

5. A pilot, and the money

In August Padmini ran a small pilot with 1,200 newly registered Surat traders. These traders received a free import of their existing Tally or spreadsheet data, a "parallel run" mode that let them keep entering the paper book for thirty days while Charkha mirrored it, and two visits from a field helper. Figure: the decision window. Only 26 days separate the start of the case from Diwali.

6. The options

Option A: buy more installs (₹60 lakh). Keep the funnel as it is and feed it. At ₹25 a download, ₹60 lakh buys another 2,40,000. Upside: it is predictable and lifts the headline numbers. Cost: at 6 per cent survival it yields 14,400 retained traders at about ₹417 each, and feeds the same leaking funnel.

Option B: lower anxiety and habit (₹45 lakh). Build the import tool, the parallel-run mode, and a field-helper programme, aimed at traders who have already registered. Upside: it attacks the forces 70 and 85 per cent of lapsed traders named, and the pilot suggests it works. Cost: it cannot be proven across Gujarat by Diwali, and the pilot's help may not scale.

Option C: sell through accountants (₹30 lakh). Give chartered accountants a dashboard to manage many clients and a commission for each trader who stays active. Upside: it turns a trusted advisor from a blocker into a seller. Cost: accountants have habits of their own, and the traders' anxieties stay largely untouched.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 2, which force is strongest, and which is weakest, for the lapsed traders? Why is a high pull score not enough to explain retention?
  2. Using Exhibits 1 and 3, where in the funnel does each force show up, and what does the pilot reveal?
  3. Option B costs ₹45 lakh and Option A costs ₹60 lakh. How many extra retained traders must B deliver to match A's cost per retained trader, and what does that imply for the registered base?
  4. Would you decide now, or buy more evidence first? Explain what you would ask Padmini to test before 30 October.

8. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. Charkha's team had invested in pull, which product teams naturally build and demos reward. The interviews show pull was already present; the binding forces were anxiety and habit, stubborn in a market where paper books are a family inheritance.

What a good answer looks like. It names the dominant forces from the evidence, reads each exhibit with the right denominator, and recognises that a weak push (35 per cent) means Charkha should target traders in whom pain is already acute, not try to manufacture it. Option A buys 14,400 survivors at ₹60 lakh, which is ₹416.67 each, from a fresh pool. For Option B to match that cost per survivor it must create 4,500,000 divided by 416.67, or 10,800, extra active traders. On the existing 96,000 registered traders, that lifts month-3 survival from 15 per cent to 26.25 per cent. The pilot's 42 per cent leaves room to fall short and still win, but its selection bias must be discounted.

One defensible path. Choose Option B as the core, because it works on the forces the evidence says are binding and it protects the traders already acquired. Phase it so that the import tool and parallel-run mode go live before Diwali, since Chopda Pujan is the moment when a switch is least threatening, and fund the field helpers in Surat only until a second pilot, run on a randomly chosen group, confirms the lift. Hold back Option A entirely; more installs only deepen the leak. Test Option C cheaply by recruiting ten accountants within the Option B budget. Address the GST-visibility anxiety honestly in onboarding. The recommendation should state what result in the second pilot would change the plan.
case40v1-cust.jtbd.forces:
Naavik Mobility Works: The Driver Who Will Not Switch

Kanpur and Lucknow, November 2026 — an ambiguous case on the forces that move, and hold, a customer

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday 29 November 2026, Meera Pardeshi was still at the dining table of her Indiranagar flat in Bengaluru, four printed exhibits under a water glass and one sheet she had refused to print. The board of Naavik Mobility Works met at nine, and as Vice-President of Product she was to recommend how to spend the ₹6.40 crore of growth capital released for the two quarters to March 2027.

The facts she trusted were few. Naavik had delivered 1,296 electric cargo three-wheelers in Kanpur and Lucknow since January, and on paper the vehicle saved an owner-driver roughly ₹45,000 a year. In nine months it had signed 14 dealers, energised 53 swap stations, and never found a month in which more drivers joined the energy subscription than left it. Between a product that was plainly cheaper and a customer who would not keep it lay a gap nobody could name, and her colleagues had arrived that week with six different names for it.

Her co-founder's message at 10:40 p.m. read: "Pick one. Don't bring the board four options and a shrug."

2. How Naavik came to be where it is

Naavik Mobility Works was founded in March 2019 in Bengaluru by Siddharth Panicker, formerly of a Pune commercial-vehicle maker, to supply lithium packs to the e-rickshaw assemblers around Kanpur's Dada Nagar and Panki estates.

The decision that shapes everything today was taken in November 2022. Naavik's board chose a proprietary swappable pack, the 4.3 kWh N-series, and its own network of twelve-bay cabinets, rather than a fixed-battery vehicle charged overnight at the driver's home or an open swapping standard riding on a third-party network of the kind Sun Mobility and Battery Smart were then expanding. The logic was defensible. A swappable pack let Naavik sell the vehicle without the battery, bringing the on-road price of its one-tonne Bhaar 1000 to ₹2.68 lakh against about ₹3.52 lakh for a comparable CNG vehicle, and rent battery and energy back as the Naavik Urja plan: ₹5,900 a month, unlimited swaps.

The consequences arrived in order. Every new city now costs roughly ₹5 crore of cabinets before the first vehicle is sold. The 4.3 kWh pack, sized to a cabinet drawn for e-rickshaws, gives about 62 km of loaded range, so a working driver swaps about once a day and cannot stray far from the network. And in March 2026, when the N-series replaced the legacy pack, Naavik wrote off 1,100 old packs at ₹4.10 crore. The board reads every request for station capital through that write-off.

3. The market Naavik sells into

The Indian cargo three-wheeler is a working asset bought by someone who will drive it himself. In Kanpur that is typically a man of 28 to 45 running loads between Naya Ganj, the leather units of Jajmau, the plastics cluster at Dada Nagar and the feeder warehouses serving Flipkart, Amazon and Zepto. He finances about 80 per cent of the price over three to four years with a non-banking financial company, trusts a mechanic near where he parks, and earns a different amount every week.

The incumbents are formidable in a way that has nothing to do with technology. Piaggio's Ape, Mahindra's Alfa and Atul's vehicles have decades of resale depth, a spare part on every corner, and a dealer who will quietly defer an instalment in a bad month. Mahindra's Zor and Treo, Euler and Omega Seiki compete directly. Policy pushes Naavik's way — the PM E-DRIVE incentive of ₹25,000 a vehicle, road-tax exemptions, tightening rules on old diesel — while finance pushes back, pricing an electric three-wheeler loan three to six points above a CNG one because nobody knows what a four-year-old one is worth.

In August 2026 Naavik shipped 120 vehicles to a Nairobi operator, an order worth ₹384 lakh, which took two of its nine vehicle engineers for the quarter and gave the board a story about global demand that Meera thought premature.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Figure 1: the decision path. The 2022 choice cannot be undone inside the current budget.

The Bhaar 1000 launched in Kanpur in January 2026 behind a one-page cost sheet (Exhibit 3) printed for every dealer. In March, at a dealer mela on the Grand Trunk Road, marketing surveyed 420 owner-drivers and concluded that anxiety about the technology was low. Lucknow opened in April with 19 stations. By June, Urja cancellations were visible in the weekly report and were put down to the monsoon, which halves loading work, and to one Unnao dealer who had mis-sold the plan. Both explanations were sincere; both now look wrong, since October and November ran at July's rate.

In July and August, Samira Pathan ran 38 switch interviews, reconstructing each driver's decision from the first thought of change to the day they signed, or did not. In August, Keerthi Padmanabhan pulled thirty-one days of telemetry and found the fleet's real daily distance (Exhibit 4); her note of 30 September re-cut retention on a matched cohort and landed 14 percentage points below the dashboard.

Three facts arrived late. Sixty-one used Bhaar 1000s were offered for sale in Kanpur between September and November; the best bid reported was ₹78,000. On 12 September the financier behind 58 per cent of deliveries said it would raise its electric three-wheeler rate from 21 to 24 per cent on 1 January 2027 unless Naavik posted a first-loss guarantee of 5 per cent of the book. On 20 October a Gurugram contractor running feeder fleets for several e-commerce platforms sent a letter of intent for 600 vehicles, valid to 15 December.

The PM E-DRIVE allocation of ₹25,000 a vehicle runs out around February. The 34 Kanpur sites sit on five-year leases with exit penalties; dealer agreements guarantee ₹14,000 a vehicle and cannot be reopened before April; the letter of intent lapses on 15 December. And the telemetry that would best support differential pricing is personal data under the DPDP Act, which counsel has not cleared for a credit decision.

Forces of Progress: Push, Pull, Anxiety, Habit

Why a customer who agrees your product is better still does not buy it.

1. Two decisions, six weeks apart

On Monday 12 October 2026, Sharvari Pendharkar, vice-president of product at Rozgaar Skilling Labs in Pune — a vernacular skilling and job-matching app for tradespeople — opened a quarterly review with a number she dreaded. From 1 July to 30 September 2026 it took 12,00,000 installs; 2,88,000 activated, meaning a trade profile plus one lesson, or 24.0 per cent. Of those, 14,400 bought the twelve-week placement track at ₹500: 5.0 per cent of activations, 1.2 per cent of installs. Learner revenue was ₹72.00 lakh.

The previous quarter, 2,45,000 activated users produced 11,270 payers, 4.6 per cent. That 0.4-point gain cost ₹68 lakh of employer-partnership spend. On the September base, 0.4 points is 1,152 extra payers, so each cost ₹68,00,000 ÷ 1,152 = ₹5,903, against ₹500 of revenue. Rohit Sohoni, the founder, wanted ₹1.10 crore for forty more employers. Sharvari's objection was aim, not cost: 71 per cent of lapsed users agreed the app beat how they found work, then went back to the contractor at the labour chowk.

Six weeks earlier, on Monday 31 August 2026, Raghavendra Shirodkar, head of product at Sopaan Weighbridge Works in Nashik, saw the same shape in a 60-tonne pitless electronic weighbridge with cloud software, ₹14.50 lakh installed plus ₹48,000 a year. Between 1 January and 30 June 2026 his team made 142 qualified visits, issued 58 proposals and won 17 orders — 29.3 per cent of proposals, 12.0 per cent of visits. The CRM coded the 41 unwon proposals as 29 lost on price and 12 to a competitor. Re-interviewed, they resolved into 9 lost to a rival and 32 that had not decided: 78.0 per cent of losses went to the status quo, which the CRM had no code for.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

The forces of progress are four pressures acting on one person at the moment of deciding whether to change how a job gets done. A job is the progress someone seeks in a circumstance: Prakash Rautela, an electrician in Nagpur, has the job "get paid work next week without losing a day's wage", not "use a skilling app". Two forces press toward change — push, the pain of the current arrangement, and pull, the attraction of the new. Two press against — anxiety, fear the new thing will fail or cost more than it appears, and habit, the comfort and social embedding of the old. Switching occurs when push plus pull exceeds anxiety plus habit, not when the product is better.

The formulation came from Bob Moesta and colleagues in the 1990s and 2000s, built on Clayton Christensen's jobs theory, and from a method rather than a theory: reconstructing a purchase backwards from first thought to payment. Diffusion curves, attribute utility and conjoint assume a superior bundle displaces an inferior one at a rate set by awareness and price; none accounts for a buyer who agrees yours is superior and declines.

Five schools claim this ground. The interventionists, Moesta's own, would sign that the four forces jointly explain a switch and that three can be moved by the seller; not that intensities are measurable on one cardinal scale. The trigger-timing school would sign that push is made by events outside the seller's control, so the job is detection; not that anxiety relief substitutes for a trigger. The behavioural economists — status-quo bias in Samuelson and Zeckhauser, the endowment effect in Kahneman and Tversky, Gourville's finding that buyers overweight what they surrender by roughly three to one — would sign that resistance is one loss-aversion phenomenon with a measurable multiplier; not that habit and anxiety need distinct remedies. The structuralists, after Klemperer and after Shapiro and Varian, would sign that switching is predicted by the cost of change and network position; not that interviews add power beyond a ledger. The measurement sceptics would sign that forces language is a useful interviewing discipline; not that scoring can allocate a budget. Across twenty double-coded transcripts Sharvari's inter-coder reliability was 0.78 for push, 0.61 anxiety, 0.44 habit.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Experts do five things; the first two are usually implicit. Fix the unit. The forces act on one person in one circumstance, not an account. A Sopaan order involves a managing director carrying capital anxiety, a plant head downtime anxiety, and a clerk employment anxiety and all the habit; averaging the three describes nobody. Fix the comparison. Pull is relative to what is in use, including its unpriced parts: Prakash's contractor takes a cut but advances ₹2,000 before a festival. Date the push. Push is pain plus a reason to act now. Sharvari ran 60 switch interviews between 16 June and 17 August 2026, coding each by whether a trigger had occurred in the previous sixty days.

Twenty of the 60 switched, a rate of 33.3 per cent. The spread is the finding: 64.3 per cent among the laid-off, 9.1 among those with no event. Nothing about the product differed; only the circumstance did. Measure the decay. Push drains, so take the 38 cases with a trigger (60 less the 22 without) and sort them by days from event to first install.

Score, model, calibrate. Here the formal treatment lives, and most teams stop one step early. Researchers coded each force from 0 to 4 and defined N = (Push + Pull) − (Anxiety + Habit), from −8 to +8. A logistic regression on the 60 interviews gave logit(p) = −1.60 + 0.52N.

The curvature inverts the intuitive allocation of effort. A point of anxiety relief in the most hostile tail buys 1.6 points of conversion; the same point just below the tipping point buys 8.6. The last step is calibration.

4. The conditions, stated as tests

There is a single datable moment of decision. At Rozgaar there is: a ₹500 payment. At Sopaan there is not — the median won order took 7.5 months through a technical evaluation, a capex committee and a Legal Metrology clearance, so the forces run by role and stage.

An alternative is in active use. Both qualify: a chowk-and-WhatsApp network, and a fifteen-year-old mechanical bridge with a slip book. Where it fails — a first water purifier — there is no habit to overcome and only pull analysis remains.

The decision-maker bears the anxiety. True for Prakash; false at Panchvati Sugar Industries, where the managing director signs while the weighbridge clerk, Prabhakar Sankhe, risks redundancy by a tamper-proof ticket. Aggregating them recommends financing terms when the constraint is a clerk who can stall the project indefinitely.

The switch is voluntary. Where it is not, the framework misleads. When a mandate arrives — an e-invoicing turnover threshold, a re-verification rule under the Legal Metrology Act — adoption approaches 100 per cent of the covered population whatever the anxiety or habit. Within a phase-in window the forces govern when, not whether.

The push event is observable to you. Rozgaar's 29-day median lag is a detection failure, not a persuasion failure. Where no signal exists, as in most consumer categories, the only lever is to be cheap and present.

5. Hard edges

Hardware plus software. Anxiety about software is reversible; anxiety about concrete is not. Table 3 is what a switch costs Panchvati Sugar Industries, a 2,400-tonne-per-day mill in Nashik; Sopaan's proposal quoted two of its seven lines.

Sopaan quoted ₹14.98 lakh; the perceived cost of change was ₹22.79 lakh, 52.1 per cent above the quote, and the ₹7.81 lakh never quoted is 34.3 per cent of it. Against that sits a push the mill had never sized. At 2,400 tonnes a day across a 150-day crush, Panchvati takes in 3,60,000 tonnes of cane; a 0.6 per cent short-weight leakage at ₹3,400 a tonne is 2,160 tonnes, ₹73.44 lakh a season — 3.2 times the cost of change. The decision stalled eleven months anyway: ₹73.44 lakh was invisible and attributable to nobody, while ₹22.79 lakh was dated and owned by whoever signed.

Multi-product. Sopaan attached software to 9 of the 17 orders, 52.9 per cent. The eight hardware-only sites change character at commissioning: habit now favours Sopaan, so a hard first switch manufactures a cheap second one.

Two-sided markets. At Pahunch Delivery Network, a Pune courier marketplace, each side's pull is the other's supply. A rider's anxiety about empty afternoons is curable only by merchants, a merchant's only by riders; one-sided analysis yields a recommendation that cannot work.

AI-native products. Parchhai Vision Labs sells camera-based defect inspection to foundries, replacing a human inspector. Pull is easy to demonstrate, but the buyer cannot enumerate the failure modes, so anxiety is unbounded rather than specific, and no guarantee answers an unbounded fear. Habit here is professional judgement, defended rather than preferred. The remedy is to bound the anxiety: shadow-mode running with a published disagreement rate.

The organisational seam. Sopaan's miscoded CRM is the normal case. Research owns the diagnosis, engineering the budget, sales is paid on pull, so a finding that friction binds has no owner. Mature firms claim cross-functional discovery fixes this; the good ones make "no decision" a mandatory loss code and quote the cost of change.

6. Eight distinctions that separate expert from competent

Push has a half-life, measurable in days. The competent record whether a trigger existed; the expert records when. The tell is a cohort flat by channel and steeply sloped by days-since-event — 77.8 per cent at day 7 against 12.5 at day 90. The obvious reading, that early users are better users, is wrong: they are the same users on a draining force.

Anxiety is sometimes correct. A competent team manages anxiety as a perception; an expert first asks whether the fear is true, because relieving a founded fear converts customers into refunds. The tell is a guarantee that lifts conversion and lowers net revenue.

Habit is a bundle of unpriced services, not laziness. The tell is an incumbent bad on every axis the seller measures and irreplaceable on two it never measured: forbearance in a bad month, credit without paperwork, answering at 10 p.m. The obvious reading is inertia; the accurate one is a feature you lack.

Pull has no units until you name the alternative. Rozgaar's 71 per cent were comparing the app to a job board nobody had asked about, not to the chowk. The tell is a satisfaction figure too high to square with the conversion beside it.

Marginal relief beats average relief. The curve is sigmoid, so effort belongs nearest the threshold. Rozgaar's biggest band — 1,15,200 users at N = −4 — is its least responsive: relief yields 1.6 points there against 8.6 for the 46,080 at N = 0. The competent target the biggest segment, the expert the steepest slope.

Interview-fitted models over-predict populations. The 0.51 haircut is structural: consenting to a long interview selects for push. The tell is a model that fits the sample and misses the cohort by the same multiple every quarter. Trust the ranking of bands, not their levels.

Most of the cost of change is not on your invoice. The expert builds the buyer's ledger, not the seller's price list, then hunts for lines to absorb: ₹3.20 lakh of civil works and ₹3.12 lakh of diversion could be financed away without discounting the ₹14.50 lakh. The tell is a sales team seeking price approval on deals never about price.

Forces explain switching, not retention, and your customer's habit is a moat. A customer won by anxiety relief arrives with weak pull and no habit — the churn profile — so the tell is strong early conversion with fast decay. Run the forces from the incumbent's chair and habit becomes an asset to deepen: the tell is a defender answering a challenger with migration services and longer contracts rather than features.

7. Where the picture genuinely changes

In consumer products one person holds all four forces, making diagnosis cheap and intervention blunt: habit dominates, anxiety is mostly social, and the lever is to be cheap and present when a trigger fires. In B2B the forces fracture — champion carries pull, user habit, procurement and security anxiety — so the aggregate is meaningless while the maximum anxiety across roles is decisive.

Marketplaces differ structurally, because the forces are coupled across sides. Hardware differs because anxiety attaches to irreversibility: concrete, downtime, a decommissioned asset. AI products differ in the character of anxiety, not its level, making bounding rather than guarantees the remedy. By stage the honest summary is narrow: an early-stage firm cannot argue away anxiety it has no references for, while an incumbent faces habit among customers and anxiety among prospects. Beyond that, claims that the framework differs at Series A and at scale are about budget, not mechanism.

8. Three worked examples

Sopaan's shadow audit, which worked. For ₹38,000 a site, Sopaan parked a portable axle-weigh pad beside the existing bridge for fourteen days. Of the 58 proposals, 24 sites accepted and 34 declined; Sopaan won 12 of the 24 audited, 50.0 per cent, against 5 of the 34 unaudited, 14.7 per cent — the 17 orders above. Measured short-weight was 0.42 per cent of inbound tonnage against managers' estimate of 0.10 per cent, a factor of 4.2. The programme cost 24 × ₹38,000 = ₹9.12 lakh. Year-one gross margin per order is 22 per cent of ₹14.50 lakh plus 80 per cent of ₹0.48 lakh, or ₹3.574 lakh. Crediting the whole 35.3-point gap to the audit gives 24 × 0.353, or 8.47 extra orders worth ₹30.27 lakh. Raghavendra disbelieved it — audited sites start with more push — but even a third, 2.82 orders and ₹10.09 lakh, clears the ₹9.12 lakh cost.

Rozgaar's refund guarantee, which failed. Reading anxiety as binding, Sharvari had run a randomised test opening on Thursday 1 January 2026 and closing 45 days later, on Sunday 15 February: 60,000 new activations split evenly, treatment promised a refund if the track produced no interview within 60 days. Control converted 1,500 of 30,000, or 5.0 per cent; treatment 2,100 of 30,000, or 7.0 per cent — a 2.0-point lift. Then the claims arrived, the last 60-day window closing on 16 April: 630 of the 2,100 treatment payers, 30.0 per cent, got no interview and asked for their money back. Net payers were 1,470 against 1,500. Gross revenue of ₹10.50 lakh less ₹3.15 lakh of refunds is ₹7.35 lakh against ₹7.50 lakh — ₹15,000 worse, 2.0 per cent down.

The guarantee had not relieved an unfounded fear; it had priced a founded one, revealing an interview-within-60-days rate of 70.0 per cent nobody had known. Recovery meant fixing the product, not the promise: an audit de-listed 62 of 180 employers for unverifiable vacancies, leaving 118. In the next cohort, the 45 days from 1 May to 15 June, claims fell to 294 of 2,100, 14.0 per cent, and net revenue on 30,000 users rose to ₹9.03 lakh — 20.4 per cent above the ₹7.50 lakh control.

Sambal Lending Network, which mistook habit for anxiety. Sambal offers kirana retailers a ₹2 lakh line at 1.8 per cent a month against the bazaar financier's 3.0 per cent: over six months on a full draw, ₹21,600 of interest against ₹36,000, a saving of ₹14,400. Of the 8,400 retailers approved between 1 February and 30 April 2026, 798 drew down — 9.5 per cent. Sambal read anxiety and added testimonials, a helpline and branch visits; nothing moved. Switch interviews found habit that was really an unpriced service: the financier takes stock on consignment, skips a month in a bad season and answers at 10 p.m., while Sambal auto-debited on the 5th and reported a miss to the bureau. The fix was a retailer-chosen debit date and two missed payments unreported for 90 days. In the cohort approved between 1 June and 31 August 2026, 1,656 of 7,200 approvals drew down, 23.0 per cent, a book of ₹24.01 crore at an average ₹1.45 lakh. Pull was never the binding constraint.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Reading a flat conversion rate as a missing feature. Sign: satisfaction and conversion move in opposite directions. Diagnostic: what were they using the week before, and what did it do that we do not? Caught late it costs a roadmap quarter at ₹5,903 a payer.

Interviewing only those who said yes. Sign: every transcript describes a smooth decision. Diagnostic: what is my non-switcher quota, and did I fill it? Sharvari's 22 no-event respondents carried the finding.

Confusing anxiety with habit. Sign: reassurance campaigns that do not move behaviour, as at Sambal. Diagnostic: is this a fear about the future, or a service they will lose? Caught late, a year of marketing goes on an operational problem.

Letting "no decision" hide in the loss codes. Sign: price leads the loss reasons and discounting does not raise the win rate. Diagnostic: how many of last quarter's losses went to a named competitor with a signed order? Sopaan's was 9 where the CRM said 12.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The sharpest live disagreement is whether push can be created or only detected. The trigger-timing case is empirical: Table 1's spread from 64.3 to 9.1 per cent is produced by circumstance alone, and no campaign in Rozgaar's history has moved a comparable distance — so the right investment is detection. For this to be wrong, someone must show that a seller's action manufactures push of the magnitude of a job loss; no such demonstration exists.

The interventionist reply is that this concedes too much. Anxiety and the cost of change are in the seller's hands, Sopaan's audit moved win rate 35.3 points, and a framework that only says when to show up is a media heuristic. For it to be wrong, Sopaan's gap would have to be all selection — what Raghavendra's randomisation is built to settle.

The behavioural economists dispute whether the four-way split earns its keep: loss aversion with a threefold weighting predicts the same reluctance from one replicated parameter rather than four coded judgements, and a habit reliability of 0.44 suggests the extra constructs are noise. The reply: a multiplier is not actionable — be three times better says nothing about which intervention to run on Monday.

The structuralists dispute method, not content: the ledger in Table 3 predicted Panchvati's eleven-month stall without a single interview. For it to be wrong there must be cases where the ledger is small and the switch still fails — precisely Sambal's 9.5 per cent, since the retailer's cost of change was negative. Neither camp beats the other on the other's ground.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied the framework names four forces and scores them. Someone who has internalised it refuses to begin until the alternative is named; states in advance which force binds and what would falsify that — Raghavendra's randomisation exists because he distrusted his own 35.3-point result, Sharvari's 0.51 haircut because she distrusted her model; and asks whether the fear about to be relieved is true. An expert spends more effort trying to be wrong about the binding force than moving it.

12. The decisions

Sharvari killed both proposals. The ₹1.10 crore plan bought pull at ₹5,903 a payer against a ₹500 price, and the refund guarantee had already lost ₹15,000 on 60,000 users. She funded three things instead: the employer purge that took the pool from 180 to 118; a trigger-detection build reading attendance and payslip uploads to flag a contract ending, aimed at the 29-day lag; and a re-pricing proposal to Rohit Sohoni. Of the 14,400 payers in the September quarter, 2,160 were placed, 15.0 per cent. At a ₹12,000 employer fee per confirmed placement those would have earned ₹2.59 crore against ₹72.00 lakh of learner revenue — 3.6 times as much — letting Rozgaar drop the ₹500 price standing in front of its most anxious users.

Raghavendra made the shadow audit a gate: no proposal without one, deliberately shrinking proposal volume. He randomised the offer across the next 80 qualified sites, 40 and 40, to learn how much of the gap is real. And he attacked the ₹7.81 lakh never quoted — a portable bridge during changeover to remove the ₹3.12 lakh diversion line, and the ₹3.20 lakh of civil works financed at ₹10,200 a month over 36 months, ₹3.67 lakh in all, of which ₹47,200 is finance cost, moved from capex to operating budget.

Discussion questions. First: if Raghavendra's randomisation returns 11 points rather than 35.3, has the audit failed, or learned something worth more than a win rate? Second: the 0.51 haircut assumes selection bias is stable across quarters — what would make it unstable, and how would Sharvari notice before a forecast broke? Third: Sambal made its book riskier to make it larger; state when giving away the incumbent's unpriced service is the right trade, and when it is underwriting badly.

13. Going deeper

Jobs to Be Done supplies the unit the forces act on; without a job stated as progress-in-a-circumstance the scores have no referent. Non-consumption and workarounds follows: the chowk and the slip book are the real market share. Switch interviews (JTBD timeline) is the method behind Table 1 and Figure 1, and the only way to date a push event. Measuring willingness to switch turns force scores into forecasts that Table 2 shows must be calibrated. Market segments vs personas matters because forces vary within a segment and across moments. Why personas and Anatomy of a persona give the artefact a place to record the alternative in use and the triggers to watch. The self-referential design trap is the standing risk: a team with no anxiety and no habit under-weights both. Building personas from research supplies the sampling discipline, including the non-switcher quota. AI-assisted persona synthesis is where reliability bites: a coder agreeing with humans at 0.44 on habit produces confident, wrong scores at scale.
exp40v2-cust.early.adopters:
Early adopters and the chasm

Who has the problem, knows it, and is already looking for a fix — and why the honest answer is arithmetic on a finite, shrinking pool.

1. Two decisions, the same week

On Tuesday 29 September 2026, in Coimbatore, Ojaswi Bhatnagar put one number on the wall: 19. Bhatnagar was head of product at Quwwat Machine Works, founded 2022, sixty-one people in Coimbatore and Rotterdam. Quwwat sold a clamp-on vibration sensor for ring-spinning frames at ₹9,000 a machine and a dashboard at ₹2,000 a machine a year predicting bearing failure before it broke yarn. Thirty-eight mills had bought; only the nineteen independent spinning units in the Tamil Nadu belt, she argued, behaved like buyers in motion.

Her co-founder and chief executive, Qamar Hashmi, had a board paper due Thursday 15 October. Quwwat held ₹6.4 crore and burned ₹38 lakh a month — under seventeen months, to late February 2028. The paper had to choose: hire field pairs and chase the belt, or spend ₹2.9 crore completing the product so mills not looking could buy. Bhatnagar's 19 mattered because only 53 reachable mills were still looking.

On Wednesday 30 September, Oishik Barman faced the mirror image. Barman co-founded Olakh Sports Labs in Bengaluru, with five machine-learning engineers in Lisbon. Olakh's app, launched Monday 9 February 2026, read a phone video of a cricketer's action and returned a biomechanical assessment and drills, at ₹299 a month or ₹1,999 a year. In just under eight months: 4,10,000 installs, 61,500 accounts that had uploaded a video, 7,380 paying subscribers producing ₹19.23 lakh in September — annualised, ₹2.31 crore. Investors who had put in ₹41 crore had underwritten ₹120 crore; Olakh held ₹27 crore against ₹2.6 crore a month. His head of growth, Qudsia Farooqui, framed the plan due Friday 23 October as one question: were the 7,380 the first slice of a mass market, or nearly all of it?

2. The idea, and what it was invented to fix

Define it tightly. An early adopter is a customer for whom three conditions hold at once: the problem is acute (it costs money or time the customer can name), recognised (raised unprompted), and actively sought — a workaround, trial, rival purchase or budget line already exists. The third is load-bearing: only it leaves physical evidence.

Two layers of history are routinely collapsed. Everett Rogers, in Diffusion of Innovations (1962), partitioned adopters by timing: innovators 2.5 per cent, early adopters 13.5, early majority 34, late majority 34, laggards 16. Those categories are statistical, assigned by position on a cumulative curve — never a prospective screen. Geoffrey Moore, in Crossing the Chasm (1991), claimed more: for discontinuous innovations — those forcing the buyer to change a process other people depend on — the early majority buys on different grounds, demanding peer references and a complete, supported product. Between the two populations sits a gap in demand, and firms die in it while forecasting from the enthusiasts.

Three schools disagree about what follows. Moore-orthodox signs: pick one narrow beachhead, build the whole product for it, let reference density pull in neighbours; not that the chasm is an artefact of weak marketing. The penetration school, after Andrew Ehrenberg and Byron Sharp, signs: growth comes from broad reach of light buyers, and no enthusiast segment predicts anything; not that a narrow beachhead is generally right. The jobs school signs: the gap is a different job, so the answer is a different product, not a bigger one; not that services and references close it. Bhatnagar's ₹2.9 crore is where the three diverge.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Expert practice turns the three conditions into countable evidence, then does arithmetic on a pool. One: fix the unit. Early adoption belongs to a segment — a group sharing a situation and a buying process — not to a persona or person. Quwwat's unit was a mill with twenty or more ring frames; Olakh's was a player, which forced a behavioural screen.

Two: write the seeking test as an artefact you can ask for. Quwwat's test was not "does the mill care about downtime" but "show me what you did about it last year": an abandoned box, a consultant's report, a capex line. Twenty-eight of the thirty-eight had one.

Three: size the pool, not the market — units passing the seeking test today and reachable by an affordable channel. Four: price the scarce input. Five: track the pool remaining, not the wins accumulated. Quwwat had won 19 of the 72 reachable seeking mills in A, or 26 per cent; 53 remained. At nine closes a pair-year, one pair exhausts them in 5.9 years, the two pairs Hashmi wanted in 2.9. That is the chasm as a date, not a metaphor.

The one formal model is Bass diffusion, (p + q·N/m)·(m − N), for eventual adopters m and cumulative adopters N. On Olakh's ceiling of 53,550 (section 8) with p = 0.03 and q = 0.38 it yields 1,606.5 adopters in year one, 2,150.5 in year two and 2,821.3 in year three, a cumulative 6,578.2 — against Olakh's actual 7,380 in month eight. Adoption that outruns a plausible p is being paid for: ₹4.9 crore of spend bought 4,10,000 installs at ₹120 each, ₹6,640 a paying subscriber.

4. When it applies, stated as tests

Four conditions can be written as checkable claims; they do not all hold for both. Adoption requires the buyer to change a process others depend on. True for Quwwat — a mill must change who inspects what, when — false for Olakh, where a player installs an app and tells nobody. The purchase is reference-dependent. True for the composite mills, whose committees asked which peers had deployed; false in segment A, where owners decided alone. The seeking pool is small relative to the market. True for both: 9 per cent of Tamil Nadu units, and a ceiling of 53,550 against 68 lakh players. The enthusiast's behaviour differs in kind, not degree. Olakh's case turns here.

The idea is actively misleading in three situations. Where adoption is continuous — a cheaper version of something already bought on a familiar process — there is no chasm and a narrow beachhead forfeits volume. Where distribution is self-serve and one person buys for their own use, references and whole products address a constraint that does not bind. And where the category is new but the job old and universal, segmenting on urgency discards a newcomer's only advantage, reach.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product firms. A customer can be an early adopter of the firm and a laggard on the product. Quwwat's composite mills loved the sensor and refused the dashboard: as subscription adopters they flatter the forecast, as hardware adopters they are real.

Two-sided markets. Seeking must be tested on both sides, and the binding side is rarely the noisier. Olakh's coaching academies were loudly interested with no budget; players had small budgets and strong intent. A beachhead taken from the enthusiastic side builds liquidity nobody pays for.

Regulated products. Regulation manufactures counterfeit seeking. A hospital buying because accreditation requires it is in motion, but the urgency belongs to the auditor and stops at the minimum compliant purchase. The tell is a buyer asking for the cheapest conforming configuration.

Hardware plus software. Tolerance applies to software, not hardware. A mill forgives a dashboard that mislabels a fault; it does not forgive adhesive that fails in a 41-degree shed. Quwwat's second firmware revision had to ship before any beachhead strategy meant anything, which is why Quirine Hofman's Rotterdam group held a veto.

AI-native products. Early adopters here are unrepresentative in a new way: they supply clean, well-framed inputs. Olakh's model scored 0.86 on its action-detection benchmark for seekers' videos and 0.58 for first-time uploaders in poor light. The product that satisfied enthusiasts was never tested on mainstream data.

Organisational seams. The idea dies between product and sales: product defines early adopters by urgency, sales compensation by who signs. Mature firms resolve this less elegantly than they claim — usually a ring-fenced team with its own quota and an exemption from pipeline rules: a permission slip to refuse revenue, dressed as strategy.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

Seeking is a receipt, not a sentiment. The competent practitioner asks whether the pain is acute; the expert asks to see what the customer bought, built or budgeted. The tell is the discovery call's closing question: what did you try before us, and what did it cost? A customer who cannot answer is not an early adopter.

The early adopter of the category is not the early adopter of your product. Four Quwwat prospects had bought a rival box and abandoned it: two sought better prediction, two a cheaper box. The second pair signed, churned and told the belt Quwwat was expensive. The tell: a prospect who discusses price before naming the failure.

A champion is not a segment. One motivated individual can manufacture the appearance of a seeking buyer. The expert's test is counterfactual: would this purchase survive the champion leaving? Section 8's third example shows it not surviving in nineteen cases of twenty-three.

Early-adopter revenue is an instrument, not a result. It buys information about what the whole product must contain, and that decays. The tell is a team that recites beachhead revenue but cannot say what its last five customers taught it. Quwwat's twenty-eight artefacts were worth more than its ₹165.78 lakh of hardware revenue.

The chasm belongs to the buying process, not to product quality. Improving the product does not cross it if the mainstream decision needs peer references, a service promise and a procurement-friendly contract. The asymmetry: early adopters ask if they can try it next month; mainstream buyers ask who else like them uses it.

Reference density beats reference count. Ten customers scattered across four states do not help a mill in Tiruppur decide; nineteen in the same belt, on the same mill-ERP packages, meeting at the same association, do. The expert counts references inside the buyer's peer set and treats the rest as logos.

Blended metrics hide the chasm. Any average over a population 16 per cent enthusiast and 84 per cent everyone else describes a customer who does not exist. The expert splits every cohort by first-fortnight behaviour before reading retention; the tell is a dashboard carrying a single curve.

The pool is finite and the date is computable. Competent practitioners celebrate cumulative wins; experts watch remaining reachable seekers and know the quarter it reaches zero. Quwwat's answer, 53 and 2.9 years, turned Hashmi's growth question into a sequencing one: the ₹2.9 crore is not optional, only early or late.

7. By product type and company stage

In consumer products the segment is behavioural and found after launch, because urgency is invisible before the user acts; the chasm shows as a cohort discontinuity, not a stalled pipeline. In B2B mid-market it is a firmographic cluster with a channel and a documentable artefact. In enterprise the chasm is most literal, the buying committee being Moore's mechanism. In platforms and marketplaces each side has its own pool, so the beachhead must be a matched pair dense on both sides. In hardware it must also be a serviceable radius. In AI products the difference is data, not psychology: enthusiasts' inputs are cleaner, so measured quality is an overstatement exposed at the crossing. By stage, pre-fit firms use the idea to choose whom to listen to and growth-stage firms to decide when to stop; the inversion comes at scale, where an incumbent has distribution and no seeking pool and must construct one.

8. Three worked examples

Olakh: the cohort split that settled the argument

Farooqui defined a seeker prospectively: an account that in its first fourteen days uploaded four or more videos and typed a goal. Of 61,500 activated accounts, 9,840 — 16 per cent — qualified.

Selling them at nine closes a pair-year needs 9.33 pair-years at ₹32 lakh, ₹298.67 lakh: total cost ₹588.67 lakh against ₹347.76 lakh of gross profit, a deficit of ₹240.91 lakh over three years. Renewals recover it: 84 mills at ₹82,800 a year is ₹69.55 lakh, closing the gap in 3.5 years — a six-and-a-half-year payback on a seventeen-month runway.

Qatra Water Systems: the failure, and the recovery

Qatra, founded in Pune in 2021 by Onkar Sabharwal, sold greywater recycling plants to apartment societies at an average ₹6.8 lakh and, between 2021 and 2024, sold 64 — ₹435.2 lakh. The founders believed they had found early adopters: in 58 of the 64 sales a single resident pushed it through the managing committee. In 23 of the 64 that person left within two years, and in 19 of those 23 the society stopped servicing the plant. Referrals produced five further sales in three years, 0.08 per society, against the 0.5 assumed. Conviction had been mistaken for urgency: belief does not generalise, nor survive a transfer.

Recovery took re-segmenting on measured pain, then changing the commercial model, because the pain alone did not justify the capital. Qatra targeted societies buying ten or more tanker loads a month. One buying 14 loads at ₹1,100 spends ₹15,400 a month, ₹1.85 lakh a year; a plant cutting that by 60 per cent saves ₹1.11 lakh a year and pays back in 6.1 years, which no committee approves. So from Monday 5 May 2025 Qatra sold a build-own-operate contract at ₹9,900 a month — ₹1.19 lakh a year against ₹1.85 lakh of tankers, a ₹0.66 lakh saving with no capital vote. In the twelve months to Thursday 30 April 2026 it signed 41 societies at a median five weeks against thirty-four, worth ₹48.71 lakh a year. The early adopters had been there all along; only a champion could buy the old product.

Paid acquisition masking diffusionGrowth linear in spend, flat without itWhat is organic adoption at zero spend?Olakh: ₹6,640 a subscriber against ₹261 a month

A fortnight with a spreadsheet answers any question in the third column; every cost in the fourth accrued over quarters.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Moore-orthodox, at its strongest. Discontinuous innovations are adopted through peer reference, and reference networks are local, so a firm spread thin never reaches the density where a mainstream buyer finds a peer. The evidence is the history of enterprise technology categories, whose winners almost always owned a vertical first. For this to be wrong, mainstream buyers would have to adopt without peer proof — which is what bottom-up software adoption appears to show.

The penetration school, at its strongest. Ehrenberg-Bass work finds no stable, useful loyal segment: brands grow by raising penetration among light, inattentive buyers, and "early adopter" is a label applied after the fact. On this reading Olakh's seekers are an artefact of self-selection and the answer to a ₹16.77 crore ceiling is wider reach, not a deeper product. For this to be wrong, prospective screens would have to predict — and Farooqui's did: 44 per cent against 6 per cent month-six retention, a lift of 3.6 times over the blended 12.1.

The jobs school, at its strongest. The gap is a job gap, not a demand gap. The mainstream weekend cricketer does not want biomechanical analysis done badly; no whole product converts him. The evidence is the firms that completed their product, crossed nothing, and watched the mainstream buy a different category. For this to be wrong, a firm would have to cross on services and references alone — close to what Qatra did, changing only the contract.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this says "we should start with early adopters", then describes a persona. Someone who has internalised it arrives with four numbers: the pool passing a written seeking test, its reachable fraction, the number won, and the quarter the remainder runs out. They treat the early-adopter phase as a purchase of information with a known expiry, refuse revenue that would distort the roadmap, and name what they refused. And they hold two incompatible positions at once — that the chasm is real, and that it may be the wrong frame here — long enough to find out which.

12. The decisions

On Thursday 15 October, Hashmi took Bhatnagar's recommendation with one change. Quwwat would add two field pairs in segment A alone, declining the composite mills and freezing Punjab, since only A returns more than ₹32 lakh per pair-year. But it would begin the ₹290 lakh whole product at once in two parts — ERP integrations and the service network, ₹180 lakh — because 53 remaining reachable seekers set a 2.9-year clock, and a six-and-a-half-year payback begun late is one the company never sees. The two moves are in tension, and he said so.

Barman's decision on Friday 23 October was harder, because his ceiling was not a timing problem. Olakh would stop optimising the funnel, cut acquisition from ₹120 to below ₹60 an install by selling through academies where seekers gather, and accept a smaller profitable business at the ₹16.77 crore ceiling while testing — separate product, separate team — whether the mainstream club cricketer has a different job worth serving. Farooqui disagreed: a screen that predicts retention does not prove the ceiling is real, so she wanted reach tested first. The board has not resolved it.

  1. Quwwat's segment A returns ₹37.26 lakh per pair-year against a ₹32 lakh pair. Is a 16 per cent margin enough to concentrate a company on, or evidence that no beachhead here is good enough?
  2. Olakh's ₹16.77 crore ceiling rests on three estimates: 7.5 per cent seeking, 35 per cent reachable, 30 per cent willing to pay. Which would you measure first?
  3. Qatra recovered by changing its contract, not its product. Does that support the whole-product view, or the jobs view?

13. Going deeper

Market segments vs personas — what the seeking test attaches to. Your first 100 users — turning a pool into a recruitment list and a reference set. Crossing the chasm — the whole-product machinery Quwwat's ₹290 lakh bill represents. Why personas — the composite portrait as communication device, not targeting instrument. The self-referential design trap — enthusiasm substituting for a measured pool, Qatra's error. Anatomy of a persona — what makes a persona falsifiable. Building personas from research — how artefacts become a defensible description. AI-assisted persona synthesis — interview corpora without laundering enthusiast bias. Jobs to Be Done — the strongest rival frame, deciding which of Barman's options is right.
exp20v2-cust.early.adopters:
Early adopters and the chasm

1. A Monday in October

On Monday 6 October 2025, Eshwar Kulkarni, head of product at Ekagra Route Systems, opened a spreadsheet with eleven rows. Ekagra, founded in 2023 with thirty-one people in Pune and Kraków, sold dispatch and route-planning software to businesses that run their own delivery vehicles. Each row was a paying customer. Together they produced annual recurring revenue (the yearly value of live subscriptions) of ₹39.6 lakh. The company held ₹1.8 crore in cash, which is ₹180 lakh, and spent about ₹22 lakh a month, a runway of just over eight months, running out in early June 2026.

The chief executive, Ekta Rastogi, wanted to present a plan to the board on Friday 17 October. Her instinct was breadth. The eleven customers came from three kinds of business: six FMCG distributors, three dairies and two pharmaceutical stockists. All three had said yes, and she saw no reason to choose. Kulkarni was less sure. The dairies had taken fourteen weeks on average to sign, the stockists twenty-two, the distributors five. Every stockist call ended with a request for temperature-logging features no other customer wanted.

Kulkarni's question: which of these eleven customers had behaved like people who already knew they had the problem and were already looking for a fix, and where did more of those people live? The answer would decide the roadmap and the hiring of two salespeople.

2. The idea

An early adopter, in the sense used by working product managers, is a customer who has a problem, knows they have it, and is already trying to fix it. The conditions are separate. The problem must be acute: it costs the customer real money or time. It must be recognised: the customer would describe it unprompted. And the customer must be actively seeking: they have already built a workaround, evaluated a tool or set aside a budget. A customer who meets all three will tolerate an unfinished product.

The lineage is worth stating accurately. The sociologist Everett Rogers, in Diffusion of Innovations (1962), described how new practices spread through a population and divided adopters by how early they joined: innovators (about 2.5 per cent), early adopters (13.5), early majority (34), late majority (34) and laggards (16). Geoffrey Moore, a technology marketing consultant, argued in Crossing the Chasm (1991) that for high-technology products there is a gap between the first two groups and the early majority, because the early majority wants proof, references and a complete product that the pioneers never needed. He called that gap the chasm.

The sentence Kulkarni could say in the meeting without sounding glib: "We should sell first to the people who are already trying to solve this, because they will forgive what we have not built yet and tell us what to build next."

In Exhibit 1 the first two bars together are only 16 per cent of an eventual market. A start-up that mistakes their enthusiasm for the demand of the 34 per cent bar beyond the gap will forecast revenue it cannot collect. Early adopters are not a small version of the mainstream; they are a different kind of buyer.

3. How it actually works

The mechanics have five steps, two usually left unspoken.

Step one: define the unit. Early adoption is a property of a segment, a group of customers who share a situation and a buying pattern, not of an individual persona (a composite portrait of a typical user). Kulkarni chose the firm: a distributor with ten to sixty delivery vehicles.

Step two: write the three tests as observable evidence. Acute means the customer can say what the problem costs. Ekagra's yardstick was delivery leakage, the share of delivery revenue lost to missed drops, empty return trips and fuel waste, with eight per cent or more counting as acute. Recognised means the customer raised the topic first. Seeking means a prior workaround, trial or budget line exists.

Step three (usually implicit): count backwards from the whole market. The tests are filters, and each filter shrinks the pool.

Step four (usually implicit): check that the segment can be reached cheaply. Is there a channel, such as a distributors' association or a referral from a prior customer, where this group already gathers?

Step five: sell, learn and widen. Moore's advice was to pick one narrow group, build the complete solution for it, and let reference customers pull in neighbours.

Applied to the eleven rows, the tests produced Exhibit 2. Kulkarni's team phoned each customer to check the tests.

Exhibit 2. Ekagra's eleven customers, 6 October 2025

Segment values are customers multiplied by value per customer: 6 × 3.6, 3 × 3.0, 2 × 4.5. The average is 39.6 ÷ 11 = 3.6.

Distributors came fast and almost all had a prior tool. Dairies were slow and mostly had no prior effort, so Ekagra was educating them. The stockists had sought a fix, but temperature compliance was a different product. Only one segment behaved like early adopters of this product.

4. A worked example

Kulkarni then asked how many such distributors existed. His estimate for Maharashtra, Gujarat and Karnataka was 18,000 FMCG distributors with ten to sixty vehicles. He applied the three tests as successive filters, then reach and a pilot win rate.
