Each row multiplies the row above: 18,000 × 0.40 = 7,200; × 0.50 = 3,600; × 0.25 = 900; × 0.50 = 450; × 0.10 = 45.

Read the table line by line. Of 18,000 firms, 900 are genuine early adopters, which is 5 per cent of the market. That is below Rogers' 16 per cent, sensibly, since Kulkarni counted only buyers in motion today. Only 450 can be reached affordably, and Ekagra expects to win 45. At the average contract of ₹3.6 lakh, that is 45 × 3.6 = ₹162 lakh, or ₹1.62 crore, of annual recurring revenue from this segment, in addition to the ₹21.6 lakh the six distributors already pay.

The second pass. Change one input. Suppose a sceptical board member argues that only 15 per cent, not 25, of recognising firms are really seeking, since many keep a spreadsheet out of habit and have no intention of changing. Everything above that row is unchanged at 3,600. The seeking pool becomes 3,600 × 0.15 = 540. Reach at 50 per cent leaves 270, and a 10 per cent win rate gives 27 customers, worth 27 × 3.6 = ₹97.2 lakh. A ten-point change in one filter cut the outcome from 45 to 27, a fall of 40 per cent, because filters multiply. The seeking filter is the one to measure.

Exhibit 4 shows the shape: the first bars suggest abundance, the last three show the real size of the beachhead, the first market a company wins decisively before moving on.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Urgency is not the same as enthusiasm.

A customer who loves the demo and says "this is brilliant" has shown you a feeling. A customer who already pays a monthly fee for a worse tool has shown you behaviour. Count the second kind.

Early adopters are a segment, not a persona.

A persona describes a person; the early-adopter label describes a state of mind about a problem. Two identical-looking distributors can sit on opposite sides of the line.

Moore's visionary and the practitioner's seeker differ.

In Moore's account early adopters buy for strategic advantage and will tolerate rough edges. A seeker in the sense used here may simply be in pain. The second may churn when a bigger vendor arrives.

Early adopters can mislead the roadmap.

Their requests are often idiosyncratic. Ask whether the next ten customers in the segment will want a feature.

The idea cannot size the prize or price it.

It tells you who to sell to first. Nor does it say whether the segment is large enough to build a company on.

Questions to ask before relying on it.

What evidence, other than words, shows the customer was seeking? Who found whom: did they come to us or did we persuade them? Is each filter rate measured or assumed? Can we name the channel where these customers gather?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products

In consumer products, early adopters are often individuals with a strong personal motive and little switching cost, such as someone using three expense apps before trying a fourth. They are cheap to find but leave as easily. In B2B products like Ekagra, the early adopter is an organisation with a champion inside it, and the filters are costly to check but sticky once passed. The person who feels the pain is often not the one who signs the cheque, so apply the tests to both. In marketplaces the idea applies to each side. A freight exchange needs transporters who are already hunting for return loads and shippers who are already hunting for trucks, in the same lane at the same time. The beachhead is a lane or a city, not a customer type.

Size changes the picture too. An early-stage company can build for forty customers. A large company already sits in the mainstream, its early adopters are a lead-customer programme, and the risk reverses: their demands crowd out customers who do not yet exist.

7. Common mistakes

Averaging the enthusiasts. Symptom: the roadmap contains features for three segments and each customer receives a third of the attention. Misunderstanding: that every signed customer counts equally as evidence. Diagnostic: tabulate prior workaround, time to sign and who raised the problem first, as in Exhibit 2, before choosing.

Treating a funnel as a forecast. Symptom: plans quote 45 with no range. Misunderstanding: that assumed rates are facts. Diagnostic: change each filter by a third and see which one moves the answer most; then measure that one.

Declaring victory early. Symptom: new prospects ask for references Ekagra cannot give. Misunderstanding: that the next buyers resemble the last. Diagnostic: ask what a prospect needs to see; if it is "other firms like mine", you are at the chasm's edge.

Confusing a pull with a push. Symptom: customers needed many visits and training. Misunderstanding: that persuasion creates an early adopter. Diagnostic: note who initiated the first contact.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Kulkarni's decision looks like this. Before the board meeting, the team has phoned fifty outside distributors and measured the seeking rate, so the 25 per cent in Exhibit 3 is confirmed or replaced. The team can say which segment it serves and which two it is deliberately not serving yet. Each roadmap item is tied to the question: will the next ten distributors want this? The plan carries a range, 27 to 45 customers, and states which assumption separates the two.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

Kulkarni took a recommendation to Rastogi on Wednesday 15 October. Ekagra would focus on FMCG distributors for two quarters, decline new stockist and dairy work, and measure the seeking rate with fifty calls before hiring the two salespeople. His reasoning: only one segment had met all three tests, the reachable pool of 450 was large enough, and even the downside case of 27 customers, ₹97.2 lakh, exceeded the ₹39.6 lakh in the sheet. Rastogi accepted, and the board saw the plan two days later.

To go further, read about your first hundred users, which turns this segment into a launch sequence, and then crossing the chasm itself, which asks what a complete product and a credible reference look like to the early majority.

Two questions to sit with. First, take a product you know and name three customers who match all three tests today. How do you know, and what evidence would change your mind? Second, if the seeking rate in Exhibit 3 proved to be 10 per cent, would Ekagra still be a venture-scale business, and what would the owners of the company have to believe to say yes?
case40v1-cust.early.adopters:
Prakampan Labs: Which Plant Wants This Most?

A machine-health company, six industries, and a board meeting in the morning

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday 15 November 2026, Sharvani Patwardhan was still at the dining table of her flat in Baner, Pune, with two laptops open. On one was the deck for the Prakampan Labs board in Mumbai at ten the next morning, Monday 16 November. On the other, a spreadsheet her field engineer in Coimbatore had sent at nine that evening: Ma'am, please look at column H before tomorrow.

Column H said that nineteen of the thirty-four textile spinning mills in the pilot had been paying a contractor to take quarterly vibration readings before Prakampan ever called. The deck said seven.

Sharvani, thirty-six, had joined as head of product sixteen months earlier. The board wanted one slide: which industry Prakampan would commit its next two quarters to, and why. Her co-founder wanted it to say textiles. Her own numbers said otherwise, and column H suggested neither of them had the right question.

2. How the company got here

Prakampan Labs was founded in Pune in June 2022 by Pranav Sathaye, a former plant reliability manager, and Shridhar Pendharkar, who had spent eleven years building control software. The product watches rotating machinery and warns a plant when a bearing or an alignment is going bad, days before it stops. An unplanned stoppage on a critical line costs a mid-sized plant ₹2 lakh to ₹30 lakh a day, and nobody on the floor can say which of four hundred motors will fail next.

For eighteen months the founders built software that read whatever plant data already existed. It worked beautifully in the four plants that had a data historian. In February 2024 they visited sixty-one plants across Maharashtra, Gujarat and Tamil Nadu and found forty-three with nothing usable: analogue gauges read by a fitter with a torch.

That survey produced the decision that still governs everything. The founders chose to build their own hardware, a battery-powered wireless sensor that clamps to a bearing housing and streams vibration and temperature to a gateway. It took ₹4.6 crore and fourteen months to reach a production run, with a firmware partner, Ruixiang Precision Works, in Hsinchu. It created three new problems. Every sale now carries a deployment, so travel and field days. Every sale carries inventory: 2,400 finished sensors at ₹7,200 landed cost each, ₹1.73 crore of working capital in a warehouse in Chakan.

In March 2025 Shilanyas Partners led a Series A of ₹32 crore on top of ₹6 crore of seed. The paid pilot opened on 1 April 2025; the exhibits close its first eighteen months, on 30 September 2026.

Illustration 1. Company timeline; dates as in the narrative.

3. The industry around it

Condition monitoring is not a new idea in India, only an unevenly adopted one. At the top of the market Siemens, ABB, Honeywell, Schneider Electric and SKF sell instrumented packages to large plants, and Larsen & Toubro wraps them in integration work. Those offers begin at a scale a spinning mill turning over ₹400 crore will not entertain. At the bottom, thousands of independent vibration consultants walk the aisles with a handheld analyser once a quarter, charge ₹18,000 to ₹60,000 a visit and hand over a PDF. Prakampan sits between: ₹18,000 per machine once for sensor and installation, then ₹2,400 per machine per month for the software.

Two forces push its way. The Bureau of Energy Efficiency's Perform, Achieve and Trade scheme puts named energy-intensive plants under specific-energy-consumption targets, and a misaligned drive is wasted power. And the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 made plants careful about what a vendor's gateway carries out, which helps a company whose sensors read metal, not people.

Two forces push back. In several of these industries equipment is bought on unit price alone, and a monthly software line on a maintenance budget is an unfamiliar object. And exposure abroad is now material: an agreement signed in September 2026 with Prabu Tekstil Group, a textile group in Jakarta, covers three plants and 240 machines, is worth ₹1.12 crore of first-year billings, and requires a Bahasa Indonesia interface by 31 March 2027.

4. What was believed, and what has gone wrong

That textile spinning was the beachhead. Spinning mills carry the densest population of rotating machines of any industry surveyed, they cluster around Coimbatore and Surat, and the Southern India Mills' Association gave Pranav a platform at two conferences. Textiles duly produced the largest installed base, 612 of 2,195 instrumented machines, and the second-lowest conversion.

That machines instrumented was the right metric. It was in every board pack: an honest measure of hardware shipped and a misleading measure of business built, because it rewarded the industry that bought cheaply and then stopped opening the software.

That the questionnaire measured urgency cleanly. Every plant was asked at sign-up whether it had already tried to solve unplanned breakdowns. In January 2026 the form was rewritten. The earlier version asked whether the plant had "a condition-monitoring programme", which mill owners in Tamil Nadu took to mean a department; the later asked whether anyone "takes readings on your machines today", which they took to mean the contractor who comes on a Saturday. The 2025 cohort was never re-asked. Column H is the consequence.

That cement would be too slow to sell. Procurement at a grinding unit runs through a committee, so the segment was deliberately under-resourced: nine plants in eighteen months. Seven converted, the best rate in the pilot, and there are only about 180 such plants in the country.

5. The people

Sharvani Patwardhan, head of product, Pune. Her incentive is a roadmap eleven engineers can deliver; her alerting refactor slipped two quarters while the team built a Tamil interface. Unsaid: she no longer trusts the prior-fix column in her own deck.

Pranav Sathaye, co-founder and chief executive, Pune and Mumbai. He wants textiles. The association platform is his, so is the Prabu Tekstil agreement, and he believes the spinning base is a moat pharma can never give him. Unsaid: two of the six converted mills are run by men he studied engineering with.

Shridhar Pendharkar, co-founder and chief technology officer, Pune and Bengaluru. Indifferent to which industry wins, hostile to the number of them: each adds a machine type, a sampling rate and a failure library, and six means six models for four data engineers. Unsaid: the cement models work because cement machines are big and slow and easy.

Prithvi Salvi, national sales head, Chennai. He owns Exhibit 4 and its probabilities. His variable pay is on first-year contract value booked, which hardware inflates relative to recurring revenue, and his relationships are overwhelmingly in textiles. Unsaid: those weights have never been tested against what closed.

Sabari Palaniappan, field reliability engineer, Coimbatore. He installs the sensors and is the only person who has stood in all six kinds of plant. He sent column H. His position: the pilot measured the wrong thing — not whether a plant has a programme but whether a named individual loses his evening when a machine stops. Unsaid: a Tiruppur consultancy has approached him.

Pirjo Rantanen, data scientist, Helsinki, three and a half hours behind Pune in November. She built the conversion model and is its loudest sceptic: the pilot was not randomised and the segments were worked with wildly different intensity. Her loaded cost is about ₹1.05 crore a year, three and three-quarter times a senior Pune engineer at ₹28 lakh.

Rosario Patiño, customer-success lead, Bogotá, ten and a half hours behind Pune, starting her Indian calls at seven in the evening local time. She says the cement and pharma plants ring her and the mills only answer when she rings them. She backs whichever industry keeps her role out of Pune.

Shalmali Risbud, partner at Shilanyas Partners, Mumbai. She wrote the tranche condition, and has said twice that revenue spread across six industries looks like six failed experiments, not one business. Unsaid: her fund's cycle makes a visible number in June 2027 worth more than the right answer in 2028.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 records the pilot, and the prior-fix column is the one to argue about. On the questionnaire's evidence, 53 of 120 plants, 44.2 per cent, had already tried something before Prakampan arrived, from 20.6 per cent in textiles to 88.9 per cent in cement. If Sabari's count of nineteen replaced the recorded seven, the pilot figure would be 65 of 120, or 54.2 per cent, and textiles would stand at 55.9 per cent, fourth of the six rather than last, though still below auto components. Illustration 2. The two dimensions that matter. Horizontal axis, the prior-fix share from Exhibit 1; vertical axis, addressable plants from Exhibit 5. Both linear; each point carries its two values.

7. Voices

"We have 612 machines running in spinning mills. That is not a pilot, that is a position. I am not giving it up because twelve pharma plants pay us on time."

Pranav Sathaye, board pre-read call, 12 November 2026

"The conversion numbers are real and they are also a measure of how hard we pushed. Cement had one manager and converted seven of nine. Textiles had four managers and a conference stand. Swap the effort and you may swap the table. I cannot tell you that you would; only that the pilot cannot rule it out."

Pirjo Rantanen, product review, 10 November 2026

"Ma'am, in the mills the contractor already takes readings. The mill does not call it monitoring because it is his job, not theirs. Ask the owner and he says no. Ask the fitter and he shows me the contractor's book. In the pharma unit there is a man whose name is on the batch record if the blender stops. He calls me on Sunday."

Sabari Palaniappan, email with column H, 15 November 2026, 9.04 pm

"₹2.75 crore across six industries is not a company yet. Tell me on Monday which one you will own, and how you reach ₹4 crore by June."

Shalmali Risbud, Shilanyas Partners, 6 November 2026

8. The options as Sharvani sees them tonight

Option A: commit to textile spinning. Keep the installed base and the pipeline, build the Bahasa interface the Prabu Tekstil agreement requires, and sell the same product to mills in Indonesia and Bangladesh. The argument is scale: 1,840 Indian plants, forty-six in the funnel, a hardware line cash-positive on delivery. The cost sits in Exhibit 3, and the hinge is column H. If nineteen of thirty-four mills do have a contractor taking readings, textiles may be an industry that knows the problem and has already bought a cheaper answer — a very different thing from one waiting for Prakampan.

Option B: commit to pharma formulation and cement grinding. The best conversion, retention and payback, named individuals accountable when a machine stops, and audit trails that make continuous records valuable. The cost is arithmetic: 600 addressable plants and a pool of ₹40.6 crore, against a company that has raised ₹38 crore.

Option C: commit to auto components. The compromise nobody argues for: 56.0 per cent conversion, 78.6 per cent month-twelve retention, 7.4-month payback, 2,600 plants, the largest single block of recurring revenue today. It is off the table because neither founder has a relationship in it.

Option D: stop choosing an industry and choose a buyer. Sabari's framing cuts across the other three: the unit may not be the industry at all but whether the plant has a person whose evening is lost when a line stops. Testing it means re-asking the prior-fix question across all 120 plants and 105 open opportunities — six to eight weeks producing no revenue in the quarter the tranche is measured in.

Three of these are answers and one is a reason to doubt the question, and the board has asked for an answer.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Cash at 31 October 2026 was ₹14.2 crore against a net monthly burn of ₹1.15 crore, which is 12.3 months. The Series A carries a second tranche of ₹8 crore, released only if annual recurring revenue reaches ₹4 crore by 30 June 2027, seven and a half months after the board meets. Current ARR is ₹2.75 crore, so the gap is ₹1,24,67,200; at ₹28,800 of annual subscription per machine that is 433 more machines at converted plants, roughly nineteen pharma-sized plants or twenty-five textile-sized ones. The Prabu Tekstil agreement alone, if its 240 machines go live, is ₹69.12 lakh of ARR, or 55.4 per cent of the gap, tied to the Bahasa interface due 31 March 2027.

Against that: 2,400 sensors in stock, a 1,500-unit minimum reorder. Eleven engineers, four on data. One field crew that can deploy about six plants a month. And the alerting refactor Shridhar calls the only way to serve more than two industries has not begun.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. From Exhibits 1 and 2, which industries look like Prakampan's early adopters, and on which column? Which column would you drop?
  2. Exhibits 3 and 4 point in opposite directions. What would have to be true for the pipeline to be the better guide?
  3. Textiles are 27.9 per cent of instrumented machines and 11.3 per cent of recurring revenue. Which is the company's real position, and why does the choice change the decision?
  4. If Sabari's count of nineteen is right, what becomes of the beachhead argument, and is a plant that already pays a contractor a better prospect or a worse one?
  5. Pirjo argues that conversion measures sales effort as much as appetite. Design the cheapest test that separates the two before 30 June 2027, and price it in revenue forgone.
  6. It is Monday morning: one slide, twenty minutes. What does it say, what does Sharvani leave out, and what does she tell Shalmali Risbud about reaching ₹4 crore of ARR by June?

At ten past midnight she typed to Sabari: Can you get me the contractor's name at four of those nineteen mills by eight tomorrow? Then she looked at the slide reading Textile spinning: 612 machines, 1,840 plants, the moat, and at the spreadsheet saying the moat might be a market that had already bought, and deleted neither.
case20v1-cust.early.adopters:
Hundi Collect Systems: Who Is the Early Adopter?

A product decision on beachheads, urgency and the road to the mainstream

1. Opening

On Monday 19 October 2026, Hemavati Ghanekar, head of product at Hundi Collect Systems, sat in the company's Pune office with a blank page headed "Q3 plan". The board would meet on Thursday 29 October, ten days away and just before Diwali on 8 November. It expected one recommendation: where to spend ₹60 lakh over the next two quarters.

The pilot had produced 600 sign-ups, and the founders were excited. Hemavati was not yet sure the number meant what they thought it meant. She needed to decide which distributors Hundi should chase next, and why.

2. Company background

Hundi, founded in 2023 in Gurugram, sells software that helps wholesale distributors collect what they are owed. A distributor uploads outstanding invoices from Tally Prime or a spreadsheet. Hundi then sends polite, scheduled WhatsApp reminders to retailers, each with a UPI payment link, and reconciles payments as they arrive. The price is ₹1,500 a month per distributor.

The company has 38 employees and ₹2.4 crore (240 lakh) in the bank after a seed round. Monthly burn is ₹18 lakh, which gives a little over thirteen months of runway. The alternatives are plentiful: Tally's own reminders, Vyapar, Khatabook, OkCredit and Zoho Books for bookkeeping, and payment-link tools from Razorpay, PhonePe and Paytm. None is built around the weekly rhythm of chasing forty retailers for overdue dues, which is Hundi's wedge. The pilot ran from 6 January to 30 September 2026, with founder-led outreach through distributor WhatsApp groups and trade associations.

3. The situation

By 30 September, Hundi had 600 distributors signed up and 118 paying, which is ₹1.77 lakh of monthly recurring revenue (118 x ₹1,500 = ₹1,77,000). The sign-ups came from five trades. The founders read the spread as proof of broad demand and wanted to pour money into whichever trade was largest.

Hemavati's team had collected something more useful at onboarding. Each new distributor was asked one question: before Hundi, had you already tried to fix late collections, by hiring a clerk to chase dues, buying another tool or building a spreadsheet routine? The answers are in Exhibit 1. She also had product telemetry showing who actually ran three or more weekly reminder cycles in the first sixty days.

The global team saw the data from their own corners. In Nairobi, Gideon Ireri heard the sentiment directly on calls. In Melbourne, Hari Ilango saw the cohort as a statistician would. In Lisbon, Girija Hosangadi was designing screens for traders whose daily reality she had never seen.

4. The people

Ishaan Gulati, co-founder and CEO, works from Gurugram. His network is mostly FMCG distributors, and he wants a visible 1,000 paying customers by March 2027 to raise the next round. Volume is his language.

Gideon Ireri, customer-success lead in Nairobi, two and a half hours behind Pune, takes calls late into the Indian evening. Pharma and auto-parts owners, he says, phone him unprompted, often at night, asking for a feature. FMCG owners "nod politely and never log in".

Hari Ilango, data scientist in Melbourne, five and a half hours ahead of Pune, accepts the numbers but warns that the first pharma and auto-parts sign-ups came through personal referrals, so the best-looking conversion rates may flatter the segment.

Girija Hosangadi, designer in Lisbon, notes that pharma distributors need credit-note handling and regional-language reminders, which would consume the design calendar, while a generic FMCG flow needs little new work.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 sets out the pilot by trade. FMCG and kirana distributors are the largest group, at 210 of 600 sign-ups, or 35.0 per cent. Yet the prior-fix signal runs the other way. Among FMCG distributors only 20.0 per cent (42 of 210) had tried a fix before Hundi, against 60.0 per cent in pharma and 70.0 per cent in auto parts. Pharma and auto parts together are 230 sign-ups, 38.3 per cent of the total, but 85 of the 118 paying accounts, or 72.0 per cent. Of those 230 distributors, 147 (63.9 per cent) had a prior fix.

Exhibit 2 charts the final column. It makes the same point visually: two trades convert at 35 and 40 per cent, and the other three at 10 per cent or less.

Exhibit 3 prices the options in the next section. Option A assumes the FMCG pilot rate of 10 per cent. Option B assumes the combined pharma and auto-parts rate, 85 paying of 230 sign-ups, rounded to 37 per cent.

6. The options

Option A: scale FMCG. Spend ₹60 lakh on paid campaigns and field outreach to the biggest trade, using Ishaan's network. The upside is volume and a story the board will like. The cost is that Exhibit 3 gives ₹40,000 of spend for every new paying customer, which takes 27 months of ₹1,500 subscriptions to repay.

Option B: focus on the urgent trades. Concentrate on pharma and auto-parts distributors, reaching them through trade associations, and spend half the money on what they ask for: credit notes, regional-language reminders and a Tally connector. The upside is lower spend per customer and a base of references. The cost is a smaller pool, a slower route to Ishaan's 1,000, and exposure to Hari's selection-bias warning.

Option C: build first, sell later. Pause acquisition, spend ₹25 lakh on integrations and relaunch with a broader product. The upside is a cheaper quarter. The cost is that it adds no evidence, adds no customers, and burns runway while the team waits for a mainstream that has not shown any urgency.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What does "early adopter" mean in Exhibit 1, and which column best measures it? Why is sign-up count a poor proxy?
  2. Why do 35.0 per cent of sign-ups produce so few of the paying accounts? What would Gideon's calls tell you that the dashboard cannot?
  3. How much weight should Hari's warning carry? At what paid rate does Option B stop beating Option A?
  4. Which option would you take to the board on 29 October, and what would make you change course?

8. A note for the learner

This topic frames an early adopter by urgency and openness, not by size or logo: someone who has the problem, knows it, and is already looking for a fix. The prior-fix question is a direct measure of that, because a distributor who has hired a clerk or bought another tool has already shown pain and a willingness to change. Mainstream buyers, the chasm's far side, wait for proof from people like themselves. A beachhead is therefore not the biggest segment but the one whose members can become references for the next.

A well-reasoned answer rejects Option A. Its 1,500 sign-ups would be mainly the 20 per cent prior-fix FMCG group and the polite nodders Gideon describes. It buys volume where urgency is weakest. Option C is also weak, because the pilot has already shown where demand is and building more features for people without urgency gives no new evidence.

The defensible path is Option B with discipline. Hari is right that referral sign-ups flatter conversion, so treat 444 new customers as a ceiling and not a forecast. Release the ₹30 lakh of acquisition money in two tranches of ₹15 lakh, and stop to review after the first 300 cold sign-ups. Break-even against Option A is a 12.5 per cent paid rate, since 1,200 sign-ups at 12.5 per cent give 150 customers at ₹40,000 each. Even a fall to 25 per cent would give 300 customers at ₹20,000 each, still half Option A's cost. Hemavati should also tell Ishaan that 1,000 paying customers by March 2027 is not the target to optimise now. A tight base in two trades is the foundation for FMCG later, when pharma and auto-parts references can speak to the mainstream.
case20v1-cust.persona.why:
Bhugtan Systems: The Table and the Three Shopkeepers

A decision case on why a product team might model people rather than describe a market

1. Opening

On Monday, 19 October 2026, Harshita Lamba arrived at the Bengaluru office of Bhugtan Systems at half past eight, and opened a spreadsheet she knew by heart. As Head of Product she had to bring one recommendation to the roadmap committee on Friday, 30 October, eleven days away. Diwali fell on Sunday, 8 November, and the committee's decision would fix what the company's two engineering squads built through the festival season and into the first quarter of 2027.

Sales urged a premium tier for the largest merchants; design wanted a long research programme. Underneath sat a plainer question, asked of Lamba twice that week: why spend scarce weeks on invented people when the company already had a table that described its market?

2. Company background

Bhugtan Systems, founded in Pune in 2020 and now headquartered in Bengaluru, sells a collections app and a small countertop speaker to shopkeepers who accept UPI payments. The speaker announces each payment aloud; the app reconciles the day's receipts, issues a closing statement and records credit given to regular customers. Paytm and PhonePe both sell sound devices and merchant apps, BharatPe and Razorpay serve overlapping merchants, and all of it rides on rails operated by NPCI under the oversight of the Reserve Bank of India.

The company had 1,80,000 active merchants at the end of September 2026, mostly stationers, tailors, sweet shops, pharmacies and cloth traders in tier-2 and tier-3 cities across Maharashtra, Gujarat, Punjab and Uttar Pradesh. They earned money from a monthly device-and-software fee and from a small charge on settlement. Since 2023 the product organisation had planned by segment, using monthly UPI value: Segment A below ₹1 lakh, Segment B from ₹1 lakh to ₹5 lakh, Segment C above ₹5 lakh.

3. The situation

Exhibit 1 is the table everyone referred to. It shows that Segment A held 1,10,000 merchants, about 61 per cent of the 1,80,000 total, but only 19.13 per cent of the monthly value of ₹3,450 crore. Segment C held just 16,000 merchants, 8.9 per cent of the base, yet processed ₹1,440 crore a month, or 41.74 per cent of value. Segment C also churned least. In the quarter ended 30 September, 9 per cent of its merchants left, against 30 per cent in Segment A.

Source: Bhugtan internal data. Segment value is merchants times average value per merchant. The ₹1.92 lakh average is total value over total merchants; simple means of the segment figures (₹4.03 lakh, 19.0% churn) would mislead.

Lamba read it two ways. As a map of money it was clear: Segment C was where the value was. As a map of loss it was equally clear, and more troubling. Of the 44,160 merchants who left in the quarter, 33,000, or 74.7 per cent of all those lost, came from Segment A. The table said where merchants were leaving. It said nothing about why, and the roadmap had been written as though the answer were "price".

In September Lamba's research lead interviewed 24 merchants, 12 who had stayed and 12 who had left. Sorted, the transcripts did not follow the revenue bands; they fell into three kinds of person, each present in every band. Exhibit 2 summarises the pattern.

Source: Bhugtan research team. Stayers and leavers were sampled equally, so the 50 per cent here is a sampling artefact; the company's true rate is 24.5 per cent (Exhibit 1).

Hansa, a stationer in Nashik, closes her shop at nine every night and wants the app's closing tally to match the cash drawer and the bank credit to the rupee; when next-morning UPI settlement disagrees with her notebook, she stops trusting the screen. Hiren, a Surat cloth trader, earns most of his year around Diwali and Navratri and cancels in January because the speaker sits idle. Harpreet, a hosiery owner in Ludhiana, never touches the phone at all; his son does, and Harpreet leaves when he cannot see, in one glance, what came in. Exhibit 2 shows that the ledger-keepers left at the highest rate within their group, 6 of 9 interviewed, and that they were spread across all three revenue bands: five in Segment A, three in B and one in C.

4. The people

Hemant Lal, the lead data scientist, works from Austin, ten and a half hours behind Bengaluru,. He built Exhibit 1 and trusts it: the interviews are twenty-four people, the table is 1,80,000.

Hina Londhe, the senior designer, works from Lisbon. She sketched the three working patterns and argues that no one on the team can picture a merchant at nine at night with a notebook. She wants a full research programme first.

Hitesh Lakhani, head of sales, is based in Jaipur and spends most weeks in the field. Four large Segment C merchants have asked him for multi-outlet dashboards, and a rival is pitching to them. He wants the premium tier funded now.

Hari Lobo, the customer-success lead, works from Kuala Lumpur, two and a half hours ahead of Bengaluru. He has noticed that most "cancel my plan" calls cite the same complaints the interviews surfaced, though none appears in any dashboard.

5. The calendar

6. The options

Lamba had three courses open to her. Exhibit 4 sets out their costs, which she had priced with the finance team.

Exhibit 4. The three options and their costs (₹ lakh)

Source: Bhugtan finance and product estimates. Each total is the sum of the component amounts shown.

Option 1 follows the numbers. Segment C holds 41.74 per cent of value, its churn is lowest, and four named merchants are asking. It costs ₹60 lakh and two quarters, and assumes "large" is one kind of customer; Exhibit 2 shows Segment C held all three working patterns.

Option 2 follows the designer. It would yield well-evidenced personas, but it freezes the roadmap through Diwali and defers any decision to January.

Option 3 is the middle course. Twelve further interviews would be completed within the ten working days before the committee, bringing the sample to 36. The team would write three short personas and ask Hitesh's four Segment C merchants which one they resembled. It costs ₹6 lakh, but the evidence is thin and the personas could be wrong.

7. Questions for discussion

1. What does Exhibit 1 tell Lamba, and what can it not tell her? In particular, why is a table of merchants by volume silent on the reason 74.7 per cent of the lost merchants came from Segment A?

2. Exhibit 2 shows each working pattern cutting across the revenue bands. How would the premium-tier proposal change if its sponsor had to name which of Hansa, Hiren and Harpreet it serves?

3. Which option does best against Exhibits 3 and 4, and what is each willing to be wrong about?

4. Twenty-four interviews cannot support a count. For what decision are they nevertheless sufficient?

8. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. Describing a market and modelling a person answer different questions. The segment table says who is large and who is leaving. A persona says what a particular human is trying to get done, and so it does three things a table cannot: it creates empathy for a shopkeeper nobody on the team has pictured, it draws out goals rather than features, and it gives four time zones the same person to argue about. The question is whether the segment view has stopped explaining the loss.

One defensible path: Option 3, with conditions. Lamba should fund the ₹6 lakh sprint. Option 1 commits ₹60 lakh on a belief the interviews already contradict, since the large band is not one kind of merchant. Option 2 buys certainty the company does not yet need, at ₹45 lakh, and delays the answer past Diwali. Option 3 costs 10 per cent of Option 1 (6 against 60) and finishes on the day of the decision.

The three personas are hypotheses, built from a sample that over-represents churners; they decide what to test, not how many Hansas exist. Hemant Lal's table should then be used to size them: tag a sample of the 1,80,000 merchants by the behaviours that define each persona and count. Interview recording should follow the DPDP Act. The premium tier need not be abandoned; it should be re-scoped around whichever persona the four large merchants resemble.
exp20v2-cust.persona.why:
Why Personas

Discovery & Design: Customer Modelling. Why bother with personas when you could simply describe the market?

1. A Tuesday in September

On Tuesday 8 September 2026, Charvi Bansal, head of product at Bhavishya Pension Labs in Bengaluru, opened a meeting with a spreadsheet that nobody liked. Bhavishya runs a micro-pension app: a user deposits small amounts, as little as ₹50 at a time, into a pension account regulated under the framework of the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA), and pays in through UPI. In August 2026 the app had signed up 1,20,000 new users. Only 25,320 of them, or 21.1 per cent, made a deposit within thirty days. The market description in the board deck read: "Informal-sector workers aged 22 to 45 who want a simple way to save for retirement." Nobody could build from it.

Dev Chauhan, the head of growth, wanted to spend the ₹90 lakh October-to-December marketing budget on a salary-day reminder for everyone. Chaitali Dasgupta, the lead researcher, had just returned from forty-one interviews in Pune, Kanpur and Hubballi, and said the users were not one group. Bela Dutta, who led engineering, said she could ship one major feature before the 18 September product committee, ten days away. If Bhavishya picked wrongly, the quarter would go on a feature that helped the average user, who, as this page will show, barely exists.

The decision therefore turned on a question that sounds academic: should the team keep describing the market, or give it faces? This page argues that the second choice, the persona, is a working tool for making a decision, and that it earns its place only when it changes what a team builds.

2. The idea

A persona is a described, representative user: a composite built from research on real people, given a name, a context and, above all, a set of goals, so that a team can ask "what would this person do?" and get an answer grounded in evidence. A market description, by contrast, is a statement about a category of people, such as an age band, an income level or an occupation. It tells you who exists. A persona tells you what someone is trying to get done and why your product might or might not help.

The technique was developed by the software designer Alan Cooper, who began using a fictional user in the early 1980s and set out the method in his 1999 book The Inmates Are Running the Asylum. Cooper's problem was that engineers, when they lacked a specific user, quietly designed for themselves.

Three jobs follow from this. Personas create empathy, because a team can feel the friction of a named person in a way it cannot feel a percentage. They elicit goals, because writing a persona forces the team to state what the person wants, not merely who the person is. And they align a team, because forty colleagues can argue about one imagined Dinesh and converge, where forty readings of "informal-sector worker" will diverge. Charvi's sentence for the meeting was: "A market description tells us whom to count; a persona tells us what to change."

3. How it actually works

The mechanics have five steps, and the middle ones are the ones practitioners rarely say aloud. First, gather observations: interviews, session recordings, support tickets, and behavioural data such as who deposits and who does not. Second, extract the behavioural variables, meaning the things people do or want that differ between them: how often their income arrives, how much cash they hold, what a good week looks like. Third, and usually implicit, choose which variables matter for the decision at hand. Age and city are easy to record but often explain little. Fourth, cluster the people who sit close together on those variables, and test that the clusters really differ in behaviour. Fifth, write each cluster as a persona and attach the design decision it should drive.

Figure 1 shows the sequence. At Bhavishya, Chaitali's forty-one interviews and the August deposit data supplied the observations. The variables she judged to matter were income rhythm (daily, monthly or seasonal), the typical amount available to set aside, and whether the user trusted a phone app with money. She found that age and city told her almost nothing: a 24-year-old rider in Pune and a 41-year-old rider in Hubballi behaved alike, while two 30-year-olds in the same city did not. That was the third step doing its work.

4. A worked example

Chaitali tied the interview clusters to the August cohort and arrived at three personas. Dinesh is a delivery rider who is paid daily and holds small amounts of cash. Charu is a freelance designer paid monthly who has surplus and distrusts anything that locks money away. Bhagwati runs the household accounts for a family shop, whose income is lumpy and seasonal. Table 1 sets out the cohort. Each deposit count is cohort size times deposit rate, and each monthly deposit value is depositors times the typical monthly deposit.

The blended 21.1 per cent describes no one: Dinesh is at 18.0, Charu at 30.0, Bhagwati at 12.5. A uniform reminder tuned to "the average user" would be tuned to a person who does not exist.

Second pass: change one input. Suppose a salary-day nudge works only on Dinesh, lifting his deposit rate from 18.0 to 27.0 per cent. Table 2. Rider-heavy mix: depositors 12,960 + 9,000 + 2,250 = 24,210; deposits ₹77.76 + ₹135.00 + ₹45.00 = ₹257.76 lakh. Blended rate 24,210 / 1,20,000 = 20.2 per cent. The last row is a difference, not a total.

The lesson is the gap between the two columns. Depositor count falls 4.4 per cent, a dip a market-level dashboard would call noise, while rupee deposits fall 16.1 per cent, because the sign-ups lost were the high-value ones.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

A persona is not a segment

A segment is a slice of the market defined by traits, and is used to size and target. A persona is a representative character used to design for. Segments answer "how many?"; personas answer "what do they need?".

Goals outrank demographics

The most reliable persona content is what the person is trying to accomplish and what stands in the way. If removing a detail would change no design choice, it does not belong.

A persona is a hypothesis until behaviour confirms it

Chaitali's checkpoint was to test each persona against the deposit data. A persona whose members do not behave differently in the data is a story, however vivid.

Composites are legitimate, individuals are not

A persona is built from many people and must never be one loud customer or one executive's cousin.

How many personas is too many

Three to five is usual, and the reason is practical: a team can hold that many in its head. The better test is whether each demands a different decision; two that always get the same answer should be merged.

Primary and secondary matter

Cooper's advice was to choose one primary persona, the one whose needs, if met, would also satisfy most of the others. That is a prioritisation choice and it needs a reason. Bhavishya's reason was value: Charu produces 189.00 of the 307.32 lakh, or 61.5 per cent.

What it cannot tell you

A persona cannot tell you how many people it represents, nor whether they will pay. Table 1 needed the data for the counts. Personas give direction; sizing and pricing need other tools.

Questions to ask before relying on one

What did we observe, and what did we invent? How many people sit behind it? Which decision would change if it were wrong?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products

In consumer products, such as Bhavishya, the user and the buyer are the same person, and personas turn on motive and context. In B2B products the person who uses the software is often not the one who signs the cheque, so a team needs at least a user persona and a buyer persona, and often a third for the person who must approve it, such as a security head. Writing only the user's persona is the classic B2B failure.

In a marketplace, there are two sides and personas are needed for each, and the interesting design work lies in what one side's persona demands of the other. A Flipkart seller with thin margins and a shopper hunting a festive discount are linked: the seller's willingness to cut price creates the shopper's reason to come. Early-stage companies should keep personas light, built from fifteen to twenty conversations, since the product is still changing. Large companies need a shared library with a named owner, because the job there is alignment across teams who never meet.

7. Common mistakes

The demographic mannequin

Symptom: the persona opens with age, city and a stock photograph, and stops. Misunderstanding: that describing who someone is explains what they will do. Cheapest diagnostic: delete the demographics and ask whether any design choice changes. If not, rebuild around goals.

The persona nobody uses

Symptom: a polished deck, never cited in a roadmap meeting. Misunderstanding: that the artefact is the deliverable. Diagnostic: in the next planning session, count how many times a persona is named in a trade-off. Zero means the work is decoration.

The average user

Symptom: one persona covering most of the market, with a feature list that pleases everyone mildly. Misunderstanding: that a blend is a person. The 21.1 per cent rate above is the proof. Diagnostic: split the headline metric by suspected group and see if the groups differ.

The persona that confirms the plan

Symptom: the personas fit what the team already intended to build. Diagnostic: ask what finding in the interviews would have changed the roadmap, and whether any did.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the September meeting runs differently. Chaitali presents three one-page personas, each with a goal, a main obstacle, a behavioural number from the data, and the decision it implies. The group argues over trade-offs using names rather than abstractions: "Does this help Dinesh at the end of a shift, or only Charu?" The team agrees on one primary persona with a stated reason, and it names the evidence that would make it reverse course. Dev's reminder is not rejected; it is scoped to the persona it fits.

9. Closing

On Friday 18 September, Charvi took a recommendation to the product committee. Bhavishya would build the salary-day, end-of-shift nudge for Dinesh as the one major feature, and would hold the October-to-December budget back from rider-heavy channels until the mix could be tested against deposit value, not sign-ups. The reasoning followed the tables: the nudge was worth an estimated ₹29.16 lakh a month, while a careless shift in acquisition could cost ₹49.56 lakh. She also committed Chaitali to checking each persona against live behaviour every quarter. She flagged both figures as estimates.

What to learn next: the self-referential design trap, which explains why teams design for themselves when they have no persona; the anatomy of a persona, which sets out what a good one contains; and Jobs to Be Done, which models the situation of need rather than the person. Two questions to sit with. First, name a decision your team made last quarter: which group of users did it quietly favour, and who would have objected? Second, if your headline metric were split by the groups you suspect exist, what is the smallest difference that would change a plan?

Laadla Depot: Four Bands, Five Cohorts, Thirty-eight Conversations

An ambiguous case on customer modelling in Indian pet care

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday night, 22 November 2026, Ranjana Achrekar sat at her dining table in Sahakar Nagar, Bengaluru, with three documents before her: the growth team's deck, arguing for a paid membership, Laadla Plus, for the highest-spending customers; a memo from her design lead in Amsterdam, holding that the company did not know who its customers were; and a page of her own handwriting. Laadla Depot's FY28 planning committee met at nine the next morning. As Vice-President for Product she had one slot and one recommendation, and it would fix both squads' work from January to June 2027.

Diwali had fallen two weeks earlier, on Sunday, 8 November, and the festival fortnight closed with the best gross numbers in the company's history. Nothing was broken. Cash stood at ₹71 crore at the end of October against a net burn of ₹3.40 crore a month, under twenty-one months of runway. What she could not settle was worse than any option before her: she no longer trusted the categories the question was asked in.

2. The company, and a signature from March 2024

Laadla Depot was founded in Pune in 2019 by Ravindranath Arakere and Rituparna Amladi. By November 2026 it ran 41 stores from Pune to Lucknow, an app with a recurring food plan called the Monthly Bowl, vet tele-consults and at-home grooming. Headquarters moved to Bengaluru in 2022. Of 1,840 staff, 1,180 worked in stores and delivery.

Two earlier decisions shaped the room. In 2022, after a study by Likhit Insight Partners, four spend bands became the planning unit: Band 1 below ₹1,000 of monthly spend, Band 2 ₹1,000 to ₹2,999, Band 3 ₹3,000 to ₹7,499, Band 4 ₹7,500 and above. Achrekar co-authored the memo. Within a year the growth targets, the merchandising calendar and a slice of everyone's pay were written in that language.

The second was contractual. On Monday, 18 March 2024, the company signed a five-year private-label agreement with Lataa Feed Industries of Hosur, to 31 March 2029, for the kibble that anchors the Monthly Bowl. It sets a minimum annual offtake of 1,100 tonnes at ₹182 a kilogram — a floor of ₹20.02 crore a year — and a 14 per cent charge on tonnage not lifted. FY26 offtake was 1,140 tonnes. In the 183 days from 1 April to 30 September 2026 it lifted 496 tonnes: 992 doubled, or 989 scaled on 183 days of 365. On the doubled 992, a 108-tonne shortfall, 9.82 per cent of the floor, would cost ₹27.52 lakh.

3. The industry

Indian pet care in 2026 was growing fast and unconsolidated. Supertails and Heads Up For Tails had built national brands, Zigly was opening clinics, Drools led domestic volume, Pedigree and Royal Canin held the premium shelves, and Amazon, Flipkart and ONDC sold the same SKUs on thinner margins. Zepto, Blinkit and Swiggy Instamart stocked 1.2 kg and 3 kg packs: a ten-minute option in front of the subscription customer.

Regulation bore on the product at three points. Tele-consult prescriptions had to come from veterinarians registered with the Veterinary Council of India. Prepared pet food sat in a GST slab well above the loose rice and chicken a feeder bought locally. And the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governed the consent linking a store purchase to an app account by mobile number — the join the customer view rested on. Of the 4,86,000 customers active in the quarter to 30 September 2026, 3,12,000, or 64.20 per cent, had given it; the other 1,74,000 appeared only as fragments. The Animal Birth Control Rules, 2023 framed a customer nobody had named: the resident who feeds ten street dogs and buys 20 kg bags. Abroad, Lahja Retail Group of Abu Dhabi had bought ₹6.40 crore in FY26.

4. What happened, and what has turned out to be wrong

In April 2026 the growth team set a target of lifting Band 4 spend; Exhibit 1 is the table it rested on, and the deck's first slide. As a map of money it is unambiguous: Band 4 holds 17,000 customers, 3.50 per cent of the base, and ₹19.04 crore of the ₹94.22 crore of monthly spend, 20.21 per cent; with Band 3 it is 53.74 per cent of spend. Penetration rises steeply, from 4.0 per cent in Band 1 to 58.0 per cent in Band 4.

A September survey, Exhibit 4, was read as a mandate. In August Renuka Athreya, in Bangkok, noted that cancellation reasons mapped onto no dashboard field; nothing followed. In September, independently, Rohith Anaokar in Vancouver clustered eighteen months of events into five behavioural cohorts, and Rameshwari Adiga in Amsterdam ran 38 interviews across six cities in the four weeks to Friday, 16 October 2026, writing four personas from them.

Exhibit 2 cross-tabulates cohorts against bands, and is why Achrekar stopped sleeping. The cohorts do not nest; every one appears in every band. The smallest, the bulk and trade buyer at 31,000 customers, supplies 6,000 of the 17,000 customers in Band 4, 35.29 per cent of the band the membership is for; yet those 6,000 are only 19.35 per cent of all bulk and trade buyers.

Exhibit 3 made things worse. Grouped by band at the third month, retention rises from 14.0 to 57.0 per cent, which the deck quotes. Grouped by cohort over the same customers the ordering changes: bulk and trade buyers retain at 64.0 per cent and community feeders at 41.0 per cent, while first-year pet parents, the largest cohort and the focus of almost all marketing spend, retain at 15.0 per cent. Both panels reconcile to the same 21,757 survivors of 1,02,000, a blended 21.33 per cent. The windows differ too, as the exhibit notes; in the deck they sit side by side anyway.

Three things surfaced in early November. Athreya disclosed 4,118 goodwill credits worth ₹37.06 lakh in the September quarter, of which 2,883, 70.01 per cent, went to Band 3 customers at risk. Roshni Alandkar, head of retail operations, disclosed an audit finding 15,376 of the 2,48,000 store transactions logged in September 2026, 6.20 per cent, recorded against 23 staff mobile numbers. And Anaokar conceded that his fifth cohort, the 1,34,000 labelled unclassified, could not be characterised, nor reconciled against the 1,74,000 with no consent to join.

6. The people

The group sits in five cities. Vancouver runs 13 hours 30 minutes behind Indian time, Chicago 11 hours 30, Amsterdam 4 hours 30, Bangkok 1 hour 30 ahead.

Ravindranath Arakere, co-founder and Chief Executive, wants Laadla Plus live before the Republic Day sale on Tuesday, 26 January 2027, and blames timidity on price. His incentive is the Series C talks with Lagan Growth Partners; he has not said that the draft term sheet assumes FY28 membership revenue.

Raghuveer Ambalavanan, Chief Revenue Officer, Chicago, wants the membership and a trade portal with GST invoicing, and argues they are one build. His pay rides on Band 4 spend and the Lahja order. He has not said that three of Lahja's largest reorder lines are 20 kg bags on a fortnightly rhythm — trade behaviour, not premium consumer — filed under the premium tier, the only one there is.

Rameshwari Adiga, Head of Design, Amsterdam, wants ten weeks and ₹62 lakh for the persona programme; her incentive is her research budget. She is persuasive about what nobody pictures: the Indore woman who divides 20 kg of the cheapest kibble into eleven steel bowls and has never opened the grooming tab. She has not said that her four personas are already written and offered as findings, not hypotheses, two from five transcripts each.

Rohith Anaokar, Principal Data Scientist, Vancouver, wants the bands retired and the warehouse rebuilt on cohorts, at ₹1.65 crore and nine weeks of one squad. He alone has looked at all 4,86,000 customers, not a sample. His appendix, not he, says that the unclassified cohort is 27.57 per cent of the base and he cannot say what is in it.

Renuka Athreya, Customer Success Lead, Bangkok, says the reasons her team hears — the bag is too heavy for the lift, the vet slot clashes with the school run, the dog will not eat the new food — appear in no dashboard. Her incentive is a CSAT target. She said only lately that 70.01 per cent of the credits went to Band 3, so part of that retention was bought.

Roshni Alandkar, Head of Retail Operations, Hyderabad, says the stores see customers the app never models. Her incentive is the attach rate, which pays store bonuses. She has not said that the bonus is why those 15,376 transactions sat under 23 staff numbers, nor that she knew in August.

7. Voices

"Fifty-four per cent of the money and the lowest churn sit in two bands. We have a deck, a price and a January window. What are we still discussing?"

R. Ambalavanan, growth review, Thursday, 19 November 2026

"Not the money. Whether 'Band 4' is a person. Exhibit 2 says it is five people. Which of them is the membership for?"

R. Adiga, same review

"Then name the one. Tell me what she buys on a Tuesday and I will build it. What I cannot build is a table."

Rizwan Antarkar, engineering director, Pune, same review

"The 58 per cent in slide 4 is penetration inside Band 4. Band 4 is 13.24 per cent of our subscribers. Slide 11 uses the 58 per cent as though it were a market share. Nobody has asked what the unclassified 27 per cent are, either."

R. Anaokar, comment on the deck, Friday, 20 November 2026, 02:14 IST

8. The options as Achrekar now frames them

Option A: build Laadla Plus. An annual membership for Band 4 and the top of Band 3: a discount, priority tele-consult slots, free delivery. Cost ₹2.50 crore — ₹96 lakh of engineering, ₹14 lakh of design, ₹1.40 crore of marketing — and both squads for two quarters. It alone puts revenue on the board inside FY28. It rests on Exhibit 4's leading question, and on a reading of Exhibit 1 that treats Band 4 as one person where Exhibit 2 shows five.

Option B: fund the ten-week persona and jobs-to-be-done programme. ₹62 lakh — ₹41 lakh of fieldwork, ₹9 lakh of recruitment, ₹12 lakh of synthesis — freezing the roadmap to Monday, 1 February 2027. Adiga is right that nobody pictures the Indore feeder, but it asks a board for ten weeks of not building, and its personas will not be countable: 38 interviews, soon 80, cannot say how many Ritus exist.

Option C: a three-week working-personas sprint. ₹11 lakh. Use the 38 transcripts, add fourteen interviews, re-tag the event data against four behavioural definitions and publish them as hypotheses by Friday, 11 December 2026. Cheap, fast, thin: it settles nothing about the warehouse, and the staff numbers and the unlinked 35.80 per cent may have contaminated its material.

Option D: retire the bands and rebuild the warehouse on cohorts. ₹1.65 crore — ₹1.41 crore of engineering, ₹24 lakh of infrastructure — and one squad for nine weeks. It alone changes what every team can see. It installs a model whose largest cohort is called unclassified, and rewrites three teams' objectives and pay mid-year.

Beneath them Achrekar had written a fifth line, shown to nobody: are these four options, or one build and three ways of describing the customer?

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The committee sits at nine on Monday, 23 November 2026 and not again until February. The FY28 first-half discretionary budget for product and engineering is ₹3.10 crore; the four options come to ₹4.88 crore together. Rizwan Antarkar has two squads and will commit them to one piece of work; he has not said that the warehouse rebuild takes one squad nine weeks whatever is approved, since the consent model must be rebuilt anyway.

The Lataa floor does not care which cohort lifts the tonnage, and the company tracks 108 tonnes short, a charge of ₹27.52 lakh. The cheapest tonnage is a 20 kg bag sold to a community feeder — the cohort that retains at 41.0 per cent, carries a 27 per cent gross margin, contributes ₹336.82 a customer a month, and sits almost wholly in Bands 1 and 2, where no target has ever been written.

Recorded interviews, and any change to the mobile-number join, must satisfy the DPDP Act. And the growth team's pay this year rides on Band 3 and Band 4 spend, so retiring the bands in January is also a decision about somebody's March payout.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 1 establish, and what does it only appear to establish?
  2. Exhibit 1 reports that 58.0 per cent of Band 4 customers hold a subscription, and that Band 4 is 13.24 per cent of all subscribers. Why does the choice between them change the recommendation?
  3. Exhibits 1 and 3 use different windows. Does the clash between Panels A and B favour cohorts over bands, or only show that both are descriptions?
  4. Adiga's 38 interviews cannot count anything; Anaokar's clustering cannot explain 27.57 per cent of the base. What is each sufficient for, and what would make them answer the same question?
  5. The credits, the 23 staff numbers and the unconsented 35.80 per cent each corrupt a different exhibit. Rank them by the damage done to Option A, and act on the first.
  6. It is nine o'clock on Monday, 23 November. What does Achrekar recommend, what does she concede, and what does she tell the board about the bands she introduced in 2022, knowing that the Lataa floor, the term sheet and three teams' pay are written in the language she would abandon?

11. Sahakar Nagar, half past one

Achrekar turned the page over and wrote two names on the back: Ritu and Rupesh. One was a woman in Indore she had never met, who fed eleven dogs, bought the cheapest tonnage in the business and never appeared in a target. The other was a boarding-kennel owner in Band 4 who would be sold a membership he did not want by a company that had mistaken his spend for his appetite.

Anaokar could count behaviour but not name it; Adiga could name but not count; the stores could do both and were never asked. In nine hours she would choose between a product she could ship and a vocabulary she could not defend.
exp40v2-cust.persona.why:
Why Personas

Discovery & Design › Customer Modelling. Why bother with personas when I could just describe the market?

1. Two decisions, eleven days apart

On Monday 5 October 2026, Harshita Jhaveri, vice-president of product at Hamsafar Pet Care Services in Mumbai, called a meeting about a number she could not defend. Hamsafar sells pet food, accessories and vet teleconsults through an app in nine cities. In June it acquired 62,500 first-time buyers; 20,710, or 33.1 per cent, placed a second order within ninety days — a figure the board had seen unsplit for four quarters. Gaurav Hattangadi, head of growth, wanted the ₹2.4 crore October-to-December budget spent to push it to 36 per cent. Hemal Jaisingh, the engineering lead, had eleven discretionary engineer-weeks before the Diwali freeze. Jyotika Ghorpade, back from fifty-two interviews, called it an averaging artefact.

Eleven days later, on Friday 16 October, a different argument ran in Pune. Guniya Quality Systems sells a shop-floor inspection system to auto-component makers who must hold IATF 16949 certification to supply OEMs. Jaydev Hirlekar, the founder, had reviewed the cohort signed in the twelve months to 30 September 2025, now past first renewal: 180 qualified opportunities, 96 pilots, 36 paid contracts. Gokul Hariharan, head of product, read it as a product gap; Jaswant Gondhalekar, in customer success, read it as a persona failure — Guniya had a portrait of its buyer and none of the person using the handheld forty times a shift.

Both decisions turn on one question: whether a named, representative user is a more useful object to reason with than a market description. This page argues that it usually is, that the reason is partly quantitative, and that the usual defence — empathy — is the weakest of three.

2. The idea, and the four positions on it

A persona is a described, representative user: a composite built from research on real people, given a name, a context, goals and obstacles, so a team can ask "what would this person do?" and get an answer traceable to evidence. A market description is a claim about a category — age band, income decile, firm size. It says who exists and supports counting; a persona says what someone is trying to accomplish, and only that supports design.

Alan Cooper began reasoning aloud as an imagined user in 1983 and codified the method in The Inmates Are Running the Asylum (1999). His diagnosis was narrow: lacking a named user, designers substitute themselves, and being more patient and more technical than anyone else, they drift the product towards their own tolerance for friction. The persona was a prosthetic for a missing user, not a communication device; Pruitt and Adlin (2006) made it a process with provenance and owners.

Four positions contend. The goal-directed school (Cooper) treats a few qualitative personas as design targets with one non-negotiable primary; it would sign that designing precisely for one well-chosen user serves more people than designing loosely for all, and would not sign that personas need validation first. The data-grounded school insists every attribute be sourced and sized; it would sign that an unsourced attribute is a liability, and would not sign proceeding from twenty conversations. The jobs school (Christensen; Ulwick) holds the person is the wrong unit, since one person behaves differently in different circumstances; it would sign that circumstance predicts behaviour better than personal attributes, and would not sign that demographics carry design information. The behavioural-cohort school holds that personas are a lossy summary of what event data already shows; its sharpest form is Chapman and Milham's 2006 objection that a conjunction of attributes may describe almost nobody. All four agree the market description is inadequate; the fight is over its replacement.

3. Mechanics in depth, including the arithmetic

Expert practice runs in five movements, the middle two rarely written down. Assemble observations. Extract behavioural variables — things people do or want that differ. Choose which the decision is sensitive to. Cluster along them and test that the clusters differ in behaviour. Write each as a persona with its decision attached.

Jyotika's third step discarded everything the market description was built from. Her retained variables: how many animals and of what kind; whether the buyer feeds for pleasure or for cost control; and whether the animal is the buyer's own. The last does the work, and is invisible in any demographic cut. Jugal is a first-time dog parent, over-buying accessories. Hemlata keeps three animals and values the vet consult over the catalogue. Girdhar runs home boarding from a Jaipur bungalow — a small business buying wholesale through a consumer app.

The first test of a set is discrimination: do the groups differ by more than sampling noise? Figure 1 sets the persona repeat rates against the same cohort split by age.

The persona split spreads 36.0 percentage points; the age split spreads 1.5. Nor is this a small-cell artefact: the standard error on Girdhar's 58.0 per cent at n = 5,000 is 0.70 points, so his 95 per cent interval is 58.0 ± 1.4, nowhere near Jugal's 22.0 per cent (± 0.43 on n = 36,000). That is the answer to the title question: the market description is not false, it is built from variables along which behaviour does not vary.

The second piece of machinery is the conjunction problem. A persona is a logical AND of attributes. Jyotika's draft of Jugal carried seven, from metro resident to orders after 9 p.m. In a 4,000-respondent survey their frequencies were 62, 55, 71, 48, 66, 58 and 44 per cent. Were they independent, the share satisfying all seven would be the product, 0.62 × 0.55 × 0.71 × 0.48 × 0.66 × 0.58 × 0.44 = 1.96 per cent, or 78 people. The observed count was 311, or 7.8 per cent — 3.97 times that prediction.

That ratio is the test. Near 1, the attributes are uncorrelated and the persona is a chimera; above 1, they travel together, which is exactly the claim a persona makes. Since every uncorrelated attribute multiplies the represented population down, enriching a persona with colour is an instinct to shrink it towards nobody.

4. When it applies, as testable claims

Claim 1: behaviour varies more between candidate groups than within them. Hamsafar passes emphatically, 36.0 points against 1.5. Guniya passes on another axis: pilot-to-paid conversion was 50.0 per cent where the corporate quality head championed the pilot (27 of 54), 26.7 per cent where the plant quality manager did (8 of 30), 8.3 for plant IT (1 of 12) — the same 96 pilots and 36 wins, the blended 37.5 per cent describing none.

Claim 2: the product's decisions are sensitive to that variation. Usually assumed, rarely checked. A faster checkout needs no persona; a credit term only a boarding operator can use does.

Claim 3: the team cannot observe the user directly and continuously. Hamsafar's engineers have never watched a boarding operator order forty kilograms of kibble at 11 p.m. The condition is not company size but which users the decision-makers have watched.

Claim 4: the decision horizon is longer than the measurement loop. A team that can test a change in five days should test, not theorise. Guniya's firmware ships twice a year to certified plants; a named inspector is its only instrument.

The idea is actively misleading in three situations. Where variation is in circumstance rather than person — a commuter buying a sandwich behaves nothing like the same person buying Sunday groceries — a persona attributes to identity what belongs to the occasion, and the jobs school is right. Where a market is homogeneous in the dimensions that matter, as with a filing utility, personas manufacture distinctions and licence sprawl. And where a persona proxies for a power struggle it stops being evidence; the tell is needs that track one executive's roadmap.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Guniya is the hardware-plus-software case, and its numbers show the seam. Across the 36 paid accounts, 1,800 inspectors were trained, 50 per account. In the 12 where Guniya also redesigned the inspector's shift workflow, 450 of 600 — 75.0 per cent — logged an inspection every shift at day ninety. In the other 24, 420 of 1,200, or 35.0 per cent. Across all 36, 870 of 1,800, or 48.3 per cent.

The consequence arrives at renewal. The 12 redesign accounts averaged ₹24 lakh of annual contract value — a book of ₹288 lakh — and 11 renewed: 91.7 per cent, worth ₹264 lakh. The other 24 averaged ₹18 lakh, a book of ₹432 lakh, and 13 renewed: 54.2 per cent, worth ₹234 lakh. Total book ₹720 lakh, renewed ₹498 lakh: gross revenue retention 69.2 per cent against logo retention of 66.7. Had the 24 renewed at 91.7 per cent, 22 would have stayed, worth ₹396 lakh, lifting the renewed total to ₹660 lakh and retention to 91.7 per cent — ₹162 lakh a year more, against ₹1.6 lakh of redesign per plant, ₹38.4 lakh across 24: a return of 4.2 times in year one.

Guniya's buyer persona, Gajanan the corporate quality head, was owned by sales. Nobody owned Haresh, the line inspector, because inspectors never appear in the sales cycle; Jaimini, the plant quality manager, and Hitesh in plant IT were obstacles, not users with goals. Mature enterprises claim a persona library; what they keep is a buyer list. The diagnostic: who owns the user persona, by name, and does that person's bonus depend on renewal rather than bookings?

Other seams fail differently. On a two-sided platform a persona on one side implies a constraint on the other, and the arithmetic closes only when both are specified. In an AI-native product the persona must carry tolerance for being wrong: one summarisation feature delights a user who verifies and is unusable to one who forwards unread. A regulator is a stakeholder, not a persona, having no goals the product serves. In a multi-product company the set belongs to the portfolio, or two teams optimise one person in opposite directions.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert

A persona is an instrument for choosing, not describing

The competent practitioner writes a good description and stops; the expert writes one so an argument becomes decidable. The tell: sentences of the form "therefore we will not build X".

Empathy is the weakest of the three benefits

Empathy is unfalsifiable and fades within a quarter of the workshop that produced it; goal-elicitation and alignment survive because they leave artefacts. The tell: a team citing empathy has not re-tested its personas in a year.

The choice of behavioural variable is the whole exercise

Jyotika's question — is the animal yours? — created Girdhar, 8.0 per cent of buyers and 34.7 per cent of revenue, where a demographic framing would have scattered those 5,000 people. The tell: an expert names a variable she excluded.

A primary persona needs a stated measure

Cooper's rule, choose the persona whose satisfaction satisfies the others, is often put to a vote. On revenue share Hamsafar's primary is Hemlata at 49.8 per cent; on gross profit per engineer-week, Girdhar at ₹11.09 lakh; on headcount, Jugal at 57.6.

Three to five personas, and not for comfort

The sharper reason is the merge test: two personas that always produce the same decision are one wearing two names, and a set producing six answers produces none.

Personas cannot size, price or forecast

A persona has no cardinality; every count in Table 1 came from behavioural data joined to the persona assignment. Asked how big Girdhar is, an expert answers with a join. Sizing validates personas, not conversely.

The conjunction ratio measures quality, not the attribute list

Each uncorrelated attribute multiplies the represented population down. Jugal's seven predicted 1.96 per cent under independence and delivered 7.8 per cent observed, a ratio of 3.97. The tell: the expert deletes attributes.

Windows are not interchangeable, and sets decay with mix

Hamsafar's figures are all ninety-day; Guniya's adoption is at day ninety and retention at twelve months. Mix windows and the ranking becomes an artefact of measurement. Sets also drift when the entering mix changes, so experts re-test after channel changes.

7. How this changes by product type and stage

In consumer products user and buyer coincide, so personas turn on motive and occasion, and data is plentiful enough to validate clusters quickly. In B2B and enterprise the user, buyer, approver and administrator are different people with conflicting goals, so the minimum set is larger. In platforms and marketplaces each side needs its own set, and the work is the cross-side implication. In hardware plus software the persona carries the physical environment — gloves, glare, noise, a shift roster — which telemetry never reveals. In AI products the new attribute is error tolerance.

By stage the honest answer is narrow. An early company builds light personas from fifteen to twenty conversations; a scaling company is the only stage where the full apparatus pays; a large company's problem is governance, not quality. The arithmetic itself never changes.

8. Three worked examples, including one failure

Hamsafar found an 8.0 per cent group producing 34.7 per cent of ninety-day revenue at a 22 per cent margin: high revenue, thin profit, cheap to serve. Guniya's buyer persona was productive — Gajanan-championed pilots converted at 50.0 per cent against 8.3 for plant IT — while the missing user persona destroyed value downstream, at 48.3 per cent adoption and 69.2 per cent revenue retention. Its recovery was a change in who owned a persona, not a new document.

Hathkargha Craft Exchange. Founded by Himani Jagirdar in Varanasi, Hathkargha connects handloom weaver clusters to urban buyers, trading on the Handloom Mark and GI-tagged fabric. In the year to September 2025 its buyer-side thinking rested on one persona, Jhilmil, a 32-year-old conscious consumer in Bengaluru, drawn from eighteen interviews — all recruited from Hathkargha's own Instagram followers. The funnel: 2,40,000 installs, 48,000 accounts (20.0 per cent), 9,600 first purchases (20.0 per cent of accounts, 4.0 per cent of installs). Repeat purchase within 180 days was 1,620, or 16.9 per cent, and repeat buyers averaged 1.5 further orders, so orders totalled 9,600 + 2,430 = 12,030, or 1.25 per buyer. At ₹2,750 average order value and a 14 per cent take rate, contribution per order was ₹385 and total contribution ₹46.32 lakh against ₹192 lakh of spend: CAC ₹2,000 per buyer against ₹482.45 of contribution, a ratio of 4.15.

The failure was not that Jhilmil was unreal but that she came from the population already converted, so the persona encoded the outcome it was meant to explain. The re-analysis split the same 9,600 first orders by occasion: gifting 2,400 (25.0 per cent), self 5,760 (60.0), home furnishing 1,440 (15.0), with 180-day repeat rates of 30.0, 12.5 and 12.5 per cent — 720 + 720 + 180 = the same 1,620 repeat buyers, unevenly spread. Gifting was a quarter of buyers and 44.4 per cent of repeat buyers.
