The recovery is honest rather than triumphant. The new primary persona, Gulnaaz the occasion gifter, brought a guaranteed delivery date, gift packaging and occasion reminders, and a decision to stop buying broad installs. Contribution per buyer rose 34.9 per cent and CAC halved, yet spend still exceeded contribution by 1.54 times: closer to viable, not viable.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

The self-selected sample. Sign: every interviewee came through a channel the product owns. Diagnostic: what share of subjects never completed the action we are explaining? Hathkargha's answer was zero; the cost, a year and ₹145.68 lakh.

The buyer-only set. Sign: every persona has budget authority. Diagnostic: name the person who touches the product most hours per week and show me their persona. Guniya caught it at first renewal, at ₹162 lakh a year.

The average user. Sign: one headline rate reported for four quarters, unsplit. Diagnostic: split it and compare the spread to sampling error. Hamsafar's 33.1 per cent concealed a 36.0-point range.

The over-specified persona. Sign: the document runs past two pages and names a favourite restaurant. Diagnostic: the conjunction ratio; below about 1.5 the attributes do not travel together.

The ratifying persona. Sign: no finding surprised anyone. Diagnostic: which finding changed a planned item, and what did it displace?

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is whether the unit is the person or the circumstance. The jobs school's strongest form is empirical: Hathkargha's occasion split separated 30.0 from 12.5 per cent where buyer identity separated nothing. For it to be wrong, person-level traits would have to predict behaviour across circumstances better than circumstance does — Girdhar is a candidate.

The second is whether validation must precede use. The goal-directed steelman: validation is a luxury of companies with traffic, twenty well-chosen interviews surface a market's goal structure, and waiting means designing for nobody — by Cooper's argument, for yourself. For it to be wrong, teams proceeding on twenty interviews would have to decide worse than teams that waited; the evidence is thin, since published cases are selected on success.

The third is whether naming is a feature or a bug. The cohort position: a name invites invention, "Jugal would hate this" is unfalsifiable where "the 22 per cent group did not return" is not. For it to be wrong there must be decisions event data cannot adjudicate — Guniya's position, since no telemetry from a plant that has not bought the system says what its inspector needs.

A fourth is unresolved: whether personas can be synthesised from language models. One camp sees plausible responses generated cheaply; the other sees output regressing to the mean of written text, under-representing exactly the users — Girdhar, Haresh — personas exist to make visible.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied personas produces a well-sourced document. Someone who has internalised them arrives at a prioritisation meeting already holding the persona-level split of the metric in dispute; states which measure makes which persona primary; can name the attribute deleted and the persona merged; and ties re-testing to channel changes, not the calendar. A subtler sign: they will say a decision needs no personas, because the variation that matters is not between people.

12. Closing: what each team decided

On Thursday 15 October 2026, ten days after the opening meeting, Harshita took Option C to the Hamsafar product council: bulk packs and fourteen-day credit, four engineer-weeks, the remaining seven held for Option A. Her reasoning named the scarce resource — engineer-weeks before the Diwali freeze, not revenue — and on gross profit per engineer-week Option C returned ₹11.09 lakh against ₹5.26 and ₹4.30 lakh. She declined Gaurav's budget proposal because a mix shift towards any persona would move the blended 33.1 per cent without saying whether profit had moved.

At Guniya, Jaydev commissioned no new persona document. He moved the inspector workflow redesign into the contract as a priced deliverable at ₹1.6 lakh per plant and made Jaswant the named owner of Haresh, with a renewal-weighted target. The April 2027 firmware would carry a glove-mode interface designed against Haresh, not the dashboard Gajanan shows auditors.

  1. Option C serves a buyer arguably not a consumer, at a 22 per cent margin against 38 and 42 elsewhere. Profitable discovery or strategic drift, and what evidence would settle it in two quarters?
  2. The absence of a user persona cost Guniya about ₹162 lakh a year. Which function should own one, and what must change in its incentives?
  3. Hathkargha halved CAC and raised contribution per buyer 34.9 per cent, yet spend exceeds contribution by 1.54 times. When does persona work become a way of avoiding the unit economics?

13. Going deeper

The Six Ps framework puts the persona in the first P, whose errors every later P inherits. The self-referential design trap is the failure personas prevent. Anatomy of a persona says what to include and what to delete — the practical form of the conjunction argument. Jobs to Be Done is the rival of section 10. Market segments vs personas sharpens the counting-versus-designing split Table 1 rests on. Building personas from research is the sampling discipline whose absence cost Hathkargha a year, and AI-assisted persona synthesis the open question. Functional, emotional and social jobs explains why Jugal over-buys; Forces of progress turns an obstacle into an intervention, and Pains and gains into a testable claim.
case40v1-cust.journey:
Manthan Energy Works: Nine Stages and One Squad

Teaching case. Manthan Energy Works and its people are fictional; real firms and regulators are market context only. Where two exhibits disagree, that is part of the case.

1. The night before

On Sunday evening, 11 October 2026, Mrudula Mokashi stayed late in the Navrangpura office of Manthan Energy Works, in Ahmedabad. Taped to the glass behind her was a photograph of a journey map built on 10 February 2026: nine columns of sticky notes, rows for steps, actions, thoughts and feelings, and a thick orange ring around the column headed Installation day. On her laptop was a cohort report sent on Friday, 9 October, by Nitisha Ogale in Amsterdam. It did not ring the same column.

At eleven the next morning, Monday 12 October, she was to tell the steering committee which single stage of the residential rooftop-solar journey would get the Q3 FY27 product budget of ₹2.40 crore and Manthan's one spare squad. Nakul Nandgaonkar, the co-founder, wanted "one number and one stage, not a map".

Her difficulty was not a lack of data. She had three sets of it, from three parts of the company, and they did not describe the same customer.

2. The company, and the decision that still binds it

Manthan was founded in Ahmedabad in 2019 to sell and install rooftop solar to homeowners: a fixed price per kilowatt, one point of contact, an app showing generation. By FY27 it worked in six cities.

In mid-2023 the founders made the decision that still shapes every option on Mrudula's list. Rather than employ installation crews, they franchised them: seventy independent electrical contractors enrolled as Manthan Mitr partners, trained for a fortnight, given a partner app and paid per kilowatt installed. It let the company enter Nashik, Nagpur and Kochi without carrying payroll through the monsoon.

It also meant four of the nine stages — survey scheduling, installation, the net-meter inspection and handover — are performed by people Manthan does not employ, recorded in an app partners fill in when they remember, and reconciled against a CRM built for a direct sales force. Mrudula had inherited a journey she could only partly see.

3. The industry

Residential rooftop solar in India in 2026 is a subsidised, regulated and slow purchase. The national programme pays a central subsidy into the household's bank account after commissioning; state nodal agencies and the distribution companies, the DISCOMs, control feasibility approval, net metering and inspection. A 3 kW system is a project, not a product.

Tata Power Solar and Waaree carry brand trust into the home; a long tail of local electricians quote 30 per cent below Manthan with no warranty worth the paper. Financing has eased as banks and NBFCs took rooftop loans into retail books, with collections on UPI mandates under the RBI's framework. Expectations, though, are set by Zepto and Swiggy: a homeowner who watches a ten-minute delivery on a map cannot see why a utility application has no status screen.

Manthan's exposure runs outward as well: a Kenyan pilot runs on the same software, where there is no subsidy and a different grid code, and the monitoring firmware comes from a partner in Osaka, on its own release train.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The February workshop was Mrudula's idea and, by the ordinary tests, a success. Twenty-four people spent a day in a room in Ahmedabad: Mitr partners, surveyors, call-centre staff, engineers and Omana Nair's team, with fifteen recorded interviews. Each placed a dot on the stage where the customer suffers most. Eleven of the twenty-four dots, or 45.8 per cent, landed on installation day: the dust, the drilling, the scaffolding against a neighbour's wall. Six landed on the DISCOM wait, one on the net-meter inspection.

Through the first half of 2026 the roadmap followed the dots: crew tracking, a photographic checklist, a dust-sheet protocol, a handover certificate. By June, installation-day satisfaction had risen from 3.9 to 4.5 out of 5, and nobody disputes the work was good. Then, on 14 July 2026, Nihar Mahadevan funded a four-person subsidy desk in Chennai. It found commissioned customers who had not received their money — and, in chasing them, customers who had never commissioned at all, waiting for a net-meter appointment nobody had booked.

In September, Mrudula asked Nitisha to stop reporting monthly conversion and track one cohort end to end: every residential enquiry from 1 April to 30 June 2026 — the Q1 FY27 cohort, 48,000 enquiries — followed to 30 September 2026, long enough for most to reach commissioning. Exhibit 1 is the result.

Exhibit 1 unsettled the February consensus. Installation day — the stage the room had ringed — loses 482 customers, 10.0 per cent of the 4,821 who reach it, the smallest loss of any stage but commissioning. The net-meter stage loses 1,302 customers, 30.0 per cent of the 4,339 who reach it, who have paid in full and have panels on their roof. The quote stage loses 9,821 of the 17,856 who reach it, 55.0 per cent, after a surveyor has climbed the roof. The finance and DISCOM stages each lose exactly 1,607, yet one is a 20.0 per cent loss and the other 25.0 per cent, standing on different bases.

5. The people

Mrudula Mokashi, head of product, Ahmedabad, owns Monday's recommendation. She is uneasy that the map she championed sent a squad to the wrong place for two quarters, and has not told Nakul she blames the map, not the data.

Nakul Nandgaonkar, co-founder and chief executive, Ahmedabad, is raising a Series C in early 2027 and wants one metric that visibly improves before diligence. He claims to be agnostic about the stage; he has not mentioned the investor who asked why Manthan's cost per installation is high.

Mehtab Niyazi, head of the Mitr network, Jaipur, argues the net-meter problem is not Manthan's to fix: meters are fitted by the DISCOM. His partners, paid per kilowatt installed, are paid in full at stage 7 and earn nothing for stages 8 and 9 — which he does not volunteer.

Omana Nair, customer-experience lead, Kochi, holds the customers' own words and the worst conversion in the company. She believes Kerala's numbers reflect roof type and a slow utility, not a worse journey, and wants the quarter spent on survey-to-quote. Her team is measured on tickets closed.

Nitisha Ogale, data-science lead, Amsterdam, produced Exhibit 1 and will defend it, but has twice written that the stage definitions were built for sales reporting and three are inferred, not recorded. Mitul Nathwani, in Nairobi, wants the utility logic out of the core so Kenya can ship; every option on the list deepens the Indian assumptions he wants to escape.

Nihar Mahadevan, chief financial officer, Chennai, reads the journey as working capital: a customer stalled between payment and commissioning is cash spent, revenue unrecognised. He wants the quarter spent downstream.

Munira Nanavati, regulatory affairs and DISCOM liaison, Ahmedabad, deals with six utilities and three nodal agencies. Approval timelines, she says correctly, are outside Manthan's control; she alone knows how many applications are rejected and refiled, and nobody has asked her to report it.

Exhibit 2 is the one Mrudula least wants read naively. Kerala has the highest price per system and the worst conversion, so a reader in a hurry de-prioritises Kerala. Omana's reading is the opposite: Kerala's customers buy larger systems on sloped tiled roofs with a slow utility, so the journey is longer rather than worse. Nobody has separated the two, and 378 systems is too thin to split further.

Exhibit 3 was Nihar's contribution, and it cuts awkwardly. Its two largest lines, together ₹472.80 lakh, are spent before anyone agrees to buy, and each of the 9,821 lost at the quote stage has consumed a survey. Yet it says nothing of the cash tied up in the 1,302 who have paid and wait for a meter.

Exhibit 5 is where Mrudula's confidence collapsed. If the CRM is right, the DISCOM stage converts at 75.0 per cent and is a middling problem. If Munira's count is right, roughly one filing in ten is done twice, the customer waits through both, and the stage is quietly adding weeks in the three worst-converting cities. The two readings imply different projects, and the data to choose between them does not exist.

6. Voices

"We ringed installation day because that is the part of this business that walks into a person's home and makes a mess. You tell me the number says it does not matter. The number says people do not leave. It does not say they do not suffer." — Omana Nair
"Three of my nine stage definitions are inferred. 'Net meter fitted' is a photograph in the partner app: if partners stop uploading photographs for a week, stage 8 falls and nothing has happened in the world." — Nitisha Ogale, email, 9 October
"My partners are paid at installation. Ask them to chase a meter inspection and you are asking for free labour." — Mehtab Niyazi, 7 October
"I have two filings for the same Kochi roof, three weeks apart, the first rejected for a diagram error. Which one does your funnel count?" — Munira Nanavati, on the Exhibit 5 draft

7. The options as Mrudula currently sees them

Option A gives the homeowner a priced, designed proposal while the surveyor is still on the roof. Option B takes ownership of the DISCOM stage: a pre-filing checker, a desk with Munira, a status screen the customer can watch. Option C targets the net-meter stage, where customers who have paid in full go missing. Option D screens roofs from satellite imagery before the tele-call, taking fewer leads so survivors convert better.

Each framing hides something. A's lift assumes the quote-stage loss is about speed, when Manthan has never tested whether it is about price; the electrician quoting 30 per cent less appears in no exhibit. B's lift is a rate Manthan does not own, and if Exhibit 5's partner-app count is nearer the truth, the project is rework reduction wearing a conversion costume. C is cheapest per extra system, but Mehtab's partners are paid before that stage begins. D alone cuts spend as well as volume, and Exhibit 6 gives it no credit: it is scored only on systems gained, though it would cut the two largest lines of Exhibit 3. Mrudula had written, then deleted, a fifth line — change how Mitr partners are paid — which costs nothing and belongs to nobody on her list.

8. The deadline and the hard constraints

The budget is ₹2.40 crore and one squad of seven engineers, free from 20 October. Diwali falls on 8 November 2026 and installations stop for ten days around it, so anything shipping after mid-December will not be measured before the Series C diligence. Nitisha can rebuild the cohort report monthly, not weekly, and the squad cannot be split without losing a third of its output. Munira's four people cannot absorb a DISCOM project and the festive filing peak at once. Mitr contracts run to 31 March 2027, so the payment schedule cannot change without renegotiating seventy agreements. Any roof-imagery vendor must satisfy the DPDP Act: a three-week review.

9. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1 alone, which stage is worst, and what does that depend on: customers lost, the stage rate, or the cost sunk into those who leave?

2. Exhibit 4 sets the February dots beside the October losses. Was the workshop wrong, or answering a different question? What would you change in how it was run?

3. Exhibits 1 and 5 cannot both be the whole truth about the DISCOM stage. What would you do in the next fortnight to learn which is closer, and what would you stop reporting meanwhile?

4. Exhibit 2 pairs Kerala's highest price per system with its lowest conversion. Give two readings of that pairing that lead to opposite decisions, and the evidence that would separate them.

5. Exhibit 6 scores every option by extra systems commissioned. Whose interests does that serve, and who would score the options differently? Construct Nihar Mahadevan's Exhibit 6.

6. It is Monday morning. What do you tell the steering committee, what do you refuse to promise, and what do you say to the board in January if your stage does not move Nakul's number?

10. Sunday, late

At a quarter to midnight Mrudula wrote three sentences at the top of the board pack and read them back. The first said the company had spent two quarters making the best-loved stage of the journey better. The second said the stage where customers actually disappear had been in the data since April. The third she did not finish. She looked again at the orange ring around installation day, and at the thin column at the far right, headed Subsidy received, where in February nobody had put a sticky note at all.
case20v1-cust.journey:
Dakiya Services: Where the SIP Journey Breaks

Teaching case. Dakiya Services and all its people are fictional; market institutions are named only as context.

1. Opening

On the evening of Thursday, 15 October 2026, Dhwani Kulkarni sat in the Pune office of Dakiya Services with two documents open side by side. One was a journey map, drawn on a whiteboard six weeks earlier, on 3 September, and photographed before the cleaners came. The other was a cohort report that her data scientist had sent that afternoon. They disagreed.

Dhwani, head of product, had to tell the steering committee on Monday, 19 October which single stage of the new-investor journey would receive the quarter's fix budget of ₹80 lakh. The festive season was close; Diwali fell on 8 November, and the marketing team planned to spend heavily in the weeks before it.

2. Company background

Dakiya Services runs a mobile app that lets first-time investors start a monthly systematic investment plan (SIP) in mutual funds with as little as ₹500. Founded in Pune in 2020, it grew from a salaried-professionals product into one aimed at people in smaller cities: shop assistants, school teachers, gig workers, and young employees of firms in Nashik, Indore and Coimbatore.

The market was crowded. Groww and Zerodha's Coin had set the standard for fast onboarding, PhonePe and Paytm had begun distributing funds inside payment apps, and banks pushed SIPs through their own channels. Dakiya's pitch was vernacular support and a ₹500 entry point. Regulation shaped every screen: SEBI's know-your-customer rules required identity verification, and the RBI's framework for recurring payments governed how UPI AutoPay debits were authorised.

In September 2026 Dakiya counted about 2,40,000 new installs, bought at a blended cost of ₹150 per install, a month's acquisition spend of ₹360 lakh, or ₹3.6 crore.

3. The situation

The 3 September workshop had been Dhwani's idea. She wanted the team to see one customer's path from first hearing of Dakiya to a second instalment landing on its own. Fiona Calloway, a user researcher working from Melbourne, had interviewed eighteen customers in Hindi, Marathi and Tamil through an interpreter, and presented their steps, actions, thoughts and feelings as a row of sticky notes under six stage headings.

The room voted. Asked to mark the stage with the greatest pain, fourteen of nineteen participants placed their dot on KYC. KYC asked people to photograph documents and wait, and it generated the most support tickets. Exhibit 2 records the vote beside what the data later showed.

Emre Kaya, the data scientist, working from Istanbul, then pulled the September cohort, tracked through 12 October so that second instalments could be observed. Exhibit 1 sets out the result. He sent Dhwani one line: the biggest leak per person was not where the room had put its dots.

KYC is two steps, started and completed, each holding 60 per cent of the previous stage. The mandate step, in which the customer leaves Dakiya to approve a UPI AutoPay request inside a bank or UPI app, holds only 50 per cent of those who finished KYC. These people have already uploaded identity documents and waited.

4. The people

Dhwani Kulkarni, head of product, Pune, owns the decision and the ₹80 lakh. She wants one fix that moves investors, not a long list.

Devansh Tripathi, head of growth, Gurugram, owns the festive campaign. He argues for repairing the top of the funnel, since every gain there is multiplied by everything below it.

Farooq Qureshi, compliance and KYC operations lead, Hyderabad, believes the KYC flow is already as light as SEBI rules allow. He fears that any redesign will weaken verification and wants no change that adds regulatory risk.

Fiona Calloway, user researcher, Melbourne, holds the customer's own words. She says her interviews hinted at the mandate step, but the room drowned them out.

Emre Kaya, data scientist, Istanbul, supplies the counts and reminds everyone these are one cohort's data.

Exhibit 2 supports both readings, and that is the difficulty. KYC does lose the most people in absolute terms among the product's own stages, 99,840 of them. But the journey is not one thing. A customer who abandons the mandate has spent effort and then been sent into another company's app, with a limit screen in a language and rupee amounts that mean nothing to her, to approve a deduction from her own bank account. Eleven of Fiona's eighteen interviewees, 61.1 per cent, said some version of: "I did not know what it would take from my account."

The money also matters. At ₹150 per install, the September spend of ₹3.6 crore bought 56,160 completed KYCs at a cost of about ₹641 each, and 21,060 first SIPs at about ₹1,709 each.

5. The options

Option A: redesign KYC. Farooq's team and two engineers in Pune would add document pre-checks, retry guidance and a vernacular video guide. Cost ₹45 lakh; eight weeks. The team estimates KYC completion rising from 60 to 66 per cent.

Option B: rebuild the mandate step. Add a pre-approval screen that explains in plain language what will be debited, when and how to stop it; use deep links so the customer returns to Dakiya on approval; and prompt for a ₹500 limit rather than leaving the bank-app default. Cost ₹30 lakh; four weeks. The estimate is the mandate stage rising from 50 to 60 per cent.

Option C: shorten sign-up and first-open. Delay the OTP, show a sample portfolio first, and ask for permissions later. Cost ₹55 lakh; ten weeks, too late for Diwali. The estimate is sign-up rising from 65 to 70 per cent.

Exhibit 3 compares them on one monthly cohort of 2,40,000 installs, holding every other stage rate at its September value.

6. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1, which stage loses the largest share of those who reach it, and which loses the most customers in absolute terms? Why do those answers differ?

2. Why did fourteen of nineteen people mark KYC as the pain, and how can a journey map built from memory mislead?

3. In Exhibit 3, what must be true for Option A to beat Option B? Which of the estimated lifts would you test first?

4. What would you tell the steering committee on Monday, and what would you ask Fiona and Emre to do in the next fortnight?

7. A note for the learner

A journey map is the job-to-be-done unfolded across time: steps, actions, thoughts and feelings. A map drawn from opinion locates the team's anxiety, not the customer's. Here, the first lesson is to pair every stage on the map with a count and a stage rate before anyone votes. The second is that the emotional row matters. The mandate stage shows a customer thinking "what will this take from me?" while handing control to an app that is not Dakiya's.

One defensible path is Option B, now. It has the lowest cost per extra first SIP (₹712 against a current ₹1,709 to acquire a first SIP), the shortest build, and it finishes before Diwali, so it improves the quality of the festive spend. It also touches no KYC logic, which answers Farooq's concern. Ship it to 20 per cent of traffic first, so that the 60 per cent mandate rate is measured and not assumed.

Then hold Option A in reserve: B and A together cost ₹75 lakh, within the ₹80 lakh budget, so A can follow once the experiment reports. Option C is the weakest, since it is the costliest, the slowest and offers the smallest gain. The caveats: the lifts are estimates, and one cohort is thin evidence.
exp20v2-cust.journey:
Customer Journey Mapping

Finding where along the customer's path the problem actually lives

1. The review that blamed the wrong stage

On Monday, 14 September 2026, Charulata Bhosale, head of product at Bhandar Pharmacy Network, walked into a quarterly review in Pune with a number she disliked. Bhandar sold repeat prescription medicines, mainly for diabetes, blood pressure and thyroid conditions, to customers who needed the same tablets every month. In August the company had sent 1,20,000 refill reminders. Only 27,702 of those reminders ended in a delivered order.

The chief executive, Bharat Agnihotri, had a view. Platforms such as Tata 1mg, PharmEasy and Apollo Pharmacy had trained Indian customers to expect discounts, so he proposed spending the ₹18 lakh quarterly growth budget on a deeper refill discount. Bhandar's analyst, Bhuvan Sengupta, had a different view, because the data showed the weakest step after a customer had committed a refill to the cart was not checkout, where a discount operates, but earlier. Charulata had an uncomfortable suspicion that both men were looking at the same funnel and misreading it.

The stakes were concrete. A discount spent on the wrong stage would cost the whole ₹18 lakh and return nothing, while the patients lost along the way were people who would miss doses. She had two weeks of interview notes and a decision to make before the budget closed. This page follows her reasoning, because it illustrates one idea: a customer journey map.

2. The idea

A customer journey is the sequence of stages a person passes through while trying to get one job done, from the moment they notice the need to the moment they are finished or have given up. A journey map is a structured picture of that sequence. For each stage it records what the customer does, what they are thinking and what they are feeling, and it marks the points where the experience breaks down.

It was invented to solve a specific problem: organisations are built in departments, but customers live in time. Marketing sees the reminder, engineering sees the app, operations sees the van, and nobody sees the patient. G. Lynn Shostack argued in a 1984 Harvard Business Review article that services should be drawn as a sequence of steps so that failure points become visible. Richard Normann and Jan Carlzon popularised the notion of "moments of truth", the brief encounters in which a customer forms a judgement. Design consultancies such as Adaptive Path turned the drawing into an everyday tool for product teams in the late 2000s and 2010s.

Journey mapping builds directly on Jobs to Be Done, the idea that people "hire" a product to make progress in a situation. A journey is the job unfolded in time. The sentence Charulata could repeat in the meeting without sounding glib was this:

"Our funnel tells us where customers disappear; the journey tells us where they started to struggle, and those are often different places."

3. How it actually works

The mechanics have six steps. The first is to fix the actor and the job. Charulata chose one person, a customer like Chandrakant Joshi, 68, a retired bank clerk in Nashik who takes tablets for blood pressure and diabetes, and one job: "keep my medicines continuous without running out." A map of "customers" in general averages away the detail that matters.

The second step, which practitioners often leave implicit, is to set the boundaries. Where does the journey start and end? Bhandar's funnel began at the reminder, but Chandrakant's journey began earlier, when he counted his strip of tablets and found four days left. It ended not at delivery but at the next refill, because that is when he knew whether the service had worked. The third step is to list stages from evidence, not imagination: interviews, support tickets and session recordings. Fourth, for each stage record actions, thoughts and feelings in the customer's own words. Fifth, attach quantities from the product's data. Sixth, mark moments of struggle and ask what causes each.

Exhibit 1 shows the quantitative layer. It is the funnel Bhuvan had already built, drawn so that each bar is proportional to the customers remaining.

The funnel locates a loss at stage 4, where 12,000 customers vanished between cart and accepted prescription. But a funnel is not a journey. It says nothing about what Chandrakant was thinking when he stalled, nor about what happened before the reminder. Exhibit 2 adds the qualitative layer.

4. A worked example, line by line

Bhuvan's table converts the funnel into step rates. A step conversion is customers remaining divided by customers at the previous stage; the cumulative figure divides by the original 1,20,000.

Check: 60,000 / 1,20,000 = 50%; 48,000 / 60,000 = 80%; 36,000 / 48,000 = 75%; 32,400 / 36,000 = 90%; 30,780 / 32,400 = 95%; 27,702 / 30,780 = 90%.

The discount proposal acts on stage 6, where 95 per cent already pay. Even a perfect discount could add at most 1,620 customers (32,400 minus 30,780), and then only before delivery losses. The map pointed elsewhere. Of the 24 customers interviewed, 15 had abandoned at the prescription step. That is 62.5 per cent, and nearly all of them said the prescription was a paper slip at home, at a doctor's clinic, or had passed its six-month validity. The journey began in the wrong place: the reminder arrived without warning that a fresh prescription would be needed.

Suppose a fix, costing the same ₹18 lakh, recovers 4,000 of the 12,000 lost customers by checking prescription validity at reminder time. Those 4,000 still face the later stages, so the gain compounds: 4,000 × 0.90 × 0.95 × 0.90 = 3,078 delivered orders. At an average order of ₹1,850 and a 20 per cent contribution margin, the monthly gain is shown below. The second column changes one input, the delivery rate, which falls to 80 per cent in the monsoon.

The conclusion survives the change: the fix repays itself in under two months either way. The point of the second pass is to see which assumption the answer is sensitive to. A weaker delivery rate trims the gain by about 11 per cent, but a recovery of 1,000 customers rather than 4,000 would cut it by 75 per cent. The map told Charulata where to look; the arithmetic told her how much to trust it.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Funnel versus journey

A funnel counts behaviour inside your product. A journey includes what happens outside it: the drawer where the prescription lives, the daughter who orders on the parent's behalf. The funnel found the symptom; only the journey found the origin.

Where the loss is and where the pain is

Customers stop where it is cheapest to stop, which is often well after the struggle began. Exhibit 2 shows the pain peaking at stage 4, but in other products the lowest feeling lies two stages before the exit.

A map is a hypothesis, not a finding

Interviews with 24 people are evidence of a pattern, not proof of its size. Twenty-four conversations tell you the stages exist; the product data tell you how many people pass through them.

Journey, user flow and service blueprint are different things

A user flow traces screens inside the product. A service blueprint adds the back-stage work, such as the pharmacist's verification queue, beneath the customer's path. A journey map sits above both and is deliberately about the person.

One journey per actor and job

Chandrakant ordering for himself and his daughter ordering for him are different journeys with different thoughts. Merging them produces a smooth, average line that nobody has walked.

Emotion scores are coarse

A score from -2 to +2 compresses what people said into a single mark. Use it to compare stages, not to compare products or to claim a precision of decimals.

What a map cannot tell you

It cannot tell you which fix will work, what the fix will cost, or whether the problem is worth solving. It narrows where to look. The decision still needs sizing, as in Section 4.

Questions to ask before relying on it

Who was interviewed, and who was missing? Were they people who completed the journey, or also people who left? Customers who abandoned are harder to reach and are the ones the map most needs.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products

Bhandar is a consumer product, so one person moves through the journey in days. In B2B products the journey has several actors: the user, the buyer who signs and the administrator who configures, and it lasts months. A realistic map is therefore a set of parallel journeys joined by handoffs, and the loss often sits at a handoff, where nobody owns the next step.

In a marketplace, which connects two sides, there are at least two journeys that must be mapped against one another. A seller's wait for the first order is part of the buyer's wait for a listing. For early-stage companies, a map can be drawn on a wall from ten interviews in a week, and speed matters more than polish. In a large company the difficulty is organisational: no single team owns the whole path, so the map's main value is to give separate teams a shared picture, and its main risk is that it hardens into a poster no one updates.

7. Common mistakes

The imagined map. The symptom is a tidy workshop poster with no customer quotations and no numbers. The underlying misunderstanding is that a map records what the team believes. The cheapest diagnostic: ask for the source of each stage, and cross out any with neither an interview nor a data point.

Mapping the product, not the person. The symptom is a map whose first step is "opens app". The misunderstanding is that the journey belongs to the product. The diagnostic: ask what the customer did before and after the product, and extend the map until the answer is "nothing".

Mistaking the biggest drop for the biggest problem. The symptom is a team that fixes whichever stage has the lowest conversion. A low-converting stage may be one where leaving is natural, while a high-converting stage may hide misery. The diagnostic: compare the funnel with the feeling line; where they disagree, interview more.

The map that is never reopened. The symptom is a map dated a year ago. The misunderstanding is that it is a deliverable. The diagnostic: look for a decision made since it was drawn that cites it.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Charulata's review would have opened with Chandrakant, not a chart. Participants would see four days of tablets on a kitchen shelf, a reminder, and a prescription slip in a drawer in another town. Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2 would sit side by side, the loss and the pain visibly meeting at one stage. The proposed fix would arrive with its compounding arithmetic and its sensitivity, and with a named measure of success: the share of stage 3 customers reaching stage 4, which was 75 per cent in August. A good map ends in a decision someone can be held to.

9. What Charulata decided

She declined the discount. She told Bharat that a discount acted on a stage where 95 per cent already paid, and proposed instead that the reminder should check each customer's prescription date, warn them fourteen days ahead if it was nearing its six-month limit, and let them photograph a new one. Anjali Chaudhary, who ran operations from Lucknow, agreed to hold the pharmacist queue steady, and Chaitanya Rao in Coimbatore scoped the build at ten weeks. Her reasoning was that the lowest feeling and the largest loss met at the same place, and that the fix repaid the ₹18 lakh in under two months even when the delivery rate dropped.

To go deeper, learn the service blueprint next, since it exposes the back-stage causes your map can only hint at. Then study user story mapping, which turns a journey into a buildable backlog.

Two questions to sit with. If the share of customers reaching stage 4 rose to 90 per cent but stage 7 fell, how would you know whether the fix had moved the pain rather than removed it? And whose journey, among your own customers, have you never actually watched?
exp40v2-cust.journey:
Customer Journey Mapping

Where along the customer's path the problem actually occurs — and why the map so often answers a different question

1. Two decisions, two product types

On Monday, 7 September 2026, Kiranmayi Lohiya sat in a dealer's back room in Jalgaon with a spreadsheet she had been avoiding. She was head of product at Jalaj Irrigation Works, a Nashik firm making the JX-2 solar pump controller: a sealed box bolted beside a borewell and paired to a phone app that scheduled irrigation. Between 1 April and 31 August 2026 Jalaj invoiced 9,600 controllers to its 140 dealers; 8,160 were installed within forty-five days; only 5,712 were ever paired — 59.5 per cent of units shipped, 70 per cent of those installed. The ₹1,200 annual subscription was the only recurring line, so an unpaired unit meant no renewal.

Her founder, Lakhan Jagtap, wanted to pay dealers a ₹600 bounty per pairing, from ₹2.4 crore of FY27 growth spend the board wanted committed by 30 September. Kiranmayi, who had spent three weeks watching installations with Jamuna Kelkar, head of field operations, suspected this was not a pairing problem at all.

Four days later, on Friday, 11 September 2026, Lalita Kharote met the same question in Bengaluru. She was head of product at Karyavaahi Claims Systems, which ran motor own-damage claims adjudication for Indian general insurers. Its largest customer, Jaywant General Insurance, had processed 2,40,000 own-damage claims in the twelve months to 31 August 2026 under a ₹4.80 crore licence due for renewal on Wednesday, 31 March 2027, sold on a promise to cut the mean claim cycle, then 11.0 days, by a fifth. Three of the previous four quarters had gone into the adjudication workbench; the mean had fallen to 10.6 days, and Jaywant's chief operating officer wrote to ask what they had bought.

Her chief technology officer, Jitender Lamba, read the letter as a delivery problem; Lalita read it as a mapping problem. Both were about to rediscover the proposition that makes journey mapping worth its room: the stage where a number goes bad is rarely the stage where the customer's trouble began, and a funnel cannot tell you the difference.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A customer journey is the ordered sequence of stages a person passes through in a single attempt at one job, from the moment the need becomes salient to the moment the attempt ends in success or abandonment. A journey map represents that sequence, recording per stage what the customer does, thinks and feels, how many people are at that stage, and how long they spend there.

The practice was invented against one pathology: firms are organised by function, while customers experience time. G. Lynn Shostack's 1984 Harvard Business Review argument for service blueprinting was the first widely read attempt to draw a service as a sequence so failure points became institutionally visible. In product management it arrived fused with Jobs to Be Done: a journey is a job unfolded in time.

Three schools disagree substantively. The artefact school, out of service design, holds that the map's value is shared understanding across functions: it will sign that a map drawn together changes what a team notices, and not that a map must carry quantities to be useful. The instrumentation school, out of growth analytics, holds the reverse — a map is a measurement specification, and an uninstrumented map is a poster. It will sign that no stage belongs on a map unless you can count the people in it, and not that emotion scores belong beside conversion rates. The job-map school, after Anthony Ulwick, holds that journey maps are structurally conservative: they describe the path your current solution imposes, so they find friction but never discontinuity. It will sign that the universal job steps are the stable unit of analysis, and not that today's behaviour tells you what to build.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Expert practice has six steps, and the two usually left implicit are where the damage is done. Fix the actor and the job-instance: not "farmers" but Jairam Kharatmal, 54, four acres of onion near Kalwan, and one attempt at watering one plot, not a season. Choose the boundaries — the first implicit step, and the one that decides the answer: Jalaj's funnel began at "controller invoiced to dealer", while Jairam's journey began nine days earlier when his starter panel failed. Derive stages from evidence, then record thoughts and feelings as verbatims and attach volume and duration to each stage. Cut every stage by segment before believing any average — the second implicit step, the one most teams skip. Mark each struggle and name its mechanism.

Exhibit 1 shows what the segment cut did to Jalaj's 70 per cent: Kiranmayi split the 8,160 installations into distress purchases, ordered within seven days of a failure and so almost always mid-season, and planned ones.

The blended figure was correct and meaningless. The broken population was defined by when in the journey the purchase happened, not by anything inside the product: a distress purchase meant an installer arriving mid-rotation for a farmer with water to move that night.

Lalita's arithmetic needed a different care. Her team quoted median stage durations — correct for one stage, void the moment you decompose a total, because medians do not sum. She recomputed in means, which do.

Exhibit 2. Jaywant General Insurance, own-damage motor claims, twelve months to 31 August 2026 (n = 2,40,000)

Three facts fell out at once. Karyavaahi's software owned stages 2, 5 and 6: 0.6 + 1.3 + 1.2 = 3.1 days, 28.2 per cent of the cycle. Three quarters of roadmap had gone into stage 5, worth 1.3 days in all, of which a realistic gain was 0.4 — the 11.0 to 10.6 day improvement Jaywant resented. The largest stage, 3.4 days, belonged to the policyholder, where no telemetry reached.

Then she cut stage 1 by whether the claim required a police report.

The 3.4-day average concealed a 7.0-day experience for 48,000 households a year, and those claims generated the status calls: 3,12,000 "where is my claim" calls against 2,40,000 claims, 1.3 per claim at ₹46 each — ₹1,43,52,000, or ₹1.44 crore a year spent saying nothing had happened yet.

4. When it applies, stated as testable claims

Four conditions, each checkable before the workshop is booked. One: the job spans more than one sitting or more than one actor — otherwise a user flow will do. Jalaj passes decisively, crossing a failure, a dealer counter, a credit decision, an installer visit and a first irrigation cycle in nine days; so does Karyavaahi, whose Exhibit 2 names four owners across six stages. Two: a material part of the path sits outside your instrumentation. Karyavaahi explained 3.1 of 11.0 days; Jalaj saw nothing before the dealer invoice. Three: the metric you care about is a lagging consequence of an earlier state, as Jalaj's pairing rate was of purchase circumstance three stages upstream. Four: more than one function must change behaviour for the fix to work.

It is actively misleading in two situations. First, when the journey is one your own product imposed and the opportunity is to abolish it: a map of a seven-step reimbursement claim optimises seven steps and never asks why reimbursement exists. Second, in novel categories where nobody has walked the path, so mapping yields a record of the team's own assumptions.

5. Hard edge cases

In multi-product companies the journey crosses products owned by different teams, so the most valuable map is the one no single team is authorised to act on. What mature firms say is "we have a cross-functional journey council"; what works is that one named person's bonus depends on the handoff rate.

In two-sided businesses two journeys are coupled — a seller's wait for a first order is a lag inside a buyer's search — so mapping one side alone shifts pain to the other.

In regulated products parts of the journey are not yours to design: surveyor licensing governs who may file Karyavaahi's stage 3, and the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India sets turnaround expectations. The map's value shifts from friction removal to sequencing — what may legally run in parallel.

In hardware-plus-software products the journey contains irreversible events. Jalaj's installation is the type case: once the installer has driven away, a pairing failure costs a second visit at roughly the margin on the unit.

In AI-native products the journey is probabilistic: the same stage may succeed for one user and fail for the next on identical inputs, so conversion is a distribution rather than a rate, and the new stage is where the customer decides whether to trust the output.

6. Nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

i. The left edge of the map is a decision, not a fact

The tell of an amateur map is a first stage naming a product surface — "opens app"; an expert's names a change in the customer's world. The obvious reading, that boundaries are presentational, is wrong: they decide which causes can be found at all.

ii. Means add; medians do not

Teams report medians because medians resist outliers, then decompose a median total into median stages, which is void. The tell is a stage table whose rows do not sum to the total. It stops being pedantry the moment you allocate effort by stage share, as Lalita did.

iii. No customer lives at the average

A blended rate is a weighted mixture, and the mixture is usually the finding. The tell is a rate that sits mid-range and never moves under treatment. Jalaj's 70 per cent was 30 and 90; Jaywant's 3.4 days was 7.0 and 2.5. Segmentation does not refine the estimate, it replaces it.

iv. Loss is recorded downstream of where it is caused

People abandon where it is cheapest to abandon, often two stages after the trouble started. The tell is a stage with poor conversion whose usability tests come back clean. The obvious reading blames that stage; compare the volume and difficulty curves, and where the peaks are misaligned the earlier one is the cause.

v. The traveller may not be the decider

Mapping the user when someone else chooses produces a beautiful, useless document. The tell is a map in which no stage holds a conversation with a third party. In Indian fittings, pumps and tiles the installer is often the decider and the householder only approves a budget.

vi. Emotion is a routing signal, not a score

A feeling rating from minus two to plus two ranks stages within one study and is worthless across products or quarters. The tell is a score quoted to a decimal. Read a dip as an instruction to ask why, not a number to manage.

vii. Your sample over-represents survivors by construction

The people who answer your interview request are those still in a relationship with you; the tell is a deck in which every participant completed the journey. Experts spend disproportionately to reach abandoners, because the map most needs the stages they never reached.

viii. A map that cannot be instrumented is not finished

The second-order effect of mapping well is that the map becomes a measurement specification: every stage acquires a volume, a duration and an owner, and the organisation starts reporting the journey rather than the department. The tell of a finished map is that somebody can name the dashboard it created; of an unfinished one, a wall photograph.

7. Differences by product type and company stage

In consumer products one person traverses the whole journey in days, and the difficulty is reaching those who left. In B2B and enterprise products the journey is a braid of parallel journeys — user, buyer, administrator, security reviewer — joined by handoffs, and the loss sits at the handoffs, because a handoff is the only part of a process with no owner; in Exhibit 2, three of six stages belong to parties the software cannot compel. In platforms and marketplaces coupling dominates, so both sides are drawn on one time axis; in hardware the one-way doors dominate; in AI products stages carry probabilities rather than binary gates. Where the difference is overstated: evidence-gathering, boundary selection and segmentation are the same everywhere, and claims otherwise are usually claims for a proprietary template. By stage, the variation is in cost and failure mode — at seed a map is ten interviews on a wall and the risk is skipping it; at growth its job is to arbitrate between funnel-driven and research-driven accounts of one drop.

8. Three worked examples, including one failure

Jhumar Jewellery Exchange, Jaipur. In the quarter to 30 June 2026 the jeweller ran 1,600 try-at-home appointments and converted 680 into purchases, 42.5 per cent. Eleven interviews put the break after the appointment: a buyer who wanted to proceed had to visit a store for gold valuation, which the consultant could not book. The next quarter, 1,600 appointments produced 848 purchases, 53.0 per cent — 168 incremental sales at ₹68,000 average order value, or ₹1.14 crore of extra revenue in a quarter.

Kadamb Transit Network, Nagpur. The bus operator wanted digital ticket share above 18 per cent of 4,20,000 monthly trips. Mapping the conductor's journey instead of the passenger's found the constraint: validating a digital ticket took nine seconds against two for cash, so conductors discouraged it in a crowded aisle. A firmware change specified with Joana Lameira's team in Lisbon took the scan under three seconds. Over five months digital share reached 31 per cent — 1,30,200 trips against 75,600, a gain of 54,600 a month, worth ₹1,74,720 monthly at ₹3.20 of cash handling avoided per ticket, or ₹20.97 lakh a year.

Laalten Lighting Industries, Kolhapur — the failure. Laalten mapped the householder's journey for a ₹2,400 connected LED batten, concluded that onboarding was the problem, and spent eleven months and ₹1.90 crore building a polished consumer app. The year's sales reached 38,000 units against a plan of 1,10,000 — 34.5 per cent of plan — and only 4,180 units, 11.0 per cent, ever activated the app. The map had the wrong actor: research at forty retail counters found that in 82 per cent of installations the electrician chose the batten at the moment of fitting, the householder approving a budget rather than a product. Laalten then built a ₹60 per-unit electrician claim, redeemed by photographing a carton code into WhatsApp, and sold 51,000 units in six months. The ₹1.90 crore was not recovered; what it bought was the discovery that the firm had mapped the payer and ignored the chooser.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

The imagined map. Sign: a workshop output with no verbatims and no counts. Diagnostic: name each stage's evidence. Late, it costs a roadmap quarter on a problem nobody has.

Mapping the product instead of the person. Sign: the first stage is a product surface. Diagnostic: what did the customer do in the hour before this stage, and the week after the last one? Late, you optimise inside a frame that excludes the cause — Jalaj's funnel, exactly.

Averaging over a mixture. Sign: a stage rate stable across quarters that refuses to move. Diagnostic: cut it by three plausible segments; does any cut give a spread wider than twenty points? Caught late, you buy a uniform fix for a non-uniform problem — the ₹600 bounty, exactly.

Treating the largest drop as the largest opportunity. Sign: a prioritised list that is the conversion table sorted ascending. Diagnostic: what improvement is achievable here, and what is it worth? Stage 5 was 11.8 per cent of Karyavaahi's cycle and yielded 0.4 days — three quarters of roadmap.

The map as deliverable, and the happy-path map. Signs: it is beautiful, printed and two quarters old; no stage contains a complaint, a retry or a workaround. Diagnostics: name a decision in the last ninety days that cited it; ask where a customer uses WhatsApp or a spreadsheet to get around you. Late, the cost is credibility, and the next map will not be funded.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does the value lie in the drawing or the measurement? The artefact school's strongest form is not sentimental: teams act on what they can see together, and a wall-sized picture changes meeting agendas in ways a dashboard does not. Its evidence is twenty-five years of service design in airlines and banking, where the map is the intervention. The instrumentation case is equally serious — without counts you cannot rank, and unranked insight loses every budget argument to a funnel; its evidence is the many maps that produced no decision. The artefact position would be wrong if teams with instrumented funnels and no maps found the upstream causes anyway; on the evidence of Jalaj and Laalten, they do not. The instrumentation position would be wrong if drawn-only maps reliably changed roadmaps; mostly they do not.

Journey map or job map? The job-map school's strongest form is that journeys are solution-shaped: every stage exists because some provider decided it should, so a journey map can make a bad process efficient but cannot notice the process is unnecessary. The journey school's answer is that solution-agnostic steps are too abstract to locate a defect: "confirm" does not tell you the installer left before pairing. It would be wrong if job maps alone found defects at that resolution. Expert teams run both, the job map deciding what to build and the journey map what to fix.

Does emotion belong on the same canvas as numbers? One camp holds that affect is the point, since the dip locates the problem before the data do; the other, that a minus-two-to-plus-two line beside a conversion rate invites the false precision of nuance vi. Both are right about the risk they name, and no measure of journey emotion yet survives comparison across studies.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied journey mapping runs a workshop and produces a map. Someone who has internalised it asks first what decision the map must inform, then argues about the left edge of the frame for longer than seems reasonable. They will not quote a blended rate without a segment cut beside it, know which numbers are means and which medians, and can name the three people whose behaviour must change, having asked each. Above all they can say which stage they were wrong about last time and what the error cost, because a practitioner who has never been wrong about a journey has never tested one.

Discussion questions

  1. Kiranmayi excluded hardware upside from Exhibit 5 as unprovable. Could option A ever become the right answer, and what would have to be true?
  2. Karyavaahi's contract rests on one blended cycle-time number that Exhibit 4 shows to be a mixture of two populations with different physics. How should the renewal be structured instead, and who loses?
  3. Laalten spent ₹1.90 crore mapping the wrong actor. What question, asked in week one, would have caught it, and why did nobody ask it?

13. Going deeper

Jobs to Be Done is the parent idea; without the job, stages have no organising purpose. Job hierarchies and job maps supply the solution-agnostic alternative at the heart of section 10. Service blueprints extend the map into back-stage operations and would have shown Jalaj the installer's incentive directly. User flows and task analysis work inside one stage, where screen-level defects live, and Storyboarding makes a stage vivid enough for a room to argue about. Customer narratives (Day 0 / Day N) force the question of what the journey looks like after the first success, which maps habitually truncate. User story mapping turns a journey into a sequenced backlog, the natural next artefact after a decision like Lalita's. Market segments vs personas and Anatomy of a persona supply the actor a journey needs; Why personas argues for naming one; Building personas from research keeps nuance vii honest. The self-referential design trap names the failure of mapping your own journey. AI-assisted persona synthesis is least settled, since a synthesised actor cannot be interviewed about the stage you did not think to include.
